What was the most surprising thing you saw in Cornwall? Well, it's funny you mention Yorkshire. The lighthouse at Pendeen! It was so clear, the history surrounding it. And the views, of course. We took a bike ride along the coast and it was so beautiful. Ah, I see. I've always loved lighthouses. There's something so comforting about them. And that photo with the crabs. Was it as fun as it looked? Well, the crabs weren't too keen on being held, but the kids were having the time of their lives. It wasn't all fun and games, really. But that's life, innit? I mean, you've been in some tough situations when volunteering. True that. I remember when I was childminding and the kids wanted to walk along the beach and one of them tripped and cut his knee. But the beach was so clean, it was just lovely, blurred out the wound in no time. Good old crabs and their healing properties. Minerals or what? While you were dealing with crabs and cuts, I was making sure they didn't do a cycle race up the stairs. Funny how those troubles seem so trivial now. It does bring back a lot of fond memories. And look, I still have the certificate from YHA volunteering back in the day. It's like... proof I did something with my life. Well, those experiences aren't just past. They are part of what makes you who you are today. I think that's often overlooked. Yeah, you've got a point. I think about it a lot, especially now. I miss the adventure and the sense of community from those times. Cornwall brings a bit of that back, you see. It does. So, any more plans for adventures?

I've decided I need to take a cooking class. I just can't seem to get dinner together that isn’t a disaster. Oh, that’s a good idea! I need one too! Last night’s lasagna was just pasta and tomato sauce. Between us three, one of us has definitely got to learn some cooking skills. And maybe some healthy food options while we're at it. Definitely healthy options. Like my diet always ends up being chips and soda. I just don't know, cooking's always been such a hassle. But I think maybe with some guidance and recipes, it could be fun. Fun is a bonus, as long as we can actually eat it without embarrassment or ending up at the doctor's. Speaking of which, I had that Italian place recommended by someone and it didn’t work out well. Really? Did they have a claim-to-fame dish that wasn’t what you expected? No, it was just this ragu on penne that was supposed to be amazing but was just pasta in a tomato sauce. I know that feeling. Last week in Lewisham at this new place, I ordered the ‘World’s Best’ burger, and it was just mediocre. You, trying to branch out with the fancy burgers, huh? That's becoming me too. I get burgers from different places and they're all just burgers. The only food review app that has any basis on reality is if it’s your mum’s. She’d give any place that serves a decent portion two stars. On that note, did either of you see this couple on BBC Food Show last night? Yeah, that couple who was trying to make everything from scratch despite clearly having no clue. They were hilarious. But you know, sometimes I watch those shows and think maybe if I follow the recipe, I can make something decent. We should show them a simple recipe. One could even be for chips and soda, and just call it edible. Do you think if we got a cooking class, we could learn to make healthy chips and a decent soda? Sure, why not? It’s a start. And maybe over time, we can move onto actual meals. That would be a dream. Meanwhile, what do you both think about these restaurant review apps? They make it sound like every second place across the country is Michelin starred, and then you go and it’s just okay at best.

So tell me all about your weekend. I heard you went to Barcelona. Yeah, it was amazing! We strolled along La Rambla, went shopping in the Gothic Quarter, and had the best seafood paella at this little restaurant on the beach. The atmosphere, the culture, everything was fantastic. Oh, that sounds incredible. I've always wanted to visit Barcelona but never had the chance. What was your favorite part of the trip? Definitely the food. Like I said, that paella is something else. Also, the Sagrada Familia... it's truly breathtaking, especially the stained glass windows. I can imagine. I’m really jealous. You two were just away for like two days, right? Four actually. We started early Sunday morning and didn’t even make it back until last night. Where did you stay? We stayed in a hostel in El Raval. It was central, and the staff were super helpful. Nice. I heard that area has a lot of character. Oh it does. We had dinner at this tiny bistro that served tapas the whole night. It was kind of assumed we’d order everything and share. That’s so Spanish. I also really want to try that at some point. You should. The food is amazing, and the atmosphere, like I said, is really vibrant in that area. Speaking of which, have you watched “The Crown” and "Peaky Blinders"? I think you might enjoy them. "The Crown" I have seen a bit of, but haven't jumped on “Peaky Blinders”. I’ll have to check that out soon. Oh, both are fantastic. "The Crown" is fun since you get to see another side of British history. Yeah, and "Peaky Blinders" is a great show. You can catch up with our cultural heritage and everything. Exactly, that’s what I meant. Let me know what you think when you do watch. I will. So plans for future holiday ideas already in mind? We almost didn’t make this one happen. Maybe Paris soon. Paris would be amazing! I’ve got a friend who moved there; I can ask her for some insider tips if you want. Sure, that would be helpful. I’ve heard the Montmartre area is great for little cafés and art museums. Perfect, that’s what we love. Maybe next time then. Any chance of dragging me along? We’d love to. Let’s plan something together, successful holiday queens that we are.

So tell me about your journey to becoming an entrepreneur? Well, it's been a bit of a rollercoaster. I started out after university, working in finance for a while, but then I realized I wanted to do something more... creative. A bit of a risk-taker, I suppose. So, I left my secure job and started my own company. It's been a steep learning curve, but very rewarding! I can imagine! I've never had the stomach for that kind of risk. I always liked the security of teaching. Although, I must admit, sometimes it can feel a bit... restricted, you know? Even with my postgraduate degree, I've been stuck in the same role for over a decade. Teaching can be as much of a challenge in its own way though, can't it? You're constantly dealing with new kids, new curriculums... Absolutely. But at least with teaching, sometimes you get creative too - thinking of ways to engage the students, that kind of thing. And it's very fulfilling to see young minds grow. So, have you ever considered taking a jump into this side of things? Maybe start a small business on the side? The thought has crossed my mind, but I suppose it's the fear of the unknown that holds me back. I also really enjoy the predictable grind of teaching. Totally understand. Honestly though, I think it's good to have a balance in life. If I'm being completely honest, entrepreneur life can also be all-consuming. And there are definitely times where I wish I had the predictability of a steady income and the benefits that come with working for someone else. Absolutely! I just had a parents' evening last week and one of the parents asked if I'm a single parent, thinking that explains my dedication. She said it couldn’t be love for teaching. Just proves we’ve all got our struggles, regardless of our career choice. Yeah, and that's one of my favorite things about entrepreneurship - everyone thinks you're some sort of genius for taking the risk. But most of the time, it just feels like pure, unadulterated fear. It does sound like a bit of a funny world. Definitely. Although, if I could go back and give myself advice when I was 22, it would be to not be afraid to take the leap sooner.

I keep telling them to clean up after themselves but have you seen today's mess? Oh, they're always doing that, aren't they? Are you still at uni with them? Yeah, we all share a house – Rachel, Tom, James, and now Alex isn't living there but he'd definitely be the worst of all if he did. Oh no, poor you. How's the studying coming along though? It's all fine, just trying to balance life and stuff but seeing that mess every day is stressing me out. Well, at least your life is a bit like my university days then. I had five guys in our house and we always had a lot of 'discussions' on who should clean what. Exactly! But it's hard to do anything when you've got a housemate who thinks the kitchen is a public rest spot. I know it's stressful. You should probably try and talk to them next time though or even set some rules. Oh I have and they just ignore it or say they'll do it later. "I'm busy studying" or something like that. Classic. I used to think it was all fun and games until you actually have to start cleaning up after people who don’t know how to use a bin. You're learning about life, Al. It’s all part of growing up and dealing with stuff you don’t like but doesn’t go away. Thanks for the motivational speech, babe. Just trying to help the future career lady. The career lady who can’t handle a bit of mess yet. Maybe you should write an article about it – "The Cleanliness Chronicles: Adventures of a Student-Who-Couldn’t-Wait-To-Grow-Up." Yeah, I could make a fortune. And maybe we could include a chapter on how to handle studying while being annoyed. That’d be the real job. So what now? Are you going to have words with Rachel or Tom? I think so. Maybe this time I'll actually write it down or something. That might make them take it more seriously. That’s a good idea. Make it official so they can’t pretend like they didn’t know. Yeah, and then if they still ignore it, well, I can just argue that they signed off on it. Well, that’s a legal mind for you.

Right, I got us a nice big bunch of vegetables first things's first. Look at this lovely cauliflower and these carrots and cucumbers they've got deep greens. Are you still making all the usual fayre or are you trying anything new this week? A bit of both dear. You remember that new recipe for those stuffed bell peppers we saw online? And then there's the big roast this Sunday, can't be without that. Table won't be the same without it. You know what? That actually would be nice. You'll need all the veg, those new potatoes you spoke of will be perfect for Sunday's roast. They'll be in season just right, just like the recipe wanted. And speaking of Sunday, have you decided what to do about making the summer pudding? Ah, yeah! I thought I'd do it like mother used to. Use the blackberries we picked in the summer, layer it with those sponge fingers you brought back from the bakers’ last week. That should do the trick. That sounds lovely, I can already taste it. It's been ages since I made one. I think most of the heavy lifting is still the jam making, but seeing it all in the glass bowl at the end is so satisfying. And the key is to make sure they soak long enough, right? That's right, all day if possible. Like grandmother used to say, "If you can see through, it's not ready." "All through and clear through" - doesn't that it say. Exactly that. Now where are my jam jars... There they are next to the bread. Ah, thank you. Shall I just start on that now? If you're up to it, sure. I can help with peeling the apples next if you want. That would be great, the more hands the faster it goes. I know what you mean. Though in these days of automation, it's just as quick for one person. But companionship is better. True, true. You know, this almost makes me wish youngsters would learn the art of jam and jelly making. There's something about it that's lost with the new generation. Totally agree. It’s not just about preserving food but preserving traditions. I suppose it’s not just that they... Don’t know how? Don’t want to spend the time?

Oh, Dad, don't you remember when you first started doing that joke; it was about 30 years ago. You used to tell it to us at every family gathering and we thought it was hilarious, but Mom would always say she'd heard it before. Aye, it’s a good'un though, isn't it? I suppose it’s a part of my history with you lot. You know, when I was a lad, we’d have to wait till the radio finished showing its programmes before we could tell jokes like that, and then only if there was someone new to hear it at! Really? I can't imagine waiting like that to share a joke. No, it’s almost unimaginable how things have changed. And Dad, how's everything at your place? How did you and your mates go with looking after the garden? Oh, it's coming along grand. We managed between us. I've been showing Jack a thing or two about the lawns and this year it looks the best it’s been in years. He’s got a green thumb, just like his granddad! Yeah, he’s quite the gardener, hasn’t he? He can't wait for spring so we can plant more vegetables. I know. Speaking of which, how about making a plan for the season? We could have a session where we all go and do some planting. Aye, that’s a grand idea! I’ll even show you how I keep the weeds down, using some old Yorkshire methods. Dear, I reckon that’s a fine plan, but let’s keep it for the day when the weather is better. You know how we Yorkshire folk can be; we don’t want to be caught out in the rain planting flowers! Mother’s right as always. Let’s pencil that in for late spring. Right. Pencil it in so we don’t forget. Is everything still good with you and Dad, though? I mean, health-wise and all? Everything’s fine, thanks for asking. We’re managing. It’s just the usual — our knees creaking more than they used to when it’s frosty outside and the rain makes the joints ache. Aye, that’s the age, isn’t it? Not moving like we used to. Still, we’re grateful for what we’ve got and still quite capable of bending down to plant a few bulbs.

Yo, anyone seen that new health craze around? Yeah, I think you mean that probiotic water trend. I was thinking about trying it, talked to someone who swears by it. Right, that's the one. I just can't get over how much people are willing to pay for some kind of ginger flavored water and call it healthy. It's not just that, though. I've seen this one ad for a collagen drink that I'm almost tempted to try. They claim it can help with skin and even joints. Collagen drinks? That's new to me. Do they have anything behind that claim? Apparently, some studies suggest collagen peptides may help with skin elasticity, but it's not like you're drinking a magic potion. And let's not forget the placebo effect. Placebo effect aside, I find it interesting how quickly these trends pop up and go viral. Last week it was spirulina, now it's collagen. And it's funny because it's not just the drink itself, right? It's the lifestyle. Like, suddenly people who never worked out before are posting #homegym selfies because their influencer told them "after just 30 days you'll see the difference!" Strikes me that people follow these things because the core message can't be wrong – eat better, move more. It's just the packaging that changes. Still, it's silly isn't it? Like, really? Collagen drinks? For real? I guess it's also about perceived ease. Instead of cooking a meal, it's easier to "fix" your diet with a collagen drink and think that's enough. And let's not forget about technology side of things, right? Every day a new app, gadget, claiming to be the next big thing for fitness or health. Yes! Like these new smartwatches and fitness trackers. While they provide some benefit, sometimes I feel like they just sit on your wrist collecting dust if you don’t use them properly. My biggest gripe is probably just the sheer volume of health and fitness content on social media. It's information overload. Totally. And it's not even just about health. Look at how much content we're being served about what job we should do next or how we should be organizing our lives. True. Sometimes I scroll through Instagram thinking I’m behind because I don’t know how to apply for a visa to live in another country or this or that trendy skill.

Right okay so I think we need some milk. Yeah I'd agree. Yeah definitely! And bread, wouldn't it be better if we did that first. We can grab the bread while we're doing other shopping, then we don’t need to come back for it again. Yeah and tins of beans and pasta. Let’s get some basics covered. And butter! But actually, I've got no idea what else we need. Well, how about we get a list. You can look at the fridge and stuff to see what we actually need. Yeah, okay. You thinking of just bread and milk? You'll have to get more than that if you actually want a meal in the next day or two. He's right, but we're trying to remember what we're already low on. Ron, can you check the fridge, please? Sure. You also probably should get some fruit and vegetables. Yeah, that sounds like a good idea. And maybe some snacks? Oh, I was thinking of trying to make dinner tonight too. I might need some meat or something. Good thinking. Any preferences or ideas, or we can just pick up whatever looks good? Ah, I saw some recipes online for a lamb curry, maybe that could work? Sounds good. But you'll need spices for that, and a few other things. Mum, doesn’t cooking spices stuff like curry powder just keep for ages? Doesn’t it go bad quickly? No, if it’s stored properly curry powder or any spice mix usually lasts months. But we could just check, if we're not sure. If you think about it, we can make a trip to the market, they always have fresh everything and we can grab a few extras. You can also help pick things out, might make it more interesting for you. I don't know, Dad. I was just thinking it'd be easier to get stuff we need online and have it delivered if we're going to do that much shopping anyway. True. Maybe we can list everything and then decide if we just order the non-perishable stuff or if we should still do a quick trip. A good plan. Also, can we discuss our thinking on this issue with the insects while we’re at it? I saw Silas playing with his bug net this morning.

So, I got my P.E. grade today. Oh really? What did you get? Well, it's not great but it's better than I thought. I got a 7 out of 10. That's actually quite good considering how much you hate P.E. Thanks, I suppose. At least I didn't fail. Definitely not. Now, moving on, have you heard about that new science project we've got to do? Yeah, our teacher said it's about genetics and DNA, right? Yes, that's the one. I heard it's really interesting but also pretty challenging. Does anyone know any good YouTubers that explain genetics well? Oh, yeah! I think this one called CrashCourse has a whole series on genetics and it's super helpful. Oh wow, okay. I'll check that out. And have you seen on Instagram this girl who's majoring in genetics? She posts all these cool videos on it. For me, looking at her stories on Instagram helps prepare me for school sometimes. That's pretty cool. Where did you find her? Just scrolling in the biology category. Social media can sometimes be helpful right? Yeah, it can be. Although, I'm kinda annoyed with this one teacher today. She made us all write an essay for homework and in class we were really doing okay with the topic, but the homework piece was just really confusing. That sucks. But sometimes that's just the way it is with homework. Yeah, I guess. I just don't understand why we have to do the extra work. Seems like the class was enough. I feel that. But we are supposed to be reviewing and reinforcing the material ourselves. It does help me by doing some independent practice. I guess you're right. I just wish the topics weren’t so confusing on my own. Oh, and did you hear? The principal announced something in assembly today. I think it’s about something for us over Christmas break. No, I missed assembly today. What did they say? I could have sworn it was something about a workshop or a session over the holidays. I swear I saw people arguing about it, but I couldn't hear. Oh, that would be nice. Maybe it will be more hands-on or something interesting. I might actually go then. Yeah, I'll ask someone about it tomorrow maybe. Yeah, do that.

Oh, sorry about that. Just can't seem to shake this cold. You poor thing! I hope you're taking care of yourself. A bit of rest and meds. I kind of regret going to that food festival last week. You and everyone else now. Food poisoning seems to ruin a fair share of weekends around here. And to think I avoided that dodgy stall with the raw oysters... Wise. I've been meaning to get the flu vaccine, just need to find the time. Might just save you next time.Plus, with the health guidelines getting more stringent, it's a good idea to stay on top of vaccination schedules. Exactly, and it's not just about you—it's for the whole community. Hospitals are still recovering from the last year, you know? Totally, and between the colds and the flu or even just the usual aches and pains... this is a perfect moment to appreciate good healthcare. Indeed. Makes you appreciate the effort of all the healthcare staff. Have you seen the recent updates about body language recognition to detect early signs of illness by cameras in hospitals? No, I haven't, but that's an interesting idea. Could really help identify patients who need attention before things escalate. I found that through a research analysis on Lloyd Grossman's show that's been popular again. "How to Catch a Killer" or something like that, they highlight new tech in forensics and it led me down a rabbit hole into health tech. Really? I've heard it mentioned in our research circles as well. It's fascinating how far things have come. Speaking of shows, the lack of hiatus from screen time is probably not helping my cold either. Yeah, for sure. I've been plowing through box sets as well. Though, I have found one zero-obligation activity to do while lounging. What’s that? Reading. I've caught up on a couple of good books I was putting off. The plus side of a cold is enforced downtime. Wise choice. I've been eyeing that series about dystopian futures where illness detection is a given—it hovers around the themes of body autonomy and surveillance. That ties back into our tech talk. How do you balance exploring these subjects with your thesis? It's a juggling act—sometimes I worry I'm spending more time worrying about the future than working on my PhD about the past, but there's a bit of crossover in thinking about society’s relationships with health and tech.

I've used up all my vowels already. That's alright, try to build on what you have. Right! Right! You don't have to have all the letters. And isn't that often the case in life as well? True, right? Life never gives you all the vowels. Ah, another E. Yes! That's a good one. ... or is it? Oh, oh we're on the wrong track here. The game of life—always looking for the paths least taken. Or the letters least used. So, where were we with the shopping centre gridlock yesterday? Honestly, I missed a meeting because of that. And the butcher's shop, right? What a queue! The joy of living in a big city, I suppose. At least it gives us something to talk about. Indeed, and who would have thought it'd lead to a better scrabble game? We make do with what we have, eh? Literally, in this case. A couple more E's wouldn't hurt, though. Perhaps changing the board could help? Oh, don't tempt the fates! No, no. I'll just use this E to make "heeee". That'll do. That's almost as clever as my "queue" the other day. Queue was a good one. Very applicable to our late night company. Speaking of... should we post any of this... on Facebook? "Spending a lovely evening playing scrabble and waiting in long queues." Oh, I'd like to see who "likes" that! Maybe just the memes from queueing at the butcher's. Memes about queuing might just trend. "Life in a big city: The one universal truth is waiting." "When life gives you lemons... you still need to wait for the butcher." And here we are, making lemonade—or should I say scrabble—in this very room. It's all a bit of fun, really. Unless we're actually stuck in a gridlock... Then we can use it to write a book on "How to Cope with Urban Life". And "The Art of Making Scrabble from Life's Obstacles". Well, I think we have enough material for several chapters already. We could start a new genre: "Urban Realism for Scrabble Players". (

So tell me about your time in Germany working at those exhibitions. We've all heard your successful career; it sounds like quite an adventure. Oh, it was indeed! I invented and marketed various printing systems. It involved a lot of work, but the exposure and network were invaluable, especially those times at the Druck and Print shows. Wow, I can imagine! The market for printing technology back then was quite robust, wasn't it? I'm right in the middle of a local project trying to get local history set for printing. It's interesting how even now, alongside all the digital stuff, print still has its place. Absolutely. Print never goes out of style, just like these old buildings around here. Even in Germany, people appreciated quality, and the shows were always bustling. Everyone from all over Europe, but of course, the Germans - precise and methodical as always. Care to share any particularly memorable moments or challenges during those exhibitions? Let me think. There was this one year, we had a last-minute issue with one of the systems. Someone had mistakenly packed the wrong power supply or something, and it was a total panic. But, it turned out to be a blessing in disguise. It brought different departments together in a way we hadn't before. Good problem-solving in the face of disaster, I suppose. Exactly. We ended up having some of the best discussions about teamwork and preparedness right then and there. Also, there was this time an old colleague from the factory spotted me at one of the shows. We'd been apart for years, and it was like no time had passed at all. That's it, the connections and the camaraderie. Reminds me of our little community here, coming together for the preservation of these old things. It truly does. Both in your line of work, preserving history, and mine, it was about preserving a craft, even as technology was rapidly changing. There's something about working with your hands or inscribing meaning into tangible items... You've hit on something there. It might explain why despite all the digital tools out there, we find ourselves coming back to these more traditional methods. I've been thinking, when I retired from my gallery, I felt a bit lost for a bit because so much of my identity was tied to creating and displaying physical art.

So, Dad, did you hear about that strict spelling test we had this week in English today? Oh, yes! Well, I'm sure you did well. What was the most challenging word for you? It was definitely "queue". The teacher made a point that "queue" is spelled "q-u-e-u-e", and I knew it, but it still feels a bit odd! Yeah, the English language can be strange! You know, words like "queue" come from French, and that's why they have a "u" in the middle. Right. I remember learning about that earlier in the year. It's just that sometimes it feels like our language just keeps making exceptions! Exactly. It's one of the many quirks we English speakers have adopted over the years. And then you have words like "enquire" and "inquire" with different meanings but similar spellings. It's confusing! Right! And "its" and "it's". Those still get me mixed up sometimes! Well, remember this trick: if you can replace the word with "it is" or "it has", use "it's". If you can't, use "its". Got it! Thanks, Dad. That's really helpful! No problem, love. It's always a bit of a journey learning English, especially as it's constantly evolving. Evolution of language can be fascinating, though. You know, words can come from anywhere, and they often have interesting origins and stories behind them. Really? Like "quinoa"? That's a food we often use, but I never thought about where it comes from. Good question! "Quinoa" is a South American plant, popularly used as a nutritious grain. It's been adopted into many English-speaking countries quite recently but has its name from the Quechua language, which is spoken in the Andean region. Wow, I didn't know that! Language intersects with culture and geography so much, doesn't it? Absolutely! And it can lead us to learn about new ideas and ways of life. Speaking of which, are we close to reaching Bude yet? Or perhaps you want to stop at a service station? We could stop in Bodmin and stretch our legs. Do you need anything from the service station? Maybe some water and a few snacks will do. And while we're at it, I might as well use this time to check the map again... We left the M6 at Birmingham, yeah? Then we'll take the A38 to St. Austell, and from there, it's a pretty straightforward drive into Bude.

Right okay so I'm going to make homemade Yorkshire puddings. Dad uses these special tins; he says they give them the right shape. Hopefully they don't stick, though. Are you sure they're needed? We can just get some from the shop if you like. Oh, homemade’s always the best. It’s something my wife used to make. She could make a roast that would make your eyes water, right? Yeah, homemade is definitely better. But even if they stick, it's worth it. There's nothing like a good traditional dinner. Even lazy like me can appreciate a good homemade Yorkshire. Though I’ve been relying on my mum’s too much lately. Your mum's cooking’s fantastic, isn’t it? I remember coming over for Sunday roast and just...  sighs  Speaking of which, I need your opinion. Is there a better gravy recipe than the one in the book my dad gave me? It feels a bit boring. Boring's good. I mean, what more do you need than onion, veg stock, and some flour for thickening? Well, if you want to add some depth, some red wine and maybe a touch of mushroom would give it some body. My wife used to make a gravy that...  smiles  Wine in gravy? That sounds posh, but okay, I might try that. And you can always experiment, right? Who knows, you could create your own signature gravy! Yeah, and maybe I’ll figure out how to properly season stuff. Seasoning’s key. Sometimes people just throw salt on, but understanding when to add what... That’s an art. Speaking of food, do any of you know what’s wrong with the local pub’s steak and ale pie? It’s always overcooked and stodgy. I heard they switched butchers and it’s been a disaster since. You can’t even get a decent piece of meat. Sad to say that. The butcher used to deliver for my Sunday roasts. Lost my appetite for pub grub after that. Yeah, it’s like the whole town's been let down. Well, maybe we can convince Matt to come over for dinner more often. Matt cooks decent stuff, right? Not my grandson. He still relies too much on ready meals, but he’s getting there. You guys are more hands-on with food. Yeah, like I said, I’m learning... slowly.

Yo, how's studying going? It's been alright, just getting into the second year now and things are getting tougher. I've been finding the reading list rather large, but I've learned to be more efficient with my time. Yeah, I remember when I was at uni, managing time was kind of like learning how to juggle while riding a unicycle. But you get into a rhythm, right? Any big projects coming up? Actually I have a big presentation next week. It's on how language teaching keeps changing with new technology, something like that. Oh, that sounds interesting. I've been thinking of enrolling in an online course, maybe learn Spanish or something. You've got any advice? Definitely. I think the key is just to stick with it and create a routine - like making time each day to practice. And you know, using apps can be really helpful. There are some that are like a game for learning a language, which can make it a bit more fun. That's a great idea. I used Duolingo once, it was quite addictive. Yeah, it really is. And maybe try to connect with native speakers, even if it's just for a chat. You learn so much more through conversation. That makes sense. Speaking of learning new things, have you started driving yet? I've been thinking of getting my license. Ah nice, I got my provisional last year. It's been good so far, but I've been trying really hard to keep calm when I'm on the road. It's weird, you always hear these horror stories but I've been lucky so far. Yeah the horror stories can make it sound worse than it is, but you're right, staying calm is key. And I just got my first car, it's just a small one but it's mine. Do you drive regularly? Just couple of years now, but yeah, it's great. Gives me a lot of independence. Definitely. I find that driving really helps when I'm stressed, I mean you can just listen to your music or podcasts for a bit of alone time. Exactly, plus it's always fun to drive to new places and explore. I intend to. Maybe you can come along sometime and show me some good spots around here. I'd love to, why not? Perhaps a weekend trip somewhere.

I've got another cup of coffee, I've been up since 5; these are moments I love. Ooh, talked about coffee! I remember when we first started, we had this coffee machine that made the best coffee. Then, the kids, all those years ago, they were so fascinated by driving and cars. "Mummy, can I have the keys and drive?" of course, as soon as I'd glance away . Yeah, and would they try and make a donation box to sell, saying it's for charity. I have to say, in our years of childminding, making a donation box was always a hit. But in retirement, my big project has been my garden. Lovely. I’ve heard you’re quite the green thumb. Well, in retirement, you have time to visit your plants every morning. I've also been playing around with making a few banners. Oh, for what? Well, the local gardening society is having a competition and I thought, why not? It’s something to keep me busy and I enjoy a bit of creativity. What a lovely project, making banners for the competition! Yeah, and then there’s bell ringing. I’ve joined the church bell ringing group. It’s another way of keeping active and giving back to the community. I know what you mean about giving back. Yes, it's important. Speaking of, did you hear about the trip to the Gambia that’s being organized? I’ve been thinking about making a donation, maybe getting a group together for it. Ah, yes, I did hear about that trip. It's for a really good cause isn’t it? Definitely. You know, after all the years of looking after children – it’s lovely to be able to contribute to something like that. That’s so kind of you to say! But, you know, it’s also a bit sad sometimes. You think about kids and what they might grow up to be, and all the possibilities... Munchausen Syndrome by Proxy comes to mind. We've had those cases in our careers, you remember? Yes, I do. It's heartbreaking to think that parents or any adult would... I can’t even get the words out. Absolutely. But what good is dwelling too long on that? What can we do, right here, right now, to keep making a positive difference? We can at least support initiatives like the Gambia trip.

So, I was browsing on my phone yesterday and came across an app called "Seek" that's apparently trending right now. It's like a mix between Pokémon GO and Geocaching, but with plants and various flora. I'm curious to try it out, maybe on the weekend? Really? I heard rumors about it, but never had the chance to try it out. Pokémon GO got old quite quickly for me, but this sounds different. Maybe we could make it a group activity? That sounds fun! And it could be an interesting change from our usual weekend routines. We could make it a fun outing, check plants and stuff. Who knows, we might even learn something. Yeah, definitely vote yes for that. Might just encourage me to actually leave the house for once. Jokes aside, it can be a nice way to get some fresh air and perhaps even meet new people while exploring nature. Plus, I want to get into exploring more during holidays. Speaking of which, did any of you see that new zombie apocalypse movie that just came out? It got mixed reviews but I'm curious. Should we watch or skip it? We could try it on our next movie night, maybe have a "choose your own scary movie" night. You know, everyone brings a movie suggestion and then we pick one to watch. It’s a lot of fun to see what scares everyone the most. That's a great idea! But, to be honest, my stomach always does a somersault at the thought of scary movies. I guess I’ll need to man up, or should I say, “woman up” and face that fear head on. But it's not just about the movie itself, sometimes it's about the company, right? Plus, with snacks and blankets, it can become quite a cozy night in. Oh, absolutely. And the best part is the bonding that comes with it, even if we’re all screaming or hiding behind pillows. True. Speaking of snacks, I was thinking we could make something special for dinner on Sunday. Last time we did a proper dinner together was ages ago. What do you think? I’m all in for that! How about something easy yet delicious? Maybe burgers or a big salad? And sweet potatoes as a side. Or could we maybe try making something completely new this time? Like maybe some Korean BBQ or a variation of Italian we haven’t done before?

I've been meaning to ask you, have you seen these new cars that can practically park themselves? You know, with all the sensors and whatnot? Oh, yeah! I've seen them. I think it’s quite amazing technology now, isn't it? Though, personally, I’ll still need the manual feel of the steering wheel . I wish I could get one, but I don't drive anymore. Too expensive and too complicated for an old man like me. True, true. Though, I'm thinking of maybe getting a simpler, more environmentally friendly one. Something electric, maybe? Electric cars are really taking off now. Maintenance is low, just like my car was when I used to drive. Though, I've heard the range can be a challenge, still. Exactly! My mate, he's got one—says it’s great, but he’s always worried about the range when he travels far. And charging stops are still not as convenient as petrol stations for us old blokes! That's true. I've heard this new tech on the charging side might be addressing that soon. I'm sure it will. I read somewhere the new 'supercharger' stations are already more efficient. Supercharger... sounds like something out of a sci-fi film, doesn’t it ? Well, really, it’s about time we’re talking about automotive tech like it's something from "Back to the Future"! Though, us getting home is usually a hell of a lot more straightforward now. Speaking of "getting home", how did you manage with the weather today? Roads weren’t too bad, were they? Oh, it's been okay. Just couple of small delays, but manageable. Though, I always worry when you two are out and about. Yes, we do our best to plan ahead. Roads are clearer now, but you can't predict everything. Us, stuck at home, fret about all sorts of things... That's family for you. Always worrying over the things worth worrying over. But seriously, we’re lucky to have each other and a reliable way to get back home. Amen to that. Though, I have to say, those new cars might be helpful for someone finding their way home when they might not... Yeah yeah, I get what you mean. Technology might not solve all our problems, but it can certainly make things a bit easier. At least for the journey outside, right?

So, I hear you’re planning on moving to Manchester soon. We've lived here our whole lives; how are you feeling about the change? It's both exciting and daunting at the same time. I love the idea of starting anew. Still, leaving behind the familiarity, friends, and family is bittersweet. Yeah, I'd totally understand. But you've always been up for a healthy dose of adventure, haven't you? Erm, yeah, but it's not always about how much you love change. Sometimes it's just about routine and knowledge of your environment, you know? Absolutely. But think of all the new things you can experience. You've always wanted to travel more, and now you'll have city life at your doorstep. And Manchester's got a lot to offer, isn't it? Good transport links too. Plus you can visit Liverpool, Chester, and all those lovely Midlands towns if you get a car. That's true. We're planning on getting a car as soon as we settle. I've heard their train links within the city are brilliant too, but a car can be nice for weekend getaways. I’ve always found the M6 fun on a motorway journey. You get such a range of landscape and architecture as you head north. Well, at least you won’t spend ages in traffic anymore like on the M25 . Speaking of traffic, how is Pat's health in all the commotion? She's never been one for big changes and all this moving around might be. Mum's holding up fairly well considering. It's the logistics and the physical work that’s been the most challenging for her, but everyone's pitching in to help. The main concern is really finding the right place in Manchester; we don’t want a house too small, but at the same time it should be relatively affordable. There's usually a wide range of options in cities like Manchester. From apartment living to family homes. Indeed. It’s just a matter of finding what suits us best and that can take time. If I might suggest something, when you're house hunting, make sure to look for parking facilities too. Cities can be crowded and parking can be a nightmare without it. That's a great point, Michael. I hadn't considered parking sufficiently. And what about the joys of airport travel?

Mum, I can't believe you did it. Doing what dear? You nearly accelerated off the seat. Noticing the bike thief! Oh, that. It was just luck. A friend of a friend works at a local bike shop and heard rumors there was a stolen bike for sale around town. I knew it must be yours. And now you've got it back right? Yes, but it was a long day. First, I had to get concrete proof. That involved calling around, discussing with friends, seeing if anyone actually saw you leave the cycle store with the bike earlier today. You've been thinking about it non-stop, haven't you? As soon as you told me it was gone. And to think, it was right under your nose. That guy seemed so suspicious when he turned into your street. I know! But in the moment, when it was just an ordinary day. You couldn't suspect anyone. Exactly what thieves rely on. Now that it's recovered, let it be a lesson. When leaving your bike anywhere, even if you think "it's just for a minute," lock it properly. I know, I was stupid. Well, now you can have it back and keep it safe. Aye, I’ll never leave it unguarded again in my life, really. But you never spoke of the thief, did they have it claimed? That’s the odd part. The guy had no idea it was the bike that was reported stolen until my friend from the bike shop jumped on him. How? He must have just been trying to sell it off quickly? I think so. Whatever his story ended up being, he will likely regret storing that bike. So you followed legal means to get my bike back? Of course. I don’t mess around with illegal activity. It’s for the best in these situations. I’m just truly so grateful. That’s the sweetest part. Now show me your gratitude by doing the dishes. Maybe I will. Just maybe? Okay, okay. And you’ve been doing well in college? Yeah, I like it. The subjects are interesting... except for when any of the assignments feel tedious. That’s usually the case with most things. But hang in there, these skills are essential. Though sometimes social media can get pretty frustrating, huh? It can at times. But it’s also how we connect these days.

Oh, did I mention my first year's passport control story? On the way back from South Africa. I was carrying six dozen hard-boiled eggs, souvenirs for my students, and well, let's just say they got quite a squeeze to determine the contents of my luggage wasn't a threat to aviation security. Oh, isn't that one for the books! I suppose those eggs were part of a history project? Exactly! I wanted to bring back something tangible for them. But it was quite the ordeal to explain to security why I was smuggling six dozen eggs across international borders. Even with your charismatic charm, passing through security is never easy, despite the intended purpose of your souvenirs. Might have been easier to bring back ostrich eggs instead. Ah, but the children cherished those eggs. They were thrilled with the idea of eggs from South Africa! Though, I didn’t tell them yet about the security ordeal. Let’s leave that out of the educational stories, shall we? Someone should make a comedy about that. I’m sure it has the makings of a great sketch. Interesting how culture and food can tie different parts of the world together. You’re kind of like a modern-day 'Mary Poppins' with the eggs; making a daily staple into an exotic souvenir. Only if 'Mary Poppins' decided to smuggle eggs instead of chimney sweeps across London. Next silly story I could tell: trying to buy a ticket to ride from the automated machine and getting thrown out because it 'recognized' me as two different people - doesn’t learn that I have a twin! Automated machines, always understanding. Speaking of ‘ticket to ride’, have we decided the order yet? We couldn’t keep ourselves from buying every ticket board we found. Ah, yes. I remember we had a bit of confusion about train dynamics. Someone asked if you could sit on the first and last carriage at the same time. The theoretical physicist in the group said, "Theoretically, it's possible, but pragmatically, you run the risk of zero points if caught mid-journey by the station master." And almost as comical as the time the automated station announcement started explaining the mechanics of how trains work, including explaining that trains run on tracks and not on the sense of wanting to go somewhere. I saw that. Incredibly detailed and slightly nonsensical.

I've decided I need a routine or I'm just going to forget what day it is. Well, routines can help. But don't beat yourself up about forgetting sometimes. It's normal. Yeah, but the days are all blending together – do you ever feel like that? Constantly. But we've at least managed to stick to playing board games most nights, right? Absolutely. That's been my savior during lockdown. I think it's a good ritual. It forces us to turn off our laptops at least for a little bit. And to actually interact with each other. Which is...surprising given we're both lecturers now. What's that supposed to mean? Well, we spend our days explaining things to people via screens. But with board games... we have to actually speak to each other and strategize face-to-face. Mm. That's a nice contrast. I hadn’t thought of it like that. It's kind of surreal. Here we are, with advanced degrees and teaching others about all sorts of complex topics, and then we're in the living room at 9 PM, trying to figure out why the Inns and Mansions expansion to Carcassonne hasn't been equitably distributed. It's a different kind of analytical thinking, for sure. But it's been good for us. We've learned a bit about each other's temperaments and patience levels. Indeed. I never thought I’d be arguing over who gets the extra sheep in Settlers of Catan. The marital arts really do come out over those little wooden pieces. You're just really insistent on being the feudal lord of all things fluffy and wooly. Well, who's going to run a sustainable economy if not me? We need to diversify, my dear. Maybe invest in some grain or stone instead of just wool all the time. Point taken. Though, I just think the sheep give us a tactical advantage. It's all about the economy of scale, or so our game plans keep telling me. Sure. But I like to think there's room for... a bit of cunning strategy, maybe some sheep-based diplomacy? There might be a paper in there somewhere for a game studies conference. I'd read it. You know, it's interesting how games can reveal these little aspects of ourselves or our relationships. And it's a nice way to unwind, too.

So, I hear you moved to Sunderland recently. Yeah, just today. The move is done, and I'm trying to figure out where to put everything. It's quite disorienting. Right! Welcome to our little dinner gathering and help us celebrate this new chapter in your life. Why don't you start unpacking while we talk? What kind of food would you like while you're doing that? Thanks, actually, I've been thinking about trying to get some white goods for my new kitchen. I keeps coming across loads of different brands and options. Oh, that is a nightmare! Even with my job as a project co-ordinator, I still found it very overwhelming. But in your case, since you're just moving in, you might as well get the best quality you can from the start. Exactly. And have you thought about the most practical place for them? The positioning of white goods in a kitchen can make or break your workflow. Make sure there's enough space and that it's easily accessible. Mm, yeah, that occurred to me but I wanted to talk to Kerrie about her recommendations. She's lived here quite some time, I bet she has her tried and trusted brands. Absolutely, while the 'tried and trusted' might be reliable, make sure you check out some newer, more energy-efficient models too. Absolutely, and while you're doing that, perhaps look into the bin system in your new area as well. You'd be surprised how much chaos can be avoided with the right waste management plan. Right! That’s a great point, Kerrie would know that as well. On the topic of chaos, how about this food situation? Do you have any recommendations for supermarkets or local shops? You'll definitely need to familiarize yourself with the area, but for now, we can point you in the right direction. If you're in town, there's usually a Tesco next to the train station and there's always a great collection at the changing times market. And don’t forget about the local butchers and bakers. They're not just better in terms of quality but often have a more personalized service. Plus, supporting local business is always a good idea. That makes sense. Speaking of making sense, how have you been dealing with the medical care in Sunderland? Is it easy to get appointments or are there any specialized services I should be aware of?

Mum, I can't believe how much of a difference it's made getting that new car. It's like night and day compared to the old one. Oh, yes! I've noticed that. It's got quite a bit more zip to it now, hasn't it? It sure has. And isn't it lovely how equipped it is? Like the Bluetooth and all the gadgets. It makes the trip a lot less of a hassle. Well, I'm glad you like it. It's a bit of an adventure choosing a car, isn't it? Did you see the prices for some of the models we looked at? Yes, it was a bit of a shock to the system to see how much some cars cost. But this one, while not cheap, seems like a good value. What's been keeping you so busy lately? You're always talk about work. Oh, it's always something. Tonight, I'm working on the proofs for the next edition of TLS . I love the thrill of seeing what new authors are making waves. That sounds interesting. So, you prefer print or digital for that sort of thing? I'm more of a kindle person, but I know some people still love the feel of a physical book. It really depends on the reader, doesn't it? There's something about print that keeps its charm for some, while others simply love the convenience of digital. It's a different reading experience, but both have their place. I guess so. And what about working conditions? I saw a headline about how they're phasing out TLS's print edition. Yes, it's happening, but we're hoping to find new formats and ways to make the digital version just as engaging and measured as the print. Change can be scary, but often it forces us to innovate and find better ways to do things. It’s just that I love going through TLS and finding all sorts of great recommendations. I hope the digital version will be just as good for that. I'm sure it will. Plus, with digital, you can get instant access and a wider selection. But, yes, the art of curation is indeed important. It's what sets a publication apart. Just hope they don't turn it into just a list of recommendations like those algorithmically driven ones on those websites.

Remember that time we went to Majorca? How could I forget? The hotel we stayed at had the pool right next to the bar. Made for some interesting poolside moments. And don’t forget when Matt slipped on the wet tiles coming out of the pool and landed awkwardly on his back. Oh right! And then he blamed it on the towel? Yeah. That moment was embarrassing for him but hilarious for us, especially when you tried to help him up and your hand slipped because the tiles were still wet. I thought he was trying to breakdance. That’s the only time I’ve ever seen anyone accidentally bust a move out of embarrassment. It also led to the beginnings of our “Have you broken something today?” tradition. Perfect. So what else did you do on that trip that’s worth mentioning? Well, there was that night we tried to order food in Spanish. It was more of a game of charades than communication, really. Because obviously, speaking a basic level of Spanish is easy for people who don’t know it at all. It was funny though. We couldn’t understand what we were ordering most of the time, but somehow we ended up getting something palatable every time. I guess it proves food and good company transcend language barriers. We also had this one day where we went exploring the local market and tried to buy some souvenirs. Remember how we got overcharged for those silly bracelets? We knew better than to argue with the charm of the vendor. They probably thought we were in a new sitcom about British tourists abroad. Could've been a hit show if we had a camera to capture the show. And let's not forget the spontaneous karaoke night at the hotel bar where we discovered Martin's operatic talents. Oh man, “In the Still of the Night” just wasn't the same coming from him. But it’s moments like that which make a trip unforgettable. Absolutely. I miss those kinds of silly, memorable moments with all of you. Speaking of memorable, at least our financial statements are less exciting than our holiday stories. Right, Sarah ? Oh, touchy. You know I spend more time at work than having spontaneous sing-alongs on vacation. It’s a different kind of excitement. So, who’s up for trying out this new cocktail list here?

So, I hear that you've decided to take up wild winter camping as your latest hobby. Isn't it quite adventurous for this time of the year? Oh absolutely, and I've never felt more alive. There is something about being in the wild and challenging the elements, even in winter – it's exhilarating. It's fascinating. Speaking from a psychological viewpoint, I can understand the appeal. It's like a modern form of exposure therapy, where you learn to manage extreme conditions, which can build resilience and confidence. That's a compelling point. Do you believe it could be therapeutic for people, especially with the stress we see today? Definitely. I've been doing it for a few years now, and I find it is both calming and invigorating. It really places things in perspective – the simplicity of making yourself comfortable, finding food, and keeping warm. It's a form of mindfulness. Yes, and the physical aspect also can't be ignored. The physical challenge, adapting to changing weather, and the need for constant attention to your surroundings, it's almost like a form of meditation or flow state. That's interesting. So, it's both a physical and mental challenge? Exactly. And it forces you to be present. There's no room for distractions – you're either preparing for the night or focusing on surviving. It's raw, it's real. Like, my first experience was in the Highlands. There was one night where the wind was so strong, it was difficult to pitch the tent, and all I could hear was the roar of the wind and the creaking of the trees. It's a unique experience, and the solitude has given me time to reflect and think deeply. But isn't it dangerous? What about the temperatures and the risks of hypothermia or getting lost? The risk is certainly there, and safety precautions are paramount. But with proper planning, knowledge, and the right gear, it's manageable. In fact, it teaches a very important lesson about self-reliance and making wise decisions under pressure. Definitely. Preparation is key. You need to know what you’re doing, but it’s taught me invaluable survival skills and how to handle emergencies. And if you're going with others, it fosters teamwork and cooperation – strengthening bonds. That makes sense. It’s like real-world education. But what about the freedom aspect?

Speaker_1 and Speaker_2 are discussing film and literature, catching up as they head out for an unmentioned activity:   So how keeps coming up in our conversations. You still admiring Game of Thrones or have you moved on to something else? Oh, Game of Thrones's still very much on my watch list. But let me tell you, I’ve been thinking about diving into some of the books it’s based on. I heard they’re quite different from the show. Ah, you’re going classic, I see. I’ve actually been on a Woody Allen kick. Everything from "Annie Hall" to "Manhattan." There’s something about his writing and directing that still feels so sophisticated. Yeah, he's got that certain style. I appreciate it too, especially his early films. Exactly. His wit is just unbeatable. Though, while on the topic of film and literature, have you had a chance to read "Normal People" by Sally Rooney? It’s been making waves, and I keep hearing great things. Actually, I did. I found it really interesting, especially the exploration of character development and relationships. It felt very real. That's what I found so compelling. The way she captures the mundane and makes it significant. It’s also the first time I’ve read a book and could hear the characters’ voices in my head so vividly. Seems like the author's background in writing plays a big part, isn’t it? How’s it been with your work, getting to do engineering projects that interest you? It’s been great. I’ve been working on a project dealing with renewable energy solutions in urban areas. It’s really fulfilling to do something that could make a real difference. Though, I also need to catch up on some non-technical reading. Any recommendations from your end? Beyond "Normal People", I’ve also enjoyed "The Thirteenth Tale" by Diane Setterfield. It’s a mystery but also has this atmospheric quality to the writing. You might enjoy that. I’ll definitely add it to my list. We should make a point to discuss our reads soon, though. I heard about this new food fair happening in town this weekend. I know you’re not too far from... is there any particular type of food you’re looking forward to? I’m a bit like you though, wide interests, but if I had to pick something, maybe some authentic doughnuts or a well-priced local fare stall.

So tell me Sophia and James what did you both think was the best part of Grace's school Brownie Promise evening? The sweeties after the knot-tying! Yeah! There were lots of different flavours. That's lovely! So questions for me then: what would you both like to hear me read from tonight? A story with a ghost! And fairies! Okay. Which book would you like? We've got loads. Can it be 'The Wishing Tree'? Or maybe 'The Magic Door'! Perfect. Okay let me grab one then. Is 'The Magic Door' the one with the magic typewriter? Ah, yes! It is. Did you know we learnt about typewriters at school today? Really? How was it? It was cool! We saw one in the corner of the classroom. The teacher said they used to be used a lot. That's right. Where did you get told the typewriter was? In the 'old-fashioned' corner. It was really old and big. That's wonderful! Did you have a go at typing anything? No, but in class we were shown how to type on a computer. What's the 'old-fashioned' corner for then? It's where the teacher keeps things that show how things were done a long time ago, like using a typewriter or maybe an old camera or things like that. Oh, that makes sense. Can I see a real typewriter again sometime? Of course! I might have one in my room. From my grandmother's collection. You sure? Wouldn't they be really expensive if they're old? Some would be. But not all. I have a few from when my grandfather collected them. I can show you if you want. Yeah, show me! Is it like the one in Granny’s attic? No, maybe not. But I have some from around the same era. And what about the computer typing. Was it easier? I think it's interesting how things change. You can use a computer keyboard really fast once you know how and it’s easier to correct your work. But if you make a mistake on the old typewriter, you have to start again, from the start, right? Usually yes, although there was ink and paper to get corrected too. So it took more work but the end result might look neater! I'd prefer the computer! Making mistakes is part of learning, but having to start again from the beginning is a bit too much for me!

I've got to say, it's almost as though I'd planned to leave these scruffy old jeans and t-shirt out just to match the theme of our conversation, isn't it? Indeed you have now, Jenny! You look like you've just rolled out of bed and straight to the breakfast table. Well, I did just roll out of bed actually, but I hope I'm not setting the bar too low for this fine morning meal! How about you, still got your suit on from early morning meetings? No, no. I figured today’s a Sunday, might as well lounge about a bit. Though mornings are usually my jam for preparation. Oh, oh we're on the morning kick. Hence your jam pun, I presume? Speaking of which, I had such a thought-provoking conversation with one of your friends last week, you know, over the visit to that fruit farm near Malpass. It got me thinking about sustainability and village businesses really making a mark again. Yeah, it's astonishing how well those small farms can thrive. Even the roadworks around the corner seemed inconsequential while I was walking along the hedgerows, taking in all the nature and isolation. It reminded me of the time I went to explore some of the deserted medieval villages – like a different world, you know? It’s fascinating how old things can still be alive, really. Much like our breakfast today, probably inspired by a medieval farm worker’s early morning routine! Though, they definitely would’ve eaten it in silence and not talked about old houses and junk mail... Right, because in medieval times the biggest issue was getting through the week's worth of junk mail. Okay, fun aside, Jenny, you remember my old place on Church Street? Now that's one thing that really needs attention. I've been meaning to fix up the garden before selling it. We could sit on the back step, enjoy some of my lemon verbena that’s growing for pesto in the summer. I’d love to see it, if you're ever available to show it around. And have you considered like, modernizing those old stone walls? Make them less rustic and more... well, recoverable? I did, actually! The problem is whether to keep everything traditional or make it more attractive to modern buyers. The issue with my late neighbor leaving me those herbs and plants has me torn – I like the idea of preserving some unique...

So, I was browsing on Facebook yesterday and I came across an interesting article about vitamin D. You know how we all try to get sunlight during the winter months when it's much harder? Oh yeah, but I need to remember to take my supplements. Still, now that the days are getting a bit longer, I’ll try to get outside more. Speaking of supplements, have you heard about the new CBD oil they’ve got in the health shop? I was thinking of trying it out to deal with stress. Wait, CBD oil? Isn’t that related to... medical cannabis? Exactly! But it’s supposed to be beneficial for stress and anxiety, nothing illegal. Apparently, it’s got a good reputation. I read that in some places, though, it can interact with certain medications. I should probably ask my GP before trying anything new. Definitely do that. Always best to check with a professional. Anyway, shall we actually start cooking dinner? I made a video of that new pasta recipe that went viral last week. For me, please. I’m starving after this morning’s hospital shift. Right. You’re always feeding me, while I’m always feeding the animals. My cat Starling has been so demanding lately. Starling can be quite the princess. My dog, on the other hand, is always patiently waiting for scraps. I’m still trying to figure out how to deal with the dogs when I’m at work. I know what you mean. Luckily, my sister helps out with the animals when I’m away. Speaking of animals, I just saw a funny post about how GPS directions led someone to the middle of a field. Oh, I can imagine that. My nephew once ended up in a dead-end by following GPS directions while trying to visit his girlfriend and it became a whole story. Oh that reminded me, my Facebook updated me about your nephew’s new puppy over the holidays. How’s the puppy? Oh, he’s adorable. The puppy is still so much energy. Hopefully, he’ll be easier by spring. Puppies are great. Did anyone receive any nice Christmas presents this year? I received this lovely casserole dish from my niece, and she handmade a photo album with all our family photos. That’s lovely. I got this new laptop that I’ve been putting off getting for ages.

So, I was browsing TV shows yesterday and I came across an episode of "The Crown." It’s really gripping isn’t it? The way they portray historical figures and events, so comprehensive and detailed. Oh yes! I binge-watched it last week. The acting is superb, and the historical questions it raises are just so thought-provoking. I find it fascinating how it delves into the monarchy's inner workings and the decisions that shape the country’s future. Exactly! Have you seen the latest season? I keeps coming back to how they touch on current societal issues while discussing the past, it’s really sharp. Like how they handled the Tonypandy riots, for example, and the role of empathy versus power in government. Yes, I noticed that. It’s actually really good for following recent news too - like making connections between past and present events. Speaking of current affairs, have you heard about the £200 fine for not wearing seatbelts? What a weird law that turned out to be. I mean, it’s not that people don’t understand their importance, but still, it’s not like that was ever a significant issue before. Right! The news did cover the fact that most people who were affected assumed it only applied in car accidents. The government might have wanted to make a point, but it came across really poorly given the timing. It’s just another example of how communication can go awry. Indeed, it’s funny how silly things can sometimes highlight much larger issues - like transparency in laws, or the importance of clear communication. And on the topic of communication, I saw that the NHS is getting a bit of a reputation for overcharging patients now. Have you or anyone you know had to deal with that? Yeah, the news keeps recurring about that. More distressing than anything, I just tried to get a friend’s medical bill clarified. It ended up being a mess of overcomplication and red tape before they were able to get it sorted out and it really makes me wonder how they manage changing the system to prevent these issues. It's just appalling, really, that healthcare - something so fundamental - can become so fraught and bureaucratic. It’s always about money at the end of the day, isn’t it? Probably, but it shouldn’t be. I mean, you can’t quantify the importance of healthcare or the value of the care provided.

Oh, did I ever tell you about's Dad's story when he tried to make an omelette? Whole kitchen was covered in egg after he accidentally spilled the pan! Oh no, I don't think so! That sounds like a classic – do tell! Indeed, it was quite the adventure! He did seem quite proud of himself, though – “Cooking techniques are fractals,” he’d say. All very scientific for “how not to make an omelette”. Oh, yes. He was always like that – very much into structuration theory and explaining things through analogies. Even cooking. I can see that. But seriously, have you thought about starting a regular exercise routine? You know, with the rising house prices and all, maybe you can't afford the big moves you used to make, but sometimes a workout can be therapy. Plus, there are so many free things on YouTube. Well, I’ve been meaning to start something. But the problem is, this job can be so draining – transcribing non-stop all day. By the time I finish, I just want to zone out, not workout. I know what you mean. When I was writing novels, by the time I got home, all I wanted to do was sit down and tune out. But I started walking, even if it was just a quick lap around the block. You know, sometimes it helps just to clear the head. Yeah, I've found that it does actually helps. I’ve even tried doing some yoga videos online before bed to relax. But, as you say, it can be hard to start. You could try a 7-day challenge – commit to doing something for just 10 minutes a day for a week. It’s shorter than what most recommend, but it gets you started. 10 minutes sounds manageable. Maybe I’ll try that for starters. Good for you! And on the topic of routines... has anyone else noticed that house prices are just ridiculous now? Oh, absolutely. I just went to a viewing yesterday. The place was a mess, but the price was like 20% more than what similar houses were going for a year ago. I was shocked when this house we’re in...we bought it years ago for... I can’t even think about it now without clutching my wallet. Yeah, it's a good investment we made then, but imagine trying to get into the market now.

So, I hear you’re working on that new budget project. We've been chatting about it in the administration office. How's it going? It's been a challenge. We're trying to balance the resources of the different departments while keeping our expenses in line with the university's expectations. Must be tough to keep everyone happy and manage the finances effectively. I suppose this is one part where my history with finance makes me appreciate your work. Absolutely. It's not just budgeting for this year but planning for keeps coming backwards. Plus, there are always new requests from departments and it's about making those judgement calls. Right. I've been there. It's a very similar process in my field too. It just seems like there is never enough. Unbeknownst to the speakers, from behind a large bush, another voice interjects. Ah, you guys want a tip? Oh, didn’t know you were here. Who are you? I’m Tom. Just a passerby and happen to overhear your conversation. For a budget, this advice I would take quite seriously. What tip do you have? Well, coming from someone who works in the financial sector, one thing that makes the entire process easier is prioritizing transparency within your department, really focusing on where costs can be optimized without sacrificing quality. It's amazing how many areas you can find where small efficiencies add up, especially if you invest in a cloud-based monitoring system. That is actually quite useful. We have been considering investing in some software solutions to help with that but doesn’t come cheap. I can understand that. Start by looking at the software that has a free version, or if it’s a service you already use or have done side projects with, try to negotiate a deal just for the project. The idea is to use tech that automates routine tasks, freeing up your time to focus on bigger decisions. That’s a great point. Because often what takes the most time is not the big decisions themselves but the little ones—like tracking every outgo and ensuring there’s a paper trail. Automating that could really help. That truly makes sense. I might need to bring this up with our department head. It might be worth a proposal. And Tom, thanks for the input. It’s really helpful to get a different perspective.

I've decided I need a first aid box. Took me a while; these are moments people usually learn after injuries. Hopefully I don't need it. Right, isn't it? People only think of it after a mishap. Why did you finally decide to get one? I was watching this thing on "You'll Never Believe What's in Your Medicine Cabinet," right? And I realized... I had almost nothing. All I had for cuts was this old weird keepsake bandage and a whole shelf of useless stuff from my parents. Well, that's quite an eye-opener. What's in this fancy new first aid box of yours? Not so fancy, actually. Just the basics. Bandages, antiseptic wipes, some painkillers, that kind of thing. That's wise. You never know how quickly things can go wrong when painting and such. Speaking of which, it's coming together nicely. The old fence really needed it, didn't it? Yeah, it was practically falling on the cars by now. Good thing it's been mostly sunny; the paint's drying quickly. Yeah, it's about time. It sets the whole garden right again, you know? And avoids legal trouble from the council, apparently. I'd heard that if the fence's too rickety, they can fine you. An extra bonus. So, anything else you're planning with this revamp? New plants, perhaps? Well, yeah. I'd like to plant some herbs and maybe one or two trees. The bay tree in front would look good, and it's decent for cooking too, isn't it? Exactly. And useful. I've started getting into cooking more herbal stuff myself. Mrs. Higgins taught me how to infuse oils with thyme for the meat. Ah, that's advanced stuff. I stick to basic but I'm intrigued now. Maybe I'll look into it. Be my guest. Just don't expect it to show up in the next health food delivery ad. Maybe I'll stick to painting next. Did you catch that new sci-fi film with Idris Elba? Yeah, I heard about it. Didn't get a chance to see it yet, but it's on my list... I liked it. Acting was spot on, and the visuals... really made me think about using more atmospheric lighting in these films I've been wanting to make. Really? I'd never pegged you for a movie buff.

Oh, did you see that?? That's definitely not something you see back home every day. It's surreal, isn't it? I mean, we're driving through the Polish countryside in a camper and people are walking, literally walking, alongside the road. And what's with the strawberry fields everywhere? It's like they're just as abundant as those tall, tall trees. I'd almost forgotten what strawberries look like before they're in a shrink-wrapped supermarket container. Yeah, and those fields. It makes me think of the many strawberry picking jobs I did as I was studying. Those were some early years of earning just trying to make ends meet. Ah, yes - "earning" as we call it. On a different note, I've been thinking a lot about money and expenses while we're on this trip. We've barely broken even so far, haven't we? Well, that's the thing about campervan travel. The van itself is a significant upfront cost and the ongoing expenses are stealthy - fuel, camping fees, food. But the fun factor? Priceless. Priceless. Although, let's not kid ourselves, we've made some... interesting social arrangements so far for camping and stuff, to keep costs down. Oh, absolutely. And isn't it fascinating how clear-cut things get when you're travelling and trying to stay frugal? You realize what's truly important and what's just clutter, in life and in luggage. Oh, the luggage part is so true. We've done a mighty fine job of clearing the clutter from the van, hasn't it? At the start, I was tempted to bring every possible little thing I thought we might need. Yes! And it wasn't just about the physical stuff but also mentally. I've been trying to clear out my mind on this trip. Like, who needs all those thoughts about what I should be doing for work or in general for that matter? Mind clutter. That's a great term. It feels like a mini-retreat, minus the actual physical retreat. Speaking of which, I've had a little retreat in clearing out old friendships too. The trip has reminded me who's truly there for me and who's just convenient to keep around. Hmm, I know that feeling. Being honest, this trip has been... a kind of escape for me, away from the constant pressure to be in "work mode" or whatever they call it.

Mum, can I please check my phone? I haven't checked any messages during the drive today. Yeah, sure kiddo. But don't get distracted. We're almost there and we need to make sure we pick up everything we need for dinner tonight. Thanks, Dad. I promise I won't be long. I hope those exams you've been working so hard for weren't too stressful. I've heard this week of actually very good results being out for older students though. Oh that's really reassuring to hear, thanks. I've been a bit worried actually but seeing that, okay. Well, try not to worry too much, we're all rooting for you. And just like the Queen is doing an amazing job ensuring our country's in good hands, you need to ensure your future's in good hands too. Exactly, and it's not just about passing exams, it's about what excites your curiosity. Like the Hay Festival, it's such an inspirational event if you're into books. Maybe next year we can plan a trip there together or even attend some online sessions if there are any this year. That would be amazing. I've heard they often have some fun activities too, right? Yeah absolutely. They often have readings, Q&A sessions, and even workshops where authors share insights. It's a great way to get out of the academic mindset and just enjoy reading for its own sake. And in between book discussions, maybe we can also talk about the past, reminisce about our own childhood. That sounds like a good idea! But weren’t we supposed to visit some shops first? We need food and some other stuff. Yes, absolutely. But the point is, we should balance commerce with culture. As we talk about the past, we can also discuss moving house. We’re considering it at some point. It’s a big move but maybe we can start making arrangements after your exams. Moving house is always a big process especially with all these train strikes happening. I hope next year they sort that out before we make any plans. True, it can complicate travel and so much else. Hopefully, public transport gets sorted out soon. Can’t we pick up something from the supermarket instead of going to many shops? We could, but consider also we want to support local business.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I was trying to learn how to use that computer? I think it was thirty years ago now, the whole family had to help me. Ha! I remember, Mum! You were supposed to book a train online and you ended up calling the station because you thought the computer was broken. I can imagine, Nana! And here I am, teaching kids how to use AI in school. Technology sure has come a long way! Even Siri can order our groceries now. Yes, let’s not go there. Do you remember when we thought video calling was a crazy idea? Now we're on Zoom all day. But it's actually really useful during lockdowns, right? That's right, kiddo! Technology can be a blessing in times like those. Nana, is it okay if we start talking about something else? I’ve got a question for you both. Oh, what’s on your mind? It's about mental health, actually.
