Is depression like a normal thing for people who... who have tough times or does it mean someone’s really sick? That's a very good and tough question, dear. Mental health is real and it's as important as physical health. Everyone has ups and downs, but sometimes our feelings get too big and we might need some extra help to feel better. Being depressed isn't something anyone chooses to be. It can be tough to talk about, but talking about it helps. There's no shame in needing help, just like there's no shame in getting physical therapy if you break your leg. Oh, okay. I thought some people just weren't trying hard enough or something. No, no one sits around wanting to feel sad or worrying all the time. And most definitely, it’s not a sign of weakness to ask for help. Just like if you fell and hurt yourself, you'd go to the doctor, right? Yeah, I get it now. And remember, if you ever feel sad or overwhelmed, you can talk to us. We’re always here to listen and help however we can. Thanks, that means a lot. Of course, kiddo. Always. Groceries, successful train booking, and talking about important stuff. We got that all covered. Hey, what about that big clear-out at my place? Need any help sorting things out?

Right okay so I've got my new laptop plugged in and running. Let's see if it's as good as they say. Are you still using Windows 10? Yeah, this one came with it pre-installed. I kind of like it, but sometimes it gets a bit slow. "Like my old laptop..." Is this better battery-wise? I still use an ancient desktop. It's weird how it still works alongside this shiny new thing. Definitely, this new laptop claims to have a much better battery life. Idk if it's true, we'll have to see. How's your work as an instructor? You must be on your computer a lot - do you think the software and hardware meet your expectations? As much as I love language and tech, sometimes the software can be a creative nightmare! But it's all good, you get used to it. It's like retro technology sometimes - older PCs, you know? For sure! We were talking about retro tech last time. Remember when we found an old Gameboy in the attic? You wanted to know if we could still play games. Yeah! It still works somehow. That's the beauty of retro, right? Exactly, it still 'works', isn't it? Like, really old computers that run Linux from the '90s or something. I'd say, if anything, that's where the real magic is for some people. Customizing ancient hardware and software, like minecraft on an old Commodore or something. I tried, but gardening is more my speed. Speaking of speed, is this thing faster for video editing or YouTube? I've seen yours, really good and fast. That's the plan. With more RAM and a better graphics card, I'm hoping it will perform better on video and some graphics work. Let's say, comparing to my last laptop, this should be a beast. You’ll probably enjoy the software for working out. Did you know you can turn this almost into a smartwatch just with the right apps? I swear, next they'll want us to punch our phones for a work out. Punching a phone? Sure, why not? It’s not like they can... Anyway, I really want to try some of the software for mixed martial arts training. They have these cool 3D models for practicing moves. That sounds useful. So you're going to sparring with your laptop?

Oh, did I mention my first trip's passport was covered in beer spill stains? I talked about that recently. Can you believe how many times I've tried to quit? You know, I've always thought questions like 'Who am I?' are so overrated. But then, you see this bistro, and suddenly, it feels like we're part of a new narrative, right? Oh, I get that completely. You know, alongside dreams about traveling Europe, I used to tell everyone I’d be a fitness guru. Even thought I have about as much discipline for treadmills as I used to have for essays in undergrad. Discipline? What’s that? Exactly. Hence, my biggest dream now is to finally have a consistent exercise routine that involves more than looking for my yoga mat. We’re good people, aren’t we? Dreamers and all. Definitely. For me, it's also about identity and sense of belonging, wherever we are. I think most of us struggle with that, while also trying to stay true to ourselves in a way that often feels contradictory to our surroundings. Well, technology makes it easier to stay connected to friends from all walks of life, right, no matter where we wind up. True, but we’re here, and this bistro feels like it's been plucked from a Somerset village doesn’t it? But it's actually in Poland. And yet, all these design elements and the smell of the food bring us together. It’s strange how familiar things feel when you’re thousands of miles from home. I noticed a lot of foreigners here, professors, students, couple on honeymoon... Because who else but a Brit and a Lancashire lass on a self-discovery trip through Europe would end up in a bistro in Tarnow, right? Perfectly logical. But back to identity, I've realized if anyone asks where I’m from or what I do, most of the time they expect a simple answer. But almost all of us are just as complex and multifaceted as the things we love. I started teaching because I love languages but also because I found solace in being somewhere new almost every month. For me, it's about continuous learning and adaptation more than anything else. We both know our periods of unemployment felt pretty brutal at times, but it also gave us space to really think about what we want.

So, Dad, did you manage to buy the tickets for the Dorset Steam Fair? Yeah, I managed to get them online, though they were selling out very quickly. I thought that might be a good day out for all of us. Especially now that the weather’s supposed to be nice for the rest of the week. Steam engines! Brilliant! I remember seeing one at the Haxey Fair when I was a young lad. And the pride the people there had for those machines! That’s right, it is quite a big event in Dorset. They'll have all sorts of steam engines, fairground rides, and food stalls. I've been there before and I can attest that it is a lovely day out, just like you said. What about the accessibility for Grandma though? I remember last time we went to an event like that she found it a bit difficult with the uneven ground. Ah right, Ron, I know how you're thinking. But the fair actually does provide pretty good access for disabled visitors. They’ve got free parking and there are accessible pathways through most areas, though some of the older stalls can be a bit on the rugged side. But plenty of people with mobility issues go and enjoy it. Plus, if she wants, we can take her wheelchair along. That’s good to know. It’ll be nice for her too, won’t it? And maybe for a change of scenery. Yeah, it’s good that you thought of her. I’ll check if there’s any specific information we should know about the site. And maybe it’s a good idea if I could call ahead and confirm that they have accommodations if she needs the use of a specific area or anything. That’s a thoughtful one, Debbie. Yeah, do that. Seems like the organizers are pretty together in terms of accessibility. I saw they even offer audio descriptions for blind or partially-sighted visitors. Now that's what I’d call looking after everyone. Technology nowadays! I’m glad changing times mean more people are included in having fun. Absolutely, Grandpa. It’s important that everyone can enjoy these events. Alright, well, when are we planning on going? Let’s see...They’re open from 10 to 5, and considering the kids have school and you’re almost back from lectures, Thursday afternoon might be best.

Oh, did I ever tell you about when Dad was attempting to explain the internet to me when it first came around? It was like he was trying to explain rocket science. I can almost imagine it now, Mum. You’d probably been fine before then, right? As if. I'd been fine, just fine. I just didn’t understand why I had to type "www." before every website! Are you serious, Grandma? Oh, yes. And you know, I’ve come a long way since then, dear. I even have a Twitter account now. Though, let’s be honest, I’ve only posted about the lovely sunny day we had last week and a recipe for my famous rhubarb crumble. That’s already more than I thought you’d be interested in, Mum. Technology can be a useful tool. Though, it’s funny - I went to a digital literacy workshop at the church recently. Some people there were practically issuing on computers for the first time. Well, if they’re older than I am, maybe they need some of the patience I had at first. What about those internet reviews people leave on Google? Do you read those before you go to a new place? Oh absolutely. I almost didn’t go to that new restaurant in town because of the bad reviews, but they said they changed their menu and management, so I thought, “Why not?” But it was actually quite good. I do the same if I’m planning a trip or going somewhere new. Though the lack of face-to-face communication bothers me, I have to admit. I once read a glowing review of a place, only to discover it was by someone who clearly has never set foot in North Yorkshire! Accurate critique. Accents aren’t everything, but sometimes I wish reviewers would try to be a bit more specific. Our local artisan shops get such unfair treatment just because they don’t have five stars on Google. What about plans for tonight? I was thinking about perhaps tuning into that new play on the BBC. It has some reviews worth reading. Ah, theatre! The live version beats recordings every time. Though, I heard the local school’s production of “A Christmas Carol” was fantastic. Maybe there’ll be something similar this season. And there’s the local literary festival coming up next month. We could all attend if anyone is interested?

So tell me about your birthday party. You're pretty excited about's it? It's gonna be great! We're having it at our house and talked about whether to invite everyone from school or just a few friends. I'm excited about the cake! You're supposed to get a chocolate cake because it's Easter and you asked for a chocolate cake. Yeah, and then my friend Anon's brother might come. He's actually very cool, and I'd love to have him at the party. That's really nice, sharing your birthday party with friends. By the way, Anon's birthday is not today, is it? No, it's in a few weeks. But we just like to have him over because he's fun to play with. It's wonderful that you make an invitation that flexible. So have you thought about what you want to do? Any games or activities planned? Well, we thought maybe some games outside if the weather's good. And we're going to paint some radishes. Someone gave us these really nice big radishes and they said we could use them for arts and crafts. I'm excited to see how it turns out. Me too! I can't wait to see what the painted radishes will look like. It sounds really fun. That is really imaginative. And do you have a theme for the party or just a general fun gathering? We were thinking maybe a 'Throwback to Childhood' theme, because we're moving into another school year. It’s a bit about growing up and remembering the fun times. I think that's a fantastic idea. How the years are going by so quickly; it seems like just yesterday you were all little and now you're starting to have these bigger celebrations and events. Yeah, and we talked about having a small project for the party that we can all work on together. It will be a nice team-building activity. That sounds like it could be a great bond for all of you. As for Easter chocolate, did you all sort out whose baskets you'll make? We actually thought of making a communal basket. We can take turns hiding chocolates for each other. That way we're all involved and it's a bit like a treasure hunt. And we could write notes of encouragement or just happy messages and put them in as well.

Oh, so I was at work and I had to write this campaign for a new cereal. They wanted something really fun and catchy for children. It ended up being the hardest thing I've done all week. Just imagine all those sugary cereal tag questions designed to lure tiny hands into bad choices. Exactly! It was like “Would you like your breakfast to be tangy or exciting?” Erm, both, probably. “Are you tired of boring breakfasts?” Ugh, most kids don’t even think about breakfast, let alone if it’s boring. It’s like they forget kids under five just want something that’s a bit sweet and crunchy. “Pancake day’s got nothing on us!” As if that even registers with a five-year-old. It’s creative work, but sometimes it feels like a battle to find words that haven’t been overdone. And then, at home, I have to deal with our cute but troublesome cat, Luna. Luna, the most sociable cat who sometimes thinks the couch is her own personal scratching post. Yep. Today, she decided to create a new artwork on our brand new kitchen curtains. I swear, she's got a fascination with fluff. Can you get her to stop? Maybe through some speech and language therapy techniques? “Luna, the intentional redesigning of surfaces is not ideal for living arrangements.” I’ll try that next. No, I just tried the “catnip baseboards” trick that our vet advised. Now she just rubs her head on them and ignores the curtains for a bit. Progress of a sort. Speaking of progress, how’s your day been? Any breakthroughs with Mrs. Jenkins' aphasia? Today was tough. She's getting frustrated because she feels like she can’t express herself the way she wants to. That must be hard for her. It is. But we did have a moment where she managed to communicate a full sentence without any prompting. It was such a small victory but it really lifted her mood. That’s great! Little moments can make such a difference. Definitely. It just reminds me of when we were younger, our mum used to have these intricate handmade puzzles for us from the community center. Remember those? Though, mostly I remember how I'd never be able to put them back together properly. Yes! I always thought I helped but it was probably me who undid a lot of your hard work.

So tell me about that cycle ride. You said you went from Weymouth to Brighton. That’s a heck of a distance! Oh, it was a challenge. But I was quite young, about twelve, I think. My brother and I, and a few friends, we decided to do it on our bikes. I can imagine the adventure. Were your parents supportive? Well, they actually didn't know until we'd almost completed it. We set off early one morning before they'd even woken up, and managed to get about half way before they realised we were gone. You must have been quite a handful. Yes, we were. But we made it back home in one piece, and our parents were more relieved than cross. I had similar escapades when I was younger, didn’t know how to contain the energy. And you’re from Manchester, did you have similar opportunities for such adventures? Yes, we had more urban exploring, but this countryside cycle ride is quite different. I’ve always been amused by how much fun you all still have. You seem so full of life even after all the years and the retired lives. Well, after a life in medicine, especially dentistry, you learn to appreciate the joy in simple things. And now, we all have the time to enjoy them. Speaking of life, Alistair’s experience with the NHS is quite interesting. Like when he said they used to have real perks, weren’t they? Oh yes, like those sea cruises. We’d have these ‘lectures at sea’ which was just an excuse for a jolly. I couldn’t imagine getting away with that now. The public would have a field day. While you’re reminiscing about the old days, I was wondering if any of you have gone on any outlandish trips recently? Like Prague, for instance? Prague, yes! A few years back, Susan and I went on a trip that was meant to be a 5-star show, but turned out to be quite a bargain. We ended up getting this luxury hotel at half the price because of a last-minute cancellation. That’s smart. And what about the city itself? Anything stand out? Oh, definitely. The architecture is incredible. I must admit though, getting into any theatre while fully booked...we had to pull some strings, but it was worth it. I’d love to hear more about the city.

So, I was browsing on LinkedIn yesterday and came across an idea about how social media can be used to enhance social relationships. It was about how people connect more meaningfully using specific strategies rather than just collecting connections. You know how in schools, the ideal is to promote interactive learning and communication? Yeah, absolutely. In my experience as a teacher, the key is to make those connections relevant to the students' lives and interests. But that's easier said than done, right? Exactly. That's why this idea resonated with me. It talked about creating educational content not just as information, but as experiential, relatable material. It could be about using social media platforms as dynamic learning tools. That’s very interesting. Especially with the younger generation, digital platforms are their native language. But how do we ensure it’s educational and not just entertaining? Good question. The article suggested case studies using moving images – videos, interactive content, that sort of thing – to illustrate concepts. Make the content engaging, but also build it around learning objectives. For instance, using video testimonials from real people in real scenarios related to a particular topic. Or even creating educational games or quizzes that push students to think critically but still feel like they're engaging in social media activities. I think that’s brilliant. The educational landscape is shifting so much right now, and if we can align with the way students learn naturally – through social media and interactive content – we might actually be teaching them better. Absolutely. And it isn’t just about the kids; for professional development, corporations are already using video learning platforms and gamification. So why not bring some of that approach into our educational material? True. And it’s not just about the content itself; it’s also about how we structure the interaction around it. For instance, creating online clubs or forums where students can discuss the content, ask questions, and relate it to their own experiences. Exactly. It’s about creating a community around the learning material. We could also develop webinars or live sessions with experts, make them Q&A sessions where students can interact in real-time. Fantastic. What’s the potential for moving images for teaching complex subjects, like history, or even literature? I mean, interpretation of texts can be dry if explored only through reading and writing. Again, using film could be a powerful tool here.

I keep thinking of Rachel and her trip to Cornwall. Remember how she insisted that every wave was like an old friend and how she ended up swimming deep into the sea? Oh, absolutely. It was just so her to get lost in the moment like that. I wonder if she’s still got the sea tarnish on her hair. I'm pretty sure it’s washed off by now. But, talking about the sea... it really can be like old friends, right? You get out there and suddenly all your worries just seem to fade, and you feel a deep connection to the vastness of it all. Definitely. I think there is something inherently soothing about the sea. And the unpredictability of it—it’s like even the calmest days can turn on you in an instant. Reminds us we’re not always in control. True, and yet we keep coming back to it, year after year. And these trips we planned with Tom and Karen—it’s funny, they always talked about how the sea was like a mirror reflecting back who they really were. A moment of clarity or a storm of emotions. I think most of us have that one place by the sea that we return to for the same reason. It’s where we confront things, reflect on life, or just forget whatever’s been troubling us. It’s like a naturally occurring therapy session. Speaking of which, did you see that new study about the psychological benefits of being by the sea? Apparently, the rhythmic sound helps with our brain waves and can even lower perceived stress levels. Makes sense to me. I’ve always found it easier to think things through on a beach or by the coast. Maybe the fact we’re grounded by the sand, but the sea gives a sense of limitless possibilities above it. I once took a group of students to the coast for a couple of days and tasked them with reflecting on their goals. It was incredible to see how much more they could focus and open up in that environment. That's such a great idea. I might steal that for our next retreat. Imagine having a whole session where we sit by the sea, and everyone just reflects. Could be very powerful. We often underestimate the simple and natural things. Just sitting by the sea and watching it can be just as beneficial as any technique I’ve learned in mindfulness and meditation.

Oh, did you see Avril's's Instagram? She just posted that she's getting her hair done for the company dinner tonight. Yeah! I saw that. Is she going with that pink bob she's been wanting? Oh, I kind of like it! It's daring for her usual style. But have you guys noticed how often she matches her glasses to her outfit? Erm, Avril says she “considers eyewear an essential aspect of her attire. It frames her face, defines her style, and, yes, reflects her mood. She wouldn't dream of going out with mismatched glasses!” Perfect! Avril is like a walking fashion statement. Her style’s really evolved from that “Pippi Longstocking without the pigtails” phase we used to joke about. I have to say, she's got a great eye for mixing patterns. Remember that scarf she brought last visit? And her shoes are always so on point. And those boots she wore the other day were amazing! For a moment, I thought it was maybe a new trend, but no, just her own personal taste coming through. I wish I had her confidence. I mean, I love fashion, but I'm more into the comfort side than the statement look sometimes. Ah, but have you thought about perhaps exploring more statement pieces, like a bold necklace or a patterned jacket? It’s really all about finding what makes you feel good, and a little bit of exploration can go a long way! Yeah, that's a great point. I think for me, it would be about finding the right piece that makes me feel instantly put-together without feeling too much of a stretch. Maybe Avril's secret is that she’s just found the right balance for herself. So, any fashion forward plans for this weekend or next? Nothing really concrete yet. I might browse some places in town for a new bag though. I'm feeling like I need something a bit more professional for work – more structured, some nice leather or something like that. Perfect, take me along! And let's plan a little shopping trip with Avril too. Oh, that could be fun. And we should probably plan something bigger – maybe a weekend out somewhere next month or later in the year when we can all get together without work stress? I’d love that. How about we look up some weekend getaways in the UK for next spring?

Mum, I got my photography project back from college today. Oh really? How did it go? You seemed really excited about it. It was fun, but I did struggle a bit. There were quite a few technical things I didn't quite understand. But the teacher said I improved a lot since the beginning of the year. That’s great! Technical things can be tricky, but it’s brilliant you’re improving. Did your classmates like the photos you took? Yeah, some of them were really impressed. But I’m still a bit nervous about presenting my work in front of the class. What if I mess up or trip over my words? It’s only natural to feel nervous. But that’s part of growing up and learning, isn’t it? What’s the worst that could happen? You’ll get a bit embarrassed, that’s all. And even that’s not so bad, it’s an opportunity to learn and try again. You’re right, I suppose. It’s just that fear of failure holds me back sometimes. Well, that fear is quite common. I remember when I was your age, facing this new challenge at university, it was daunting but it helped me grow as a person. Yeah, but this feels different. College is tough, and the work is a lot to handle sometimes. I know. But it’s important to remember why you started, to pursue what interests you. And as for the work, it’s temporary. It eases up as you get more used to it, and the benefits are worth it. That’s encouraging. Mum, doesn’t your job at the reception sometimes feel like too much? It does sometimes, to be honest. But I’ve learned to manage my workload and prioritize. And there are definitely days where it’s more challenging than others, but the people I work with and the job itself are rewarding in different ways. It’s about finding what makes it manageable for you, really. That’s a good way to think about it. I guess my nerves are just part of growing up, though scary sometimes. Exactly! And there’s always laughter to help, right? Have you seen any funny comedian videos lately? Oh, yeah! Who was the last one you watched? There’s this one guy, Olaniyi Olatunde, he’s hilarious! He came on Mock the Week recently.

I seen them muckers last night's match. Looked like they'd lent one of them Jefferies boys a kit they don't fit 'em proper! Oh, isn't that the life, though? You get a fit of the journals and can't just watch the match without nitpicking everything else. But actually, I've been thinking, we need to nail down how we're gonna fill out that application form for the community grant. It's due at the end of the week, and if we fuck it up, there's no second chances. Now, now, let's not go there. What's the big problem with filling out a form? It's not the filling out part. It's the narrative bit. We need to make it sound like a golden opportunity instead of just a... Why don't we tackle this together? You know I'm all for detail, Bob, or as much as one can muster before bed this side of midnight. "Detail" is putting it lightly! Yeah, but he's right. We're good at spin; we can turn a modest gesture into a groundbreaking initiative. You're right. There's no harm in trying to make it sound good. I'm all for making things sound "proper". Just don't make it sound too much like smoke and mirrors... You're always on the lookout for shabby workmanship or less-than-honest dealings. But trust me, the community project we're proposing is good foundations. If it's as good as you say, we just need to get it written in a way that makes it jump out at the reviewers. You know that narrative technique from my literature class? Where you build up to a climax? I wasn't aware we were writing a novel. It's all writing, see? The art of persuasion. You show them why this needs doing, the impact it'll have, and how it's a beacon for the wider community... That's not a bad approach. We can talk it through. But between you and me, we're up against competition from all those other projects... I know what you mean. There's always someone with better credentials or a better story already in place. But we have a unique angle - using the resources we've got in a creative way to make it a win-win for everyone.

Ah, it's's been a while since we've had a decent talk together. How are you, then? You look a bit concerned. Aye, I am. You know, things have been on my mind lately. What's got you down, sweetheart? Is it them kids, work, or just the current state of affairs? Erm, a bit of everything really. But specifically, I've been thinking a lot about Katie. Oh, yes. Your daughter. Has anything new come up with her? Well, I was thinking of bringing her over here to live. You know, to be closer to our side of the family but also for her to get a proper British education. Ah, I see. That's a big decision. It also means she would leave her life there for a little while, right? Yes. But she's getting older now, and I think it's time. She's been so open about missing her grandparents and cousins. I know. You’re thinking of all the positives for her, and that's commendable. Exactly. But it's not just about us. It's also about the studies and ensuring she's comfortable here as well, you know? Absolutely. But have you discussed this with the family and all? What's been the general reaction? Oh, it's been mixed. Some are thrilled, of course, others are a bit skeptical. Mixed reactions. Seems about right for any big change in the family! Exactly. Anyway, I was thinking, given your experience in teaching, you might have some advice on schools around here and what to expect. Ah, I can do that. I've kept up on things even in retirement. Brighton has some excellent schools. I know a few heads personally. That would be incredibly useful. Alright then, what's the plan? Are you thinking of having her boarding or just living here with you? Ah, she's not that old yet. I think just living here. But I'd still need to arrange her schooling here. I see. Well, that's certainly doable. You'd need to look into the admissions process for British schools from abroad. It can be a bit tricky, but I can help with that. That would be a huge help. Of course. And speaking of schools, have you given any thought about her integration process? Making friends, getting used to living here? We have, yes. I suppose that's a bit of a worry, but I hope she'll adapt well.

So, I hear that you've recently had to sit on an interview panel. How'd that go for you? To be honest, it was quite an experience. Hadn't interviewed anyone in many years. It was a bit challenging to get back into it and remind myself of all the dos and don'ts questions you need to ask and so forth. Yeah, it can take a while to get into the swing of things again, especially with all the new equality and diversity guidelines. But did you pick someone suitable for the position? Yeah, we actually found a great candidate. I think it's going to be a really good addition to our team. But it's interesting how the whole selection process has been changed over the years. More emphasis on inclusivity and making sure you're not inadvertently biased in any way. Absolutely, and making sure the invitation to interview is properly checked and that kind of thing. Speaking of which, I had to prep for a job interview myself recently. It was very different from the ones I used to do as an academic. Oh, how so? Well, the questions were much more firmly centered around real-world application of concepts. It wasn't just about showing off theoretical knowledge anymore. I found myself having to think through how certain subjects I study could actually be applied in a practical setting in a way that I hadn't before. Yeah, that's a good sign, really. It's about seeing whether the academic work you do has real-world impact. Speaking of practicality, my daughter has just learned how to ride a bike without stabilisers. She's so proud of herself, but it also got me thinking about how I could apply some of the principles of learning and motivation from my teaching to help her through different challenges. That's terrific! Learning to ride a bike without the extra wheels is always a milestone for kids. How did you help her with the process of learning? Well, it's mainly about building confidence, isn't it? So, I encouraged her, praised her and she got to pick out her first helmet herself. You know, these small things can really make a difference. Definitely. Positive reinforcement and independence - two powerful tools. Funny how those principles apply across different domains. Exactly! And now that we're here in your home, let's talk about something else.

Right okay so I think what we need to do is first move these pieces apart so we can actually see how this whole thing works. Right, sounds good. You mean the game isn't working because it's all stuck together, huh? Exactly because if it was easier to put together, they probably wouldn't make a game out of it. Okay, it says here we need to turn it upside down and slowly pull apart these two pieces... Remember when we tried that and it just flew off the table? Oh, I suppose we could say we're testing the game from all angles! What's that about being a chef and living in the States? Does it really make a difference being there compared to here? Oh, absolutely. The mentality around food is completely different in the US. There's a lot more of an emphasis on portion sizes and convenience foods. For me, it was the amount of fast food places. It's everywhere, even in smaller towns. Where did you work, while you were there? I was at a few restaurants in New York, mostly fine dining places. The techniques were different, and they relied more on pre-made sauces and stocks whereas here, especially in smaller, more traditional restaurants, you make a lot of things from scratch. So, American children—they must love that, right? Like a dream come true? Kind of, but you kind of grow out of it quick. And then you realize, oh, actually, I miss the different types of food here. More spice in the food, you know? I noticed a lot of kids there love burgers and fries but were quite adventurous with other types of fast food and desserts. They'd have entire meals of desserts! It’s like a different world. Education for kids is also quite different. More focus on standardized testing, sports are huge, and so much influence of media on children's preferences and interests. Speaking of media, what’s it like watching those kids’ shows? Like, do they have the same TV here? Yeah, some things are similar, but there’s a lot more screen time across the board. And the ads! Always selling something, even to kids. But it’s interesting how certain shows and characters can be like celebrities there. We had some extended family visit when I was living in LA, and the kids were glued to the TV watching like these reality shows and YouTube videos that were basically just people watching themselves play video games.

Oh, did I buy a lot or what? I was just today in the shopping mall and ended up picking up a few things I've been eyeing for a while. Ah, so you're now officially the household goddess of shopping! Why am I not surprised? Between us, you could start a boutique and fill it with your purchases. Now, why do I sense a hint of accusation there? All in good spirit, I assure you! I thought I needed a new summer dress for our trip to Spain and while I was at it, I couldn't resist buying a few tops to match. Spain, huh? That's exciting! So what's the scoop on the clothes? Show me what you've got! Okay, alright! Let's start with the dress. This one——it's a light, pastel blue sundress. I thought it would be perfect for strolling through the Spanish towns or perhaps a dressier evening on the beach. Very nice! The color is nice and subtle. It'll match most of your accessories too, right? Exactly! And the material is lightweight and breathable. I also bought a couple of tops. This one is a nice cotton blouse perfect for layering under, say, a light windbreaker in the evenings. And this white blouse? You already have five of those. But it's different from the others! It has this cute, delicate embroidery around the collar and it's slightly more structured. Plus, who doesn't need another white blouse? It's like the basic pillar of any wardrobe! So, next up, you'll be buying a new white blouse every time we go on holiday because it's essential to the "trip wardrobe". Well, I wasn't planning on it. But, alright, so I also got this yellow top . It's bold and definitely for when I want to feel sunny and vibrant. Clearly, you're preparing for a spectrum of emotions during the trip. Exactly! You need appropriate attire for all those sunsets and tapas bars. I see. And don't forget the black power suit for when we have a serious conversation about the meaning of life over a glass of wine. Oh, you're just trying to get out of shopping with me, aren't you? Maybe successful lecturing isn't just about wise words and theories, but also about mastering the art of shopping as a strategy of marital harmony.

So, James, did you manage to catch the Aviva Premiership match between Exeter and Bristol? Oh yeah, it was a great match, Dad. Exeter won, 34 to 21. Right at the end, Exeter broke through and scored the try, but the real excitement was when Bristol's player, Henry Stretton, made that amazing sprint and almost caught up with the Exeter winger! And here I am with no idea what's happening! Ah, but you get to see the excitement on our faces! Rugby's a bit like family to us in this house – always engaging, always unpredictable. Yeah, it's great. Though, let me tell you, even though Exeter was the underdog, they really pulled through. The way the forwards worked together was brilliant! It's all about teamwork, isn't it? Just like in school, when you're all working together towards a common goal. Exactly. And speaking of which, speaking of joining a team, Oisin, how about we sign up for that junior sports team next term when you’re back at school? Oh, we can't have the poor boy missing out on his rugby adventure just yet! Though maybe tag rugby or something similar? Less injury, more fun. Yeah, definitely tag rugby. And maybe cricket too? I started learning a bit about cricket last year, and it's quite fun. There you go. Just like finding the right kind of game that suits each of you. Maybe even football for a bit. It's all about trying things together as a family and seeing what sticks. Right! So, Oisin, when we head up to the backyard later for some stargazing after dinner and cake, maybe we can talk a bit about sports and dream up some fun things to do together after school. And in the meantime, let’s make sure we’re all set for bed after our little celebration later. I might need all the help I can get to get Oisin to bed on time after all the excitement today. Yeah, definitely! And guess what I learned from the rugby match? There's a little thing called visualization where players imagine the game before it happens to perform better. Maybe we can try some of that for sports practice! Now you’re talking about joining the sports team... I like the sound of that visualizing thing. Maybe we can all give it a go?

Right okay so I'm going to have another one? Really? On the road already? Yeah. Hopefully this one is more talked about than the first, you know. You were right though, it is really nice to have the other one, the breaks, the time together – but man, two is kind of overwhelming. But in a good way? Or a "oh my god" way? Both actually. I mean, I love them both so much and it’s so rewarding but... physically, mentally, it's tiring. I had such lazy weekends last year with your first one. Birch Street's closest park was our go-to. Is that still something you're up for? As much as my village now has a whole "Birch Street recreation area?" Yes, definitely. We want to get into a routine of going out, as much as it can be unpredictable. Plus, the fresh air is good for both of them. And it's funny because it's so far removed from the sterile, controlled environment or even just the... academic world? I’m really trying to keep that sense of play and learning through all their curiosity. That'll be great, I think. My niece loves parks so much. Stills at that age where everything is fascinating, right? Well, they keep you on your toes, but yes, fascinating. A couple weeks ago, we were at the park and she kept pointing at all the leaves saying “leaf!” “leaf!” It’s all about the simple stuff and they just can't get enough of it. I remember those "minute-to-minute adventures" phase. When did she start speaking? I don't remember teaching her languages during your PhD or was that side of things? Oh yeah, she started babbling really early but actually saying words around 18 months. She’s picking up quite a bit from my own projects, really. There’s a slight bias towards English first but she'll say words in both languages sometimes and we do little games or songs. That's so cool! I used to try with my siblings but it's tough, isn't it? And mixing them up all the time. It is, but it’s so good for those little brains. And almost unintentionally, just being around the research helps. She watches with great interest. I started reading her languages stuff even. She still doesn’t understand much

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new board game from's called Anon. Seems like a cool concept. Yeah, I've talked to someone who played it and said it's a right brain teaser! Mind if I ask you something though? Sure, fire away questions. You've studied linguistics, right? I'm trying to get into accent and dialect work but I'm not sure how to approach it professionally as an English language instructor. Any tips? For sure! As a linguist, it's always fascinating to study dialects. Accents, though, are more about phonetics. I recommend enrolling in some courses that focus on phonological variation or even just starting by listening avidly to different accents and dialects. Plus, apps like "Sounds of the UK" can be a great starting point. And if you want to mix fun with your research, try out certain TV shows or podcasts known for featuring various regional accents, like The Archers. Cool, that's really useful! And you're into guitar, right? I was thinking of buying a new one, any recommendations or even tips on playing techniques that aren’t common? Totally, I’ve been playing for years. Honestly, most guitar techniques aren't that hard to pick up once you get past the initial learning curve. It’s all about dedication and practice, really. For a new guitar, look into solid-body electrics for versatility if you want to experiment with different styles. As for techniques, hybrid picking is one that can give you a distinct sound if you're into acoustic or folk styles, and if you're into something a bit more complex, learn some basic fingerstyle patterns. True that. I’ve been picking up MMA lately; finding it a great way to clear my head and stay active. Any combat sports in your day, or just for fun? Nah, I stick to keep-fit for me. But I’ve seen your stuff on socials, solid movements there! Just remember, regardless of the sport, protecting yourself is key. While you’re dealing with the physical stuff, are you on top of your personal protective measures like insurance or advanced first aid knowledge? Yeah, for sure. I have a rough first aid kit always handy and I keep my travel insurance up to date if I’m going to a new place for a show. That’s smart. I should probably look into that as well for my travels.

I've decided I need a first car. Dad was telling me today that you lent your car to Alex for his driving test practise. Oh yeah, that was last week. I need to make sure he gets back on the road now, though—he's supposed to have passed by now if everything went smoothly. What kind of car was it? Mine's going to be a used one, I think, just to save some money. It was my old Ford Focus. Bit of an old banger now, but it still runs fine. Yeah, okay. But I mean, have you had to pay for any expensive maintenance on it or have any big issues? Well, among other issues, we did have to replace the gearbox once—ended up making me a bit lighter in the wallet—but apart from that, it's been quite reliable. The biggest issue at the moment is the MOT, which is due in a few months. So you think it's still worth me getting a used car? Absolutely. New cars depreciate so rapidly, it's ridiculous. Plus, for learning, it doesn’t matter as much because you're most likely going to pick up a few scratches and whatnot. If it’s reliable, that’s the main thing. So, what tips do you have for buying a used car then? Make sure to take it for a spin before making any decisions, obviously, and if possible, take it to a garage to get a pre-purchase inspection done. That makes sense. I've also thought it might be worth considering the running costs—petrol, insurance, etc. Yes, absolutely. Some cars have surprisingly different fuel efficiency or insurance premiums, so those are all important to check. You want to keep those costs as low as possible while also getting a reliable car. And insurance? There are some companies that offer discounts for new drivers, so shop around. We could sit together later and look through some quotes online. Don’t make any rash decisions but also don’t wait for too long. If you're going to buy, it’s best to do it soon so you can start practising. Alright, great, thanks. You could even maybe help me pick it out if you’re free over the weekend? I’d be happy to. Do you have a budget in mind yet or any particular make/model you’re interested in?

Oh, Brenda, I haven't seen that look on your face for years; it's like seeing Jeannie and Joe again when they first moved back to Hull! Grandma isn't going to believe this! Oh, dear! You two and your inventions! Ah, socialism at play again, I see. Erm, Brenda and Joe, we can't even get keepsakes right. Remember when Joe would bring home these... odd items from his travels, and you'd create entire stories around them? Yes, he brought back this tiny, hand-carved stone from India, and you insisted it brought good luck in exams! And the time he came back with a small, old compass and said you were going to navigate us to success in life? And then there was that big, empty jug from the travel expo. You said it was for achieving "full potential"—as long as you filled it with whatever you were striving for. Now that was a busy jug! Right, right. Well, seeing as they're visiting this time around, can I help make arrangements? Maybe we can serve some of that famous fish and chips Brenda insists on? Ooh, that'd be lovely, Barbara! But don't go putting in all that work. They're here to enjoy us, not to be waited on hand and foot. Yeah, but doesn't Granny love when it's a proper "do"? Let's not burden them with too much "do," though. They're not here for a feast in the kitchen. True. Okay, how about just tea and sandwiches? We can sit in the garden if the weather's good. And maybe some cake? That sounds perfect. And Joe, I hope you aren't planning anything too strenuous. You know how that finishes you off for days. Ah, Brenda, you're as coddling as ever! Just making sure health and happiness go hand in hand. Now, shall we set the garden table? Go on, you two, I'll be there soon. Oh, something else. I found this old photo album during their last visit. Maybe it's time to show it around. Oh, I remember when we found the old family photos at Grandma's last time! That was a good day. Seeing them laugh and reminisce was... it was like seeing our own youth come alive again. Bringing out the old suitcases of memories. Mmm, that would be nice. Yeah, why don't you set a side table with the album and some tea so when they come, there's something to sit and chat over?

Alright so I heard you've been banging on about pirates today. What's got you so excited about them? I talked about pirates in the playground and we thought that they're really cool. Yeah because they have treasure and swords and a kind of secret life on the sea. And they say "Arrrr". I see, and what about eating? Were you good about eating your dinner today? Yes, I had my peas and carrots, and Mum said I was good because I ate everything. And I had sausages. They were tasty. So what about the Shakespeare week? You're going to Stratford soon, right? That's correct. We're planning a family day out there next week. It'll be fun! They have lots of activities, plays, and workshops. Plays? Like in a theatre? Will we see real actors? Exactly! And you might even get to take part in a workshop. I'm hoping they'll have some fun activities for you both. That would be so exciting! And while we're on the subject of fun activities, you know about the circus workshop we're also going to? Yes! Ah, in a real circus? A real big one, like in a tent? Indeed! You'll learn about balancing, juggling, and all sorts of circus tricks. Okay, it sounds... big. I hope I can do it. I'm sure you'll be great! And then there's Easter, right? Did you enjoy the Easter egg hunt? Oh yes, we had a lovely time. It was nice to see you both dive in to find all the eggs and enjoy some treats. I found the most eggs! I must have four or five! I found two! But they were chocolate ones and very yummy. That's the most important part! You did great. On a different note, have either of you been into magic lately? Perhaps done some simple tricks? Magic? Like with cards or pulling rabbits out of hats? Exactly like that. And while that's... a bit advanced, maybe we could look into some beginner magic tricks for you two. Really? Can we learn how to make things disappear? Yes, disappear! I'd like to try. Alright, that could be quite the project for us. Maybe for the next family fun afternoon. Also, I've been interested in animation lately, especially stop-motion. It's quite involved, but it could be another fun project.

I've got an incredible story to share. It's from when I was teaching in Saudi Arabia and decided to sail my boat from Jeddah to Cyprus. You're kidding right? Was this the time they thought the boat was a vessel of... trouble? Yes! Indeed, it was. I've always been a bit of a adventurer, and this was right up my alley. And how did that turn out? Of course, I read up on all the necessary permissions, but apparently, "necessary" and "enough" have entirely different meanings in certain cultures. So, you didn't know you were in a bit of a pickle, eh? Oh, not at all! I was all set. I even took a few weeks to prepare, soaking up advice from local sailors who had done similar voyages but, as it turned out, the knowledge doesn't always translate. Go on, Susan. You know we're all ears - or should I say, whatever extent our ears have at this stage? Well, I set off one morning before dawn. The boat, as I said, was small but fantastic for the open waters. I must've been about 100 miles offshore when... the Saudi Coast Guard showed up. The Coast Guard? More like a whole naval fleet. They thought, for some reason, that I was attempting to transport alcohol. Which, let me clarify, I was not. From Jeddah to Cyprus on a sailboat. With no large amounts of alcohol anywhere nearby. The irony would be sublime if not for the fact that you just got arrested for, essentially, sailing too enthusiastically. Exactly! They were concerned because they could have saved me from myself... but also because of the general... paranoia around anything that smells like adventure and freedom in that part of the world. Did they suspect you were smuggling? Smuggling what? I had more dental magazines on board than... than I can explain. Oh, Susan, the dental magazines now become the most logical cargo to inspect! Yes, well, it seems that, in my preparations, I also made sure to pack every dental journal I could find. For successful cross-cultural communication, you know how it is. I can only imagine the interrogation.

I've decided I need a new bathroom. The current one just can't handle how many showers we all take at once. Oh, that sounds like quite an ordeal. You know, we're lucky. I've heard of Istria first from Jamie Oliver. He has this show; every episode is about exploring food around the world. He was amazed by the truffles here, and of course, the seafood. Right, mum? Yeah, I've read a bit about that. Stem cell therapy; it's potentially very groundbreaking. Although I worry, like all new medical advances, about access and affordability for everyone.

So, I hear that Cambridge University Press is working on an exciting new online linguistic tool. Is that right? Yes, we've been deep into development for a few months now. The main goal is to create a comprehensive platform for language learners and researchers to explore the nuances of modern language usage – dialects, syntax, everything. Wow, that sounds fascinating! The hope is to provide not just information, but personalized support in language learning. Imagine an AI assistant that can offer real-time feedback on pronunciation or grammar! Cool! I can already see the implications in our research. It must be challenging to balance accuracy with what's feasible to implement given the nuances of language study. Definitely, and keeping it user-friendly while still containing depth is a tall order. But I think your team is up for the challenge! How are you planning to validate the tool's usefulness? We're partnering with language departments for beta testing. Also, we’re planning a focus group with language learners and researchers to gather feedback before the official launch. That’s smart. I often find that tools like these need continuous user-centric development. Any plans for the future? Genius! An open-source community might achieve something truly revolutionary. Have you taken into consideration the likely criticism from purists that such a tool might dumb down the study of linguistics? Absolutely, and we're actually planning to address that in our initial user guide and ongoing support forums. The idea is to clarify the blurred lines between language learning for practical communication and academic research. That's wise. It's about making the tool accessible and respectful to both audiences. I look forward to seeing where this goes. Me too! I might try to get involved in the beta testing. Maybe for my own language learning, but it'd also be invaluable for our own project assistant role. Definitely consider that. We're aiming for a strong theoretical base with the tool. It could be very beneficial for anyone working in language-related projects.

Right okay so I think this should be it. Yeah I'd hate to leave too early or too late. Right exactly. It's supposed to be tea and cake by around two. I've been meaning to ask you, have you seen these McDonald's adverts? Which ones? The ones with various football teams. Yeah, it's quite the thing, isn't it? That's a great point.

Bro, so I was at the station's ticket office today trying to book a train for a day trip to London and.... What happened? You don't usually need help with that. So, how was your school day today? Did anything particularly exciting happen? It was pretty standard to be honest. Science was okay, though the teacher told a particularly bad joke. Oh, so you're saying you think's Dad's religion is like the Matrix? Exactly! He’s still figuring out his reality right now—like which button to press and why.
