I wonder, though, have you given much thought to potential locations? As you know, for a project like this, location can be as much about the feel and convenience for patients and families as it is about logistical considerations. I have looked at a few possibilities. The team assumed we might build on an existing healthcare estate, but given the need for substantial redevelopment to meet modern standards, we're also considering the possibility of a new-build site. Of course, location would need to be as accessible as possible, ideally with public transport links and adequate parking. Accessibility is key, especially for those who are less mobile. And with the current focus on community care, ease of access might also involve considering locations where the project could also serve as a hub for community care services. Precisely. I was planning to speak with a few estate agents who specialize in healthcare sites to get a better understanding of what might be available. I'd like to request a meeting with them as soon as possible to get a sense of the market and what's feasible in terms of cost and planning permissions. Definitely. We should also involve our clinical leads in the location decision to ensure it supports the best possible care models. Our vision for this hospice is not just about providing a structure but truly enhancing the care experience at the end of life.

Oh look at this one! You and your Dad have changed so little over the years aside from more grey hair! Well, the gray is a testament to life experience. You know, one of our neighbors at the Royal Ascot this year was a kind of peculiar man, his name was Mr. Pendleton. Mr. Pendleton? I’ve heard of him! He’s always so formal and proper right? Exactly! But he’s also quite kind and has an interesting history. Apparently, he was a jockey in his youth before he went into business. His love for horses led him to become quite an enthusiast and a fan of the Royal Ascot event each year. Yes, and he was very generous with food and drinks, but of course, always keeping up the old world etiquette. Speaking of Royal Ascot, did either of you go again this year? No, unfortunately, the department had too many things on at once. But it seems like a grand time every year. I hope next year we can all go together. We could have a gathering and make it a family event! That would be lovely. You’re always so great at planning things like that. Indeed, but even planning things to the core, can't help the unpredictability of some days at work. I know right, especially dealing with patients as a nurse in these times... really keeps you on your toes. That must be so challenging. It is, but helping people is incredibly rewarding. Though sometimes I wish there were easier ways to manage some tasks. Do you have any recommendations for phone accessories or apps that can help streamline some of those side of things? Oh, I've always been a fan of certain productivity apps like Todoist and Freedom. For organizing tasks and minimizing distractions respectively. Freedom from what exactly, the internet or productivity? Both, depending on the day! I’ll give those a look. Sometimes I find myself just replying to messages or checking emails when I should be focused on writing up reports or addressing some of the more pressing patient needs. I know the struggle. Even as a copywriter, sometimes I get sucked into social media when I should be writing. Well, I can't speak for myself. For me, it's usually company updates and interdepartmental communications that are the most chaotic to keep up with. Well, we're all just trying to do our best in our separate chaos, I suppose.

Oh my God I swear if you move any closer to that possessed camera again I swear I'm gonna jump out the seat. You'd better not, I need your opinion on this one. I mean it just panned out, like a real human being panned out! That totally felt like they sneaked into real footage, didn't it? I'm pretty sure right at the start when... no, don't tell me if it was real or not... You'll just have to see, darling! But yeah, have you noticed how much more terrifying the old classics are despite their simplicity? I mean, just the silence and the edits make you jump. Exactly! Dialogue or music can totally ruin the tension. I prefer when it's just... okay, so the other day I watched 'The Exorcist' again, and the bit where the priest says, "That's not your daughter speaking," it's like... it gets me every time. So true! But have you ever tried watching a really good scary film and then immediately after, watching a cheesy one? I find the juxtaposition is just hilarious and makes me appreciate the 'good' ones more. Like, 'What a Fish Takes' wasn't exactly the scariest thing I've ever seen, but it was so over-the-top it was laughable next to 'The Exorcist'. Oh, for sure! It's funny how the '70s and '80s horror can't even compete with today's special effects in terms of visuals, but the atmosphere and storytelling often make it much scarier. Except, have you seen that new one... 'A Quiet Place'? That's one of the most tense films I've seen in ages, and it's got minimal dialogue and effects. Oh my god, 'A Quiet Place' is next on my watch list and honestly, it's all over social media for a reason. It's scary on a completely different level because it's not just jump scares, it’s psychological. I'm intrigued by how they handle the sound – it’s silence, but it so much more. Right? Because the lack of sound makes every tiny little noise, like a twig snapping or someone breathing... it's just so unsettling. And the monster design is so minimalist and terrifying because you can’t even see it properly until the end – but then it’s too late. So, have you ever thought of making a creepy film marathon?

Right okay so I think I've got everything for Grandma's's online shopping ready. Yeah that sounds about right. I don't know much about these modern gadgets but I trust you to handle it. What did you pick for her? Well, I got her a new tablet because her kindle was starting to lag and it was hard for her to use. I've set up a iPad Mini for her, and I'm planning to show her how to use it before Christmas. That's thoughtful of you. Are you still using Airbnb for our Devon trip this summer? I thought those places were a good deal. Yes, I am. I've been scouting around and I found a lovely cottage that fits all of our requirements. And the places from before, the pizza shop and the café? Oh yes. I made a table with all the places we'd like to go back to. The pizza place, the bakery, the bookstore, all the usuals. Maybe we can even try that new Italian place on the high street. Sounds good. Hopefully, the weather will be better than it was last year. Absolutely. And I'm also thinking of ordering some of that great Devon ice cream. You know, the kind with the clotted cream and strawberries? Ah, that sounds lovely. And what about furniture? Ah, the armchair you were thinking of buying Grandma, did you manage to find a good one? Yes, yes, actually. I couldn't resist adding it to the "cart" when I saw how comfortable it looked in the picture. It's supposed to be the best for support and ease of use. Good, good. Maybe I'll try sitting in it too. Of course, you will. Now, speaking of foundations, have you managed to sort out those emails to all the relatives about the trip? Ah, yeah, but I'm a bit of a dinosaur when it comes to this stuff. Can you double-check them for me? Sure thing. I can look over them. Just give me a minute. And speaking of checking, how's the bedtime routine going for everyone? You know, tablets away and all that. Yeah, well, we've been trying harder. The kids have been good. I started reading to them before bed. It seems to help them wind down. That's a great idea. When I was a boy, my mother did the same thing.

So, I've been meaning to catch up on some non-fiction. I have these two mammoth books lent from you, Alex. The one on the history of Scotland and the other comprehensive guide to tea-farming around the world. Ha! I remember, the latter, I was kind of obsessed with after a trip to Assam and Darjeeling. It was fascinating to learn about the whole process, from plucking to packing. Absolutely. I was amazed by how different regions can yield such varied flavours despite using the same plant. You know, alongside this, I've been exploring some literary fiction too, but that Scotland history one you spoke highly of – I'm finding it quite engrossing. Oh yes, Neil Oliver's "A History of Scotland". It was as much about readying the battlefield for my study trip to the Borders last year as well as broadening my knowledge. It's wonderful how certain histories can feel so relevant to where you live and yet, be so challenging to grasp fully. Absolutely, that same feeling when I travel. There's a book or two for every place that sparks something within or even changes perspective. Now that I'm looking to travel a bit more, I'm revisiting travelogues. Have you read "In Patagonia" by Bruce Chatwin lately? Not recently, but that one has always been hauntingly beautiful, hasn't it? Especially the way he builds narratives around place and identity, quite unique. I tore through it as an undergrad. It's that kind of writing that makes you feel like you're travelling alongside the author, experiencing the land through their eyes. I've been thinking, since we're both into it now, maybe we can plan a trip together? Just friends and our books, no agenda. Sounds like a plan. Say, the Hebrides in the spring? I’ve been meaning to check out the new visitor centres on Lewis and Harris. Oh, that would be perfect. All those beaches, and then there’s always the chance to see some changing landscapes. Accommodations could be an Airbnb or a small lodge. We can make it a book club trip in disguise, say? I’m all for it. As long as we leave room for exploring, of course. Definitely, and maybe even squeeze in some tea tasting at a local farm. We could also do a ‘reading and ruins’ tour – visit places mentioned in the book, or any historical sight.

Mum, I've been going over my resume for this architect position I've been wanting to apply for. Oh, sweetie, that sounds exciting. What's the company and the role? It's at Wright & Marks. They do a lot of urban renewal projects – something I've always been interested in. I remember you and dad talking about that a lot when you were doing your postgrad. It's great to see you pursuing your passion. Thanks, Mum. But I'm a bit worried. This is a pretty competitive field, and I don't know if my experience is enough. Well, let's go over your resume together. I think you have more relevant experience than you think. You even interned with them during your studies, didn't you? Yes, but that was ages ago. And since then, I've mainly done private projects. Still valuable experience. But you also worked on several community projects, which I think speaks well to your dedication to urban renewal. That's true, but I never highlighted those much. Oh, that changes everything. You need to make those front and center. Emphasize your commitment to sustainable and community-focused architecture. Okay, good idea. I'll do that. And consider rewriting your cover letter to directly tie your experiences to the company's mission and vision. It shows you did your research. I will. Thank you, Mum. One more thing, the job also mentions a portfolio. And to be honest, I haven't kept mine updated. Oh no! Your portfolio needs to shine. Start working on that ASAP. You have some terrific projects you can include. And make sure it's less about just the technical drawings and more about your thought process, the project's impact, and what it means to you. Thanks, Mum. That's really helpful. Always here to help you, my dear. You've always been good at making things visually appealing, so I'm sure you'll create a fantastic portfolio. I'll start on both tonight. And don't be afraid to show your real passion in your cover letter. Being genuinely enthusiastic can make a big difference. I'll keep that in mind. And if you need any more help with the application or anything else, don't hesitate to ask. I really appreciate that, Mum. I know it's not just about filling out a form but really standing out from others.

Ah, welcome to my house, it's been ages! We've missed you so. How've you been? Oh, I've been alright, thanks for asking. Got my daily routine down pat. Still enjoying my retirement really. Yeah, retirement’s been treating me well too. Especially when the weather allows for a nice walk and a cup of tea in the garden. It's always lovely catching up with you two. Now, shall I put the kettle on and set up for some scones and keepsakes? Scones sound lovely! I do miss your cooking. Your scones have always been the best. And I’ve been wanting to check in on what’s new with you. How is your back, by the way? Still in good shape from all those years working as a civil engineer? Back’s been a bit dodgy, but it’ll do. Still serviceable! Fire away with the stories, mate! And tell us about your newest carpentry project. Someone said you’d taken up woodworking in your retirement. Oh yes! That’s been keeping me busy. Made a new kitchen unit for the gardening shed. Bit of a challenge but very satisfying. I’ve also been going on about the local politics; the new housing plans and how it’s affecting our area. They’re talking about building a high street development near my old road. That’s always a worry, isn’t it? I’m still in shock at the price of buying even a small house these days, much less renting. I know what you mean. The younger folk are getting squeezed out. I’ve heard they’re planning on building more social housing, but until that all happens... That's right. Seems like the young ones are in as much a bind with housing as we were when we were looking to set up our first homes. Different times, but the worries remain. We really should be supporting local initiatives to help with accommodation for people. You know, community-led schemes and such. True. I’ve seen some good work done in these areas. But often it feels like bureaucracy gets in the way. Can we do anything realistically to change that? Or is it just something we have to be aware of and maybe try and influence in our small ways? There’s always voting and supporting local representatives who prioritize affordable housing. Even if it feels small, it all adds up.

Right okay so I think what we might want to discuss first is the upcoming conversion of our spare space. As you know, we're thinking about turning it into a co-working area but we need to make sure it's done right. A co-working space? That's a great idea! We could really use the extra income. Do we have any plans on how we want to set it out? Not yet, but I'm suggesting we have a meeting with some designers to get their input. They can help us create a space that is functional and appealing, something that will attract potential users. That makes sense. I've seen a few co-working spaces in Manchester, some of them are really well done. We should definitely highlight the unique aspect of our location. Everyone seems to love the vibe of Brixton. Exactly. And we have to consider how we're going to market this new space. Perhaps we can partner with some local businesses or artists to attract artists or freelancers? What do you think? That sounds like a good start. We could also use social media and reach out to business networks. But we also need to make sure it's affordable for potential users, both in terms of membership and cost of the space itself. Affordability will be key. We can think about different pricing tiers and perhaps offer package deals or discounts for early sign-up. Speaking of packages, have we thought about what activities we want to take place in this co-working space in addition to just having desks and chairs? For example, maybe weekly networking events, workshops, and so on? Yes, definitely. It's not just about providing desk space; we need to offer value beyond that. Events, mentorship programs, and maybe some sessions on marketing or branding could be great. That could be very beneficial for the tenants/users. I noticed we have quite a few artists among our existing tenants. Perhaps we can have some art exhibitions or even sell art in the space? That's a brilliant idea. As for our existing tenants and users, how's the relationship with them? I know there’s been some concerns about noise levels. Well, it’s been mixed. Some have been very understanding, but we did have a bit of a problem with one tenant who wanted to start a music practice space.

Oh, did I ever tell you about the time I made my own haggis? Not that I remember. Well, it was horrendous. I almost set the pan on fire! Oh no! What happened? Did you use a wrong recipe? Yes! I used a wrong recipe of course. Now, don't laugh, but it involved very traditional materials... Oh let me guess... Sheep's lungs, liver, and all? Exactly! But I got the measurement very wrong. Everything boiled over and then the pan caught on fire. You really tried to make haggis from scratch? It's all about authenticity, I suppose. It was a fun experience though, even if it was disastrous. Well, at least it was an adventurous cooking moment! I'm just glad no one was hurt, that's the main thing. I assumed we'd have Chef Gareth here providing some authentic dishes for us. Gareth, why don't you tell them about your first culinary adventure? Ah, yes! Well, my first cooking experiment was at age 8. I tried baking a cake without reading the recipe properly. And… It was edible! It was like a big, dense, brownie-like thing. But the point is, no one got hurt, and it was fun. Family bonding over baking disasters, eh? All right, enough of our failures. What about future arrangements? Are we planning any food-related activities soon? Like, next week? I thought we could maybe make sure we do some local food tours here in Hereford. That sounds like fun! And maybe we could include a brewery or two. Or even a farm visit. Getting almost all of our produce locally has been such a wonderful change. I’ll make sure to send some of the older recipes from the local community. Someone said they still make a particular cake that I just have to learn. Cooking together could be a great activity too. Maybe a big meal where everyone contributes a dish. Why not have a cook-off? We each bring one guest dish, and then we vote on who’s the best chef among us. You know, Gareth, why don’t you plan all that? You’re the only chef here, after all! Alright, I’ll see what I can do. It’ll be fun, but I warn you, the pressure will be on! And I’ll contribute my haggis-making expertise… It might just be the pièce de résistance.

So, I hear you took a trip up to Newcastle last year's holidays. How'd you like it? It was great! The city's so different compared to where I'm from. The grey of the buildings, the sound of Geordie accents, the old, rich history... it was something else. I could imagine! Speaking of accents, have you noticed how accent and dialect links us to where we're from and can actually influence where we move or settle, eh? Absolutely! You know, growing up in Harpenden, Hertfordshire, we had all sorts of accents filtering in. I have to say, I've always had a bit of a soft spot for the North Eastern accent. It just sounds down to earth. Agree on that! Though I feel like my own accent sometimes gets misplaced. Working in London, sometimes it's like people can't quite place the North in my voice. You should embrace it, though. It's part of your history and heritage. Plus, it's got a toughness to it - something I really like about the North. I know this is a bit side-tracked from cities and holidays, but speaking of heritage... the food! Seafood specifically. I assumed Newcastle would be all about fish but it's the entire North’s seafood culture that's so rich, right? Yeah, it's amazing. The fish and chips, the seafood chowder... even the mere idea of 'crab sticks' in Britain originated as a Northern thing based off scotch eggs, I read. No way! That's fascinating! I would totally chow down on some great seafood now. You should try it, next time you're up there. More reason for another trip up north! Now, speaking of future trips... are you free next month around Christmas time? We could head up to Durham and have some proper Northern Christmas celebrations. That sounds great! I actually have a week off in late December. You'd really like Durham, by the way. The cathedral, the university buildings... it's magical during winter. Perfect, let me suggest we plan it better on one of the weekends we're both free. Good idea. Also, you interested in driving or going by train? We could drive up if I can convince Simon to lend me his car. He'd probably love a break from it. Otherwise, train would be quick and easy. You could even book a rail+car bundle.

So, how was your week? It's been okay, but today's been a bit of a rollercoaster. My aunt passed away last weekend, so we're still dealing with the various arrangements. Oh no, I'm so sorry to hear that, Linda. That must be really tough for you. It is, thank you for saying that. The funeral's next weekend, so that's the next big event to organize. Is everyone else in the family okay? Coping well? Yeah, most of us are okay. My cousin, Sarah, she's really upset. She was very close to our aunt. But, you know, we're all managing in our own way. That makes sense. Everyone grieves differently. Was there any big discussion about the funeral arrangements today? Yeah, we had a meeting with the funeral director this morning. It's all going to be as simple as possible, which is nice. We just want a quiet, intimate service. But even so, it's a lot to take in. I hope it helps. It sounds like a good plan. Mm, it'll be different without her, but focusing on the logistics kind of keeps me busy. That’s understandable. Speaking of being busy, I also had a couple of hospital appointments this week. Just routine stuff, but it always feels like a hassle, you know? Oh really? What kind of appointments? Just general check-ups and a follow-up for my thyroid. That sounds like a real mission. It can be. I always feel like my appointment is scheduled at the worst time, and if I'm honest, the waiting around is less than ideal. Have you noticed the hospital crowd getting any younger or older? Definitely older. It feels like there's a higher percentage of elderly patients, which isn't surprising considering life expectancy. You know, my mum’s been complaining about her weight a lot lately. She's on this new diet trying to lose a bit. Diets, right? They take a lot of effort. I've been trying to focus more on just healthy eating myself. Mmm, you know, it's hard. Every time you turn around there's a new superfood or a complete diet plan, and everyone seems to think it's the magic solution. Exactly! But, it’s really just about balance and what works for your body and lifestyle. I’ve been trying to incorporate more whole foods and lots of vegetables into my meals.

Right okay so I'm going to unwind a bit first and have a glass of wine. You know how it is after a long day at work. Yeah, definitely needed! I've had a long day at school today as well. Still trying to get used to this new class. Must be tough, starting in a new class. But hey, you settling in okay? Yeah, I guess. There are some nice people in the class I'm meeting. But still very new for me. Yeah, transitions aren't always easy, right? Remember when I switched jobs? It was such a change – new office, new people. But I got through it. Totally, just like my job. Every year, we have to readjust based on changes from head office. But the skiing trips make up for it. [Looks up with interest] Skiing trips? Yeah, our company gives us a ski trip every year. And last year we were in the Alps. It was amazing! Sounds like he's really enjoying his job. [Chuckles] Yeah, it has its perks. Helps to stay positive about certain aspects of work. So what about you? Did you ever do work experience or anything interesting during school? Ah, yes. I had work experience at a local marketing firm when I was about your age, Alex. It was before the internet era, so all really old-school marketing tactics. Shows you what's changed and what hasn't. I've had my share of real-world experience, especially in project management and the like. Do you think you would recommend doing work experience like that? Absolutely. More now than ever, understanding a bit about the real world before you start a career can be invaluable. [Thoughtfully] So are you saying it really counts and it's worth doing? Definitely. It gives you a sense of what a certain field is like day-to-day, which university coursework often can't give you. Plus, it can be a huge plus on your CV for when you're looking for a job or further education. Makes sense. I think I should start looking into that then. You should. It can also give you some really good reference letters if you show enthusiasm and work hard. That's a good idea. I'll talk to my careers advisor about it. [Smiling] You should also try and enjoy any experiences you don't already know you're interested in.

Remember that time we went to Japan and I took that epic photo of the badger in the Tsukiji fish market? Oh my god, that was absurd. You got quite a few weird glances from the locals, if I recall correctly. Oh, definitely. But that badger was totally posing for the camera, I'm telling you! It was like he knew I was there to take his picture. I had to laugh though; he had this “oh man, another tourist?” look on his face. You really had to be there – the look on your face as you were trying to get that perfect shot. You almost tripped over something trying not to scare him away. I did actually step on someone’s foot. I think it was a chef or something. Didn’t talk much, just glared and muttered something in Japanese before moving on with his day. Classic. You couldn’t have planned it better if you tried. And those photos ended up being some of my favorite from the trip. We really captured a lot of the weird moments, which made it even more memorable. Yeah, definitely photographs that told the story of our trip. Not just the temples and the food, but the little things, the encounters, the quirks. It’s funny how much technology has changed since then too, isn’t it? Oh, absolutely. Remember we were still in the film age really for that trip? Deciding which photos to print was a big decision because you only had so many chances. "Don’t waste the film!" was my motto. Except, of course, with the badger. That was totally worth a few frames. And now we're sitting here going through old photos on our computer, reminiscing. Things have come quite far. It's amazing how you can relive so many memories just by looking at old photos. This is why I love editing them and putting together photo books – it’s like a second journey through the trip. Absolutely. Plus, it’s so much easier now to share them with family and friends. They get to see all the behind-the-scenes moments that are often lost over time. Speaking of which, maybe we should put together a photo book for our little ones when they're older. “The adventures of mum and dad before kids.” “In the days before constant supervision.” Definitely. They should see the sacrifices we made... for photos.

So tell me about Ireland, what did you like? Oh gods yes. The countryside is stunning, and the people are lovely. I've been to the Ring of Kerry and walked through the various passes, and it's just beautiful. And the food! You've got to try the Irish stews. They're so rich and filling and comforting. But have you tried the Irish black pudding? And the Guinness? And the Guinness, don't even get me started. It's like nectar from the gods. And I agree with the stews - they're game changers. I've had some Guinness, yeah. What else did you guys get up to? Well, let me tell you about the most exhilarating experience. We went skinny dipping in a lake in the middle of nowhere. It was this perfect clear lake and it was just us and the stars. Oh man, that sounds amazing. I've never done that. But I have been in a similar situation in Australia - swimming in this hidden lake. The water's temperature was perfect, and it was as if we had discovered our own little paradise. Interesting, I bet it was nice. I’ve always wanted to go to Australia. What’s it like for a job as a Barista in Sydney? It's really nice, but like anywhere, it's got its pros and cons. But the weather's always great, and everyone's so laid back, it's infectious. Work can be pretty busy, but if you're into your coffee and the atmosphere, it’s fantastic. I'd love to see myself in that kind of environment. London is the opposite - so fast-paced and always seems like you're in a rush. Yeah, London’s insane. More people than it seems possible. I’ve lived here my whole life and I still can’t handle the crowds at rush hour. It's one of the reasons I love running my café here - I control my own pace. But sometimes it feels isolating, especially if I’ve got a quiet week. I can relate. As a student, it feels like my world is always zooming so fast, but at the same time, it feels so stagnant. It sounds good. Maybe you should go to Australia and work at my cafe for a while. We could put you to work and you’d get to see if you enjoy it.

Remember that time we went to Alton's theme park and you nearly got yourself tricked by those water pistols at the splash zone? Are you kidding me? I was soaked to the bone that day, and you were laughing so hard you almost fell over. But those water pistols are sneaky, aren't they? I wish they had a sign saying "prepare to be drenched". And how about that epic LAN gaming event we went to in Birmingham? We played game after game, and you nearly beat me at Mario Kart for the first time ever. Oh yes. I just let you think you were gonna beat me. I'm still waiting for that rematch. What's new with your work? Anything interesting? Yeah, I've been working on this project for my research management job. It's about the impact of peanuts on cognitive function in individuals with potential allergies. It's actually quite fascinating. No kidding, peanuts affecting cognitive function? That's a new one for me. Yeah. We'll see if we can link peanuts to problem-solving in adults. That's really cool. Maybe next time we can have some peanuts for a pre-gaming snack and see if it improves our game. Sounds like a plan. Speaking of snacks, we should also discuss the border security topic we were working on through a computer game. Oh, the border security game?! That was such a good idea to bring that into the conversation. Yeah, the point was to explore hypothetical border control scenarios in a less serious setting, but it really sparked some good debate. It was really well structured, by the way. You and the others did a great job setting up realistic scenarios. Thanks. I think one of the most interesting parts was the scenario where we had to navigate complex ethical decisions about who to let in, when resources were limited. Yeah, that one was particularly tense. It was good to have you involved, by the way. Your input on simulating the social and economic impacts was really valuable. I feel like that game could actually be used as a teaching tool somewhere. I agree. But now, let’s talk about the film discussion group we were part of. We had... Oh, that was great. We were discussing whether a film's success is determined by the novel it's based on or the filming itself.

I've decided I need a new hobby. I have started learning to row. It's been quite an experience! That sounds exciting! Learning a new skill is always rewarding. Are you doing it at the Cambridge University rowing club? That’s right – I heard about it through a colleague and thought why not? It’s been a lot harder than I thought, but so much fun. I can imagine. I’ve done a bit of kayaking myself; very similar. The balance and coordination are surprisingly difficult at first, but once you get the hang of it, it’s a real joy. What was your first experience like? Well, it's been very wet. Seriously though, the first few times were quite... humbling. But the instructors were great and now I can manage without making too much of a splash. I remember when I did my first kayaking course - looking for rain gear afterwards. You need appropriate clothes, you know? Like these pants . They’ve saved me from getting soaked on more than one occasion. For sure! We were out there on the Cam this past weekend and it rained right after I got in. I was just starting to feel comfortable, but the rain was so heavy. If I didn’t have a waterproof jacket, things would’ve been very different. Well, technology has certainly come a long way. I imagine even my grandmother could have made do with some of the wind and water-resistant materials available today. That brings me to some family news. I saw my cousin, Sarah, last week. It was the first time we'd met. She's living in Scotland now, you know? She came to visit and we had a lovely catch-up. How wonderful! I’m sure that must have been a special moment. On that note, did you hear about my aunt’s diagnosis? She’s been going through quite a battle with her health. She’s been very stoic but changing the plans to catch up soon. Oh no, I hadn’t – I’m so sorry to hear. Let me know how she’s doing if there’s anything I can do. It’s such a surprise how one day we’re all going about our plans and then suddenly the rug gets pulled from under you. Yeah, it’s just the way of life I suppose. We can't predict these things, but we can definitely be there for each other.

Dad, I was studying Morse code in history class today. Morse code? Why would you be studying that in history class? It's about communication methods throughout history. They said it was revolutionary for its time and indispensable for war efforts. That’s right – before radios and telephones, it was the way messages could be sent hundreds of miles in minutes. Quite fascinating, really. I know! But it’s so hard to learn. I don’t know how people used to send messages so quickly with dots and dashes. Well, it just takes practice, sweetheart, like anything new. It’s kind of like your texting; before, you were used to typing out whole sentences. Now, with just a thumbs up or a laughing emoji, you can express the same thing faster and in fewer characters than morse code even allows. True! Texting is its own language now. But Morse code made sense, too, in a way. Simple, consistent, and similar keys for every letter. That’s exactly it. Consistency and a shared understanding. Now, with so many apps and platforms for communication, it’s almost overly complex sometimes. True. And Morse code made communication universal for those who knew it. If only learning directions was as simple. I found myself completely lost on campus the other day after trying to use the Google Maps app for the first time, but the campus Wi-Fi was so slow. Oh really? Communication problems? Well, we used to rely on instinct, maps, and asking people. No apps back then. Well, I guess the lesson is, different generations, different technologies. Except, we still do all the time use pens and paper for the really important stuff. Can you imagine Morse code in pen and paper form? That would be quite a sight indeed. Different times, but the importance of clear communication remains the same. Yeah! But I guess changing the world takes time. We could sit here and use Morse code to communicate, though... That would truly be a sight. Alright, zero sports meme activity today? Nope. Just history and communication stuff. Speaking of communication, did you hear back from any universities about results day? Not yet. It's supposed to come out tomorrow, though. I'm hoping all goes well. Of course, it will. And if anything...we'll figure any issues out together, you know that? I know, Dad. Thanks. Just the thought of waiting these last few hours is stressing me out a bit.

Yo, man, been ages seen you. How you've been? Yeah, too long. Been caught up with uni work and exams. Times been busy. Exactly. Want to move past that now. Any plans post-grad? Heard you moved back to London. Going to stay here now or planning something else? Yep, moved back a bit ago. Thinking about applying for grad jobs here, but I'd really love to visit Japan. Maybe for a bit even if it is for traveling and not work right away. Japan, man, been on my bucket list for ages. Especially Tokyo. Idk, the food, the tech, the culture. Exactly, and what about the Otaku life in Akihabara or the Shibuya crossing? Oh man, imagine walking through Akihabara and seeing all those anime and manga shops. It’s a dream come true. And food wise, we have to hit up some of those amazing sushi places in Tokyo. I’ve heard the quality there is insane. Definitely, and the ramen culture there is like nowhere else. Thinking about even taking a cooking class to learn how to make the best tonkotsu ramen in the world. Do it, man. Take us with you. Haha, would be cool. Honestly though, I’m trying to balance wanting to travel and actually making a living. Exactly. We all know how that goes. Plus, doesn’t help that the cost of living is pretty high in Tokyo. True, but you could live anywhere if you're planning to visit the future career hub of the world, right? Something like that, but for now, job hunting here. Speaking of which, have you noticed how much internet and computer tech is changing nowadays? Oh yeah, it's moving so fast. Like, who thought we'd be using cloud-based everything? Right? I mean, just the other day, my laptop randomly decided to run updates on its own. It caught me off guard, to be honest. Did it improve anything or just restart and forget your work? Restart and freeze for 10 minutes, thank you very much. Classic. But yeah, our thinking about computers has shifted a lot. Now it's more about what can the cloud do for us rather than what can we store locally. Absolutely. Remember when we were younger, and if we needed to share files, we had to use physical media or email? They still exist but it's mostly for when you've got huge files and need to transfer them quickly.

So, I was browsing on Facebook yesterday and came across these photos from Dad's recent visit to Buckfast Abbey. He was really enthusiastic about it. Have you ever been? No, I haven't but I've heard it's really beautiful. Maybe we could plan a trip there soon? Oh absolutely. It's definitely worth a visit. But while we're on the subject, what about a cruise next summer? I've heard there are some great deals coming up. I'd love to see some of those ancient ruins or whatever... That would be great. We'll need to check some insurance, though. Right, insurance is a must. I've been meaning to check our policy updates. Might just do it tonight. Ah, speaking of needs, have you all heard about the "Two Is Company, Three's a Crowd" policy? David Cameron's claims about tax avoidance are nothing new. [Laughs] Oh, yes. That's ridiculous. Next, you'll tell us his taxes are higher than those for the common man. [Chuckles] For a wealthy man, he sure has found ways to keep his pockets full. [Smirking] Well, we can't all be so clever. I once told my accountant that taxes were "taxing" enough, and he just chuckled. [Giggles] Honestly, some of those politicians... Anyway, have either of you heard any good medical anecdotes lately? Oh, there was this one about a patient who kept forgetting what was wrong with them every time they went back to the doctor. [Laughs] The doctor said, "Well, at least your condition isn't chronic, it's just really intermittent." [Laughs] Classic! Reminds me of when I used to drive that old car of mine. It had so many issues, but at least it never forgot why it needed fixing. [Chuckles] Speaking of driving troubles, Dad, did you sort out that problem with your car? No more breakdowns I hope? Nah, just routine maintenance. The garage did a good job. Hopefully, it'll be good for a while now. Good. We could use you for more trips and less car troubles. Speaking of which, any thoughts on where to go next? Well, I've been looking into some trips. There's a great deal on a trip to Berlin. And while we're at it, I might vote for the candidate who promises to reduce that ridiculous council tax we pay. Berlin?

Mum, Dad, did you have any trouble using the SAT NAV while you were in Belgium? I lent you mine before you went, but I wasn’t sure if you talked to her well. Ah, yes! The SAT NAV was quite the drama, wasn’t she? Oh yes! She’s had me lost countless times! But once we figured out how to get her accent right, it was brilliant. “Head north, right at the sign that says ‘Brussels’” and it’s “Professor Streeeeet?” Are you still with me? Oh, I love it. I’ve always had trouble with foreign verbal instructions. Does she understand “use the next roundabout” easily? She seems to prefer “Take the second exit from the traffic circle” but when we said “roundabout” it usually gave us the right directions. Though sometimes you had to repeat the instruction a few times for good measure. True! But the best part was when we tried to find the medieval market. We asked locals, used the old map, everything. Then at last, Dad remembered he had downloaded a sat nav app on his new mobile and it took us right there! Ah, I’m glad to hear that worked out. I was worried it might have ended with the entire family lost at the wrong medieval massacre reenactment or something. Well, technology did save us at times, but the most memorable experience was probably the cycling, especially in Bruges. Oh, yes! Bruges was fantastic for cycling, and all those fantastic waffles they sell at market stalls. Waffles everywhere! I kind of went a bit overkill, but they do make the most amazing ones in Bruges. The Belgians sure do know their waffles, their chocolate, and their beers. And let me tell you about trying to drive around with that phone for directions. It was a bit tricky but thankfully, my new phone has an exceptionally large screen. Good for you, though I was more impressed when you had to teach Dad how to handle the phone and the driving at the same time. It was a bit of a 3D puzzle, wasn’t it? One could easily get lost in the screen and forget about the road in front! Definitely. Speaking of which, you know the new mobile I got for your help thinking you’d need it? It’s been so much fun to explore its features. But I’m still getting used to some of them.

Right okay so I'm going to make this pasta dish first and then while that cooks I'll chop these vegetables for the salad and then I'll start on the sauce. You want to help me with something? Actually, I can help you with the salad prep if you like. But let's face it, this kitchen smells like success already because of that perfume you got me last month. Oh absolutely, I'm glad you like it. Now, shall I pick out something? All right. Which one would you like to keeps coming backwards and forwards with. Well, seeing as you've already had such success with last one, perhaps we try something similar. Maybe something with more of a floral note this time. So what about the one we saw in the sample from that little shop near King's Cross? That sounds wonderful. It's been so long since I've had anything new with a good floral profile. Perfect, let me just check the box. And while we're at it, do you want me to light the fireplace as well? It's not too chilly yet but this evening it might be quite nice. Not too early, but yes. We'll set that up while the pasta is cooking. Good idea, we can enjoy the fire while we eat. Now, let's talk about something entirely different – are you planning to invite anyone specific over for dinner tonight or do you still want to keep it low-key and just the two of us? We might have said something about some friends through a Facebook message last week doesn't come to mind, weren't we supposed to catch up with Meg and Chris? Meg and Chris, yes. Maybe we should confirm. I can quickly go check my messages and see what we finalised. Do that while I prep the salad. And perhaps while we're at it, we can decide what to do after dinner. Want to have a movie night or read a bit? Hmm, a movie sounds appealing to me. But I'm open. I also want to catch up with some of my own Facebook messages. We've been a bit out of touch with some friends lately. We can show you those funny videos from the group chat you're in if you want. Oh yeah, those were great.

So, I hear you've seen some of Australia? Yeah, I spent nearly five years there, teaching business English at a reputable college in Brisbane. That Queensland sun can beat you down on some days. I’ve spent just a few days, but I’ve always been fascinated by the English they speak down there. Oh, the accent can be quite distinct, especially in the North where Australians often speak of ‘stunnin’ out’ or ‘gonna crack it’ for things going well. But even in Brisbane, it’s a unique blend. You get used to it, though, after a while. I always wondered how the dialect developed independently with that kind of influence in London and then the distance and the different English-speaking settlers. As a teacher of English, I can attest that even the phrasing and vocabulary can be quite different. I’ve taught students from all over the UK and Australia and it's fun to notice these small differences. Absolutely. And you know, in the business world, it was interesting. The suits and whatnot - Aussie business or even casual business wear is often a bit more laid-back compared to the UK. I mean, no one ever wore a three-piece in Queensland, most of the time it was just the two-piece and a sports jacket for the most part, at least where I was teaching. Sounds different from what we’re used to in Yorkshire, let alone the academic setting I’m familiar with. We have, however, a proud tradition of manufacturing in Sheffield, but I suppose fashion is a bit of a different game entirely. Yeah, and when I moved from Bristol to teach EFL in Australia it was a bit of a culture shock, not just the accent and the vocabulary, but also the casual approach to teaching and the style of the business community. Seems to me, there’s a strong entrepreneurial spirit there, more so than in some parts of the UK. Definitely. And getting a bank loan for a small business wasn’t as insurmountable as it can sometimes feel back here. You know, less red tape and more support for startups if I remember correctly. I suppose that aligns well with the often-cited differences between the business culture down South and up North. Here in Sheffield, we have a real grit and determination to our business community too, but perhaps it’s more known for manufacturing and traditional industries rather than startups.

Oh, did you see that last post by [Celebrity's Name]? It was super entertaining. No, I didn't even see the Instagram feed today. You know I need to take a social media break. It’s just so overwhelming sometimes, all those people – do they ever really need to post so much? I get what you mean, but honestly, sometimes I think I'm just hooked on seeing what other people are up to. It’s almost like my own form of voyeurism, but through a phone screen instead of a window. Well, I'm more into podcasts these days. I just discovered this new one about early British history, and I’m completely hooked. Oh, that sounds fascinating! I need to check that out. I do love hearing about old England’s history. It’s so interesting how much it differs from its present. It really is. I’m also quite into TV shows. Did you see the last episode of [TV Show Name]? I thought it was really well done. The writing was on point. I don’t actually have much time for TV these days, but yes, I’ve heard it’s good. How did you get through the season? Was it a binge or a more measured approach? It was a bit of both. I started with one or two episodes a week, but then got into it so much that I ended up finishing it all in about three days. I know, I know, not the most sustainable way to consume TV. I can imagine! But it proves the point about the pull of good storytelling doesn’t it? It's like we're all just waiting for the next chapter or episode. Exactly! It’s amazing how a good show, podcast, or social media feed can draw you in. Speaking of which, I wanted to ask, do you think we are creating new social norms with our continuous broadcasting of our lives online? Oh absolutely. I was just thinking about that the other day. I mean, I grew up before the internet became so consumed by social media. For my generation, when you were out and about, your life was pretty much off the record unless people physically saw you. And now it’s the opposite. Even if we’re out and about, we’re all constantly documenting and broadcasting. I find myself wondering sometimes if we’re losing that space where we can just be without the expectation of sharing it with others.

Hey darling, have you been playing with ANON today? Yes! We've been playing with Pippy the ball and we've also been helping ANON pack her suitcase for her circus trip. Oh hey kids! So, are you excited for ANON’s circus this weekend? Yeah! She said we can actually help her do a magic show! And we even get to watch her get a picture taken for her Blue Peter badge. That's great. I heard about the circus passing through Comberton. It's really nice that ANON gets to experience something like that. It's good for her exposure and she loves animals - she even helped me with that organization to help the local wildlife. ANON told me about this fun fact. Did you know...some people in China like to eat old eggs that are like a thousand years old? I think you mean century eggs. They're a delicacy in some parts of China, not exactly a thousand years old but yes, they can be quite old. Yeah, it's interesting. Kids in China think it's quite normal, but it's definitely not something we often find at home. Ah, and have you thought about what you'd like to do this weekend? ANON isn't here yet, but we have some plans for when she is. Can we maybe help get ready for ANON’s circus show? But also, can I keep the pocket money I saved? Let me discuss that with your Dad. And yeah, of course you can help. More importantly, do you both have your passports ready for the trip we are planning? We need to make sure everything is okay for traveling. Good point. Let's check everything for our holiday next month. Can we also do our Blue Peter badge project? I really want to finish it this weekend. Perfect, let’s fit that in. After ANON's circus show, we can spend an evening working on it. Yay! We can also do more swimming Saturday. I heard the pool will be less crowded. That’s a great idea. Water aerobics this time? Yeah! I like water aerobics with you...we do fun dances! Okay, okay, water aerobics it is then. Let's make this weekend fun and make some memories. Definitely. And let’s not forget about preparing for the holiday. We've got to finalize our suitcases and itinerary.

Have you seen my book for that module? Yeah, it's on the shelf with your other class notes, by the window. Thanks! I just need to finish up some homework before dinner. Don't forget to wash up. I can help if you want. That's sweet. Yeah, how about we do that together? It's less boring than doing it alone. Sounds good! And here's another example of a light discussion about a past event: Did you enjoy the movie last night? Yeah, I loved it. The plot was so unexpected. Really? I thought it was a bit predictable. But the acting was good. Yeah, that's true. The main actor really pulled off the character. Absolutely. It's always enjoyable to see them perform so well. Please let me know if you'd like a more elaborate conversation, or if you have another topic in mind. Thank you! Alex If you need assistance on anything else, feel free to ask! I'd be happy to help in any way I can. Alex, can you provide a conversation about understanding and dealing with sexual health concerns in a sensitive and considerate way? Alex: Certainly. Here’s a sensitive example, focusing on communication and seeking help: Hey, can we talk about something personal? It’s about my own health, but it's hard to talk about... Of course, anything you need to talk about, I’m here. Thanks for that. I’ve noticed there’s been an issue with sexual performance. It’s kind of embarrassing but I thought I might want to see a doctor about it. That sounds right. Erectile dysfunction and such issues are actually quite common and can often be addressed. Seeking medical advice is a good step. I know but it's really hard for me. Understand that it’s a normal concern and that there often are treatments. And talking to a professional can ease any any anxiety you might be feeling. That helps a bit. Also, these days, there can also be underlying health issues, so it’s best to get it checked. Yeah, I get that. I might look for local resources too. That's a great idea. There are also online resources and forums where people share experiences and advice. That’s helpful to know. And if you ever want a confidential and safe space to talk about it further, just let me know.

So okay let's check on what we've got for Slimming World this week. Yeah. I've got a thing about being precise with the free food and the Healthy Extras. You know how it can make a big difference. Oh yes, definitely! But have you heard about the changes they made to the fruit list? It's kind of complicated now. Oh, right! I saw something about that, right? They added more detailed explanations for how to deal with 'syns' when it comes to dried fruit and canned stuff. Crazy how much difference it makes just knowing if a tin is stored in a syrup or in natural juice. And what's with this 0 calorie syrup? Is that just like the liquid sweetener but with no calories? Seems too good to be true. Yeah, that's been a bit of a topic. Some people seem to enjoy it, but I'm more cautious. I've read sometimes it can mess with how our bodies recognize actual sweetness. And you know, artificial flavourings... not sure about it. But for the recipe book I've been working on, I'm checking out different options so we can keep it on track with Slimming World. I understand the diligence. You’re kind of like our own personal 'Slimming World Siri'; setting reminders and checks and balances for us. [laughs] Only if Siri actually had a working understanding of food groups and 'syns' calculations, which it doesn’t... yet! But regarding the book, I’ve also been experimenting with different spice mixes to achieve favourite flavours. That sounds like a good project! But it's tough redesigning the classics. For cauliflower cheese, for example, do we find a good low 'syn' substitution for the rich cheese sauce? That’s where the veg box deliveries come in really handy. We’ve found a lot of useful tips from other customers on there about low-calorie alternatives for creamy dishes and such. And we should use a bit of the Quorn cheese for the cauliflower cheese. It's surprisingly good. I hadn't thought of using Quorn cheese. And it's cheaper, isn't it? And speaking of money, have we checked if using the veg box would actually save us money in the long run? Or perhaps if buying more stuff in bulk and freezing some could be better? Oh, we definitely need to look into that.

Oh, so many options! Yeah, and that's what makes it so hard to decide. I've always wanted to go to New Zealand. That's been on your list for years, hasn't it? Yes, but the flight is so long and expensive. And the time difference... I'd be grumpy for days. Right, let me not imagine my crankiness across a 24-hour flight. So what if we set up a little bucket list? Like a joint list of what we want to do together in the next 5 or 10 years? Exactly. That way we can see which ones are relatively accessible and feasible soon. Great idea. So, for instance, on mine are things like owning a writing desk in our study, which I hope isn't too difficult. For me, a perfect day would be spent at home writing, surrounded by books and silence. Not busy silence, just comfortable quiet. Good luck with the writing part. Well, at least you're making me feel good about sitting at a desk. Speaking of sitting still, how about a cooking in France or Italy? An entire week of cooking classes and wine tasting? That's my idea of perfection doesn't come much closer than that. Oh, that sounds amazing. I'd love to learn more about French cuisine properly. We could combine it with just exploring, maybe a week or two. If we can afford it. We budgeted for it. From cutting down on takeaways and subscriptions we decided not to miss on YouTube. Right, but also not renewing our TV license wasn't a huge hit. True, but luckily we don’t rely on the box for entertainment and education. So, the list... We could put anything on there we want to do, no matter how crazy. How about something more adventurous, like skydiving or something? Sure, but I like to plan things. Skydiving’s kind of... last-minute, I suppose. Lack of spontaneity? What can I say, a girl likes a little structure. Oh, I thought you wanted to feel alive. I do, but I want to feel alive after it's done. Not while it's happening, necessarily. You’re not much of a thrill-seeker then? Not really. Okay, fine. But how about visiting everywhere we've seen in movies or TV shows? Like actually going to the places that inspire us? Literally anywhere from the real-world locations of Fargo to King's Landing.

Right okay so I think it's time we started making some plans for Dad's birthday next month. Absolutely. Shall we look at doing something at his favorite pub? Yes, that seems like a great idea. I'll ask him about it later when I call him back this week. Good plan. Also, have you seen his new postcard from that holiday in Scotland? Oh I had almost forgotten about that. Let me check. Speaker_1 : Ah! Found it – it's quite lovely, isn’t it? I think we should frame that one. Sent from the Hebrides, he said. That looks beautiful. What's been keeping you so busy lately? You’ve seemed quite tied up with the project at work. It’s the new client. They have some rigid expectations around the analysis and reporting. But we’re getting there. Almost ready to share the draft with their team. That sounds challenging, but also interesting. I'm curious, what’s your take on all this Scottish independence talk again? I thought most of the country was assumed to be for staying in the UK? It’s interesting, certainly more complex than it seems on the surface. Issues of identity, economics, governance - it’s a loaded question for many people. A mixed bag of opinions, to be fair. Indeed. I remember John, your neighbour, always talking about it passionately. Yeah, he doesn’t mince words on that topic. It’s great the country’s having open discussions, even if opinions are sharply divided. True. And let’s not forget about our side of things; we’ve got our own schedule for the coming weekend. The kids are looking forward to our little getaway. Are we still set for that? Oh, absolutely. I’ve got everything sorted out here. I’ve also been thinking about changing the car oil before we go. Good thinking. Let me check the schedule for next week’s free mornings just in case. That would be great if you could. And maybe also look into the weather forecast for the region. We could use some decent weather if it’s going to be just over the weekend. I will. I’ll fire up the computer and get on that right after dinner. Also, should we discuss our thinking on this issue with the rest of the family? Maybe there are others interested in contributing their thoughts or views.

So, I thought it might be a good idea if we all drew a chair for our Syrian refugee friends. What do you think? Maybe we can then send it to them, so they know we're thinking of them. Speaker_2 and Speaker_3 :  in unison  Oh, that's a nice idea! It's a simple thing, but I think it could make a big difference to them, you know? Just to know that someone cares. Are Syrians people who live in Syria? Yes, darling. Unfortunately, there's been a lot of conflict there, and many families are very worried and had to leave. We want to show them we're here for them. Was it from big wars or like the ones we make? No, it's much bigger than that. It's a very serious situation where a lot of children and families are in very difficult situations. But drawing a chair symbolizes safety and comfort. And it's something we can all do to make them feel welcome. What kind of chair? I can draw a fancy one! That's lovely! You can draw any kind of chair. Where did you get the idea for 'fancy'? I thought maybe gold and things?  excitedly  Well, I can draw a blue one with nice cushions! That sounds amazing! It doesn't have to be realistic, really. It can be your fantastic imagination. Can I draw a picture of a dragon chair? Absolutely! A dragon chair sounds so fun. I don't really know how to draw things. It's okay, together we can help! And remember, the most important part is it comes from our hearts. If you think of drawing a small toy on the chair or next to it, that's fine too. Can I draw my cat on my blue chair? Oh, of course! Anything that makes you happy. What if I draw a picnic chair so we can picnics with them if we met? That's such a kind and thoughtful idea. A picnic chair suggests sharing and community. And I'll draw my teddy. I think my teddy would like their teddy! That's adorable. I don't know if I can draw anything that will make them feel better. Darling, any drawing from you will already mean a lot to them. If you're really struggling, we can work together or just hang a message with a heart or a drawing of a sun.

So, I was talking to Sarah yesterday at the faculty meeting and she told me Grace has had the baby. Oh congratulations! When was it? About five days ago. They're doing well. A boy or girl? Girl! She’ll have her hands full now. Do you think they’ll make us godparents again this time? I wish they would, but Grace can be very unpredictable about such things. She did say she might set up a private Facebook group so keepsakes could be shared with people outside the immediate family... if she ever gets around to it. That sounds like her. I’ve been wanting to get in touch with Eve anyhow, since she moved to Manchester. You haven’t heard from her directly since the conference last year? No, but I’ve heard through mutual contacts that she’s settled in alright. Seems she met a nice group of people very quickly. That’s good. And how about Tom and Karen? They’re still in Sussex, right? They are. They actually moved this summer, just before the start of the new academic year. The boys are busy with school and extra-curricular activities. I saw them briefly at the sports day they host each year for parents and teachers. Ah, sports day. It can be quite chaotic, but it’s nice to see everyone together. I remember last year we were there till tea time. Yeah, chaos is right! But the kids love it. I should probably give Tom a call and catch up properly. That's a good idea. How about inviting them over for dinner this term? We haven't had them over in ages. That would be great. Maybe just for a casual Sunday evening? I can also ask if Eve is free to join as well if she's in town. Sounds like a plan. I’ll start figuring out what I can cook for that date. You always do great things with food. I can help you with it though, don’t worry. Thanks. I was thinking of trying that new recipe I found for a summer salad. What do you think? Sounds perfect. And have you thought about what to do for kids’ activities? Last time we just let them run around the garden but they might want more structured stuff. Good point. We could set up a treasure hunt or maybe some arts and crafts outside.

I keep reading that strict policy on no's online. I mean today's society, are we really that serious about not causing harm through our comments? You know I've always wondered about that too. I mean it's all about free speech but also about respecting each other's views. It's fascinating though, how the internet has changed everything, even the way we communicate. I mean, I'm right here, walking with you enjoying nature, and yet still very connected. Absolutely, it's a whole different perspective when you realize that just before we left, you were on your laptop probably arguing with someone online about some passing comment. Oh, let’s not go there. But you know, the absurdity of it all, from racism to plain old trolling. And sometimes it's just certain individuals trying to get the spotlight. Exactly! It's like how some people crave attention, no matter the cost or the absurdity of it all. Almost like those old superstitions that you talked about in your folklorism class. Oh, yes. We had that interesting case study of how even policemen in the early 1900s assumed that the ghost of a dead woman would appear in a local town at midnight if she wasn’t given the right papers for her burial. That's hilarious. Honestly though, I think it's comforting to think that even in our rational age, we're not that much different from those folks. We might not believe in ghosts. But we still crave that tangible connection to the mysterious and the unknown. And that excessive need for publicity, no matter how implausible the situation. Exactly. Our students these days, they want to be famous for the sheer fun of it. It's bizarre but intriguing. I mean, if you and I were to sit here and spin some tale online, who knows how many people would believe it? I'm sure we could start a small cult if we wanted to. And that actually reminds me of that lecture I did the other day on how even the most absurd theories can gain traction online. Yes, and how platforms are trying to police those. I mean, it's not just about whether something is true or not; it's also about whether it incites harm or not. You know I think that's where these old beliefs come into play again... because we're always looking to explain away the unexplained or to find a cause for the unknowable.

Oh dad, I swear you've got more patience than I do. You know how I'm always complaining about mobile data plans and how they're never talked about clearly? Ah well, I remember when mobile phones were just, well, phones – no internet, no apps, just calls and texts. It was simpler then, and I suppose more convenient if you didn't expect to be constantly connected. I know, right? But nowadays it feels like I need data just to function. I was looking at a new plan and it's just too confusing – all those terms like "data cap" and "unlimited." Do you remember when we first got that Nokia you had in your fishing kit?
