And it's not just the sounds and grammar, but how we use language to identify ourselves or signal belonging to certain groups. It's so nuanced. And ever since I took that course, I've been listening to people around this area, on the train, in shops, and it's funny how you can still pick up hints of traditional accents but mixed with newer influences. Like the way the 'g' in "going to" turns into 'a' at the end, or the way 'th' sounds are influenced by the Cockney 'f'? Exactly! And it's not just from London either, I'm seeing it in Cambridge and even over in Sussex where I went on holiday. But it's not a blanket change—there are pockets that resist more than others. Which I guess ties into what’s happening with English globally, right? The way the language is adapting in international contexts, especially with the increase of English as a lingua franca. Oh, absolutely. Your PhD on World Englishes is probably covering all this in depth. I always found it so interesting when people talk about "standard English" and whether we really mean UK or US English, or if it’s somewhere in between for global communication. Well, my initial question was trying to narrow it down for my dissertation but realistically, English as a global language isn't something you can tie down easily. It’s like almost every region or culture is adapting English into something unique. Just like how languages borrow and adapt over time.

So, how was everyone's weekend at school? Did you all enjoy the school dinners today? Oh, yes! I had a pizza, and it was yummy! Me too! I had fish and chips and it was so good! That's great to hear! I'm glad you both enjoyed them. Did you have a chance to save some money for the school trip? Yes! I saved 10p from my pocket money! I saved a pound! Well, that's really responsible of you both. Remember to keep saving; the trip will be here before we know it. Can we have more school dinners instead of taking in our lunch from home? I suppose that could be arranged sometimes. However, most of the time it's better to bring in your own lunch as sometimes you get creative options at home that the school can't offer. But at Granny's, she makes the best spaghetti bolognese ever! I'm sure Granny's cooking is delicious, but remember different homes have different routines and rules. Where Granny lives, the time of day and what's prepared might be more suited to when you're there. So, can we eat at school more often? Like I said, sometimes we can, but it's best not to rely on it all the time. Your own lunches from home are usually much better for you and give you some choices you might not get from the school menu. What about the tennis tournament that's coming up? Ah, yes! I just spoke to your teacher about it. Seems like the weather's looking good, so it should go ahead. Do we need to bring anything special for it? Of course! Remember to bring your tennis racket, some water, and a snack if you'll need one. Can we practice before it happens? I'm sure we can arrange that. I know there's a park near us where we could practice. Can we talk about something else? Like clowns. I heard they're at the circus in town and I'm scared. I know clowns can be a bit daunting for some kids. But remember, clowns are people like us, but they just choose to put on fun and silly costumes to make people laugh. Yeah... I kind of want to be a clown one day. It looks like fun. That's very kind of you to say, but being a clown is a lot of work and practice.

So, I thought that film we saw yesterday was pretty good, don't you agree? Yeah, it was. I liked the cinematography, but I thought the plot needed a bit more development. I thought it was okay. Just a bit too dramatic for me. Oh, isn't that often the case with movies these days? More flash than substance! True. Although I do appreciate when directors try to provoke a reaction. It keeps things fresh even if it doesn't always work out. Well, I suppose, but sometimes you just want to be entertained without all the controversy. I hear you. Speaking of controversy, did any of you read about the debate in Cambridge last week about the national curriculum? No, but I’ve heard talk about it. It seems to be all about changing the way we teach history, right? That's part of it, but there's a lot more to it. They're also discussing how to accommodate more diverse or even alternative perspectives on historical events within the main narratives. Interesting, but isn’t that just different ideological interpretations? I’m worried about facts becoming too flexible in the name of inclusivity. That’s a valid concern, but also, can't we learn more by hearing different perspectives? Exactly, it’s about balance. Teaching students to critically evaluate multiple sources can only strengthen their understanding of history. I'm not so sure. I always believed in a clear, chronological approach doesn’t leave much room for it. As a teacher, I think that kind of understanding would be beneficial if executed properly. Challenging the students to look at events from different angles can make the subject a lot more engaging. That said, I'm also worried about skills. With so much focus on alternative narratives, are they also going to insure kids can write a proper essay or understand changing economic policies? Good point, but maybe it's a case of integration? Education isn’t binary. You can teach multi-perspective history while also developing those skills. That makes sense, but it’s not an easy thing to implement in the classroom. True, and that’s why it’s such a contentious topic. It also touches on the larger issue of what universities expect. If schools are changing the way they teach, aren't universities thinking about how this will affect higher education degrees and their entry requirements?

Remember when we used to sit around the fire as children listening to our grandfather telling these stories about the war? He was such a good storyteller, wouldn’t let the tea go down without finishing a tale. Oh yes, I remember that – “Uncle George” we'd call him isn’t that right? But those weren’t just stories, were they? He really fought in the war. Indeed, he did. I found some documents about him online for my research once. So how is that tea? Think we’ll ever experience another summer like this one? The heat, it’s been unbearable. It’s been hot but then again, we’ve just been down to the garden most of the time. The grandchildren loved the paddling pool. Reminds us of when we were young. And this tea’s lovely. Just made it this morning, so the taste is still fresh. You’ve got the knack of it, bless you. I always told you this was the right cup for the garden. So who’s this new police officer that’s been round lately? Seems very keen. Oh yes, Officer Richardson. I think he’s one of the younger recruits. Stands at over six foot, hasn’t met a rule he doesn’t obey by. I noticed that, yes. There’s one thing about the police: as long as they keep the area safe, we don’t mind them. And with the recent disturbance in the park, I think we’re all thankful for them being vigilant. It's just part of the area, isn't it? Used to be so peaceful. Seems like the young ones today don’t respect a quiet neighborhood anymore. That's true, but then again, we had our own mischief back in the day. There was a time we'd knock on doors changing the furniture inside just for fun on a dare. Oh for heaven’s sake! Imagine doing that now and getting in trouble. We were lucky truly. The stories we could tell! And yet, it was good fun. Unbeatable bonding almost. Though, I laughed at the thought of asking our older self if they’d want to go through it again and got a “Not on your life” as an answer! But it’s interesting how beginnings change us. I often think about this armchair here. My grandmother had it from our great aunt when she passed.

"Baby one more time" . Remember when we used to drive these roads all together? Whole family and everything. Well, now I guess this is the last time for a while. Yeah, it’s almost surreal now that I think about it. Time really does fly. Exactly! Next time I’m back, there’ll probably be another baby at mum's and possibly a ghost at your place . Ha! Don’t forget we got another keepsake for you alongside the ghost - a whole lifetime of knowledge and bags of useless advice, courtesy of your father. I’m sure you've already started with that, just like you have with Emma. I bet she’s read more about mortgages than she has English novels! And what about your own? You’ve progressed from "I don’t know, let’s go with £200,000" to actual research, barely? Well, English language instructor and finance advisor, apparently. All round useful. Not to mention I’m discovering how fun it is to study while the rest of the world watches Friends reruns. At least you’re finally using your knowledge for something useful - understanding your finances, or understanding why nobody tore their eyes away from the screen during 'The one where they all moved'. Exactly. Shows like that help with English too, you know? Idioms, doesn’t come much more real than Joey saying "How you doin’?" to a chicken. I just hope your English students don’t get into side conversations about Phoebe’s “Smelly Cat”. If that were to happen, I think they’d be more engaged than they were in Mr. McCann’s class! Definitely. We could sit here and go through all the iconic shows from our childhood, but what’s for sure - we’ve seen our fair share of sickness in family. Yeah, I couldn’t help but think of the years of Chinese takeaways leading to the great health kick. True. There’s something about the real job of getting better that makes those 24-hour soups and noodles worthwhile. Absolutely. Food’s central to memory, just like company. You know, I still remember that one time.. Oh... the time when you took a packet of tomato soup into a theatre? Exactly! What can I say, a man on a mission across the youth of Bedford. I remember having to drive back to get it when you realized it was still in my car.

Right okay so I think we need to decide on the first move's menu. Grace has told me that her mum loves traditional English food, and clearly the fish option is a big hit at home. What are your thoughts? I really like that. A traditional English menu sounds lovely, but I suppose we do need to keep some kind of balance. Maybe we could do a fish and a meat course? Something like fish pie or fish with a bit of roasted veg, and then perhaps a main course of lamb or beef? That's a great idea. Fish pie is a winner in our household too. And we could do a vegetarian option for anyone who might not want meat. What about the cake? Does anyone have any ideas? Might we consider not making a cake but perhaps hiring a lovely cake maker in the area? I've heard of this place in the market that does incredible traditional cake designs and they could add a personal touch which would be lovely. That sounds perfect. And we should definitely check out the local fish shops and visit a few to see if they have any top quality fish that’s been caught that day. Perhaps we could even pick some up ourselves if we time it right. Also, when arranging the seating, have you thought about making sure Grandma has a seat that’s easy for her to get in and out of? Maybe near a window where she can enjoy the view? Absolutely. Her comfort and wellbeing are paramount. Maybe arrange to seat her at the head of the table, it feels traditional and gives her a central and respectful place. And have you thought of the photos? I was thinking maybe we could put some family photos round the room, it doesn’t have to be all over the place just a few in strategic locations might stir up some lovely memories. Yes, I was planning to bring the photo albums. Seems like the right opportunity to pull them out and just let the crowd of photos do the talking. On that note, maybe we could arrange some of those books or albums near her place setting so she can look through and reminisce if she wishes. And candles. Definitely some lovely candles around the room. Lighting is so important to setting the mood. And we should probably handle the logistics of who’s bringing what dish, when and so on.

I've decided I need to get my wisdom teeth out. Can you believe that? Yeah, talked to my dentist the other day. He said they're coming through at quite odd angles. Exactly – do you have any idea how painful this is? You're a drama queen. It'll be fine. Now, don't start complaining to me about French food. Are you kidding? Have you not noticed? There's always too much cheese, and I fucking hate cheese. Get over it mate. Not when it's everywhere in every meal. Try finding something without it. Hence your stellar diet over here? Exactly. But, seriously, thinking about getting the teeth sorted out over break. Oh, good on you. Just make sure you keep warm or you'll end up with a cute little hole this side of Christmas. Thanks, just what I need. Well think of it this way, you can enjoy the local cuisine properly next time. Right, as if I'd go back for more. Probably not, but we’re here, and it’s not so bad once you get through a painful extraction. I know that. You should've mentioned earlier. We could have planned something together. Yeah, good idea. Let's do it. If you're going, I’ve got to meet my parents next week. Back in Cambridge. You aren't stuck here forever then? No, but for now, we're here. Funny how we just decided on this, isn't it? And I thought I was going to have a real summer of not A summer of no... what was that again? Nothing much, just hanging around, enjoying the sun. Enjoying? Well, I thought it'd be better than studying this summer. You're also talking about exams, yeah? Yeah, and then thinking about moving house next year. All this and still worrying about my wisdom teeth. It all seems to pile up, doesn’t it? But we've been through more, remember? Yeah, we have. That’s what friends are for, eh? To laugh and grumble together about our big plans and even bigger grievances. Exactly. So, you're taking the train back to Cambridge? Yeah, my parents will pick me up from the station. And when are you heading back? Not sure yet. If I go back for that procedure, might as well stay a bit longer. And check if I can pack some essentials without having to rely on this cheese-loving culinary culture.

So, I thought it might be nice to find some lactose free recipes. Grace has been having issues and we realized it's not just about dairy products but also cakes and sweets. Are we still making cakes? That seems time-consuming. Yes, but we can use substitutes easily. I've found some really good tapioca and almond flour recipes. It could be a fun project that makes Grace feel included. Can we use those chess and draughts set for money when we play? Pleeease? Well, seeing as those coins are really just lazy ways of keeping track, I don’t see why not. Might just encourage math skills too. Speaking of games, have you thought about Chinese New Year? We could do something little. Can we have a dinner with red and gold decorations? Why not? We could also do a little craft project together, maybe even make some lanterns. I heard they also do a lot of acts of kindness during this time. What kind? Like helping with chores at home without being asked, or even bigger things. For instance, in some places, they send cards and gifts to the elderly or those who are alone. That's really sweet. But for kids, perhaps we could do smaller, more practical acts. Maybe making a small gift or card for someone who helped us or write a thank you note to our teachers. I like the thank you notes idea. But it has to be nice, like with stickers and drawings! Absolutely, and if you're feeling brave, you could even tidy up the garden or try helping with dinner a few times, as a nice surprise for Mum and Dad. And speaking of unique celebrations, do either of you remember last summer when we had that spa day at home? We used to changing the colors of our hair with food colorings. YES YES YES! Can we do that again? But for Chinese New Year, like we can each pick a color and so we can make it fun! That does sound like a good family tradition. But maybe we stick to less permanent colors just in case the kids want to reverse it later. Do you think Grace would like that? Let's ask her. For now, let's all agree to: 1. Set up a small craft session to make thank you notes and maybe a few simple decorations for the dinner.

Mum, I can't believe what happened yesterday. Oh Grace, what happened? I was at school and we were having a big celebration for the end of term. They had a competition where they let the students pick their own Alice in Wonderland character to dress up as. That sounds so fun! It was, but while I was walking out to get a snack, I tripped and fell. Oh no, are you okay? Did you hurt yourself? Yeah, I landed on my knee pretty hard but I thought it was just a scrape. You need to take care of that. Let me take a look. So, I was feeling a bit silly about it anyway and then I noticed - oh, Mum, I have this big scar now. Where is it? On my knee. It's a bit swollen too. We need to clean it and put some cream on it. And maybe we should ask the school what happened, make sure it was safe? Sure, I've already told Mrs. Thompson. She said the floor was a bit slippery and assumed I might have been in a hurry. Still, we should make sure there weren't any other factors. Yeah, but I'm more concerned about the scar... I always hated scars, especially if they're silly or can't be hidden... Alright, don't worry about it too much. Mum, doesn't it freak you out sometimes that there's the internet now? Everything about us is out there, including things like scars, instantly if we share it. It's true, Grace. The internet has a lot of positives, but it comes with a certain level of permanence and exposure to things we might not want shared or seen by everyone. Exactly! Especially now with all these changing rules about data and privacy. Right. Anyway, I was thinking after this accident, I might look into getting something cool for my scar so I don't have to be embarrassed about it... like some sweet costume or medical alert pieces of jewellery. That's actually a great idea! There are so many platforms where people share amazing work. I can look into that with you. Thanks, Mum. That'd mean a lot. You know I'd do anything to make you feel better. So, um, can I also get you something for the accident? Like a gift?  laughs  What can I possibly need a gift for?

So, I was talking to that group of protesters who've been coordinating efforts regarding these wind turbine applications. It's been quite an education, and clearly they're passionate about protecting their land. Are they still involved with the solar panel applications as well? Same group, although they face questions on both fronts. It's quite involved and tiring for them, I'm sure. The sheer number of planning applications that get approved without public consultation... it's very concerning. The local council... they keeps coming up with these proposals. It seems like they're pushing for development to meet some kind of 'target', without fully considering the impact on our landscape and communities. As company directors we had similar issues in our time. It just seems like there is no balance. Exactly! And once an application is submitted, even if the locals object, the outcome isn't always what you'd expect. Planning Appeal processes are tedious and costly—unless you've got deep pockets, your voice seems to get drowned out. Did they discuss potential strategies or tactics to make their efforts more effective? Yes, we talked about that a bit. Primarily it's about being well-informed and planning actions thoroughly. For instance, the need to research the logistics of these turbines, the noise pollution, the impact on local wildlife... It’s a lot of ground to cover to make a persuasive case. Absolutely, and while they have the passion, perhaps they could use some expert advice to bolster their arguments. I could see how as a group, they could benefit from speaking with ecologists, architects, and maybe even some engineers? Yes, definitely. Plus, it's about understanding the technical innovations that could make alternative energy sources viable while minimizing local disruption. I mentioned to them about seeing some examples in the news or in research about the potential for advancements in energy storage—if we could get to a place where it's cost-effective and practical to store wind or solar energy when it's available but not required, it’d really turn the tables. That's a key point. As I see it, the problem isn’t the energy sources themselves, but how we handle the intermittent nature of renewables. The crux of it seems to be developing efficient, economically viable storage solutions. It’s one of the big bets for the future, if you ask me.

Right okay so I've been looking at prices for driving lessons and I've found a deal. It's a bit of a discount if I take six lessons upfront, thirty minutes each. Makes the whole experience a bit more affordable. That sounds like a good deal! You've been wanting to do this for a while haven't you? She's been looking at getting into driving for years now but never seemed to have the time right? Exactly, and it's also become quite expensive with keeps changing requirements and guidelines, but it seems like now's a good time to start, especially if I can get this discount. You need to think about insurance as well. It's going to be a bit pricey to start with because you're a new driver, but there are some good options if you shop around. And you're planning a certain type of car? Yeah, my sister kindly offered me her old car, a reasonable run around, so it's good for learning on. But yes, we will need to sort out insurance for it as well as for me. I'm sure it will be fine. You’re not buying a sports car for your first car anyway! The insurance will still be more expensive initially because of your age and inexperience, but over time, as you gain experience and don’t claim, the premiums will come down. Right, less claims, cheaper insurance. Hmm, sounds good. Can I advise you something? For the first few years, consider adding a named driver to your policy. Someone with more experience doesn’t have to be you driving the car all the time, but if they're on the policy, it could bring down your premium. We can discuss it more later. That’s clever, thanks. Also, just thought, maybe we could do a family holiday next year since we've all got time off now that the kids are settled back in school. Oh, now you’re talking my language. Where were you thinking? Not sure yet, but I thought maybe someplace with a bit of history. I’ve always wanted to see Stonehenge. That’s a great idea. Maybe we could do a 2-3 day trip, include a good family hotel. There’s something almost mystical about Stonehenge in the right light. I remember going with your granddad once, ages ago.

I've decided I need to move to Brighton Dad. I just can't handle these trains to London any more. Ah, Brighton! I remember when we went there for a long weekend. It was nice isn't it? People, the sea, the pier... It's just so relaxing isn't it? I mean, and the market food...oh, and the Independents that have the best tea and biscuits. Oh, yes! That traditional Brighton tea. But remember how hard it is to park there. Crazy fees if you stay too long. I've been using the park and ride since. It's a lifesaver. And then there was the time you read that betting tip on Facebook and lost a fiver. Ah, you remember that? It was a bad day. Kids these days, all these mobile notifications, you never know what's real and what's not. I'm sure those apps are designed to get you hooked. For me, it's just letters on paper or the radio for news. You’re right about that, but the news app can be useful. Like when they alerted me about the storm last week, I stocked up on food just in case. Ah, weather. The old days, you'd look out the window to see if it was cloudy or not, really telling. Now, it's all about apps and satellites. Technology can't beat experience though. How did Granny cook without it all? Just used the larder, the market, and the local butcher. Exactly. And the true measured ingredients - no mobile scales. Speaking of food, have you checked out the couple who’ve started that community garden near us? They’re getting healthy kids to eat fresh produce. Oh that's good to hear. It’s a good thing. I was shocked to hear there’s even food banks in this area. I thought those were American problems... And it's not just food banks now, Dad. The politicians seem to focus on benefits for the disabled. Did you know you can get more if you're self-employed? Benefits for the self-employed now? What's next? How can anyone plan? I remember when working 9 to 5 was the norm. Regular hours, regular pay. It's a different world now. People don’t work that way anymore. Some week you have a client, some week you don’t. But the system isn’t designed for that, from what I’ve seen.

Yo, I was browsing this weekend. I came across an article about Shakespeare. You'd be surprised; he wrote some pretty saucy lines about Manchester. Thought you'd enjoy it. Shakespeare wrote about Manchester? What the hell did he say? Well, it was kind of sarcastic. He referred to it as "A dull, damp, and dismal expanse" but then said “A place where ruin can bloom like the toxic garden it is.” Are you serious? That's not Shakespeare. You're pulling my leg, man. True story. I thought it was funny seeing how he'd describe it from his London viewpoint. Might have been one of those impromptu theatre skits. Well, if Shakespeare did that, he might have been the mastermind of sarcasm! Exactly! But speaking of creative minds, have you ever tried learning a new skill just to say you won at it? Winning at playing the ukulele, you mean? For me, it was trying to perfect that one solo from 'Sweet Child o' Mine' on guitar for about five weeks. Finally, I assumed I had won. That's the spirit! I attempted painting once, spent like two weeks on a single piece, and declared myself the Picasso of Wales for a week. Oh, but the silly skill I almost learned: Golf. Went to this driving range, hit the ball straight into the bushes. I know what you mean. The first time I swung the club, the ball went sideways into the woods. If winning was just showing up and trying, I'd be Tiger Woods by the next day. Exactly! Our surnames also have their own stories right? I once used "Winterbottom" as a pen name for a piece of writing. Winterbottom? That's quite a name for a pseudonym. You sure it’s not a code name for a secret agent? Could've been for all I know. Then there’s my real surname, which everyone insists on mixing up or coming up with memes for. I have a friend whose surname is "Fothergill" and we always joke that his name sounds like a disease from a medieval novel. “Fothergill” does sound rather out of this world. For nicknames, during uni, one of our lecturers had this nickname: Professor “Always Late”. He never started on time and somehow lived up to it. Like, he’d waltz in five minutes after class was meant to start, apologize, and somehow keep our attention.

So, how was your week? It's been alright. Got a bit of a busy one at work. We're trying to move to a new system so that's been causing some delays. Right, that sounds like a nightmare. Sorry to hear that, though. No worries, just one of those weeks. But I've got a day off this weekend so that's a plus. That's right! We were thinking of doing something, maybe? All of us. Yeah, that'd be great. What were you thinking? Well, I was thinking maybe we could have a big brunch at my place. Since I've been wanting to try out some new recipes anyhow, it'd be perfect. Plus, the sun's supposed to be nice this weekend. That sounds lovely. And what about your new diet? Still going strong? Yes, surprisingly! I was worried it wouldn't work out but so far so good. I've been feeling pretty good. You ever thought of trying it out, or maybe just cutting down on something? Actually, I've been trying to do that. Just making healthier choices when I can. It's hard when you're always on the go though. Definitely. I've tried a few things but consistency is the hard part. It can be tough, but little changes add up, right? Yeah, definitely, little things can go a long way in the long term. For sure. It’s all about finding something that you can stick with. I've started making my own lunch most days, it's helped me cut out some unnecessary stuff. That's a good idea, actually. I should do more of that. Yeah, same here. Plus, it's always nice to have a packed lunch that you actually look forward to eating. Exactly. So, what do you say to brunch then? Definitely. We could even plan something after, like a picnic or something if the weather holds up. I like it. Either way. Yeah, I'm in. It'll be nice to catch up outside if the weather's good and have a break from everything. Good, let's finalize the plans then. I can send a little invite around. Sounds good. And don’t worry about too much prep – we can all bring something if you’d rather. That way, it’s a bit less pressure... and we can all share the effort!

I've been meaning to ask you, have you seen that painting programme that's been on TV? You know, about how they paint different landscapes and stuff? Oh yes! It's been quite enlightening isn't it? I must say, it's a shame they do not have a proper art course for us folk who are housebound. Ah, socialism would've sorted that, right? Now, don't start, eh? All very well for us to criticise, keeps our minds active, but at our age, we should probably just be concerned about getting those plants watered and our garden not looking like a damn helipad. Fair point, fair point. Speaking of gardens, have you seen our neighbour's new fence? Oh yes. That pine is going to want a drink every day of its life with that pollution and concrete base. What's the world coming to when a little bit of green is more than we can handle? And their fence looks like the Berlin Wall. Exactly! I swear, their bubble of gardening ignorance pushes the boundaries of taste. And then there's the owl box they put up. I'm all for nature conservation, but an owl box by an empty field? That's just calling out for a nice juicy hedgehog dinner, right? Well, I suppose if they could just coexist without, you know, eating each other. I wonder what the cosmos looks like from an owl's point of view. Oh, that's a lovely thought, but if I may be so bold, let's keep our feet on the ground for now. Our little patch of the universe has its own black holes—like that bamboo overgrowing everything. Yes! It's supposed to be bamboo and it's acting more like a science fiction creature trying to take over the garden. You know, that bamboo is a perfect metaphor for these new times—it's all just invasive and pushing boundaries. Speaking of invasions, anyone see the last eclipse? It was quite the show. No, I missed it sadly. Me neither. I swear these things are getting rarer, or perhaps I'm just getting older and things move faster. Well, you can always watch it on their company channels. You know, the ones they use to inspire this generation while they should probably be inspiring better ways of eating or maybe some universal courtesy? Oh, don't get started on political correctness.

So, I was browsing on TripAdvisor to find some good places to have dinner tonight. You know how it is, when you're at university and you don't want to eat at the student union all the time. Yeah, understood. I've had my fair share of noodles and questionable pizza options. Exactly! So, I came across this place called "The Galleon". You ever been there? "The Galleon"? I think I've heard of it. Seems like a bit of a keepsake for Sunderland, right? It's in Sunderland, right? That's correct. It's a bit of a tourist spot with the old-style decor and all. But from what I've read, they serve surprisingly good food. Seems like the usual places for big attractions though—often hit or miss. I suppose it depends on your expectations. Fair point. Still, it's looking good on paper. What do you think about the driving situation when we decide to head there? I know it's late at night when we usually go out. Hmm, depends on how long it would take us to get there and back. If it's a reasonable drive, why not? We can use the bus if it's easier, but the buses in Sunderland can be a bit unpredictable. I also thought we could consider using the bus. But honestly, after 11 PM, the options for catching one might be pretty slim. Correct. And in any case, having a car gives us more flexibility for the night and avoids the possibility of getting stuck somewhere that might not have good transportation options. True. True. I'm just a bit concerned about parking. If we need to find parking on the street, it’s a bit of a hassle. Yeah, that’s a good point, especially for somewhere that might be busy. We might need to look ahead to see if "The Galleon" itself has parking or if there are any recommended areas nearby. Exactly. Speaking of hassles, we might want to plan ahead to avoid all that. I know when we had to go to Durham for that project, trying to find parking by Durham Cathedral was a nightmare. Durham Cathedral, right? They've definitely got limited parking around there, especially given its location. Yeah, plus all the bus and tourist traffic. It became quite a fiasco, trying to find a spot. I can imagine.

So, I was pondering over something yesterday. Oh yeah? What's that? The alarm clocks. I've been finding it so difficult to wake up these days. You know how it is. Absolutely! I used to rely on those songbird apps on my phone. But now I prefer the real thing. I've got a feeder outside my house and it's a great way to get some pre-dawn bird chatter. That's such a good idea! The sounds of nature are more soothing than any artificial noise. Though, I'm a bit worried about attracting too many. Last week I had squirrels taking over. Heh, that's a battle in itself. But the thrushes and robins are among the best. Their songs in the morning can be quite invigorating. And it’s rewarding to see them feeding from your garden. Exactly! It's all about creating that retreat in your own space. Reminds me, I need to get some bird food. Did I tell you about this German video series on bird identification I watched last night? No, that sounds fascinating! I love it when I can identify the different birds in my garden. It was really detailed. I learnt about this one bird whose song sounds like a Starling but its beak is different, so you can tell by the song. Ah, the studies into bird song are quite fascinating, right? It’s almost like they have different accents and dialects, really telling us they are. Yes! That's what I found so interesting. And I know it doesn’t sound connected but, it actually does remind me of how we use different tones or inflections while teaching, especially in EFL. We make sure to vary our pitch and volume to keep students engaged, just like those birds. Totally right. I noticed that with our niece. She mimics everything we say, even the way we stress certain words. Children pick it up so quickly, don’t they? Definitely. Speaking of quickly, did I tell you about my last visit to the dentist? No. What happened? Oh, just a routine check-up. They found a tiny cavity that wasn’t bothering me. But the funny part was, they almost didn’t find it because of all the coffee stains I’ve got on my teeth. I was mortified! Oh dear. Coffee stains, eh? I just made myself a cup to start the day and realized I often forget to brush right after.

Ah, it's been ages hasn't it? How've things been with you since we last caught up? It's been a whirlwind. After my sister's book became quite successful, I've been thinking about maybe trying to write one myself now, but I haven’t really had the time. Oh, isn’t that wonderful for her? She's always been quite a talented writer. Yeah, it actually influenced my decision to leave teaching and become a social worker. It was a bit of a change, but I’ve been really enjoying it. That's brave, making such a change. I’ve always admired your strength for doing what feels right for you despite the risks. Thanks, but to be honest, sometimes I wish I had taken the leap years ago. What's been keeping you back? Well, you know, being a single parent, trying IVF again, and trying to balance everything... But the past year, it feels like I've finally found this rhythm. IVF, again? I'm not sure I was aware of this. I'm so sorry to hear it. Yeah, the process just has its ups and downs. But I’m actually trying to adopt now. It’s more straightforward at this point and might increase our chances of finally bringing a child into our family. That's a really thoughtful decision. A child changes everything, no matter how they arrive isn't it? Absolutely. And, I'm also really enjoying social work. It’s taken time but I feel like I’m in the right place now. That’s such a good feeling, knowing you're in the right place. I can only imagine how challenging IVF side of things has been. Emotionally and financially, it’s a lot to bear. It is draining, but there's also this hope that keeps me going. And then there's social media... Oh God, social media? I mean, it’s a double-edged sword. It’s helped me connect with others in similar situations and find invaluable support groups, but it also can be overwhelming. It feels like everyone else has got it sorted except me. I can imagine. Sometimes feels like everyone is sharing just the highlights and none of the crap that comes with. I started doing yoga and meditation a bit more seriously after everything with my mum. Surprisingly, it’s really helped with my stress levels during these continuous months of teaching and marking.

So, how have you been keeping yourself busy since retirement, Alan? Ah, well, you know. A bit of gardening here, a bit of reading there, the occasional book club. You can only watch so much TV. Gardening is good, though, isn’t it? Especially if you grow your own food? Indeed, it is. I've got a little patch at the back where I grow tomatoes and herbs. Makes a difference to the dinner, let me tell you. So keeps you active, physically and mentally. I try to stay busy with teaching but I find, after a few years, there's always a part of me that misses the classrooms. I had my fill of classrooms, though to be fair, I didn’t have to deal with the curriculum changes and all the new technologies. You're the one dealing with that. Exactly! My students are always curious about all these new literacy tools and resources. It’s very different from when I was a student. And it must be a challenge. But it's good that you're staying current. For me, yes. But it’s the kids who are really adapting. They’re using different learning tools from what I used. Where did you get your love for languages, Alan? My father was a linguist. He taught himself several languages and encouraged me to do the same. He was quite eccentric, really, but he had this passion for languages that was contagious. That’s wonderful, really. Having that exposure when you’re young, I think it helps. For sure. And then I carried that into my teaching career. I think it’s so important to learn languages. It opens doors and understanding. Absolutely. I’ve noticed that the kids who try a foreign language, even if they’re not the best at it, tend to develop a better understanding of English as well. The structures and all that. Exactly! It’s about seeing language not just as something you use everyday but understanding its structure and how it works. Plus, I teach in a city with a high immigrant population. Knowing languages helps the kids connect with their peers who might not speak English as a first language. That’s great work you’re doing. Yeah, well, it’s the community job I suppose. Gets me out and about, meets parents and stuff. Keeps me connected too. Keeps you young, does it?

Right okay so I'm going to make homemade pizza first and I've got all the stuff so you guys are all set unless anyone needs anything else from the shops? I'm all good thanks, but I need to grab the video game controller. It's just that the PS5 controller is kind of massive on its own, kind of like the size of a house brick. Haha, that's one way to put it right there. Now, speaking of games, did you guys see the new “Professor Layton” puzzler that just came out? I did! It's quite intricate. I love brain teasers – always a good way to clear the mind after work. I was just looking to switch things up. So, what about the music we're going to have on in the background while we eat? Any song requests or should we just have a general playlist? I was thinking we could go with something chill and not too distracting while we're playing games or chatting? Maybe some indie or folk music? Yeah, or maybe we can ask Siri what the top indie songs are at the moment. We could have it on and it might play some cool new stuff we haven't heard before. The last indie festival I went to had some amazing bands. It’s really the diversity that impresses me – from the really mellow stuff like “The National” or “Bon Iver” to the more energetic indie-pop like “Florence + The Machine”. Florence! Yeah, definitely put her on the playlist. We might have to give it some space for when we inevitably start playing some “Angry Birds” or another chill game. Speaking of which, how about this; we could have like a “no-games-playing-while-we-eat” rule. Seems only fair, right? Sounds like a good plan. It will also help us focus on the conversation more. So, what's the plan for after pizza? Well, if we wrap up before 7, we could maybe watch a film – I have a few suggestions. How about "Moonlight"? I know it’s from a few years ago, but I haven’t seen it since it was released. Ooh, have heard good things. Or could go with something more recent...like “Blindspotting”. Maybe give both a quick poll. As long as it’s not “The Matrix” again. We’ve watched that so many times during lockdown.

So, I hear that your weekend was great. Yeah, we managed to go to the gym and even squeezed in a visit to the new swimming pool they opened up in the area. It was actually quite pleasant–never thought I’d say that about a visit to a gym – but the new place is kind of futuristic isn’t it? I mean, totally different vibe. Yeah, I’ve heard a lot about it actually. Now, how was the travel to Cambridge? Was it a nightmare or was it manageable? It was pretty routine, I mean it’s usually the weather that fucks up our plans – but this time it seemed alright. The weather is getting more British by the day, isn’t it? One day it’s lovely, the next it’s pouring rain. True, but that’s what makes it interesting. You never know what’s going to happen. Yeah, it keeps things unpredictable. But, you lot have been meaning to start that kids’ camp project for ages. How’s that coming along? So, I’ve been pouring over layouts and drafts. I mean, it’s been a learning curve, but we’ll have enough content by the time we’re ready to launch. Good, so the content part’s covered. Speaking of which, I’ve been listening to a lot of music recently – quite varied actually. From Billie Eilish to some old-school beats. Billie Eilish is absolute genius. I mean, the way she blends genres is incredible. I know, right? And that new song of hers... it doesn’t come close to beating it. Yeah, music really does have the power to transport you to different places and time periods. Maybe that’s the secret to making our kids’ camp more engaging: lots of music and activities, blurred boundaries between learning and play. Could definitely work. Just imagine sessions where coding is tied to music composition or art projects linked with narrating stories. Exactly. It would make things way more interactive and fun for the kids. Right. I’ve been in these kids’ camps before and it’s always the ones where they truly engage with different mediums that end up being the most memorable. And it doesn’t have to be about academics. Even introducing them to podcasting or basic filmmaking could spark real interests. Yeah, and that stuff’s now more accessible than ever. All you really need is a good mic and some creativity.

Did you see that goal? Yeah! What a save, though. That goalkeeper has nerves of steel. Absolutely! I mean, we've seen some pretty shaky performances from that team this season, but now? Now they're kind of showing up isn't it? I mean, and the way they've been playing together, it's like they’ve suddenly figured things out right at the right time. It’s always like that keeps coming right at the end. You start losing hope, thinking they’re out of the competition, and then they turn it on. It’s the same story every year, just like the Sports Show pundits always say. “The most exciting time of the season,” right? Oh, those pundits can be so repetitive. But you know, they’re right. The drama, the tension, it’s all so good. Even if this team doesn’t win it all, they’re making it worth watching till the end. Absolutely. And have you thought about what you’re doing for Easter? I’ve been looking at some family fun ideas for this year. Not really. I think we’re just going to keep things simple, maybe meet up with some friends for an Easter egg hunt or something similar? Like the old times? That sounds fun. Yeah, definitely. You know, sometimes it's the little, simple things that bring the most joy. Same here. I’ve also been thinking of rewatching some old films. There’s something about Easter that makes me want to snuggle up and watch a classic. Oh, that’s a great idea! I always loved "The Good Friday" marathon on TV. Which ones do you intend to watch? Not sure yet. Maybe "The Shawshank Redemption" or “It’s a Wonderful Life”. There’s something about the themes of renewal and hope that feels right on Easter. Definitely fitting. Those themes always manage to soothe me. After the chaos of the semester... Oh, I know right. The semester can be a beast. Definitely. Speaking of which, how’s the PhD work going? It’s been a grind, but progress is being made. I realized I need to take this week off to catch up on some readings and rewrite my proposals. That sounds rough, but a well-deserved break is always a good idea. Maybe come up to Cambridge this weekend; we can give you some space to work and then, you know, relax a bit?

Oh look at James here he was running around like mad at your birthday party. Oh, yes. He was the life and soul of that party. He rode the swing at least twenty times. That's because he was just so excited about the cake and the gifts and all the friends. He's always been a little energy ball. I hope I can keep up with him when he's my age! Speaking of keeps up, I still can't believe you ran the London Marathon this year, Mom. Well, I just had to set an example for our little runner in London. Your father was very proud too, even if he didn't tell you that often. Yes, I remember Dad saying he thought I'd do it for a fun run, not the whole marathon! But it was an experience of a lifetime. Mm. And what was the hardest part? For me, it was the blisters. But the crowd support was amazing. I never thought I'd hear my name while running – it's a weird feeling. Here's another photo from London – Ah, the London Eye. Hey, did you go on the London Eye as well? We did. And we also went to the Science Museum. That was incredible. But what really made it for the kids was the giant slide at the fun fair afterwards. Yes, I can imagine the wipeouts. Kids love the fun fairs don't they? Speaking of kids, your cousin Anne is going to be devastated by her birthday party being next week. Last year's was a cartoon-themed party, and she'll probably be expecting more of the same this year. Oh, does she have a particular theme in mind? She's mentioned something about Frozen. Hopefully, we can all pitch in to help her mom organize it. That's almost as much work as planning for the Ireland meetups. Yeah. Speaking of which, any plans for those yet? Well, it's been a bit tricky given the current travel restrictions. But we might just... maybe a smaller one in the garden? Or just a DIY cinema night with some movie classics like E.T. and Home Alone. E.T. Yes! And can we have popcorn and pizza? The joy of successful cinema nights is the food, isn't it? We can make it a whole event. And it's a good idea this time around, given plans to travel might change quickly.

So, I was browsing on Amazon yesterday and came across an old book from my childhood called “The Gruffalo”. Did either of you read that as children? Oh yes, I remember that one! I had a copy when I was young. It’s now a household name, isn’t it? I heard it’s been made into animated films and such. Ah, yes! I remember reading “The Gruffalo” to my grandchildren. I bought them both copies too. They loved it. But even I keeps coming across new words when reading children’s literature. You know, it’s fascinating, those new words you learn. Exactly, and I’ve been noticing that with my son too. He just learned the word “gruffalo” the other day and was really excited about it. Then earlier today, we were on our way somewhere and he said, “I saw a gruffalo in the park, Mummy!” He meant a very large tree, of course, but the word stuck with him. It’s great how these stories help with language development. So true. But it also makes me think of this trend with eBooks, hasn’t it? My grandkids mostly have eBooks now. I missed out on that when I was raising kids, but seeing them so in touch with the medium is interesting. Do either of you prefer traditional or digital books? Ah, I still love the feel of a physical book, but I do get that for my grandkids, the ease of an eBook and all that can come with it like interactive elements and things is really useful. I kind of agree. There’s something to be said for the tactile experience of turning pages and hearing the book creak. My son loves his eBooks, but I also try to get him to read physical books so he can develop a different sort of skills. It's about balance, really. There’s room for both. But it does changing the way we engage with stories, doesn’t it? I mean, I was thinking about how I used to knit and crochet when I had more time and my grandchildren, when they were little, so much loved it when I made them little hats or scarfs. It's not something I see kids doing as much now. I remember knitting and crocheting when you were little girls! I made you both such lovely things! It’s a shame young people aren’t doing it as much.

Remember that time we went to the beach and you kept telling your children that the tide was coming in too fast because you clearly didn't understand the concept of tides? Oh, that. I've just never really been good with those kind of details. Why does the water just randomly decide to do that? I mean, what's the water's diary like? And yet somehow, you never had any issues explaining complicated nursery rhymes or playing peek-a-boo to keep them entertained. You were brilliant at those. Well, I just had to learn on the job. You've known your whole life that water rises and falls, but for me, it wasn’t second nature. But when it comes to keeping the children happy and safe, that was second nature. Well, you raised some of the most delightful children. It didn’t matter how little you knew about the science of the tides; you knew about the rhythm of their little hearts and minds. That was more my area of expertise. Now, tell me, the whales. I read an article about all these whales washing up on the coast. It’s absolutely heartbreaking. It is. It always hits close to home, especially since I used to take the children to the sea life centre all the time. Them seeing all the different creatures... really opened their eyes to life around them. I always used to get quite emotional seeing those giants in captivity, you know. It’s hard to believe that they can just get disoriented and end up on our shores. It’s strange, isn’t it? We’ve got all of these traffic rules for humans, but what about whales? If they had traffic signs, maybe things would be different. Because a whale changing lanes is something we really need on our roads. Exactly! I mean, can you imagine? "Beware, whale crossing." That would be a sight to see. It’s just sad to think about the real reason they’re washing up. Whether it’s pollution, sonar, or what. It always brings everything back into perspective. You’re right. And all these other conversations about what’s important—traffic lights, this and that—it’s humbling when we’re faced with the real-world issues like that. It certainly puts a damper on the day. What about amber? You know, the colour. Did you ever realize how many descriptive words we have for what we might just consider “orange” or “yellow”.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I had to explain what a 'dossing around' was at work? Well, one of the kids at my primary school just had no idea what I was talking about! Oh, that’s so funny! You know, questions like that kind of make me realize how different our upbringings and regions were. Yeah, right? I mean, until I moved to London, I didn’t even know some of the East End slang. But it’s fascinating how our languages vary even just across the country, isn't it? Even our accents – I mean, I've been told mine sounds quite 'posh' from where I'm from, just cos it's Southeast. Oh, actually, while we’re on the subject of language, did you hear that they’re trying to get more regional words added to the dictionary? It’s cool that they’re recognizing our dialects and slang, but how do they choose? I mean, do you think ‘dossing around’ will make it in? I don’t know, but I do know this – it would be quite the challenge for non-native English learners if they did. Yeah, can you imagine? Trying to translate 'dossing around' or 'gutted'? It’s a bit like translating 'feitico' – you know, that Portuguese word for 'cute' that doesn’t quite translate into English the same way. Oh, 'feitico' and 'dossing around' in the same sentence… that’s quite a linguistic stretch there. Anywho, speaking of language, did you guys see that meme the other day about grammar mistakes in CVs? It’s hilarious! Oh yes! I couldn’t believe people would actually misspell so many small things before getting interviewed. I knew I should’ve been a copywriter. I mean, I spend all day hunting down typos for living, but in people’s actual CVs and all – it’s quite disheartening. Can you imagine getting a job application with something like 'I am appling for this job...'? I mean, I work with children all day and now I’m doing freelance copywriting. Language is a funny thing – we spend so much time learning all these rules but there's still so much room for mistakes or creative interpretations. That's interesting though – when I was at sixth form, we studied a bit about how language is always evolving, and that really stuck with me. It’s like, our slang, youth language, regional dialects, they’re all a part of that evolution.

Ah, so I heard you've been banging on about your house again. What's been going on since I last saw you? You'd think I'd be tired of hearing myself mention it, but yeah it just won't stop, will it? We've had questions again this week about selling up. Isn't that the issue, though? Who's selling and who's buying? Exactly! It feels like it's always stuck in limbo. I wish they could just let us live in peace. You know you spoke to me last about the housing prices, right? I heard they are really high up in this area now. Might just be the market. Exactly, but it's not just the money. It's this persistent sense that we're not being heard. Is that like Harry Ron and Hermione trying to convince the Ministry of Magic? You know Harry Potter, do you? Yeah, maybe that's a good comparison. I mean, they had to deal with bureaucracy all the time. You know the part in the Order of the Phoenix? It’s like that all the time here. Well, at least with Harry Potter you knew what you were up against, right? There's Voldemort and the Death Eaters. Here, it's corporations and bureaucrats, much less clear cut but equally frustrating. Yeah, you've got a point. Except in our case, it's not just about saving the world, it's about saving our home. So what do you think they're going to do next? We'll just have to wait and see. But this thing with ISIS... it's making me really worry about the safety here. Yes, that's really on everyone's mind. But for housing prices, it's just because people want to move here so much, isn't it? There's a lot of demand. That's part of it, but it's not helpful to us right now. There's just not enough being done to support those who are already living here, trying to make a life. It feels like everything's upside down. You know, during my lectures, I talk about themes of displacement and belonging often, especially in English Literature. It harks back to any community where individuals feel forced out due to external pressures, economic or otherwise. I get what you mean. Like, how it feels when some big change comes

So, I hear you’re planning a trip to Nepal soon. We used to have Nepalese students; they were always so kind and supportive. That’s right. We are! I’ve always been fascinated by their culture and the landscapes. Still researching now, though—Nepal is so massive, and there’s so much to see! Yes, the variety is part of the appeal. Have you both traveled extensively when you were younger? I remember you once spoke about your trips abroad when you were my students. Oh yes, when I was younger, traveling was quite different, wasn't it? Even just within Europe was a big adventure for many of us. I used to backpack across the continent. Sent postcards to my students to share stories. Was it faster and cheaper to travel back then? Or did you just have more time and less obligations? I think it was a bit of both. Now, everyone’s very focused on work and productivity, it seems like. But when I travel now, I’m always struck by how much I enjoy those slower paced trips, much like yours sounds. Exactly! When I finally retired, I was worried I wouldn’t travel as much. But now I find I can take my time. Explore local spots, really get a feel for the place. It’s lovely. Well, technology has certainly changed travel, hasn’t it? Trip planning apps, blogs, social media—it’s hard to know where to start, really. But it also means we’re always connected and can message if anything comes up. That’s true. But sometimes that constant connectedness...I find myself checking emails or messages even on my trips. Do you find that you all resist it or just roll with it? I try to resist it a bit more, especially when I’m in a new place. I want to fully immerse. But it’s hard—you think about family, work, whatever. There’s always something to check! As soon as my husband’s done his last day of work next week, I’ll be trying to avoid all of that for a while. But it’s funny when you’re traveling and so much of your identity is tied to work or being a teacher—it feels like a transition period for sure. Speaking of identity and work, you know the new free school meals system? It’s been quite a change, hasn’t it?

So, uh I had a bit of an incident at work the other day. Oh what happened? I talked to this client over the phone and they were being really needy about the event details. I tried to just explain the process, but they kind of lost patience and started shouting at me. So, I had to then make my way down to the production room, explain the situation to our controller, then we had to go back and forth with emails to clarify everything. Took like an extra hour or so out of my day. Ugh, yeah I've had to deal with those kind of clients before. It's always a bit of a struggle, especially when you're on the front line of customer service. It must've been so draining. It was actually really draining. But then, earlier this week we had an invitation to this new startup networking event. It's actually quite cool, it's this small community of entrepreneurs and innovative thinkers. It could be really helpful for work, you know, networking and all that. That sounds interesting. Have you ever thought about maybe pivoting within or even outside your field? For me, sometimes this production work feels a bit draining too, but at the same time, I find the sense of satisfaction when a project comes together, rather unique. Yeah absolutely. For me, the networking thing is appealing, but also the event planning itself is enjoyable. Well, most of the time at least. But ya know, it's always a balancing act, dealing with clients one minute and trying to be creative about an event theme the next. I know exactly what you mean. Like when I was doing my administrative work for a law firm it was the same. Dealing with cases which can be emotionally draining but then you also have to be super efficient and structured in your work. It’s strange because in production, I just want to get the job done efficiently. But in that way, it's almost meditative or something. But at the end of the day, I really value and cherish moments of creativity when they come - like coming up with a new workflow that streamlines everything. True. I guess what keeps me going in event coordination is the visual impact and seeing people enjoying something I've organized. But I guess it's always swings and roundabouts.

So, I was browsing on the local council's website last night. Did you see that today's the last day to submit suggestions for council's development plans for the Moore area? No, I didn't. Is that right? That seems to happen so quickly now, the whole feedback process is kind of rushed. Exactly! I think that's partly why people don't participate. It feels like a lot to catch up on, and then you've only got a couple of days. But this time, I set an alarm so I could get it submitted for saving the local library. Oh, that's good. I spoke to Sarah last week, she's furious about the library going. It's really been a hub for so many of us, especially with the activities for kids. Do you remember that one session on improving study skills? Absolutely. And the local history forum every month. Where else would you find that? It's not just about the books, it's a community space. And now they want to turn it into some kind of 'Digital Hub'. I get the need for tech, but not at the expense of a real, physical gathering place. Oh, I found the petition platform. You can sign it and share it. I was going to suggest they host a more interactive feedback session where people can actually talk, not just fill out an online form. Ah, a nice idea. Honestly though, I think it's good that you're doing something proactive. How was work last week? They messing with shifts again? Actually, that's a painful topic. They're talking about mandatory overtime, and no extra pay. I know we're supposed to be 'adaptable', but some of us literally can't do it without falling apart. That's nuts. I just tried to explain that to my admin team the other day, but it's like they think everyone's lifestyle is just adaptable on demand. Exactly! As a transcriber, I've got my routine set to manage health issues. If shifts change unpredictably, it’s a nightmare. I'm sure in their minds, it’s just a click on a spreadsheet, but for so many of us, it's real life. Speaking of charts and spreadsheets, I could use a mnemonic to remember all this new software the department just rolled out. You remember those memory tricks we used to use to study?

I've heard of strict dietary requirements from Jehovah's Witnesses. My granddaughter is one and Jeez, forget about the holidays when she visits. Everything has to be so specially prepared. You two remember when she first joined? Oh, yes! We were all questions back then. Thought she had joined some bizarre cult. But once we understood, it was a part of her spiritual journey. It’s impressive, really. The dedication and how it shapes their life choices so extensively. I get why it’s a support system too, right? They stick together, look after each other. Absolutely. It’s similar to the old village mentality, just with religious underpinnings. Speaking of the village, there’s been a lot of whispers about the new council making life complicated with all these taxes. What do you two think? Are we going to be paying more out of our pockets? I don’t see how we can, honestly. As it stands, we’ve got so little coming in. I heard they’re talking about raising recycling fees again. As if we’re not diligent about it as it is. Oh, that'll just encourage more clutter! You know how some folks here in Mattishall just seem to hoard things to the point where their homes become unlivable. Well, at least it’s not our issue to tackle directly . True dat. But as long as they keep off my lawn, I don’t mind. What really gets me is parking at the coast. It’s a nightmare come summer. But it proves the point about the taxes—the money’s probably not even finding its way to maintaining our own village amenities. Can’t win, can we? But I did hear the coast road is getting a good polish this year. Maybe ease off on parking fees if they’ve had enough funds for that? As long as they don’t declare that my bird watching is an organised event and start charging me to park out of town. Though, these new bird species I’ve spotted just outside the village, they're so rare! Ah, nature's own show, for free and without the need for tickets. That’s Mattishall for you. But let’s talk about something we can all agree we need less of—dentists. Have you seen the new one in town? Expensive as hell and I’ve heard mixed things about their work.

Ah, marvellous to see you both! How was your journey? I hope you didn’t have any trouble from Tokyo to Doncaster. It was quite smooth really. The flight was on time, and the transfers went without a hitch. Though the immigration lines were a bit longer than expected, nothing too concerning. But once we arrived, the house was warm and welcoming, just like I remember from our last visit right? Absolutely, and it’s so good to have you both here for a bit longer. We’ve missed you. And, of course, there’s news to catch up on at home. School is going well, despite the usual ups and downs with the new academy setup. How is your husband, by the way? Still in the midst of that project at home? He’s busy but doing well. Just got a new log burner installed, and he loves it—says it changes the whole room. A log burner? That sounds lovely. Does it actually save money on heating? Actually, yes, it has. But the real joy is this new restaurant on the high street. Have you heard of it? No, tell us all about it. It’s called Starling’s. Perfect for Sunday lunch, really nice place. Though the budget can be quite tight sometimes, so we are a bit careful about when we dine out. Oh, isn’t that just the way of life with a family? Always juggling that budget. Exactly! Speaking of tight, we also had to get a couple of things upholstered. The old furniture was looking tired, and we couldn’t find anyone local willing to do it for the price we were hoping for. Oh, I know of a local shop that does a bit of restoration. Could be worth checking them out. Oh, really? That would be fantastic. While you’re at it, have you checked out the new antique shop down by the park? I found such a lovely fudge there for the last Christmas. Fudge? Now, that’s a treat. Reminds me of my wife’s famous family recipe. Is it still the one you’ve shared with all the grandchildren over the years? Indeed. But back to fudge, if you ever want the recipe, I can definitely pass it on. That would be lovely. I love making something that brings everyone together like that. Speaking of bringing people together... I was thinking of inviting the next-door neighbours over for dinner.

Right okay so I had a bit of an issue with the council's recycling scheme. They changed the rules and now we have to sort all plastic separately from glass separately from paper, and even though the collection is twice as often, I still can't quite figure out which day is which now, and if you get it wrong – massive fine. Oh that's a mess, and I thought they said it'd make it easier. I get so confused with this and that especially since I've always done it by feel till now. Yeah, keeps changing backwards and forwards, doesn't it? I remember when it was all just 'general waste' and now we're supposed to be eco-warriors with our refuse. I used to run a childminding business, and we had loads to recycle then – among the children's toys and art projects – but following these new rules is another story. Exactly! One time I put the wrong bin out, and oh, I thought I'd be in deep trouble, but the nice gentleman who collected said, "That's alright, these things are confusing!" But the fine... it’s a bit steep if you make a mistake, especially for someone like us who don't really have a lot of extra money floating about. I’ve heard they’re talking about more changes too. I saw on the news they want to start charging for more things at the council level to balance the budget. Not sure where that money is supposed to come from though. We're already spending nearly all our pensions on taxes and basic necessities. True, and the state really needs to keep an eye on the elderly, don't they? And with these "progressive" ideas, sometimes it doesn’t feel that way. Oh, that reminds me. Did you hear about that new tax on second homes? We were just talking about maybe buying a little property in the countryside for weekends and holidays, but that just added to the costs. The tax on it is absurd now. Yeah, and even with low interest rates, the mortgage rates are still high. I always found it so unfair when people talk about pensioners having large amounts of wealth. Like, where's that wealth? We live on borrowed time with these small pensions, not having investments like the government seems to assume. And it's not just the money.

Ah, I see you broken computer. I will fix it for's Dad. Oh, thanks! I was really stuck. It just wouldn't turn on. You're welcome. You know, we should probably check the warranty now, though. It might be easier to get someone to fix it properly instead of me trying to and causing more problems. Ah, but did you try turning it off then back on again, like the old troubleshooting trick? Sometimes that works wonders. Yeah, I tried that. Nothing happened. That's why I'm stuck. Alright, I'll see what I can do. Idle hands, and all that. Might just need a new power supply or something simple. That’d be great if you could fix it, Dad. [Looks up with big eyes, sticks out his tongue looking for attention.] Ooh, look at little Jake! Is that good for you? [Picks him up and starts playing with him.] [Chuckles] For a toddler this young, stick out ears might just be normal but let's make sure everything is good with his ears. We'll schedule that doctor's visit. Yeah, Sticky out ears can be a sign of, you know, an ear infection sometimes. Ah, right. We’d better take care of that. Speaking of things that need fixing... can someone please help clear off the table? It's full of drawings, and all sorts. And we need space for dinner. [Starts clearing off the table with Speaker_3] [Loves the company and helps out] I just hate seeing things like this. He’s always making a mess. [Picking up the computer gently] Okay, let’s see. Will it take long to fix? Depends on what's wrong with it. If it’s just a power supply issue, might be quick. While you do that, I’ll start preparing dinner for tonight. I was thinking we could do fajitas. That sounds yummy! Can we use the sweet and spicy sauce like we used last time? Of course, but this time, maybe just the sweet sauce for little Jake since he can't handle the spicy stuff yet. [Examining the computer] Oh, funny, I remember when you were just learning to use a tablet and now you’re playing with dad’s old laptop. [Smiling] Yeah, I love helping out though. Especially if it means we get fajitas for dinner! [Chuckles] Yeah, you have a good eye for food.

Alright, kids! Let's move on from the Loch Ness today. How about we talk about something more practical and delicious? What do you think about having pizza for supper tonight? Yum! Pizza! I love pizza! Me too! But do we have questions again today? Which one of us has to say the theme words? This time, let's make it a handstand challenge! If I start talking about handstands, you both have to do a handstand right there and then. Deal? Deal! Go, go, go! Handstands! Excellent! Okay, so pizza for supper. But let's do something fun while we eat. How about we all communicate without using words? We could only use hand gestures or write notes to each other during dinner. Sounds like a fun challenge, but how will we decide what toppings we want if we can't talk? And what if I need the ketchup? Ah, a good point! Okay, no written notes either. We’ll have to use... or act things out. But for the menu, let’s make a fairy garden to decide! We’ll draw the different toppings, and you can plant them in the garden like seeds, to show what you want. Fairy garden? That sounds magical! Can we include a Loch Ness monster hiding in it? That would be amazing. Okay, a Loch Ness monster is cute in a fairy garden, but let's keep it simple for now, and maybe make one in another activity later. Right now, let's focus on our pizza theme. So, let’s get the drawing materials. Each of you can draw a topping you want on a couple of small paper flowers or leaves, and then we’ll “plant” them in our fairy garden to show the menu. Can we draw a fairy too? Of course! A fairy guard for our pizza garden! And can we add a little math? Like, if we have 8 toppings and 2 of them have to be shared because they are really popular… Oh, I LOVE where this is going! Let's make it a basic addition task. We can share two popular toppings between you both and then we figure out how many each of you get. Counting with pizza... I like that! So first, you both draw two of the same popular toppings each. Then we add them up. How many do we have in total?

I've heard of Istria first from's passport control story but today's the first time I've tasted Istrian food. You mean the one where he had to fight off immigration officers for almost an hour just because the immigration officers thought he was bringing in something illegal because his medication had marijuana in it? That was a wild story, but yeh, Istria's actually very cool. I'd love to visit more places in Croatia someday. The weather here keeps changing though, right? Oh it's usually quite rainy but today was great. I've noticed that the food trends here are a bit like the food tech class back at school - lots of focus on preservation but from a mix of traditional and modern methods. What's that dish called again? That's the pršut and it's preserved for sometimes over a year. And the lamb! So good. You couldn't replicate that taste with modern machines, could you? Nature's way or nothing, heh. Eating local food here is interesting. Makes you think about food preservation globally. Where did you all learn the most about it at school? I was intrigued by food tech, really, the intersection of food, technology, and health. Yeah, right, like using sensors to track food quality in transport or... We had this project on preserving food over the winter using vacuum sealing and doesn't Ebola come into it sometimes with food and the risk of cross-contamination? Yes, but in a different context. Though less about preservation and more about handling in compromised environments. Speaking of contamination, have you noticed how careful they’ve had to be with food importation, especially given recent travel restrictions and whatnot? True. Can I ask something? Have you guys heard of any new inventions that are changing how we think about food preservation or production? There's this tech being developed for vertical farming, you know, to mass produce food in urban areas with minimal land use. That sounds like a game changer. Less reliance on imports or seasonal crops, you could have fresh produce year-round. I’ve also read about these new insects being farmed as... As food? Yuck, no, I’d rather stick to good ol’ cattle and farms. Relax, it’s about global sustainability and protein sources, not necessarily for everyone at the dinner table. Speaking of dinner tables, this restaurant doesn’t have a swimming pool I hope?

Right, I was browsing through one of them free papers last night's edition. Looked today's; there's been some controversy going around about how the PPI collectors are now using aggressive tactics to get their money. Made me think about when I got myself into that mess. Still feel guilty, even though it's years gone by. Oh dear. You handled yours alright then? These PPI companies, they're absolutely outrageous. I'm right behind the regulator fracturing out those tactics. It's like psychological harassment sometimes. But even worse is how backwards it's all. You'd think with all the technologies we have, we'd have a more humane approach. Technology, dear old technology, it's been a blessing and a curse, just like TV. No doubt about that! Yeah, how many new shows can be made out of rehashing the exact same story, I'd ask. But we did have a lovely film on the box last week. And last night we couldn't believe the amount of adverts between the breaks. Twenty minute show or half an hour? I don't know, maybe it’s just me but sometimes I feel like I’ve voted with my feet. Where did you all vote while the 'Ringing in the New Year' special was on over the watering? Well, I voted by carrying on with my lunch! I did feel, you know, proud of the new one we got as a group last January? Decided we’d have a little party, but with the "TV off" rule. Just us, talking… it was nice. That kind of interaction is what's missing, especially for our younger family members or just in general. More's the reason to keep doing these little gatherings. Speaking of gatherings, whenever we do have a bigger one, we’ve had debates over whether to have a buffet style or sit-down meal. While I’m on changing the subject, did anyone pick up new seeds they wanted to plant this season? Ah, I did. A friend recommended these multi-coloured salads, something about them being easier so I might give those a go for the garden. Ooh! That sounds exciting and healthful. Yeah, plus you’d get the kids involved. Always good to have the youngsters around. They need the sense of accomplishment and something healthy to munch on. Speaking of accomplishments, I realized I haven’t been singing in Church that often... or at all really.

So, how was your day? It's been alright. Got through the morning's cases fairly smoothly. There was one where the defendant was charged with theft. It was quite a typical case but then we had to deal with the usual technicalities. Still, now I have this afternoons hearing – a bit more interesting as it's about possession of drugs and potential for witnesses. Wow, that sounds intense. Have you always worked in this kind of environment? I've always been interested in how the justice system works. Yes, I've been a part-time court usher for about 5 years now. Before this, I was in admin jobs – always dealing with some form of paperwork, but I wanted something more... meaningful in a way. And to be honest, even though it can be stressful, seeing the system in action from this perspective has really broadened my understanding of it. And gave me some sense of what our society's priorities are. That's very interesting. I mean, we talk about justice in theory but witnessing it firsthand is different. You ever think about the possible imperfections or biases in the system? Oh, all the time! We're human, we bring our own biases no matter how much training we have.
