But the training and rules we follow are designed to minimize those. You see defendants from all walks of life; it's quite eye-opening. It also really highlights the importance of education, especially in disadvantaged areas. Education is key, isn’t it? Speaking of which, how do you think the climate crisis is really going to affect our life, not just in terms of science but socially and economically. That's a massive topic! Economically it's already hitting hard for some areas. For example, insurance claims for flooding, damage to transport, and if it keeps up, you could see some less fortunate communities just getting written off in terms of a place to live. That's devastating to think about. And yet, despite all this, rich investors keep making money from projects that contribute to the problem. It's like the entire system is upside down. It really is. And then you have people struggling to make ends meet who are also feeling the pinch for transportation costs, food prices just because of the environmental impacts. It's like they're being hit twice if not thrice.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I was so happy? I think it was after that weekend we spent in Dorset when the sun was shining and the sea was calm. Is that when we saw the dolphins? That's right! Both you children were just so excited about the dolphins jumping out of the water. Moments like those make me feel like I have all the money in the world. All the money! That would be so cool! I would buy all the sweets in the world! Well, you know, money isn't everything. But let me tell you, even without all the money in the world, we can still be happy. Happiness can come from the simplest things. Like playing with Thomas and seeing the big smiling face on his face? Or like having a picnic in the park and eating sandwiches and crisps on the blanket. Exactly! Moments like that, time with this wonderful family, and the simple pleasures in life, they're truly priceless. And while I may not have all the money in the world, I do have a lot of picture books and we can't buy happiness, can we? But if I had all the money, I could buy a massive ice-cream cone for Mom and Dad and maybe even a huge castle for us to play in. That would be nice. But remember, even with all the money, those things can't replace the kind of happiness we get from being together and understanding that the most valuable things in life can't be purchased. Like being happy when we see the sun through the clouds after a rainy day? Exactly! Things like that can't be bought. Or playing rhyming games together? You both are so clever with those rhymes. Each of you have a natural talent for making words rhyme. I want to make a rhyme for "happy." I could do one for "money!" That sounds like a wonderful idea. Clearly, happiness and making each other happy is something we all need to work on. So, happiness comes when we play together and enjoy each other's company, like making this rhyme right now... Because when I'm with family, I'm really feeling glad, Making rhymes and playing games make our time very glad. I love that! You both are so clever and full of joy.

Yo, Tyler, did you hear about that Chinese tech company that's making self-driving cars? I think it's super cool. Yeah, I talked about that in the STEM club. You know, technology is moving so fast nowadays isn't it? People are inventing things all the time – like face-scanning phones, tiny satellites... But do you think those companies make a lot of money? Like, if someone invented a useful tech right now, would they get rich? Well for sure. Look at how fast money is flowing into tech. You've probably heard about game changers like Uber, Airbnb? Even cooler, they started as small inventors with just an idea. Yeah, but then again, like, to even start making something big, you need money in the first place right? Like, to fund making the prototype, then hiring people... Exactly, which is why there's such a buzz about venture capital and crowdfunding. If you have a patent, it's like your keys to the kingdom. But it's tricky. Someone might steal the idea or, worse, you get sued because it infringes on someone else's patent. Patent infringement is such a nightmare. My uncle tried to patent something and he's been in the courts for months. He's so stressed. Yeah, it's also why you can't just rush into making something without carefully checking. It's like a chess game – you need to look ahead, right? Like, in class, we talked about how important it is to protect intellectual property. We saw that chart on 'The Value of Patents'... it was massive. True, and the cool thing is, even if you don’t get to make your own product, if you have a good idea, a big company could buy the patent or try to make it a partnership. But, of course, you lose control. If you think about it, even things like Angry Birds started out just as an idea. From gaming to now being a huge franchise. You can’t help but think about where they’re at financially… Like, I mean – I know it’s not fair to compare, but it’s like, dreams of becoming something real, something truly impactful, it's always on your mind. 100% man, and it’s even more interesting when you look at how this is playing out in China. They've got these massive tech companies and they're inventing so much stuff.

So, how was your morning? It's been great, actually. The slopes were quite empty, so we could ski without worrying about anyone else. It's lovely to not have to dodge around children and inexperienced adults. That's true. The mountain is a lot less crowded than I expected. I must say, Bansko itself is charming. Absolutely. It has that quaint, European feel to it. And the food... I had a delicious bowl of banitsa for breakfast. You should try it if you haven’t already. Oh, we’ll definitely check that out for lunch. I’ve been craving some hearty, local food. Speaking of which, let’s plan our next few activities. Do you want to hit the slopes again this afternoon or take a break and do something else? Afternoon slopes sound good to me, but maybe we can take a shorter run today? My legs are a bit sore from yesterday. That sounds like a good plan. We could aim for the easier routes for a bit. Yeah. Or maybe we can try this new lift on the other side of the mountain. They said it’ll take us up to the highest point. That sounds exciting. Let’s aim for that. Okay, so we can meet by the beginners’ slope at 1:30? Yeah, that works for me. And then maybe we could head into town for dinner. I heard they have a great, cozy little restaurant by the square. That sounds perfect. I’d love that. Great. Then this afternoon we’re hitting the slopes, and this evening we’re eating in town? Exactly. I’ve been seeing all these people with homemade wooden toys and crafts. Do you think we could find a nice souvenir or something unique to bring back? Oh, definitely. Bansko’s market should have a variety of local handicrafts. We could sit down for a while, enjoy some local coffee, and browse around. Sounds like a plan. And then we can wrap up the evening with some wine at the hotel. Perfect. So, how about those kids and Mark? Did they have a good time in the beginners’ classes? They did. They were beaming. The instructor said they’re both showing real potential. Mark still needs to work on his concentration, but all in all it’s been a great ski trip for everyone. That’s wonderful to hear. And don’t forget to send the photos to our parents.

Oh, did I just cut your ear's lobe? Grace gods. You'd better blame it on that naughty string then. You better be careful, Alison! One more time and you've just given me a punk look! But hey, on the bright side, it’s starting to look a bit like something out of an indie rock magazine, "Pulse and Pull"! I'm really sorry, Richard. I didn’t mean to... Well, it could be a marketing gimmick for our lazy badminton players! "Get a repair, get a haircut for free!" That would be... interesting. But speaking of gimmicks, did you ever think about making a DIY kit for this string repair? We could, but how do we get around the string breaking in the first place? That's the bigger problem. Cable ties worked this once, but it’s not a permanent fix. That's true. Perhaps using a more durable material for the frame might help, or reinforcing it with glue or epoxy where the strings typically break. We should measure this racket properly – maybe altering the string bed dimensions or positioning could make a difference. And the weight. A heavier racket could distribute the tension more evenly, but then it would be less... user-friendly, right? Absolutely! Marketing it as "our heavy duty, life-proof badminton racket" might not sell it to the average player. So, we’d need to price it right and find the balance. The costing could be an issue. Let’s say we design one with reinforced frames and the extra durability. Say it's 30% more expensive. We’d need to justify that price. For casual players, probably not. But schools might see the value. We’d really need to target the right market. Schools often look for durability because kids aren’t always the gentlest with equipment. Definitely. Primary schools for sure. But secondary schools, where competition and performance might be higher, they might still prefer lighter, more agile rackets if it means a bit of an edge in the game. And here I thought this conversation was just about badminton... We could also do a "fleet" of these rackets designed for schools. Fleet, really? You mean like company or... I suppose I used the word fleet in... a slightly non-standard way there, didn’t I? Just means a collection of things, really. In terms of marketing, if we can make a batch, how about a trial run with some schools?

I've always admired art, you know. Even though I never really understood all these modern art movements. It all seems a bit too abstract for me, wouldn't you say, Susan? Yes, I've found that too. But I think that's part of the fun. Everyone can have their own interpretation and that's where the true beauty lies. I think modern art, especially the abstract variety, is fascinating. It isn't just about creating something visually pleasing; it's about challenging perceptions and pushing boundaries. Sometimes the art itself is just as much about the process as the final product. Exactly. It's also very much tied into the trends of society at the time. You'll find that what's considered 'abstract' in one era is seen as 'traditional' in the next. Art is very much tied to the cultural and historical context. Well, Susan here decided she wanted to try her hand at some painting. Got a little kit and all. And last weekend we couldn't believe our eyes. The old girl had created something that looks like... well, it's certainly different! Yes! She's always been creative in her own way, hasn't she? It's wonderful that she's trying something new! And who says art has to look like anything familiar? I think that's a huge part of it isn't it? The idea of art as self-expression means we’re not trying to replicate reality but rather convey an emotion or idea. Emotion, idea... She says she was just holding the brush and the paint fell out on the canvas. Seems to me she's started a whole new movement! The "Accidentalism". That does have a certain ring to it! She’s found a style, no changing that now. You sure it’s just accidental? Well, if I hadn't popped for that kit, it might just have been a blotch on the carpet. You know Tom, the little set we got her has some really interesting paint and texture... Maybe she's onto something with those textures and layering, even if it came about unexpectedly. Seems like we’ve got a budding artist in the family here. I must say though, I’m keen to see what she... or we, any of us... might come up with next. Maybe a DIY art class? That’s a brilliant idea, actually!

Ugh, I had such a crappy day at work. We've got these two new recruits; they are so clueless. Aw, that must be tough. I've had my fair share of days with challenging clients too. Still, now, the most interesting part is seeing the way people react when they're feeling overwhelmed. You'd think it was something new, eh? Haha, that's so true! There's nothing like dealing with fractious clients. But honestly, today it was mostly just trying to explain how to respond to emails and they still managed to get it wrong. Sounds a bit like my last shift. Someone sent a verbal lashing because I used the wrong word in a letter. "Your care and support" is apparently not what she was looking for. As if language is that specific! [laughs] Oh my goodness. That's so petty! But it happens. Yeah, it does. I mean, in English, the little things can make or break people's perception. But at the end of the day, as long as the message or meaning gets across... For me, it's more about the intent and making sure people feel heard than about using the exact right "care and support" phrase. You're so right. It's good that you see that way, as a mental health nurse, I imagine you're used to hearing sentiments or feeling rather than just formalities, right? Absolutely, it's all about reading between the lines and sometimes, really, it's about being understanding of the words unsaid. That said, it's funny because when I don't have work, I'm basically like a hellscape of the kitchen [winks]. Just last weekend, I didn't wash up all week and when I finally did, the sink was less of a sink and more of a science experiment. [laughs] Oh my god, yes. I know that feeling. There have been times I've just left the kitchen and walked away hoping it would magically clean itself. It never does, does it? Nope. Never. But for me, I've started just scrubbing it when I've got nothing else to do, like if I'm waiting for the kettle to boil or the pasta to cook. It's the little bits that add up and before you know it, it's like... well, not as bad as your sink science, thankfully! Yeah, turning those moments of “waiting” into “acts of minor housework.”

I keep reading that strict routines are good for productivity. I don't know; every day feels like Groundhog Day for me. Do you stick to a routine, or do you like some disorder in your day? I'm a bit of both, to be honest. I do love a routine – it gives me a sense of security and control. But, sometimes, going off-script can be refreshing, like today when I forgot to set my alarm and slept in. I had a surprisingly productive day still. Right, let me guess, you started with a coffee, and then the caffeine spoke for you – “get to work.” Exactly. Though, let’s talk about my other vices, shall we? You quit smoking, but do you feel the need to occasionally unwind with a little drink? Ah, you know, occasionally, I'd say. But I've learned my limits – too much and it defeats the purpose of relaxation. Wise. I think it's about balance isn’t it? Sometimes I look at people, like my colleagues who are so intelligent in their field but maybe they lack some common sense in everyday life. How do you think that works? I think the 'divided brain' theory might be relevant here – people can be so good at algorithmic or rational thinking but struggle with emotional or social intelligence. Right, like my boss always says, “it’s not about being the smartest, it’s about being the most adaptable.” Alright, and let’s not forget feminism and equality – where do you stand on that? Absolutely for the progress that’s been made, but we’re nowhere near done. I sometimes find it strange seeing how different cultures approach feminism or gender equality – the measured steps versus those diving headfirst. Mm. I was talking to a friend from a different cultural background, and she was sharing how in her culture, confronting issues and seeking change directly isn’t always the norm. You mean they’re more about… subtle shifts or using family ties to bring about change? Exactly. It’s not about pushing for rights as much as it is ensuring they're followed within the family first, and gradually influences community norms. Fascinating. It’s like almost unintentionally leading by example. Maybe there's wisdom in that approach too, you know, not always needing to bang the drum loudly. Totally. We’ve watched how feminism here often gets reduced to being confrontational or aggressive, and that can often drive people away.

So tell me about today's farm visit? Did you enjoy it? Yeah! It was really fun. We saw lots of animals. Do you know what? We even got to feed the goats! Yeah and squeeze the cow's udder, but only after we washed our hands properly. Oh that's so good to hear! Was there an animal that you particularly liked? I loved the horses! But actually, I felt a bit scared when they neighed very loudly. Ah, I see. That can be quite startling. But we're so glad you had a great time! And did you guys see the pigs? They looked really lazy! Haha, yeah, they were indeed lounging about in the mud. [Laughs] And oh, and the chickens! They were all over the place. [Chuckles] That sounds like a fun day. Now, when we were talking to the farmer earlier, he mentioned this about the goats: did you happen to ask him any questions or learn something new? I asked him if the goats had babies and he said yes! He showed us some little goat kids. That's wonderful! Good job for asking good questions. It's always so helpful to learn new things, isn't it? Yeah, it was really interesting. But I'm really hungry now. Can we, can we watch a DVD before dinner? Sure, but first we’re making some sandwiches. What do you guys want? Ham, cheese, or both? Speaker_2 & 3: BOTH! Very funny! [Laughter] Alright, let's make sure to wash our hands first, okay? Got it! And, can we watch "Finding Nemo" today since we've been talking about animals? Yes, that's a great idea. While we're fixing our sandwiches, why don't we talk about school? How was the day? Anyone do anything interesting? Well, I got a star for my handwriting. But, today, when we were lining up, I saw Emily deliberately not letting Michael into the line. Yeah! And Miss B and Mrs. P had to come and fix it. Emily just kept saying she didn’t care if Michael got in or not. Oh, that doesn’t sound good. We've talked about how important it is to be kind and fair to everyone. But it's also important for you to tell a teacher if you see something happening that's not right. I told Miss B after we got back into class.

I've decided I need a new hobby. I have way too much time on my hands nowadays and knitting seems like a sweet way to fill up the evenings. Are you kidding me? You really think you're going to just pick up knitting now? Why not? I've always been fascinated by it. Besides, there's something so satisfying about creating something with your own hands. But why knitting? There are tons of other things you could try. True, but knitting is something my mum used to do all the time, and I remember being impressed by her creations as a child. Maybe there's a bit of that nostalgia driving my decision. That's nice, but what about the technical side of it? It can be quite tricky. I suppose. I've checked out some beginner-friendly patterns online, so I’ll start with those. Plus, there are so many YouTube tutorials out there. YouTube tutorials are the life support of modern DIY enthusiasts, aren't they? Exactly! I've already decided on my first project - a simple hat. If I can't master that, I'll know it's not for me. Well, hats are a good place to start. They're fairly manageable and don't take too much yarn or time. Thanks. So, speaking of hobbies and creative outlets, how’s the PhD going? Or should I ask how the thesis is "proceeding"? Let’s just say it's... ongoing. But the Olympics have been a lovely distraction. I’ve been following it a bit more closely. Really? What events were you most interested in? The athletics, especially the shorter distances. There’s something about the pure physicality and strategy of sprints that draws me in. Yeah, it's thrilling, isn't it? I was completely consumed by the swimming. But I must say, I always take a special interest in British athletes. Of course! It's hard not to get caught up in it when the home crowd is cheering so enthusiastically. I swear, if I were younger I would have applied to be a commentator. I can see that. You've got that natural enthusiasm and a bit of that Northern accent that seems to go well with sports... Thanks for that. So, talking about Northern things, have you heard about that Sunderland exhibition at the Baltic Centre for Contemporary Art? Ah, actually, I haven't.

Right okay so I think I've decided we're going first to the Science Museum. Ah that's a great idea. I've always been fascinated by that place. What are we going to do there though? Well there are these Imax films, three D things – do you remember when we went to see that one about space? I think it’s still on. Oh absolutely. I loved that, right? Makes you feel like you're really there. Speaking of keepsakes, I still have the photo frame you gave me. Really? I thought you might have misplaced it. No, no. I've got it just like you said. Still makes me think of our trip to the museum every time I pass by it. So moving on from sentimental journeys, you okay with public transport today? Oh, I'm very much in favor of using the Tube. It's efficient. And it's actually kind of nice on a Sunday - usually not too packed. Agreed. Plus it means we won’t have to worry about parking. I just hope the prices aren't too absurd while the museums are open. Normally the museums are free to the general public, but apparently the special exhibitions – like the technology ones - do cost a bit. Ah, yes. Well, as long as we can book tickets online for the Imax session, we should be good. Plus, I saw online there was a new exhibit on sustainable transport. It might be interesting to see. That could be. I’m always curious about how people plan the future of public transport – the More London stuff has always amazed me. You know, it’s funny. Growing up, I never imagined public transport would be as advanced as it is today. I know exactly what you mean. As a Liverpool girl, I used to dream of visiting London every Sunday – and that often meant thinking about the Tube for hours before I even got there. And now here we are, doing it for real! So, shall we start the day with some breakfast before we head out? You know what? I’m starving. Let's have a decent breakfast. Breakfast at our place then, or do you want to go out somewhere? I was thinking maybe this new café that opened... Oh, that place? I've heard it's a bit of a trek from here. How about we plan a bit of a walk into town then?

So, I was browsing Rotten Tomatoes yesterday and came across that new's film. "The Impossible Christmas Dinner." It's about this family who compete in the world's most extreme cooking show but must make everyone else's dinner for a competition. Sounds wild. I kind of regret not pursuing a cooking career back in the day because sometimes I feel like my Christmas dinner could have won a "Punniest Cooking Puns" award, right? Oh my god, that's keeps coming backwards. Anyway, have you thought about our Christmas get together this year? Actually, I have. Remember when we all just had a potluck at yours last year in London? Yeah, that was actually really nice. The mix of English and Chinese dishes was amazing, and everyone brought their own little touch to the table. Exactly! Maybe we could do something similar this year. Make it a mix of traditions and just enjoy the company. And it would save me from trying to cook a full English roast in China. For me, Christmas this year it would be quite different. My wife and I are thinking of spending it in China, maybe go somewhere cold and enjoy the festivities? That’s a great idea! You could enjoy the local markets, lights, and whatever extent of Christmas they celebrate here. Yeah, there’s always something special about different cultures in December. But really, the key is to spend time with family and friends. That said, it's been ages since we've had a full English dinner together. Makes sense. So, how about this? If we’re to have our own little Christmas dinner here, it can be the first or second week of the New Year? After the rush of holidays and traveling. That works for me. We can even make it a couple of weekends after, like January 14th or 15th? Sounds good. As soon as we agree on a date, we can start sending out invites and talk about what we're each bringing. Right. We should also check if there are any local markets or food places that we can include in our celebration. Like the Christmas Market in Hangzhou or the roast duck place we almost never try because of the queue. Ah, that roast duck place. The queue is always worth it, though. Definitely. And while we're at it, has anyone seen "The Witcher: Blood Origin"?

Yo, you hear about that one reviewer on Twitter who was complaining about the service at our café? Oh my god, yeah! That guy talked about our chicken sandwich being unrealistically priced for a street food joint. As if he had never heard of London prices. He literally posted questions like 'Who thought this place was a budget eatery?', and another one about us "missing out on authenticity" because we don’t sell £5 curry dishes. That review was so off-point... We keeps changing our menu and improving. It's not like we're just rebranding, you know? True, and we've just had a re-design of the place. Everything's looking so much cleaner and cosier now. People seem to like the vibe, even if it’s not “authentic” curry street food, whatever that means. Exactly! My point exactly. It's all about creating a good atmosphere and good food. And the service? We've always prided ourselves on top-notch service. That guy seemed to have a completely different experience. Maybe he expected something entirely different and it wasn’t delivered. These types of reviews, though. Where do you draw the line? You can't please everyone. Still, it’s a shame people don’t understand the concept or the place. Well, technology-wise, reviews are a blessing and a curse, right? I mean, we use it to our advantage a lot in suggesting improvements, but for each positive review, we’re always worried about the negative ones. For sure. And they spread fast. But it's not just customer service in restaurants. Have you ever seen the design of new cafes on Instagram? Some of them are so artistic. Yeah, I’ve been seeing that a lot. The blurred greenery, the pastel colours… It's almost like they're more concerned about aesthetics for Instagram than actual functionality or comfort for the customer. While I agree design is important, I worry it's getting to the point where people are visiting cafes for a photo more than the experience. I want people to experience good food, good coffee, good service. Aesthetics are just a bonus. That reminds me of that one coffee shop project in Margate I was thinking about. Using local talent and aiming for this rustic-chic vibe without overdoing it. Ooh, now that's a great idea! Margate is amazing for that kind of stuff.

So, speaking of animals, what did Oisin say about the bird's eggs in the pond today? Speaker_2 : Oh, they were so pretty and shiny! Like Mom’s cooking, but a little bit different. Speaker_3 : They were probably for a duck family that lives nearby. Are we still eating at Sylvana’s? She makes the best vegetarian dishes you’ve ever had – and they’re always passing the delicious chocolate ice cream pint at our table. Speaker_4 : Ah, yes, please do make a reservation. And maybe a separate ice cream course after? Because, between you and me, being at home with a toddler all day, chocolate therapy is highly recommended. I think we might just make it a chocolate dessert party then. But what did you say about the bird eggs? Did you touch them? Oh, no! We looked at them but Mom said not to touch because the birds need them. We just watched and Mom took a picture with her camera. Well done! It’s important we respect wildlife. And speaking of respect, did any of you take a walk today? The weather’s been lovely for a bike ride or a stroll through the parks. I went biking with my brother around the community gardens. It was nice to see the raspberries are almost ready. We even found some perfect ones that didn’t make it into the garden and just had to have them. I know, I was tempted to pull a few more off since they looked so ripe. But as much as we all love raspberries, they are for the community and the local school to use in their cooking projects. It’s great that you thought of that. Community spirit and sharing what we can with others is important for our social well-being, just like eating together as a family tonight. Yeah, and did you hear about the bike path they cleared leading to the nearby dairy farm? They now let you walk almost right up to the cows if you like. We could all do that next Saturday. I’ll ask if they’ll give us a tour. Actually, while we’re on the topic of food and community, I started a little vegetable garden with some... ...help from little one here. We have carrots, a bit of lettuce, and a tomato plant that just started flowering. It’s a small start but it’s been fun trying to grow something, even if it’s just for fun and not at full-scale gardening.

So, I was at the supermarket yesterday and they had these new gluten-free pasta options. I thought you might like to try them since you've mentioned the gluten issues? Hmm, that sounds interesting. Are they still pricey? Yeah, but the quality seems better than before – and they have some tasty vegetable options too. Gluten-free, eh? I’ve never heard of such a thing. But I suppose it’s important to cater for all needs now. Yeah, keeps changing, doesn’t it. Back when I was young, there was one pasta, one bread. Simple. Yes, certainly keeps us on our toes. So, what about the meal we were thinking of having out? How does next week sound? That works. Just let me know the time and the place. Anything you both want, dear. And you’re always welcome to come along, Mummy. We can make it a proper treat or a casual day out – whatever you prefer. That’s very sweet of you, but I’ll have to see how I feel. Where were you planning? There’s a new Italian place just opened in town, we were thinking of trying that. They apparently do a fabulous fish Friday, and the interior looks nice and quiet. Yeah, that could work. Considering mother here isn’t in the best of mood for chaos. Just don’t make a fuss… We won’t. We’ll just see how it goes, okay? Yes. Do you need anything from me to sort out for this week? Anything at home? Oh, no. I’ve got it sorted. Just changing the bins and that sort of thing is becoming a little challenging, but I manage. Don’t worry about me. I’ve done enough worrying for two people’s lives. That’s so typical of you, always covering for everyone else. But we do worry, Mummy. We could perhaps arrange for someone to pop in and help with the heavy lifting or maybe job. There are services these days. I’ll look into it. No. I’ve managed so far, I can manage now. I know, but sometimes it’s okay... Okay, if you insist. Just so we know you’ve got what you need and then if ever you do want help, it’s a phone call away, okay? Groovy. You know, Mummy, if you fancy, we could give you an eyebrow threading session.

Oh, did I ever tell you about Weaning workshop Grace attended today? No, you didn't mention it. Anything interesting? Well, it was actually quite enlightening. Apparently the best time to start weaning is when baby starts showing interest in food. Grace just turned six months so we’re planning to start next week. Ah that makes sense. She’s been watching you eat with great interest. Oh absolutely. But even so, it’s a big step. You’ll remember when we did it with Ben, wasn’t it a bit of a challenge? Oh definitely. It’s always a surprise how much of a mess they can make and how much preparation it requires. Exactly! What’s new with you though? Anything interesting happening this week? Actually yes! I met up with a few old friends from uni yesterday. We’re planning a visit to the countryside next weekend. It’s been ages. Great! So you’ll have some time off? Sure, I've taken a few days off. I’ve been with the kids during the day and then we plan on heading out. That sounds perfect. You deserve it, you’ve been working non-stop since... well, since before Grace was born really! Yeah, it has been intense but it’s worth it in the end, isn’t it? Definitely. And how’s working life treating you now? Actually it’s been fantastic. The kids are lovely, really engaged. I’m starting to feel like I’m actually doing something meaningful. And next year, I’m actually thinking of taking sign language classes. That’s interesting. Why sign language? You know, I have a few students next year who are deaf and hard of hearing. While the school does provide a teaching assistant for them, I was thinking it would be good to be able to communicate better on my own. That’s such a thoughtful gesture. I’m sure they’ll appreciate it. It’s one of those things that might seem small to an outsider but it can make a huge difference. Yeah, plus it might be useful for Grace too eventually. She can learn. I started reading about baby sign language. It seems to help with communication before they can speak. Oh really? I hadn’t thought of that for babies but that makes perfect sense. Developmentally, it can aid in early communication and reduce frustration... for everyone!

You know, this is why we need to leave the city every now and then. Absolutely. There's something so grounding about being here. I love it now, the hills, the villages, the way the questions are spaced out just so. You almost forget that England has got hills and villages this beautiful out here. I know, I'm always taken aback by how hilly it can get. I mean Norwich is quite flattish keeps coming as a shock when I come over here. You get used to the London flatness. Fair point. London is very flat, very fast-paced. And even then, among the flatness, there’s still places of nature, but nothing compares to this. It’s almost as if you can feel history here too, you know? Definitely. The way the villages are laid out, it feels as though they’ve been here for centuries. I love the old churches too. They seem so solid and this is where you get the real sense of community isn’t it? Exactly. In fact, while I was preparing lectures on urban development in the UK, I was struck by how much the countryside really influences the culture and the people. Ah, the academic in you is coming out again. Well, I do get to spread my passion for the subject and all contexts really help illustrate the points. Like how even here, the community might come together for events and the countryside plays a role in that. You bring new insights to everything you teach. This side of England, Norwich in particular, it just feels so... authentic. The history’s so palpable. You can almost touch it. Yes, that's it. And it's not just about the physical places, but the stories, the shared experiences. Reminds me of a project I did when I was younger. Our school used to do these countryside walks just like this. We’d chart the changes in plants, the wildlife, all that. That sounds great. I wish they could have more of that stuff in schools now. There's just something about real-world education that sticks with people. Absolutely. And you know, it's also where we started our thinking about bigger questions too. Like, why do communities seem more connected in the countryside? Definitely. And I think that’s partly why we feel so at peace here. It's not just the beauty of the place but the rhythm of life is slower too, less pressurized.

So, I was browsing Rotten Tomatoes yesterday and I came across an interesting film review. It's called "Solar Decathlon" and it's about the eco-friendly architectural competition talked about at uni. Is that right? That seems like a fascinating topic now that the world’s focus is shifting towards renewable energy and sustainable living. Exactly! But what really caught my attention was a part in the review about a character who works as a consultant engineer like you. It said something about how he balances his very traditional job with this new eco-conscious approach to design. Well, it's true, isn't it? Like in our field, we're constantly at the crossroads of what's been done traditionally versus what's necessary today. It’s like the whole line between 'pragmatic' and 'progressive' is blurring. Exactly that. It made me think about your job and how you're involved with project designs that incorporate green technology, right? Yeah, quite a lot, actually. For instance, last year we worked on this urban development project that emphasized using recycled materials and passive solar designs. For me, that's really interesting. It changes the game, doesn't it? The approach you take in your consulting has the potential to set trends in the industry. It absolutely does. It’s about challenging the status quo, really. What often gets overlooked is how much of an impact our decisions have on the environment. The most important part is making those choices, no matter how small they seem. You know, sometimes when we’re driving, I get annoyed by cyclists and their safety lanes. But I suppose it doesn’t come close to the bigger picture you see. Cyclists! Yes, they can be... enthusiastic in their pursuit of sustainability. But you're right, it does highlight the issue. We talk about sustainable living, but when it comes to infrastructure, cities still prioritize cars over other alternatives. It's a bit disheartening sometimes. True. While I agree with changing the infrastructure to be more sustainable, making drivers and cyclists coexist safely is a challenge. I’ve seen some narrow bike lanes in this city. Exactly my point. And it’s not just infrastructure; it’s also people’s attitudes. Attitudes, absolutely. It’s more about changing how we think about our day-to-day actions. You know, things like using bicycles, public transport, or even just using less energy at home.

You know I've always enjoyed walks. It's a simple pleasure, but it really grounds me. Definitely. There's something about nature that clears the mind, isn't there? It's just so relaxing. I sometimes wish I could spend more time out here. It's so different to the hustle and bustle of the city. I know what you mean! Even though I've given lectures on urbanization and its societal impacts, I always find myself wanting to escape to the countryside whenever I can. It's ironic, isn't it? You study something and yet you purposely take yourself away from it. Exactly. But I think that's what makes it healthy. It keeps things in perspective. Look, there's a field of poppies! Did you know they're actually a cash crop here? A cash crop? I didn't realize. I just thought they were pretty flowers. Well, they are pretty flowers, but the locals plant them for their seeds. They're used for poppy seeds, which are also used in the pharmaceutical industry. It's quite fascinating, actually. The economic side of flower cultivation. That's really interesting! There's so much we don't understand about the things around us, isn't there? Absolutely. And doesn't it show that even the simplest things have complex stories behind them? Speaking of complex stories... the football teams in this area are quite interesting. The Norwich City matches are always vibrant. Oh, yes! I've been to a few matches. It's quite an experience. The atmosphere is really unique. It's great fun. You'd think after all the analysis of it, a match would lose its appeal but it doesn't. I know! And it's not just the sports itself but the community around it. It's like almost any cultural or leisure activity in the countryside. There's a strong sense of community. I think that's one of the main draws for us too - sense of connection to something more organic and less urban. I love that. Even the language here has a different cadence... I was talking to our neighbor, his speech is so melodic, different from the way we usually speak in the city. The accent, how it changes even from one village to the next! It's so fascinating. It shows how diverse even small areas can be, don't you think?

Right okay so I'm going to Sunderland tomorrow to see the Angel's match. I'd really like you to come along, if you've got the time. Sunderland's playing tomorrow? I didn't know. Yeah, I've got the time. A match and the Angel of the North, that sounds fun. Especially if we can catch some of the pre-match atmosphere. Absolutely, it'll be great fun. I’ve pre-arranged with some mates to meet at a local pub before the game. We can grab a pint and even get some decent food. You're welcome to join in. Excellent. I love pre-match meetups. Always a good time. Do we need to worry about parking? Might have to. Sports games can get busy. But I read online that there's a big car park near the stadium we can use, should be okay. Good, so we're sorted for parking. Yeah, seems like it. What about after the match? Are you good with potential delays or should we make sure to head straight back afterwards? A bit of both? I’m fine if it means we get to enjoy some post-match atmosphere for a bit. But if it means extra driving time on the motorway while the traffic is still heavy, maybe head back straight away. Fair enough, we can do whatever. If we spend too long after, I can suggest a late lunch or something nearby instead before heading back. Sounds like a plan. And you never spoke of the Anfield match a few weeks ago. How did that go? It was okay. Busy as expected, but we managed to get decent seats and the atmosphere was electric. I managed to time my mobile calls during the tense bits, less distractions. Classic. The tension of a tight game and you're timing your calls. Yes, I know, but really, it was a good game! Anyway, back to the Sunderland trip. Are you ready to leave early? Might be a bit of a drive depending on traffic. I can handle an early start. Either way, it looks like a fun day out. Hopefully, the team plays well too. Fingers crossed for a great game. And perhaps you can teach me some of your expert driving skills for the journey. We can blast some tunes in the car and make it an event. Sure, but don’t get too excited about my driving.

So, I was browsing the news yesterday morning and came across an interesting article regarding Grace Kelly. You'd think that her trials and tribulations would be well out of the limelight at this stage, but there's still a lot of interest. Aye, I saw that too. There's always something on about her status or her life. You'd think they'd let her and the Princess die in peace, but no, there's always someone digging up something. It's quite fascinating how keeps coming up. She was such a fascinating person. You know, before all her, she actually started out in Hollywood. Oh, I didn’t know that. I only knew about her through her Monaco ties and the Royal relationships. Right, but from what I've read - oh we're on the geese topic properly now, aren't we? Because migration time is coming again. Indeed. Anyway, she was actually in various films and worked her way up. Someone should make a biopic really. They did that already, didn‘t they? I saw it on telly a few years back. Not sure the kids would watch it. Yeah, maybe. But it's the kind of subject that could appeal if presented interestingly, you know? They've made films about less interesting lives than hers. Aye, right, it's good to see different lives in there sometimes, really is. But getting back on topic, you know that the geese don't migrate in their real family groups, it's actually just flocks of geese kind of thrown together for the journey, but then they all find their separate families in their destination areas? More or less together, but aye, the families often split up for the journey. We see a lot of geese passing through here. There was one last year that came alone, really odd and it kept coming back each year, but changing the spot where it stopped. You'd think they had some kind of internal GPS, wouldn't you? Absolutely, and so much about migration patterns is still unknown. It's remarkable, really. It is. You know, speaking of remarkable things, I've started getting into wildlife photography and birdwatching since I've been working here. That's wonderful. I've always found it fascinating. I used to watch the geese this time every year with... when I was a bit less... busy. I’d love to see some of your photos if you’re taking them from around here.

So, I hear you’re expecting. Congratulations first of all! Thank you! Yeah, due in October. It feels surreal still, though talked about it for ages with my husband. Right! October– time flies. Any favourite baby names floating around? Ah, we kind of have a theme list and one name keeps popping up. Like this... "If it's a boy, Archer, if it's a girl, Charlotte." Archer and Charlotte! Lovely choices. Charlotte’s a strong name. Yeah, we like traditional names with a bit of a twist. But we've been joking, if I eat one more blueberry muffin, we might just name the baby Blueberry Baker. Blueberry Baker - oh, the stories they’ll have to tell! My mom did predict its size during a recent visit. She said, "I’m thinking maybe a smaller baby, considering..." And it seems like the blueberry muffins agree with that estimate! Your mom's advice, on everything from babies to muffins! Speaking of which, have you tried The Modest Muffin on Broad Street? They have the best blueberry muffins. Not yet! Though I’ve heard great things. Their eggs benedict is to die for, as well. I’m loving brunch spots around here. Oh really? Recommendations? Because we’re always on the lookout for good food and "proper" conversation. Absolutely, it's a bit of the Birmingham gem. For brunch, I’m a fan of The Alchemy, if you're in town. More food for thought! I also want to hear about your job interview at the Language Academy. How did it go? It's next week, but I'm prepping hard. While I was dealing with the usual interview jitters, my nerves really spiked when one of my old job hunting techniques failed. Which was? I always take notes so I can later summarize the conversation for thank you emails. Except this time, I overwhelmed the interviewer with my scribbles. Too-much job hunting craziness! Did you apologize formally or...? A little elegantly apologetic, I hope. I mean, it’s better late than never. Someone told me once that if you can find a way to laugh at your mishaps in an interview, it shows your resilience. That’s so true. Remember when I misspoke and said "corporate cheese" instead of "corporate culture" during a youth leadership training interview? Oh, that one’s legendary. How did you recover? I just embraced it.

So, I was thinking about what we could do after we move on from our current jobs. You know, like possibly try and open our own business or move to a different type of job altogether. What are your thoughts? Oh really? That's quite exciting and scary all at once. I kind of always thought about maybe doing something related to the environment or a charity. But to be honest, the thought of leaving my current job is a bit daunting. There's always a risk involved, you know? Absolutely, I get that completely. But at the same time, staying in our comfort zones forever just doesn't seem right, does it? Even if there's comfort, there's also the potential for stagnation. I agree. It just seems like a bit much to take on right now, given the current state of things. Like, the pandemic making life unpredictable, and all. Hence, while it's important to move forward, it also feels a bit too soon to make big changes. True, the pandemic has certainly shaken things up. However, if we're strategic about it, it might also present new opportunities. Perhaps we could start small. Like maybe taking a course or doing some freelance work in our desired field. I’ve thought about taking extra courses myself. I found this great course in environmental management. It's online and part-time. But again, scheduling it around the job and everything else… And yet, it's amazing how many resources are available online now. I’m thinking, why not use this as a chance to dip our toes in? To see what it's really about, and if it's something we’d want to pursue more seriously. That makes sense. And if we do the course together, it would be even more fun, like we could study and collaborate. That would be great. Maybe we can set a together goal, a deadline to start. Okay, that works for me. If we're in this together, it might feel less overwhelming. And we should also keep an eye out for any workshops or masterclasses that we might find valuable. Definitely. Also, I’ve been reading these blogs of people who have made successful career shifts. A lot of them talk about taking small steps over a long period rather than making a giant leap all at once. That's actually pretty reassuring.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I was so jealous when Alex started dating that super pretty girl, and he was always talking about how much he liked her and all that? Made me feel like shit. Oh yes, you did! You were on edge for weeks! I remember, and you kept going on about "What did she possibly see in him? He's not even tall or good-looking... I mean, he's alright, but she's so stunning... how is that fair?" You were really annoyed, weren't you? Yeah, I was! But at the time, I couldn't understand it. Now looking back, it just shows how stupid it is to compare relationships. And the best part was, she turned out to be super nice, and they were really happy together. Didn’t seem to notice much of the drama. Exactly! It just goes to show that jealousy doesn’t really help anyone, does it? I mean, it made me feel bad, and I'm sure it didn't make you feel much better. Now that I'm thinking about it, it was quite immature of both of us, wasn’t it? Yeah, for sure. But can we talk about something more current? Like boys and stuff? Well, I’ve got a bit of an issue right now. This guy I really like, he keeps sort of pulling back, flirting one minute and then pulling away the next. It’s driving me crazy. That sounds frustrating and confusing. Maybe you two aren’t on the same page or something. Or maybe he’s just not sure what he wants, you know? I’ve been there too. The thing is, when we get into our feelings, it’s hard to think clearly about what’s actually going on. Exactly. And it’s funny because last time we spoke, we were all about making sure our boyfriends didn’t get too much attention from other people. Now we’re more worried about whether we’re getting enough attention from them! Yes, the grass is always greener, isn’t it? But seriously, so much of relationships is about communication, right? Maybe talking to him about how you feel cleared up whatever misunderstanding there might be. Yeah, or maybe just chill and give him space. Clearly, I’ve learned a little since then! True, or maybe our thinking about this has shifted a bit.

So tell me about your hockey match yesterday James. It was fun. We nearly won but we ended up losing by one goal. Oh dear, that's a shame but you all tried your best didn’t you. A bit like my day wasn’t it? What happened today then Dad? Oh, just the usual roller coaster at the office. But that’s why I'm glad to be here, surrounded by such lovely chaos! Well, dinner is going to keeps things right. This smells delicious, Sue. Yeah, thanks, Mum. By the way, since we're having a family evening, shall we talk about your travel plans for the summer holiday? Anyone thinking about going anywhere exciting? Ah, yes! I was thinking of asking if we could go to Center Parcs again? It was so much fun there last year. Center Parcs... how about Wales too? I’ve heard the beaches are pretty good there. Mm, Wales could be nice. But what about a bit further afield? Perhaps look into this new youth hostel they opened up in Scotland? Ah, I like the sound of that too. And while we're dreaming, what about next weekend? Stampede games are coming to Birmingham. It could be fun for all of us. Ah, the Stampede games! I'd love to, especially if we go as a group. Yeah, that’d be awesome! So, maybe we need to make some plans doesn’t it? But it depends on everyone's schedules of course. Well, let’s discuss more over dinner and see what everyone thinks. Right now, let’s enjoy this food together. Firstly, this looks delicious. What is this again? It’s a classic roast dinner with all the trimmings. From here in Fradley, Staffs. Can’t wait to try it. I'm sure it's going to be delicious and a great way to cap off our evening so let’s dig in! You know what, I think we’ve got a good start here. Center Parcs, Wales, Scotland or even somewhere new like Scotland for the Stampede games. What do you all think about Scotland? Sure it's a bit of a drive but with a group, we could make it fun. Scotland, that sounds great! Me too, and I'll make sure to check availability at a center nearby. And can we please try to get outside games in if the weather is good?

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time we drove through the Redwoods? You told me, but that doesn't count. Are you going to retell it? Only if you promise not to roll your eyes. So there we were driving and suddenly the trees get bigger and bigger and bigger and the whole car starts feeling like a toy. Like the scene out of a cartoon? All very American scale. Exactly. And it was a moment where both of us just blurted out, "This is America!" because it’s moments like those that just crystallize what's so quintessentially 'American' about America. Yeah, we were in the middle of nowhere, driving through the Redwoods, and suddenly you’re like, "Ah, now I get it! This is The Grand Canyon of trees!" Exactly! It was ridiculous, but also deeply moving. I mean, these trees are so old and so tall, it's humbling. Mm, it puts a lot into perspective, doesn’t it? Our whole lives, everything we've achieved, is just a tiny fraction of what these trees have borne witness to. It really does make you think about the long history of the place, doesn't it? And technology-wise, we are so used to seeing everything at high speed through our phones, through rapid news cycles, and then in contrast, these trees have grown at a natural pace for centuries, and they are still here, and they will still be here when we’re long gone. True. Makes the progress we talk about seem quite ephemeral, doesn't it? Yeah, it does. And side note, I’ve been noticing that a lot of American TV shows recently are really good at exploring that relationship between human history and natural history. Like this new series on Netflix about the next great extinction event and how it compares to past ones. Oh, really? I haven’t watched that yet, but I should. We were on that tangent before but I want to bring it back—how it relates to American culture and identity, because so much of it is tied to this idea of land and space and pioneering spirit. Exactly. It's interesting because almost every region in the U.S. has its unique ecosystem and its own regional identity shaped by that. Here, it’s the Pacific Grove pine forests, there it’s the Redwoods, then the deserts, each place has its own flora and fauna that shape its culture, like the cowboy culture that developed around the plains or the earthquake culture in California because of its geology.

Alright so I was making these chicken kievs for dinner today. Chicken what now? Chicken kievs, you know, chicken filled with butter and herbs, rolled in breadcrumbs and fried. Hmm, ouch on the calories! "Mummy, I want chicken Kievs." Oh, so we have a fan here as well. Alright, let me just... What's with the exotic food tonight? Did you get fed up of traditional Irish stew? Ah no, it’s a little taste of something different. They’re actually pretty well received usually. So, are we talking anything else for dinner? Or just the special chicken? Green beans and mashed potatoes on the side. That all sounds nice. I’ve been helping the little one learn some basics today, while the 'Rugby World Cup' match was on the TV. Did either of you catch the highlights? Yeah, I saw them. Ireland’s team did quite well against the Wallies today. Wallies, hmm really? More courteously, 'Wales', and they did play a competitive game. Sorry, the lads at the pub this morning were calling them 'Wallies' all through the match. More importantly, what’s the plan for visiting Granny on Sunday? Ah yes, we should’ve had that conversation earlier. We should all head over and spend some time with her. Since she’s not been feeling well lately. Definitely a good idea. She was looking forward to some family time. "Granny will be happy to see you." We could even bring some of this... if they’re not all devoured. I’ll make sure to send a reminder to everyone later today. So, just to confirm, the Rugby match is on this Saturday? That's right... though I'm not sure we'll get a good view from here. Might have to set up something outside if the weather holds up. Though we must keep the afternoon free for visiting Granny. Speaking of which, I might drive with you guys. Can I do that? Of course! We can all ride together. Hey, what do you think of the chicken Kievs plans, little one? "Does baby want chicken?" I think we'll wait on the chicken until dinner. Speaking of diets and all... And speaking of snacks, are you still having trouble finding all those photos from last summer? I could help if you want to look at them together. Ah, the perks of modern technology. Right, I've been having some trouble locating everything in Dropbox and Flickr.

So, I got us a nice treat today. Oh yeah? What is it? I bought a set of vintage Moore cups and saucers on eBay. They're just lovely. That sounds great! Did you get any interesting designs? Yeah, one of the saucers has a pretty floral pattern and the cups have this really simple but elegant gold rim. Vintage items are great. I bought a few antique books and a vintage typewriter once. Really? Where would you get those from? Thrift shops and antique shops in the city. But I've been avoiding them lately. Why? Work's been crazy lately, been working extra hours. And also, my big project at the office is nearing an end. They gave us a little leaving do last week. Oh, congrats! That must have been nice. What did you do? We had a good lunch at a local restaurant and got some gifts for the team. That's lovely. So what are you up to on the day off before the official leaving date? I'm thinking of clearing out some of the clutter at home and then maybe visiting the local community market this weekend. They have a nice selection of local foods and crafts. That sounds fun! I might join you. I need to pick up some groceries anyway. Sure, that would be good. We could also try the new bakery they have. And maybe you can help me get ideas for what to make with this buckwheat bread I bought last time we were there. Buckwheat bread, huh? I've never tried it before. It's actually really good! You can make toast, use it for sandwiches or even bread pudding. Bread pudding? That's a new one. I've only made it with traditional white bread before. Yes, and it might be a good change of pace. We can make that when you come over. That sounds like a plan. I'll make sure to pick up some sweet potatoes or apples to add some extra flavor and health benefits. Yeah, sweet potatoes are great for recipes. I also thought about making dinner. I was thinking about trying out a new recipe with some leftover roast chicken. Oh, I love leftovers. You can make a lot with that. I could bring over some veggies... That would be perfect. I'll make a recipe for stir fry with the chicken and veggies.

So, how was your week? It's been alright. Got a bit of a headache with some paperwork for my business. Hopefully I don't get talked to about money laundering again. Is that still a thing you have to worry about? Yeah, questions keep coming up. It's just because sometimes clients I work with, they have companies overseas and sometimes the checks seem a bit off. I'm pretty sure it's all above board, I just have to deal with it. You must get a lot of visits from the bank for that? More than I'd like. But I'm lucky I've got someone in the company who's really good with all this stuff. It just takes up a bit of time. And the kids, how are they doing? Ah, they're alright. Little Emily is still getting into everything, but I suppose that's normal for a four-year-old. And Jack's thinking about applying for university next year, so we're going through applications and stuff. It's all so expensive, though. Yeah, it's crazy how much this is all costing. I'm just hoping that all their hard work pays off in the long run. Where did you all study while you were growing up? I'm currently at sixth form. I'm not sure what I want to do yet, but probably something in teaching or perhaps business, maybe law. And you, Alex? Yeah, I went for a postgrad in education actually. It’s all about what you're passionate about and where you think you can make a difference. True that. I've always wondered how you went about finding the right path. I mean, did you or did your parents have the idea or was it more of a personal exploration? I think for me it was a bit of both. My parents were professors, so they were always encouraging education, but they also let me explore my own interests. From a young age I was very interested in business and that's where I ended up. Yeah, I think having some influence from parents or people you look up to is great but it's also about finding your own way. I thought I might want to be a lawyer first but then got into education and have never looked back. That makes sense. I just feel like there's so much pressure to have everything figured out right now.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time during Grace's sign language class? Oh, talked about that! No, actually. Is there a story there? Yes! We were supposed to sign this kind of long sentence about the weather and I accidentally inverted the order. So while everyone else was signing, "It's sunny today and I'm feeling happy," I signed "I'm happy and it's sunny today." That's brilliant. You turned it into like a philosophical statement. I can imagine. Yeah. Everyone just stared at me for a bit then burst out laughing. They probably thought you were making a profound point about individual happiness and the impact of weather on it. You should have stuck with the philosophical angle. Well, that aside, any news or plans for the upcoming event that we were looking forward to? Yes, actually. I managed to get some pretty decent deals on some materials we still needed for the decor. Should be able to get more of that done this weekend if things go smoothly. That's great to hear! How's the sign language class going? You seem really enthusiastic about it. It's amazing! Although I'm finding it tougher than I thought. But it's so rewarding doesn't it? Oh, definitely. Speaking of things that are tough but rewarding... Yes, I was thinking about that. We've been discussing when to start solid foods and all that. Because a dinner changing table is all we really needed on our to-do list, right? I guess so! But seriously, it's quite overwhelming. We've heard different advice from everywhere. You know what? Maybe we can ask [name of family doctor or someone more experienced] next week when we're over? Maybe set up a quick call or meet-up. I'm sure she'd be happy to give us some advice. Oh, that's a great idea! Maybe there's even some kind of workshop or seminar this month we could attend... Or just a quick Google search? I've tried, but there's just a lot of conflicting information across the web. Yeah, and it's all about trust sources. You've been doing this before, any advice you can share? We can use all the help we can get. Well, I think the best advice is to observe the baby's cues. If they're showing interest in food, being able to sit up when supported, and seem to be swallowing well, then maybe it's time.

So, I hear that Cambridge University Press is strict with language use. Oh yes, they’re very particular about which dialect they feature in their texts. You can’t even use Indian English in certain contexts. It’s fascinating, the nuances, though! I’ve noticed that too. You really have to be mindful of the market they're targeting with each publication. It’s not just about the text, though. The formatting and layout also vary by region. Right, I’ve seen how different the layout is for UK vs. US editions, even of the same book. Exactly, and I’ve been reviewing some materials in preparation for their Latin American editions. The line spacing, among other things, is quite different. And the language even sounds different, doesn’t it? Even within the same language. Definitely. It’s important for the text to read naturally to the user in the region it’s being published for. And this is why we have to be careful with those dialectical changes or even just the variations in spelling and terminology. Sure, like “lorry” vs “truck”. And “lift” vs “elevator”. Absolutely, so it’s interesting because we can't just do a straight translation or even an adaptation for regional markets. It’s more like a localization, where we consider not just language, but cultural nuance as well. It’s a painstaking process, but that’s what makes it so rewarding doesn’t it? Oh, definitely. And it’s such a good skill to have, especially in publishing. That it is. And it’s definitely something we don’t get a lot of training for, at least not extensively. True. It’s more of a learn-as-you-go type of thing. But it’s changing the way we view language, especially in an era where global communication is key. I suppose that in itself is another form of research, just in real-time, isn’t it? Definitely. It’s like a mini linguistic study each project. Or perhaps a case study on the dynamic of cultural exchange through language. I love that idea, actually. And the sense of responsibility is quite unique. I know. You feel like you’re not just editing or translating, but also contributing to the cultural exchange and understanding between different regions. It’s a big job but it feels like we’re doing something meaningful. And hopefully, from a language research perspective, it helps advance our understanding of how language varies across global communities and regions.

Yo, mate, so I've been thinking we should definitely move forward with that charity rally. You know how we wanted to do something cool and adventurous after our grad years? Absolutely. It's been on my mind too. A trip to Mongolia sounds epic, though I kind of regret not knowing how much of a bureaucratic hell the visa application would be. Honestly, that's the least of our worries right now. We've got to start by getting the applications in. Which reminds me, have you managed to get those passport photos done? Not yet, I was thinking of taking a trip to town today to get them done. Or maybe we could print some at home if we have good quality photos to scan and print. Printing at home can be tricky but faster than going to town. If we can get passports scanned into a decent resolution, we can print them at home. But I'd still suggest going to town for the first version, just in case. Makes sense. Off to get those done then. Also, should we start putting those ads on Gumtree? We were thinking of selling a few of our old tech items and maybe some second-hand gear to raise more funds for the rally. Yeah, that’s a great idea. We need all the money we can get. Let’s get that sorted ASAP. And can you also look into what we’re eligible for in travel grants? Maybe the uni has some resources for charity work or something? Will do, mate. Oh, and by the way, we’re probably going to need some advice from someone who’s done similar charity events. Maybe we can talk to that pal of ours who went to Africa for a project? That’d be awesome, thanks for remembering. Maybe we can meet up or just have a call with them this week. Gotta cover all the bases. On that note, have you dealt with the donation part? We were thinking of setting up a page, but maybe we need to talk to the charity first to see what they can provide us with in terms of support? I was on it. I’ve had a chat with the charity. They’re really supportive but it seems we need to show some initial progress or commitment on our part before they can give us a proper backing.

Oh Ana, I swear if you move any slower you'll actually start to leave a reverse trail. You wouldn't believe the night I had. You two hooked up at the party at uni isn't it? Yeah, we decided to scope out the situation and had way too many tequilas. Enough that you hurt your arm and ended up at the hospital at 3am? Oh my god! Yeah! I thought I'd just pulled something but when I couldn't get it to stop throbbing, I knew it was time for a trip to the hospital. I came with you didn't I? Yeah, we made quite the pair, following the doctor through the corridors making sure each other stayed awake. Did they give you anything for it? Just told me to ice it and rest. Ugh. It's still so sore. I hope you took it easy today. I tried to. But when you’re as accident-prone as I am, anything can happen. You need to be more careful. That was nasty. Hey, at least it made for a good story, right? Aye, definitely, but still. Next time maybe a bit less tequila? We'll see. So hows the studying going? It's been a struggle, to be honest. This arm pain isn't helping. Seems like the whole flat hasn't been having a great time, huh? Exactly. I mean, I've been feeling pretty exhausted lately too. Because who needs sleep when you can party? True. But honestly, I think it's also the pressure of exams. I know. It always seems like we have too much to do and not enough time. Did you hear about the new assignment Matt's got? No, what's that about? He got a massive essay due in like three weeks. He's thinking of skipping the reading week just to get it done. That's not a good idea. We all need that break, otherwise everyone's going to burn out. Exactly. We should hang out this break, even if it's just watching movies or something. I'd say yes to that. A movie marathon and some decent food. That sounds like what we all need. Yeah, it would be good to just forget about uni for a bit. Are we talking this week or during reading week? Why not both? We could do something casual this week and then have a proper break during reading week, if you're free.

So tell me about the birthday party. I heard Grandma's speech was quite touching. Yeah, it was. She was talking about when she and Granddad first met and all the years they've spent together. There were quite a few people crying by the end, including me, a bit. It's just so nice isn't it? I remember those summer weekends at the house out at Scalby. It was always so full of laughter, especially when all the aunts and uncles came over and set up their instruments. Yeah, and how would they try and get us kids to sing along, even though we had no idea what song it was supposed to be. But they were having such a good time. And I think that is what makes those family gatherings so special - the joy of being together, even through the chaos. Definitely. And the food, of course! Aunt Mary's Yorkshire puddings are still the best. How does she manage to make them so light and fluffy? I think it's because she uses old-fashioned weights. She said at one time, before we had all the modern measurements, this is how you'd make sure everything was just right. It’s fascinating how traditional methods can often lead to the best results. And then there's the politics of the family games. Remember that one year, there was an argument about the rules of Twenty Questions? It was quite something. Oh, yes! There's always a bit of friendly competition, isn't there? It's all part of the fun. But what really struck me this time was how everyone contributed to the party. Your friend, Emily, helped with the decorations, which were lovely. The living room looked beautiful. Yes, and seeing everyone come together like that, making sure it was a special day for Grandma and Granddad, it was really heartwarming. And think about all the years and laughter we've shared. It's really what family is all about, isn't it? Definitely. You know, after Grandma's speech, I was thinking about all the stories I've heard over the years. I wish I had paid more attention when they were told so I could remember them better. Me too. We often take for granted the stories our older family members share. I suggest you sit down with them sometime and ask them to tell you all those stories again.

Dad, did you remember to pack our water bottles? We're going to be thirsty on this long journey! Always thinking of practical things! Of course, I packed them. We also have our nice packs of pens, pens for any potential roadside games or journalling if you want to write about our trip. That's a great idea! I love road trips because you can actually have time to... I don't know, write and draw. It's so different from how we have to rush with homework all the time. You know, it's funny, during one of my exams, I forgot to check my pen for ink before starting and I panicked for a split second thinking what if it just says down to zero ink? Yeah, that sounds like a "whoops" moment. And what about lunch? We could stop at this place we pass, The Dutch Kitchen or whatever it's called. Ron told me they have nice sandwiches there. Sounds good! And it's funny because it's so far from what English Cuisine looks like or even Cornish! But that's what makes this trip interesting. Also, can we plan when we’re going to have our dinner or supper? I know Cornish pasties are great but I wonder if we can try the entire local dining experience over the next week or so. Absolutely. We can plan all sorts of wonderful meals while we're there. Speaking of, we still have to sort out where in Cornwall we'll be staying. I hope it's not too complicated to find the place. I know what doesn’t come in handy is when the directions are too complicated and we end up lost or stuck finding our accommodation, but I do hope we can make it to Holland and Barrett in some less touristy town for some decent herbal teas and a few treats, maybe for the trip or for the little luxuries while we’re there. Yes, that's a great spot to stock up. And we should grab a few things for your IBS if needed. You know how sensitive you are to certain foods. Don’t worry, there’s always something we can do for that. Thanks for always being on top of such things. I appreciate it. It does get stressful when plans go awry and you have to deal with the physical aspect of traveling, like managing my diet or just the general stress of moving house.

"Those biscuits look amazing, thank you. Can I take two? Also, just trying to remember, have you updated the whole extended family on the retirement party plans for mother?"      "I gave a quick call to Uncle Tom this week, he’ll be there for sure. But looking at the list, I think we need to get confirmation from a few others. Is there a good chance it will rain on the 20th?
