Or perhaps a temporary tattoo of the Deathly Hallows symbol for them to use in the escape room. Mmm! That’s such a good idea! Alright, now let’s figure out if we need to go to Morrisons to get anything. We should check but any last minute items might already be here or we could use DIY alternatives if we're really short on time.

I've decided I need a new car. I have to admit though, I've been browsing more on Facebook than at car dealerships sites. It's kind of funny, really. Most of my car research is coming from social media. That's typical of our generation, isn't it? We're always connected and for better or worse, Facebook has become a part of our decision-making process. I've also posted a couple of times about my car troubles, and surprisingly, got very helpful tips. Right, most people on my feed just blab about their Thanksgiving gatherings. But there was this one group for car enthusiasts that had some amazing first-hand advice. Yeah, even for academics, the internet and social media can be a goldmine for information—if you know where to look. And sometimes the advice from real people is more practical than reading a review by a professional journalist. Exactly! I mean, have you seen the ads these days? Everything looks perfect and it's all about sleek designs and fancy tech. But then you look at a Facebook group and people are talking about real-life experiences, like, "Yeah, this model might look great, but the running costs are pretty high" or "The seats in the back are really cramped if you're over 6 feet tall." Spot on. Well, technology-wise, I was considering a car with some built-in smart systems. You know, things like automated driving features and in-car WiFi. They're pretty cool. I'm not sure I'm comfortable with cars making decisions for me yet. You're not on the "let's just get rid of the steering wheel altogether" side of things, then? No, I like having control over things like navigation and parking. Though, to be honest, the lane keeping assist stuff really could be useful in heavy traffic. You know, it's interesting to see how cars are sort of becoming computers on wheels. I mean, some models now come with these software updates like you'd see on your phone. That's true! And have you seen some of the safety features? Like, auto emergency braking. I could see that being helpful if you're distracted or just not in the best driving condition. Absolutely, and then there's the whole debate about driverless cars in the future. Some companies are thinking a lot further ahead than just hands-free now.

Yo, I got my sales shift at work today. Oh really? How was it? You're still doing that part-time job? Yeah, needed the extra cash. It was pretty normal, really. Nothing exciting or drastically different from the usual, but the boss seemed in a good mood which kind of made the day slightly more manageable. That's good then. Anything interesting that happened? Not really, just a bunch of regular customers coming in and out. But I did have to deal with that one lady who was really particular about which DVD case she wanted to buy, she actually started questioning me about the artwork’s meaning on the cover. Did you say something about it? Well, I didn’t really have much to say but tried to be helpful. I mean, the artwork's importance usually depends on the individual’s perspective, right? But she seemed to take it more seriously than I expected. That’s quite a discussion for a DVD case! Did you mention the film “Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs” ever comes up in or as a topic related to that? I’m catching up on that while we’re talking. Oh yeah, the film. There’s actually some pretty neat ideas hidden in it beyond the obvious kids’ fun stuff. For instance, the concept touches upon consumerism and the environmental consequences of the wacky invention gone wrong. It’s like a gentle jab at unchecked technological advancement mixed with a moral lesson about responsibility. But then again, most people probably just enjoy the food-themed science fiction without diving too deep into those layers. That’s interesting. I was watching it and the mom’s character stood out to me. She’s such a strong, nurturing figure and yet, if you look closely, the film doesn’t shy away from the challenges of single motherhood and a family trying to make ends meet. Exactly. And even beyond that, feminism and empowerment can be found in the daughter’s character who isn’t afraid to question conventions and follow her heart, literally taking matters into her own hands to change her world. I didn’t think of it that way, but now that you mention it, it’s quite progressive for a kids' film. It’s one of those films that has layers of meaning that are accessible to adults too, without making the kids feel left out.

So, Phil, did you keep any of the Tony Blair stuff? You mean these books and whatnot? Nah, gave most of it to my mate. He's more of a collector than I am. I see. I must admit, even though I wasn’t a huge fan back in the days, today I do sometimes wonder what could have been if the whole New Labour project didn’t lose its way. True that. Now, with hindsight, it seems like it was all so focused on rebuilding after Thatcher that it maybe overlooked how much support was needed for ordinary people once we had that stability. Right. I mean, the NHS got billions, which was great, but then education, the council housing – all those things were suppose to follow. Instead, we got a lot of “PFI” and making sure the economy kept chugging along while the benefits just seemed to disappear for a lot of folks. Yeah, it felt like we were promised a “third way” and instead it was more like we just got caught up in neoliberalism with a bit of warm talk on the side. Now that progressive income tax this, fairer trade that – most of it just talk. Politics often is. Where did you get the idea for this job, driving a taxi in Finland? It’s not every day you get the chance to leave Liverpool and still keep your Manc accent while working. Plus, I had enough of the political drownings at home. Sometimes you just gotta vote with your feet, you know? Shows there’s more to you than just the badge on the door. How’s the football culture here? Coming from Liverpool, the Merseyside derby would be my reference point, but I suppose you don’t have one like that here? Nah, but there’s a strong rivalry between these Finnish clubs, HJK and FC Inter Helsinki. Similar banter, different teams. So, are they as confrontational in their rivalry as Everton and Liverpool are? It’s different. You wouldn’t see as many actual violent clashes, but the passion is there. I’ve had guys arguing for forty minutes just trying to decide which team is better. That’s one thing we have in common then! It's all about the pride of the region. Did you have kids interested in football when you were at home? You bet. My youngest used to think if you played football, you had to follow Liverpool or Everton.

So, I was browsing on LinkedIn yesterday and came across an interesting recruitment opportunity for a language research specialist at a company involved in developing AI and Natural Language Processing systems. That sounds really intriguing. You know I've always been quite fascinated by AI. It’s just so futuristic, but also kind of scary when questions of ethics come up. [Unrecognizable voice, possibly of a bot or a recording] Yes indeed. Language and AI, right? Fascinating and I'd love to know more. However, my knowledge is extracted from an older dataset so I’m not up to date on the latest technologies. Hahaha. Well, it’s quite an interesting field, definitely. I’ve been listening to some BNC recordings just to get a feel for how language has been evolving over the years. It’s quite comprehensive though, the BNC. Hence your interest in language research? Because I want to assure you, being at the interface of technology and language is creative yet very challenging. Absolutely. I spend a lot of my time thinking about dialects and sociolects, which I find fascinating. But yeah, the application to AI is really where my interest is right now. [Continuing the recorded dialogue] Language variations are indeed fascinating, but the integration with AI can be so complex. Striking the balance between linguistic accuracy and algorithmic processing can often become quite intricate. Ah, the balance issue. Honestly, as an editor, it's similar for me. You're always trying to balance the creative aspect with readability and technical correctness. We might achieve this balance in different ways, but the underlying struggle is quite similar. True. I think one of the big challenges is making technology sensitive to nuances in language. It’s hard enough for humans to understand the different ways people use language in different contexts, let alone for a machine! [Contrasting voice now] Yes, human language is full of nuance and context, which are difficult for machines to fully capture. From inflection to dialect, language is a complex and multidimensional phenomenon. I totally agree. I think that's part of what scares me about moving more heavily into automation. If a machine can't capture the nuances, so much interpretation is lost. Exactly! It's like the project I’m working on. We are trying to develop more culturally sensitive chatbots, but it’s like... how can you program empathy or humor into a machine?

Yo, mate, did you finish reading that stuff? Yeah, nearly. The interns have been great, but I wish they'd take a bit more initiative sometimes. You're right. They're quite idealistic, don't they? Like the world’s gonna change with their journal entries questions. But it’s part of the learning process, I suppose. Speaker_3 : Excuse me, I couldn't help but overhear. Tattoo discussions during dinner keeps it lively, doesn’t it? Oh, we're just talking about the new one I’m getting. Decided on a little London skyline. Yeah, very cool. I like the idea of capturing cityscapes in ink. That’s actually quite interesting. Tattoos as a form of travel memorabilia almost. Reminds me, have you booked your Christmas plans yet? Just started looking. Thinking of going to Leeds? Leeds sounds like a good shout. The market there is always buzzing around this time. I’m more of a stickler for tradition. Planning to spend it with family. Not much for decorating though. Where did you get that great new kitchen idea from? Online research and a bit of Pinterest, really. Decided on the bright and airy design. Love it, it’s gonna look amazing, especially with your mother’s garden herbs in there. Now that is a great combination. Shows there’s love in the food, you know? Definitely. But it’s the redesigning the lounge that’s giving us a headache. Too much stuff to clear, not enough time. You should have done the measured drawings months ago. But hey, we've got the next month for that. You think? I was hoping by now we were done. We'll get there, but changing the layout takes longer than I thought. It’s like moving a small house inside my house. I can relate. My biggest project is trying to find my old college essay about tattoos as self-expression. Might be for a meme. Speaking of essays, I’m still working on those. Editor’s life: endless papers and Christmas just over the horizon. Yeah, and I’ll be running around universities with interns. A good time to learn. You guys are just focused all the time. You need to book that trip, like I’m doing. Work-life... Balance? True that. Maybe we all just need a Christmas dinner planning session, separate from work. How about we make a pact to actually enjoy a sit-down dinner without work talk this Christmas?

So, I thought about going to that pilates class last night's online. I'd really like to start getting back into regular exercise. Ah, that's great, you've been saying that for ages, Alison! You should definitely give it a go, the benefits are amazing! Yes, and I saw that class was at a local studio down the road. It's not too far from our homes either, so I can just walk or perhaps cycle... I bought a new bicycle recently and it's sitting in the garage collecting dust. Oh, really? That's excellent! I'm actually considering a cycling club myself – it's supposed to be fun and great for fitness, despite the risks from lazy London traffic. Might just encourage me to actually start cycling. You really need to though, driving through London traffic even just on the Tube can be pretty stressful. I imagine cycling's a much healthier alternative. Definitely. London also has some very nice spots for cycling, when you avoid the main roads. Off we go, this blackout cake will be finished in no time! A blackout cake? I haven't made that for ages, it’s a classic but it always turns out so well. I use a special recipe from my mum, but the key is in the cocoa powder. Yes, I also follow a traditional recipe. It's basically a spongy chocolate cake without any butter, nice for when you're avoiding dairy or just want a lighter cake. But isn't it called "blackout cake" because it was popular during the war and all the ingredients were rationed? That's right! The name is thought to come from the "blackout" period during World War II. People would cover their windows to block out any light that might be seen from the skies. Seems fitting the cake's name has that dark history to it, doesn't it? Very fitting. And speaking of history, have you tried that new Italian place in town? Julie and Tom said it's great. Not yet, but I was thinking we might plan a little dinner out next Friday – make that a little trip to the Italian place for a change. If we're honest, we've been stuck at home trying different recipes, but sometimes you just want real Italian food, no? Absolutely! Or perhaps we can go to the Chinese place that just opened in the city center.

So, I was talking to Lily yesterday after class and she's still annoyed about Grace's new job. Yeah, I heard about that. It sounds like she's worried Grace has taken a step back in her career. She just can't understand why Grace chose to leave London for that role in Manchester. It's like she views it as less prestigious, you know? It's funny, we've all had moments like that, don't we? Looking back at someone else's choices and wondering if they've made a mistake. Exactly! She's worried she's 'missing out' because Manchester’s not London. But the truth is, Grace just wants a change of pace. She’s looking to settle down, maybe start a family. Yeah, and who can blame her? I mean, London is great but it's intense and expensive. She might want a bit more balance in her life. And yet, Lily still can't get over it. She sees it as a setback. But the thing is, for us in academia, it's never just about where we are geographically. It's about what we're working on, who we're working with, and the impact we can make. And while the 'prestige' of the university might seem important, the real prestige is in the work we do and the students we can connect with, influence. London or Manchester, the academic landscape is less about A to B and more about what we achieve where we are. Absolutely! And Grace is probably going to do some fantastic work there and make a real difference in her new community doesn’t matter if it's Manchester or the moon. Except, we've got to find her one of those lunar posts the next career move... Oh, wouldn't that be something? I'd totally be on board for getting professors to moon schools! It's ideas like that which could really shake up education. While we’re dreaming big, though, we really should set up a dinner with all our friends sometime soon. We haven't all been together for ages. Brilliant idea. We could take advantage of the fact that we're all in the same city for the moment. It'll be nice to catch up, and Grace could share her new experiences in Manchester. And we can formally welcome her to the Manchester branch of our academic network.

So, I was browsing Rotten Tomatoes yesterday and came across that new's film. I'd really like to see it. Have you seen it yet? Ah, you're talking about that new studios release? No, I haven't had the time. It’s just, the days are getting a bit flooded with work questions and some kind of new company policy thing that everyone’s talking about and I’m still getting my head around it. Understood, right? Life as a company director can be quite demanding. By the way, did you hear that keeps coming up in celebrity gossip about a possibility of another marriage? Yes, I've seen the news – it’s quite scandalous isn’t it? I mean, personally, I think two years is a bit quick but to each their own, I guess. Exactly! Also, making me think of that TV show on radio last Wednesday. They were discussing how much of the celebrity life we believe is actual and how much is curated. Do you think we ever really know the truth about those celebs? Oh, absolutely. I'm a bit of a conspiracy theory buff myself. But honestly, the more I learn about the business side and the agencies that manage these people, it’s hard not to think they pretty much control every move and word. It's all scripted. Honestly, sometimes I wonder why we can't just look at people's accomplishments or personalities rather than their scandalous lives or current gossip. It must be exhausting being a celebrity. Indeed. You know, sometimes when we’re talking about celebrities, I almost forget that they're just regular people who've had the opportunity and circumstances that allowed them to become... well, the people we gossip about. True. Speaking of regular people, how do you feel about career progression in our field? I’ve been thinking about doing my MA, maybe getting into a bit of academia. What about you, any aspirations beyond where you are now or do you feel you’ve found your place? Honestly, I’ve thought about going back to education too. It might be a good time to consider advanced studies – I’ve seen some of our industry moving towards requiring more specialized degrees and certifications. And besides, it might also be a great way to network and get into research projects that interest you and have the potential for real impact.

"Put on your Sunday best/ and meet me at Jamaica Inn…" You know these lyrics, don't you dad? It sounds so cool, and talked about even more when we book our studios for the holiday in Cornwall. Aye now, the old Daphne du Maurier tale do bring questions back to the days of smuggling and sea tides. "What did you mean by ghost ships then? Were they just tall tales or fractals of reality? Well lass, it was a keepsake for decades alongside local stories. Captains and taverners blabbing, you know. Like how lazy chaps would misroute cargo for fun, sticking lamp lights to scare off watchers in navy colours. Might have been down to drinking or boredom. Oh god, making the railways of Cornwall look like a modern tech. But there's more to it. In the rain, the black cliffs and greened gorse fields, it's like a sketch from the Wizards of Oz. You know, between the yellow brick road and the turrets, Cornwall has that feel. Yeah, it has that differentness to the English countryside. You’re always waiting for a while for Glinda. Aye, and we’re stopping at Bodmin Moor? There’s a bit of Sherlock Holmes about the moor, loads of clues for pseudonyms perhaps? Though I think we’ll still be wanting signs to Bodmin itself, as I’m sure John wouldn’t write down ‘wrong turn here’ on his notes. Or would he use a secret code from "The Dancing Men"?! Morse code or even braille, but for writing in pebbles or sand. Now that’s Morecentric Holmes thought, aye. But for the safety of our journey it'll be plain old English signage. Speaking of which, are we really insured for a cartoonish crash into a wind turbine? You know like in those fantastical novels where everything can happen… Like, next we’ll pass somewhere Arthur’s castle would be in these fairy tale boundaries. Aye, so long as it doesn’t turn into a real ‘Jabberwocky’ showdown, we’re good. As long as there are no crazed looking weeping willows swinging towards us, plus no sudden Cheshire smiles leading us into portals or “Invisible Chariots” You’ve been reading Carroll too often, young Sherlock. But seriously, there’s lots of wind farms around here, part of the power we use in the modern day. Yeah, and they're these towering, straight-up structures, a bit like the architecture across Oz.

So, I was at this party last night and someone was showing off this new game called “Neighborhood of Decay”. It’s like a survival game where you have to collect resources and avoid these unrealistic monsters. Ah really? Sounds almost like it was from the war, you know, searching for resources and all. Yeah, kind of, but the theme of survival in a post-apocalyptic world is pretty fascinating, right? Absolutely, fascinating. But it’s always struck me how we romanticize survival when actually, most people didn’t get to be like players, collecting points. That's a very valid point. I used to play games like “Army of Two” and it never even slightly felt like the real thing. But back in my day, “Pong” was considered cutting edge, and now we have virtual reality. It’s crazy how far things have come. But speaking of creative survival, have you heard of those people who swim across the Channel? That’s a different kind of survival challenge, for sure. No, I haven’t really. Is that a thing now, for sport or what? Oh yeah, it's quite popular. You’re in the water, the tide can change at any moment, the weather’s unpredictable – and you’ve to keep going, really focusing on your physical and mental endurance. Sounds hazardous to me. I remember during the war, we had to ration food and water. It was a serious survival challenge. One time, we even used to get a little bit of butter and spread it thin over two slices of bread, and that would be our day. Nowadays, the survival challenges are more about avoiding zombies or finding the best loot, which if you think about it, the war was less about adventure and more about survival in the rawest form. True. I used to complain whenever I had to do some exercise, but swimming the Channel? That's next level. I’ve heard it’s bonkers tough, but people do it for charity and stuff. Yeah, it's a bit more purposeful than most survival games. But for me, I find survival in my daily commute, figuring out how to make lunch on a zero budget or deciding whether to pay for an extra bus fare. That's almost as challenging. I laughed at the thought of having to ration anything more than just freedom once, but I suppose coping with today's prices is a different kind of survival too.

Mum, I've brought this list. I need you to help me with moving house. Oh, okay sweetie. Let me see what you've got there. Are you still planning to move into that new apartment in London? Yes, mum. That's still the plan. But I need to make sure I make a list of everything I need to pack and organize. And you need my help? Sure, let me give it a proper once over. Thanks, it's a bit overwhelming. You'll probably be the only one who actually takes note of things like 'non-flatware for the kitchen' and 'essential weaver fish from my London life'. Weaver fish? What on earth have you got now? Just this little thing from my flat's communal seafood haul. It's a small piece of nostalgia. Make sure you don't forget the things that actually matter. You're heading into a whole new chapter of life, after all. Yeah, I know, I know. But it's funny, this weaver fish... it reminds me of late-night cooking with friends. You know, when we were all jet-lagged but still managed to cook up a storm. Those were the days. But seriously, about this list – let's prioritize the essentials first. Pack as much as you can but don't forget to consider your health as well. London can be overwhelming, even without jet lag. Yeah, I need to make sure I doesn't dwell in that. And how are you doing? Emotionally, I mean? Moving away, starting fresh... it can be tough. It's strange, mum. There's excitement, but also a lot of uncertainty. I'm leaving behind friends and family, yet I know this opportunity could open doors for me that are closed here. That's part of growing up, honey. You'll make new friends, and we can plan visits. I know, and I do look forward to that. But just hearing about what's happening around here, like your lunch clubs or your bingo nights – it makes me want to stay close. Your mum's gone and got herself two new friends already. We can set up weekly calls and you can catch up with everyone digitally. That sounds fine, but still, I'll miss the spontaneity of being here. I know, that's... that's hard. So, practical matters first. We need to check if everything on this list makes sense.

I've decided I need more plants in the flat. I just can't leave these ones to die. That sounds like a great idea. Plants really brighten up a space. Yeah, and I think it’s also a kind of stress-reliever. I just feel calmer when I'm tending them. I completely understand that. I mean, I've also started to think about my own stress levels. Maybe we can even pick up some for my desk here during our next grocery trip. That would be lovely, and actually… you’ve been looking a bit rough with all the late nights. Maybe I can pick something up that's also good for air quality like a peace lily or something. Yeah, or even a spider plant. They're super low-maintenance. Exactly! And I've seen some really cute looking ones in home decor stores around here. Plus, there's a little corner by the window in the kitchen where it could get some good sunlight. So, you were saying about the hairstyle this morning. You thought it might be a good idea to try something different? Yeah, I’ve had the same cut for years. I might be brave and do something new, perhaps even a bit shorter. What do you think? I think it’s a great idea. New look, new year sort of vibe. You’ll really stand out in your lectures too. No pressure. But seriously, I might try something like a blunt bob or even the latest trend, which apparently is a chin-length cut with subtle layers. Sounds like a plan. And who knows, you may inspire some of your students with the courage of a new look. Right. Inspiration is a job perk they don’t really advertise. Before we talk about my changing hairstyle though, I wanted to touch on the NHS plan for next year. Did you hear that? Yeah, I caught a bit of that on the radio. They want to make changes to the funding structure and introduce more community-based care? Exactly. I think those could be really positive moves but of course, the concern is the transition. I’ve seen reports that we might see some short-term gaps in services. True, change can be challenging. The issue will be during the implementation. But if it works out, it could lead to more efficient use of resources and...

Oh, did I ever tell you about that one time I discovered that the black plague is actually caused by rats spreading parasites causing the disease from Asia to Europe? No! Is that true? That's right! But it’s so ironic because sometimes I feel like my bank account is going through a "financial black plague" considering the amount of money I spend at the student union. And here I am, trying to get a job at a coffee shop. You'd think it's some kind of new 'work plague' because it’s the only thing that seems to be hiring. Might just be the "work plague" among students looking for part-time jobs. But anyway, did you guys hear about the new policy at uni regarding smoking on campus? Yeah, I heard they're going to designate smoking areas and also offering support for students who want to quit. Feminism strikes again, right? Providing support for people who want to stop smoking - that's really positive though. For sure! We should appreciate it. It's not just about health but also about making different choices in life. Regarding quitting habits, I started counting every time I need a coffee. If it’s more than five in a day, I know I’ve got a problem. Can't quit without my coffee, though. Speaking of habits, have any of you started reading up on the history of the black plague? I started reading this book and it's fascinating how it spread and the impact it had on society. Oh, that reminds me. Did you know the phrase “quarantine” actually comes from the black plague? The Italian phrase for 40 days was "quaranta giorni." Really? I had no idea. That's super interesting. It's amazing how old history still affects us today in our language and concepts of public health. Yeah, and on that note, I’ve been thinking of advocating for a bit more mental health support for students. Our university loves to talk about student wellness but it seems more like lip service than actual support. For sure. And it's not just the university, most places like to preach about wellness without really providing resources. It’s like the new plague of carelessness. That’s a good point actually. We should probably discuss that more among our group or maybe even with the student union.

So, I was thinking about what we've been talking about regarding friendships. I've noticed that as we grow older and our lives change, it can be tricky to navigate which friendships to prioritise and which ones to let go of—or at the very least, phase out. Yeah, absolutely. Especially when some kind of conflict or distance has already established itself. Exactly. It feels somewhat ghosting but also, you can't spend as much energy on everything and everyone. Our lives are increasingly busy. But even so, it's hard to address. You don't want to hurt people's feelings, but you also want to focus on nurturing relationships that feel nourishing and dynamic. True. I had this friend from grad school. We were super close, but post-grad life took us in different directions. We tried to stay in touch, but it was clear that our priorities and values had shifted quite differently. It felt hard to let go—almost like an ending—but also, we weren't really in the same spot. That's it. It's not like it was ever a dramatic conflict, just a natural drifting apart. But how do you actually... phase out a friendship without it being awkward? Well, in my experience, most of the time it's just the natural course of things. People move away, get new jobs, start families, or just grow into different lives. It's more an acknowledgement of the space rather than an active decision to cut ties. Honestly, the hardest part for me was letting go of the idea of what the friendship could have been, rather than what it actually was at that moment. That makes sense. Sometimes, we dwell on the possibility of what could have been more than we do on the reality of what is. It also makes me wonder, if one decides to phase out the friendship or lessen the contact, is there a right way to do it, or is it just as inevitable as the drifting apart? I think it's very much like any relationship; it's all about communication—if possible. Not everyone is receptive, though. Some friendships are just naturally time-limited. If you're lucky, you outgrow the need for them without feeling the need for a formal goodbye. That's true. I mean, some friendships are seasonal or circumstantial. They serve their purpose at the time and then it's okay to move on.

So, I hear you've seen some of the latest exhibitions at the art gallery. What did you think of them? Oh, they were fantastic. There was this one particularly, all about various forms of impressionism. It was really well curated. I spent about three hours walking through it. Oh, that sounds great. You always had a good eye for art. Did anything stick out to you? Yes, there was one particular piece by Monet. I'd never seen it up close before. The brushwork was so expressive and vivid. It was like being transported to another time. That's great. I've always loved Monet's work. Do you think I could have seen it from my London exhibitions? Possibly. They're quite keen on getting international pieces but of course, it can be hit or miss. Speaking of travel plans, how's your upcoming project with your Italian friends coming along? Oh, that's going wonderfully. We're planning a big show in Rome next year. It's going to be a mix of modern and traditional techniques, really pushing the boundaries. That sounds amazing. I'm sure it'll be a great success. I'm sure the logistics of arranging all of the works of art will be quite the challenge though. It is, but it's worth it. There's nothing quite like the feeling of bringing people together through art. Speaking of challenging things, how is your writing in progress? You mentioned you were working on another book? Oh, that's right. I've been deep into it, but things are moving slowly. I've always found the first drafts to be the hardest. Yes, I know that feeling. The blank page can be intimidating. I try to write for a few hours each day, but it's hard to keep that up consistently. Exactly! But once you start making progress, it's hard to stop. Have you read my last book? No, I haven't gotten around to it yet, but I've heard it was well received. Ah, thank you. It's about my experiences in Vienna and the influence of art on my life. I see. I can imagine there's a lot of cultural depth to draw from there. Absolutely, growing up in Vienna was incredible for my art education. It's something I've often heard about when discussing art history.

I keep reading that if you eat before the gym you'll burn more calories. Yeah, talked about that recently. Got all confused about whether to be hungry or full when going to the gym. Hmm, personally, I find if I haven't eaten at least an hour or two beforehand, I hit the wall about halfway through my HIIT training. Makes sense, you’re running out of energy. But it’s also about digestion time, keeps coming up. Totally. I suppose it’s one of those things where everyone’s body’s a bit different, so there’s no one-size-fits-all answer. Exactly, but what about when you read online about the best foods before a workout? Like oh, you have to eat this perfect banana with almond butter exactly 15 minutes before you exercise or your body will wither away and die? Right? And these people are usually so strident about it, too. “Absolutely, you must or you’re wasting your time.” It’s all very scientific when you’re reading it, but when you apply it, it’s kind of assumed we all have the same digestive systems and the same workout routine. And not to mention the variables! What if you’re doing an hour of yoga versus a 30-minute high-intensity run? And isn’t it funny how as English folks, we sometimes feel we’re always supposed to be “on time” and "proper"? Driving on the right side of the road, it’s like there's the expectation that we must arrive precisely at the gym at 6:00 am if that’s your scheduled time. It’s true. There’s this pressure to perform, isn’t there? To be on time, eat the right things, do the right exercises... It can feel like we’re being pulled in every direction and it’s hard to know what advice to follow. It’s like we’re expected to juggle a million balls at once. I find myself sometimes worrying about whether I’m doing it just right when it comes to health and fitness, because there’s always someone saying you’re doing it wrong. It’s intensified even more when you consider gender and societal expectations. There’s this pressure on women especially to present a certain way and follow certain rules, even when exercising. Oh god, yeah. The thinking you’ve got to look a certain way at the gym or you’re not taken seriously.

I've decided I need more hand-thrown mugs. They're so much better than anything from the shops. Ah yes, I remember when you used to make pottery. You got quite into it for a while. Did the hand-thrown mugs come out of that? Yes, I make my own now. There's something so satisfying about sitting down with a cup of tea and drinking from something I've made myself. It's lovely that you keeps coming back to it, isn't it? You'll always be the artistic one, even if you're not in the classroom as much anymore. I just love the feeling and the sound of clay between my fingers. It's almost therapeutic. And the look of them. So imperfect and beautiful at the same time. Exactly! And they're so much better for the environment. No mass production, no plastics. Now, onto something entirely different - how's the weather been treating you? Oh, it's been quite wet. Good for the garden, not so much for me. I prefer drier weather, but the garden loves the rain. Speaking of which, I saw a huge spider in my garden yesterday. Well, huge to me , but I suppose it was probably average for a garden spider. Oh really? I never mind spiders. I think they're fascinating. Just don't get up too close unless you want a close look. No, no. Except for one time. There was one who had built a web in the window and I just had to try and move it. Let's just say it was a bit more aggressive than I expected. Spiders are just doing their job. They don't mean to scare anyone. It reminded me of your garden. I was over there the other week for a gardening session. Your flowers and vegetables are always so well kept. Thanks! It's hard work, but it's so rewarding. And it's great for the birds. I've noticed almost as many birds as spiders lately . I was just thinking about decorating. We've talked about it before. Maybe now's the time, since you've got so much free time to help. Decorating? Oh, there’s lots I’d love to do! But first, we need a DIY day where we actually get a bit done. Maybe next week then? Sure, if the weather permits, and if there’s no power cut.

Mum, Dad, did you hear about Luke and Emily's trip to Paris? Oh yes, they’ve been planning it for ages haven’t they? Yes, Luke told me they're heading there over the weekend. Did they ask you about tips or anything? Well, they asked me a bit about where to stay and what to do, but I told them to look up some of our old travel guides actually. We've got some great tips in there. Oh that's a good idea. I remember how much they enjoyed our DVD of French Riviera when they were younger. Maybe they could watch it again for inspiration. I can ask them if they did watch it. Might just remind them to bring an umbrella, though - you never can predict the French weather! And make sure they check out the Eiffel Tower and the Louvre. Definitely. And if they go to a cafe, order a croissant - the real deal, not just a fancy bread. And don’t forget to try some wine or whatever drink is their style. They’re both quite adventurous with food. I bet they’ll try plenty of new things. Right. And if they’re planning on visiting the markets, remind them to haggle a bit. It’s all part of the fun, really. Yes, it’s important to interact with the locals, but always be respectful. Also, is it a good idea for them to exchange some money before they go? What about using cards all the time? These days, most places in Europe take cards, but it’s good to have some cash on hand, especially for food and local shops. And some coffee shops might only take cash. And always keep the cash and cards together, but separate just in case. Okay, that’s a lot to remember. I’ll make sure to mention all that. Speaker_2 and We could sit down later and actually plan out some of this out – make a list for them. Sounds like a good idea! And what about our own holiday later this year? Should we start deciding where to go? Oh, I was thinking about perhaps Scotland. The scenery is breathtaking this time of year and maybe we could rent bikes or go hiking. I’ve got some brochures if you want to take a look. Scotland’s a lovely idea. I just need to check the dates and see what the boys are doing.

So, I thought that Cassie from 10 Things I Hate About You was so relatable. Totally! I mean, deep down, who hasn't fantasized about giving that kind of long, impassioned speech to someone you've just kind of... not really liked yet? Exactly! And that awkwardness when she and Patrick were trying to get into the pool and just couldn't help but laugh at each other? Yeah, and when he found out she was actually nice and they started hanging out, how would they ever explain all that silly stuff to her? Like, they'd have to just pretend it never happened, or something. I know, right? So what about school? How was the new teacher for English? Um, she's all right. Quite strict, actually. But we learned about The Canterbury Tales this week, which was interesting. Cool! Did she mention anything about our homework for next week? Yeah, we have to write a short essay on one of the characters from the book. I'm thinking maybe I'll do it on Chaucer himself. He seems pretty interesting. I was thinking maybe the Wife of Bath. She’s so different and interesting, you know? Yeah, she’s certainly got personality. Speaking of school, have you heard about the trip to London next term? Yeah, I've heard whispers about it. We might actually get to go to the British Museum! Really? That's amazing. Last time we talked about that, it wasn’t even certain yet. Yes! I just hope it doesn't get cancelled. London would be so much fun together as a class! For sure. We should start making a list of things to see and do. The last trip I went on, I didn't get to see half the places I wanted to. True. Like, do you think we’ll get to go to Camden Market if we want to? I hope so, but I think we might need to ask one of the teachers if we can fit that in. Mmm, maybe. We should almost definitely ask if we can have some free time to just explore or go shopping. Yeah. It's amazing how different it is from Cambridge! Definitely. But it's fun to see where the film was set too, this time. Right! In one part of 10 Things I Hate About You, they go to the mall and have that whole drama with the restaurant and the fake date.

I seen on Facebook today someone was showing off about their grandkid getting chicken pox. Oh, yes? Had chicken pox when I was a child. Still relatively common, though hopefully, less so with vaccines. And isn’t it one of those diseases people used to have as a rite of passage? More like a rite of suffering. keeps changing backwards and forwards with people showing off about their kids. It is odd. I’ve always found social media to be a mixed bag. It’s like the whole world trying to one-up each other. But back in my day, or even earlier than that, people didn’t share such personal moments so publicly. It’s a funny old world now, innit? Did I ever tell you about the time when… No, but I'm sure this is it. The story about the time when you… Where did you get that from? You must have predicted it. No, but seriously – when I was a childminder, we had a little girl come in covered in chicken pox. The poor girl had spots all over her, and she was so silly about it, she even tried to cover them with glitter. Glitter? That’s quite advanced for a child with… Chicken pox! I don’t understand why people are so obsessed with showing off about their children’s milestones or health issues on social media. It’s almost as if… As if getting chicken pox or having a new baby is some kind of status symbol now? Or perhaps it’s just changing ways of sharing and validation. People always seek validation one way or another. But for chicken pox?! I just can’t see the appeal. It’s like with OCD – there's a funny show about it, and it’s one of those things that people almost brag about being 'a little OCD'. I think part of it is that certain conditions or experiences are normalized in media. But also, our thinking about them has shifted. For example, discussing mental health more openly has helped, but often, it’s done in a way that’s more for show than genuine help or understanding. I’d rather just not have the spots, if I’m honest. Well, at least we can talk about it freely now. But also, what about the intimacy of health and personal issues? Pre-social media, you shared such things within a very close circle.

So, I hear you took a holiday recently to Germany, or was it Holland? No, definitely Germany. It was a bit of a spontaneous trip but turned out to be a great one. Was it the Black Forest? Yeah, part of it. We went through some of the south and ended up in some beautiful villages. But getting out into the countryside, it was brilliant. And the language? Was it difficult? Well, I thought it would be a bit tricky but actually, a lot of people we met, especially younger generations, spoke good English – much better than I expected. But, you know, we tried to use a bit of German too just to be polite. Did you pick up any useful phrases? [Laughs] Well, I learned how to say "thank you" and "excuse me," and "where is the bathroom?" which comes in very handy! [Chuckles] Classic. And did anyone stop you and try to engage in English, thinking you or your friends were American or something? Actually, yes, plenty of times! The different accents can be quite misunderstood. [Laughs] Good thing they didn't think you were all from up north or else the stories [starts imitating a northern accent] "Oi, you lot are from the north, innit?" [Everyone laughs] Speaking of accents, did you notice how they pronounce "Buch" and all those words with "ch"? Yeah, definitely different from here. I mean, "Buch" sounds more like "Book" but with a stronger "ch" sound. That's right. And their "W"s in words like "wein" – they pronounce it like it's "vayn," not "wayn." Yes, that's a great example of the High German pronunciation. While here in Kent, we tend to pronounce it more like "wein," eh? I remember when we had that German exchange student for a week. She was just getting used to our way of saying "Bath" and all the regional words we use here in Kent. Again, it's about those regional variations. Over in Faversham, we have our own set of quirks too. Like saying "stang" instead of "saucepans." [Laughs] And don't even get me started on the "grass" v "hoss" debate across Kent. [Chuckles] That's a classic. My dad always says "hoss" and gets teased about it now and then. It's funny how little things like that can get us all chatting away about where we're from and how we speak.

Yo, man, did you hear any of the latest?? We've got Grace VanderWaal; her new album is lit! I was listening to it during my commute; it gives me all the feels. Ah really? I heard it was quite the show, but I kind of stuck to questions on this week's assignments. We had one where we'd analyze the market trend of a specific food product and design a marketing plan for it. Ah, I see! I've got another keeps coming up. Think about it - if I'm stuck with an internship, is it worth it to be in a big name place or try smaller, lesser-known ones with more hands-on experience? That’s a bit like choosing among culinary schools. You can go for big brands with recognition or smaller places specialized in certain cuisines. It depends what you want to gain from it, I suppose. For me, the small ones often let you explore techniques in ways the big places might overlook. True. Plus, it’s all about who you meet and what you learn, right? Absolutely. It's about building connections and being able to apply different skills in the end. You’re kind of in the position where you need to figure out what genuinely sets you apart and what you want to do long-term. Spot on. And then there's the piece about job prospects after you graduate... A friend did an internship at this tech firm and got in through that, really good for her. Yeah, those connections help. I know through my culinary classes we had a real fire-cracker chef from London guest the other day. The influence was palpable; we were all eager to discuss our kitchen experiences and planning our next moves in career. Kinda like your music influences me, I guess. Who are you listening to now? Just finishing this new Sónar series. The electronic vibes and the atmosphere it captures is so unique. It reminds me of working late on new restaurant concepts after a long day of cooking. It’s that same creative build-up feeling. Sounds like we're on the same page. Mind if I finally ask—where are you with real job plans post-studies? You thinking of sticking with the culinary path more seriously? Yeah, I’m job hunting actively in Devon. There’s a growing scene here and a need for solid, skilled cooks.

Right okay now I know it's exciting that we're first station's Dad's birthday but today we need to focus on what's going to happen for the holidays don't we talked about that schedule the other day? Yeah we did isn't the trip to Durham next weekend, though? Yes, that's right. You need to make sure your books and assignments are all up to speed so you can take a bit of time off without struggling right? Erm yeah but like how about we check up on that keeps coming up on the radio. That coffee shop deal... I think it's a loyalty card thing. Right, the one where if you buy a certain amount you get a free coffee. Might just do that to make sure we get the best out of it. But let's get back to the schedule. Okay, but like what about after the trip? We're going to do all the standard stuff right? Yeah, the summer holiday, we've discussed it, relaxing, maybe a few trips to the beach, or whatever you want to do. But also, remember we need to get a new sleeping bag for camping. Right! Oh and I need a bed. My old one is too small now. Exactly. Let’s make a list for shopping so we don't forget. What else have you wanted? Well, like loads of stuff but I really need that new game for the console. Okay, add it to the list. Now let's talk about transport and all that. Right, like we're going to Newcastle next, weren’t we? How are we getting there? Probably the train. I can look if there’s a loyalty promotion for frequent travelers. Seems like the More for Less deal might help a bit with the costs. Right! Good idea. And by the way, while we're planning, maybe we can also talk about work arrangements a bit. This business idea you've been on about, do you still plan to do it next year? Yeah, for sure. I've been thinking it through more, but I need help with the structure. Of course! You’ll need a solid plan for finance and health and safety even if it’s just a pop-up shop or something. Oh I realised. I’ll need to check if there are any regulations for running a domino drive, or whatever.

Right okay so I've moved to Sussex I figured you'd be one of the first people I'd call and let you know. It's a bit of a different vibe from Milton Keynes but the tea is still good. Hi mate, isn't it great though, the change of scenery! But tell me, have you dealt with all the joys of setting up in a new place? Like sorting out a new phone number and all that. Oh man, that was a nightmare. Two weeks till everything transfers. Which means I've got until then to be stuck on a pay as you go deal... I just hope we don’t have any internet outages. I’ve been using your old recommendation for the best broadband plans, have you been staying in London? Yeah, been around, been around. The whole broadband issue, it’s a constant battle - oh we've had our share. Though I have to say, our broadband's been surprisingly stable the past year - hope it stays that way. You didn’t move out of MK without me giving you all the advice on broadband deals did you? Well, I went off on a tangent as always. But anyways, so jobs this side, it seems quite different. Higher pay but also higher costs of living. Still, the extra pay more than covers it, I think. Yeah, that’s often the case isn’t it? Higher costs, higher income. I’ve been looking into some side gigs to boost our own budget – you know, freelancing as an analyst, things like that. How does one navigate that as an English language instructor? It’s interesting. I found that there’s quite a demand for one-on-one lessons, especially for people prepping for the Cambridge exams. Also online platforms have expanded the reach, but you do have to deal with the usual issues of the digital world. Seems like the flexibility is worth it though. Definitely hear you. I’m actually thinking of doing a bit of Spanish or even Korean online tutoring on the side next year. I’ve always wanted to but never got around to it. You'd do great at that! I tried my hand at Spanish tutoring before but found teaching in general to be quite rewarding and challenging in its own way, unlike analysis which can get monotonous. Speaking of languages, did you hear the new Korean drama I’ve been watching?

So, I hear that your sister was recently diagnosed with breast cancer. How have things been for her and your family? It's been a tough time, to say the least. We've all been rallying around, you know? Family time has been drastically different, but in a way, kind of brought us closer together. Yeah, I'd imagine. A diagnosis like that can change a lot. Have they started treatment yet? Yeah, she had surgery to remove the tumour about a month ago and is currently undergoing chemotherapy. It's a whole rollercoaster. You'd think it's just physical, but the emotional side affects everyone. Absolutely. Does she seem to be managing okay in terms of her mental health and coping with everything happening? At times, but of course, it's up and down. We've been trying to be there for her as much as possible, offering emotional support. It's hard for everyone, though. Ron, my husband, seems to be taking it the hardest, you know? Always worrying about potential outcomes and things like that. I can imagine. Ron's like that, always thinking about the future. I'm sure it's been a real strain on him. How have the kids been taking it? The kids? They’re kids. They don't fully understand at their age, so it's interesting watching their reactions. Our youngest, Lily, she's five, hasn't really grasped the scale of what's happening, so she's been acting mostly normal. But then sometimes in the evening, she'll come to me or her dad and just be all clingy, and you can tell she’s picking up on our anxieties. That's the heartbreaking part, isn’t it? Children can be so perceptive, even if they don't fully understand the situation. How have you and Ron been coping together as parents and partners through this? It's been tough, to say the least. We’ve had our disagreements, but we've also learned to really lean on each other. We make sure to take time for ourselves too, not just for the kids' sake, but for our own. We try to go for walks together, or schedule these little 'couple' evenings just to talk without distractions. It's helped. Sounds like you two are doing an amazing job of balancing everything. It's good to hear you're finding ways to cope and support each other.

So, how was everyone's weekend? We had a family fun day. Went to the swimming pool and did some team sports. I've been trying to get better at tennis, but I still need practice. Want to have a game later today? Sounds great! I'd love to. Why don't we just have it in the garden later if the weather stays nice? And how's school been for both of you? Any particular subjects you're struggling or enjoying? Well, I've got my keeps coming up soon and it's a bit stressful. But I really like my English, Mr. Smith is such a good teacher. Yeah, I’m really enjoying PE. We just started football and it's actually fun. I never thought I’d say that about football, but our coach is really enthusiastic making it enjoyable. That’s wonderful to hear you enjoy PE so much. Simon, didn’t your school have a referendum discussion recently? Like, voting on something in the class or school? Oh yeah, we talked about what or who to vote for in our favorite sports players this week. It was quite fun. We're planning to do that again for anything voted by the school council. Voting and debate can be so important for development. It teaches decision making, understanding different points of view, and respecting others' opinions even when they differ from yours. Honestly, I feel like it’s good practice for bigger discussions in life, like really understands politics and everything. Definitely. And what about you, Toby? How’s the thought of apprenticeships or further education been settling with you? Well, my teacher said that to get into a good apprenticeship or course in engineering, the grades matter. So I’m definitely working hard in that. And that’s really good to hear! You’ve also been interested in football management, haven’t you? Yeah, but I know you have to study a lot of business for football management. I'm considering taking some business courses or maybe even starting my own little business after university. Like, something in sports for sure. Starting a business is a huge step but it's also an amazing opportunity if you're passionate about it. We can talk more about business and even see about perhaps you and Emily could work together on something, just for fun and maybe even get a little bit of experience.

So, I hear you're planning a trip to Lancaster soon, isn't that right? Yeah, I am. I haven't been up there in ages, and since I've taken this job I need to make the most of time. It's just a weekend away, but I kind of want to see if universities there would be a good fit if I ever decide to do a masters. That sounds exciting! I've heard Lancaster is lovely. Yeah, especially if it's a calm weekend like they keeps coming up with. Think about visiting the coast too, right? I hear Morecambe is really nice. Oh definitely, I've been to Morecambe a few times. The promenade and the beach is great. Have you heard about the cockle disaster places from around 2004? Yeah, that's a tragic story, isn't it? Mm, it really affected the community. But Morecambe's still recovering and it holds quite a lot of charm. You will try the fish and chips, right? So many good places there. Oh definitely on my list! Also, I might visit Lancaster University if I can. I'm really interested in their language department, but I know it's competitive. You know, it's also really nice place otherwise. I used to have some relatives there so I've been a couple of times. Honestly though, visiting universities can be overwhelming. I remember writing my dissertation, it really felt like my world shrunk down to that piece of work. I know what you mean! But it's part of the deal, isn't it? I kind of see it as necessary evil to get to do something I really want. Indeed. It’s strange looking back, but I wouldn't trade the experience. The careers I've seen people go into after getting a masters is incredible. Yeah, and I’ve heard it really opens doors. But first things first, I need to finish this stage of my career. I do worry sometimes, though, especially with things like redundancy these days. Makes you think twice about what's stable in life. Totally get that. Though, having family helps a lot to not let the job define your sense of security. Yeah, my family has been supportive. We just got through my brother getting out of a pretty uncertain spot at work. It's amazing how things can turn.

Yo, mate, did you hear about that new band?? They's supposed to be gods gift to music these days. Nah, I don't think I have. What band are you talking about? It's this new metal band that just came out of Sheffield. They're called "Iron Wraith". I haven't heard of them. What kind of sound do they have? Kind of like early Black Sabbath with somecore influences. Really raw and heavy. Sounds interesting. Have you managed to get tickets for any of their gigs? Yeah, lucky me. I managed to get some for next Saturday at that pub on High Street. Wanna come along? Yeah, sure mate. That sounds good. So, aside from music, what else have you been up to lately? Ah, you know, same old. Just trying to keep up with studies and football seasons. You been playing much? Yeah, pretty much. There's a big match coming up on Thursday between the village teams. Been training or practicing much? We've been doing quite a bit actually. Just trying to balance it all with homework and the like. I know the feeling. Any new hobbies on the horizon or are you sticking with the olds? Ah, honestly, been meaning to take up ukulele for ages but just can’t seem to find the time. You tried any new hobbies? Actually, yes. I started a bit of woodworking and working on fixing my motorbike. Been quite fulfilling in a weird way. Gives me the chance to use my hands and focus on something different. That's cool, mate. That really takes patience and skill. More power to you. Thanks, you too. On that note, did your family say anything about this weekend or holidays? Nothing really concrete. But my mom keeps hinting at trying out a new recipe that she calls 'heaven on a plate'. Sounds promising, though. I'm sure it will be. She always manages to cook up something amazing, even if it's just spag-bol for the fifth time. Haha, exactly. Anyway, how about those mates of ours? Anyone gone on any new adventures or found new interests? Yeah. I heard Jimmy joined that local cycling club. And Sarah started painting again. It's amazing to see people finding new passions. Really? That's great to hear. We should plan something together with Sarah... a painting night maybe? That could be fun.

Oh, did I just kill Sydney or's it Adelaide? Oh my, nope! It's Melbourne, actually. You just gave all of Australia the flu. Wait, wasn’t Melbourne supposed to have a special rule because it was a capital at one point? Ah, no, that was Canberra, mate. Melbourne just suffers the same fate as any other city in this game. I still can’t believe how quickly things spread. It’s like seeing history, but with a board game. And I just have to say, whoever thought of putting a biochemist card is a genius among us. Oh, oh! Bio-discovery just might save us from Melbourne. We’re looking for a cure, though. And if we can get it by the next round, it's all over for the virus! So, plans for the next round? We should connect New Zealand if we can. That might give the virus trouble. But we need to figure out what the cards say. Did we interpret that right? Well, according to this, if we have four players visiting one city, it gets an epidemic, but if we have a cure in play, it doesn’t. So, working together is key now. But it's tough when we can't see everyone’s cards. That’s true. We just have to communicate better. We also need to stop the outbreak in Melbourne. If we don’t, it's over. I really should have played my “sewer upgrade” card last turn. Don’t worry, you can store it for the next game. That’s so typical of me. Always saving for the future... Anyway, the next person draws cards, and... Wait, I think we’ve been dealing with this wrong. Our “researcher” cards don’t just add connections. What do you mean? If we play two researchers... We can research a cure from one already drawn card. So, we might already have what we need! That could change everything! So, let's try that! Who has the cards? I have one researcher, but I need to check my cards... I have two regular cards and the “emit” card. I think we need one more researcher to pull it off. Wait, didn’t someone draw a researcher in the first round? I did! I have one. And if we play the sewer upgrade... Though, that’s a bit too late. Then let’s focus on the cure research!

So, speaking of birthdays, did you both remember that our's is coming up soon? It's practically World Book Day. Oh, yes! It's the birthday book! Mummy, can we have a breakfast party? Yeah! And after breakfast, can we do something fun? Maybe watch a CBeebies pantomime? That sounds like a fun idea! I think we could make it a special day. Can it be my birthday party too? Pleeease? I'm sure the CBeebies performers would have loved that kind of magic. Speaking of magic, I have an idea for a fun birthday activity. How about we have our own little pantomime? We can make costumes and even pick a story from a book. I love that! Can we be Cinderella and the Prince? I want to be the fairy godmother! Okay, we can figure all that out. Now, for the birthday itself. We can have a nice family breakfast and then our little performance. After that, we could go to the park or maybe even have friends over if it's nice. And can we have Mommy read us a story from her birthday book? And maybe you can help me pick out a new story to read for Mother's Day as well. Your great-grandmother used to always tell us a story about a kind lion who would say "Always be kind to others, for a kind heart is the true king's treasure." Do you both remember that? I remember! We talked about it at school on World Book Day. It was really nice. Yeah, and we should use a phrase like that on our pantomime stage! Excellent idea! We can use sayings from stories for our own little play. Mommy, can we start planning? Can we make invitations? We can start thinking about it and even start some crafty bits for the invitations this weekend. How about that? Yay! And can we make it a surprise? Like a surprise pantomime! [smiling] Of course, we'll make it a surprise! You two can help me think of secret plans this weekend while we read... Do you think we can also have a DIY treasure hunt?

So, I hear you’re considering moving again. To be honest yes. The commute to London is getting ridiculous and the flat we've got now is so small. You two are always on about moving somewhere bigger isn't it? You must have seen half the country already? Oh no, don’t make me count. But seriously, the market for house prices in London is just not healthy. I've been looking at some nice places in the South. Not too far from family and it’s much more manageable. True. We've been thinking Hertfordshire or maybe some of those new developments around there. Something with more space for all the gadgets, and I can have a proper kitchen where I can cook. Space would be lovely. Cooking-wise, I've started following a lot of plant-based recipes lately. I should probably get a decent kitchen too. That's great, you know where I've met my dietitian friend? She’s got the most amazing little garden in her backyard in Sussex. She grows her own herbs and it’s all very alkaline. That sounds lovely! For me, it's all about finding that balance between taste and health. But I’ve tried gardening before and it’s just not my thing. I might stick to plant-based but don't expect me to grow my own food. [laughs] It’s not like we’ll keep you away from a kitchen or the joy of takeout though, right? [chuckles] Absolutely not. But you never know, once you have a bit of space and a decent kitchen maybe you’d want to try. But it's not just about the kitchen. I've been thinking about finding some social groups around new hobbies if I do move. Socialising in new areas is always the tricky bit for me. You could try local language exchange meetups or something related to your teaching skills. It’s a great way to meet people while keeping it relevant to what you know best. Yeah, and there are sure to be new restaurant openings after all the developments. True but I want to do something local and meaningful. Like joining a community garden, but as I mentioned, I’m not exactly green-fingered. Alright, alright, no gardening. [smirks] But almost all of those new developments have local social groups or platforms where you can meet new folks who share similar interests.

So, I was browsing on Amazon yesterday and I came across an old edition of ‘The Lion, The Witch and The Wardrobe’ and it was selling for an absolute song. You love your books, Alison! Did you get it? Yeah, I couldn’t resist because it was the exact one my father used to read out loud to my sister and I when we were little. I had similar experiences with my dad. He used to read out loud to me as well. I think it’s a lovely ritual. It really creates a bond. Exactly, and I used to love the way my dad used different voices for each character. Oh, we had a similar experience. My dad used to even make the narration different. He’d have this booming voice for the narrator and soft, gentle voices for characters like Mr. Tumnus or Lucy. And do you still have those old teddies or toys from when you were little? I used to have a cute little teddy bear, but I don’t know what happened to it. I still have my teddy, but he’s been with me through so many moves; he’s quite worn out now. I used to have this old plastic tea set from when I was four or five, and I always insisted on serving tea to my mother with it. That’s so sweet. I also remember a set of wooden blocks and they were always taken on family trips. Well, I’m the eldest of five so we had to make our own entertainment. I can only imagine. Speaking of blocks, I just tried to learn a bit of Italian. Do any of you speak other languages? I speak a bit of French, thanks to school. I used to be fluent in Spanish but it’s rusty now unless I use it every day. That’s understandable. I often find that if you don't speak it regularly, it can slip away so quickly. The accent is probably the hardest part for me – unless you are a native speaker, it almost feels like you’re just pretending. I find pronunciation is the biggest barrier. The rules just don’t seem to match our English phonetics! I agree. But it’s fun to learn and explore new dialects or languages. We should really try to learn one new phrase a week. Maybe in French or Spanish?

So tell us about your trip to the Lake District then. Oh yes. The Lake District was lovely. The weather was superb. Well most of the time. We had the occasional rain downpour but nothing that couldn't be managed. You mean the kind of rain that questions if you're just being drenched or if it's raining and hailing simultaneously? Yes, exactly those moments. Oh absolutely. But apart from that it was lovely. We managed to fit in a walk at Windermere and a trip to Grasmere, and of course had to have some gingerbread. Gingerbread sounds great! Did you get a chance to buy any to take back to share? Oh, we did but we ate most of it on the way back. It's irresistible. Yeah, I recall one time going with family as a child, wandering around trying to find the best gingerbread. That reminds me, did you stop at any of the quaint little towns while you were there? Yes, we spent a night in Ambleside and it was very picturesque. All the little shops and tea rooms along the water. And the food? Delicious. Traditional English dishes with a nice twist. It really does seem like a perfect holiday spot. Well, apart from the rain, obviously. Aye, but there’s always something special about a cloudburst over the mountains. Adds to the drama. Agreed. Plus, it gives you a good reason to huddle into a cozy pub and enjoy a warming ale. Speaking of pubs, did you visit any notable ones during your stay? More than one. The one that stood out was the one above the lake. The views were stunning and the atmosphere was lively. We even got to see a bit of live music. That’s amazing! The ales are excellent, especially with a meal.

I've decided I need a new kitchen's online shopping bag but today. Need to clear some space. Whole council will be over for dinner tonight. Oh wow, that's brave of you! Are you sure you're up for that? It's just like clearing the decks before battle. But, totally understand. I've been thinking about my news links too. Seems like they're challenging the traditional modular approach. As an engineer, it's fascinating to see how these projects are pushing boundaries. And their next landmark launch or whatever, it's like a whole festival around it. I'm curious to see how it shapes our understanding of space travel. It’s kind of assumed now but the 'Rocket Man' they’re using; the tech is actually rooted in some work done right here in the UK. It’s a local hero story in tech without being a cliché. That's really cool to know. I actually have a couple of engineering colleagues who were involved in some of the initial studies. Shows you never know what you're working on could impact the world. But it proves the point too, how tech can kind of influence society and our understanding of things in ways we might not realize yet. And let’s not forget about those side projects, like bio-engineered food or something? I saw a piece about it. Ah, yes. Those 'lab-grown steaks' they're working on. But, it’s interesting how such innovations can reduce our carbon footprint. Speaking of leading by example and all that. Did you guys see the latest from this eco-friendly rapper? He's real about his music and his lifestyle. Yeah. Honestly, I didn’t pay attention past their company being praised for being carbon neutral. But yeah, celebrities making this a talking point can't hurt.

I keep telling James to turn it off. "We don't need the Satnav to tell us where to go, clearly the pub is opposite the traffic lights." He says it's voice-controlled so he can listen and do the driving, but honestly, sometimes I think he just likes the sound of his voice. "Like a fancy GPS that makes you feel smart, right?" And yet somehow still gets us lost. You know what's funny? Back when I was in my early military days, we relied on fucking maps. I mean verbal instructions, and I used to have to check in quarterly just to avoid getting lost. Was it that big a problem? No, but when you're driving around in a heavily restricted area, you make sure you know where you are. Satellite guidance seems like a godsend when you think about it. Someone should tell the Saudis next time I or Reg go over there. Oh, no kidding. James and I tried getting to the Riyadh Zoo once. Took us the whole day and we ended up driving in circles more often than not. Sounds like a bit of an adventure though. Adventure, yes. Lost is another story. Can you imagine explaining to your battalion commander why you couldn't find the damn base and "the map led me here?" I'll pass on that kind of adventure, thanks. Speaking of which, when’s Reg moving out the next time you two go to Saudi, Peterborough’s going to miss the two of you. We’re hoping to ease off on the international trips soon. The job’s going well, but it’s been taking a toll on our routine here. Yeah, I could sit on the back of a lorry or plant a garden more days than not these days. Makes you appreciate the simple things. Us too. But we promised to help him with the decorating over spring break. It’ll be nice to have a bit of a break from work. Yeah, plus you’ll get the real job of getting him settled in and out of his current place. Don’t worry, we’ll make sure he has plenty of late night company and early morning decorating sessions to keep him busy. I’ve got my paintbrush already ready. Just need to make sure I remember where I put the ladders. Don’t worry, we’ll make sure he’s exhausted by Monday morning.

I've decided I need to take a bit more control over my own health. Started taking probiotics and thinking about cutting out some of the sugar. You wouldn't believe the difference just a few changes can make. That's great! I've been journaling questions for my daily reflection and it's really helped me tune in to what my body needs. Mindfulness can be really powerful that way. Ah, mindful practices and gut health? I've got a keepsake plant here, a gingko biloba. You know it's one of the oldest surviving tree species and thought to have cognitive benefits too. These plants, they're like tiny little bio-factories. Sentient, almost . Oh, big thinkers around here - sentience in plants, that's going a bit far. But I get you, they do have this unique way of communicating with each other sometimes, right? Fungal hyphae networks, that sort of thing. Actually, yeah, that's really fascinating! So, on the health note, have either of you noticed any specific changes with this lifestyle adjustment or new practices you’ve tried? I started walking regularly. Just made it a part of my daily routine and found it to also really help with stress. It's odd how something so simple can have such a big impact. Definitely. And in terms of advice, if anyone's thinking of making changes, I couldn't recommend Omega 3 and some key vitamins taken together. Just been looking into things and found that it's helped with inflammation and even mood. I should look into that. Also, less stress about the garden, more togetherness, right? I mean, it's fun to manage it, but sometimes I get so caught up in trying to perfect it that I forget to just enjoy it. Definitely. We could sit together and do a sort of check-in every week – on the plants, but also on ourselves. Imagine, a self and a garden check. "How are you today? How's the soil?" That's definitely a health question. "How's the compost getting along with your nitrogen levels?" We've got a fine chemistry going on here then. But I like that. Connecting with nature... it's oddly grounding. And maybe that's part of why it's good for us? Exactly. What can we make this a regular thing? Though we are busy, maybe a quick check-in outside with a coffee or tea?

Mum, Dad, and everyone, I've been thinking about our accents. Do you ever wonder what our voices are like to people from outside this area? Honestly, not really. We’ve got our voice, our accent. What matters is the content, not the way we say it, right? But sometimes people can struggle to understand us, can’t they? I remember when I first started working, I had to explain to some patients what I meant when I said certain things. It was weird how they heard it. Hey, I saw this thing on TV about voice recognition – it’s supposed to be really accurate these days. I’m sure it could handle our accents just fine. Yeah, but that’s technology. And sometimes technology can be a bit off the mark when it comes to hearing nuances in regional speech. That’s true. But at the same time, sometimes our accent can be very strong in ways that aren’t helpful, like when you're on hold and the automated voice says, "Did you say…?" and you’re like, "YES! Now press two!" Everyone chuckles. Now that you mention it, I think most of our troubles come from misunderstanding rather than accent, don’t they? Like when you all were little and I used to say, "This place is like the seventh circle of hell," and you’d take it literally and want to know why you weren’t allowed in there. Oh man, that was rough. Seventh circle of hell and all. What were we, six years old? But it proves a point about the way we communicate. Sometimes the issue isn’t the accent but understanding intent, context. That’s very thoughtful of you to point out, Jessie. Growing up, I also always wondered about marital problems. How does our living environment affect them? Hmm, good question. I think it really can. Not having a calm, peaceful place to retreat to can escalate tensions. Like when your mum and I were struggling – it didn’t help living in a small house for so long. If we'd had more space, maybe things would have been different. That makes sense. It's like the idea of a physical and emotional space. Some of my friends who have gone through similar things say it’s like living in a pressure cooker. Yeah, and what about the stress of wanting to do things?

So tell me, did you manage to sort out who was running the Halloween games for our party this weekend? Yeah, I've got my mate Chris who's very knowledgeable and creative. He's been doing this at his school for years. Plus it just so happens his birthday is a few weeks before Halloween, so this will be his birthday present.
