Yeah, and we also thought about how we can ensure there's a little something for the adults too. Perhaps a wine and cheese tasting area or something less intense. Absolutely. Now, about the main event, the Baked Alaska. Have you both decided who'll be helping me in the kitchen? We need a few volunteers to help with the preparation and serving. I can help, and I also asked [friend's name] if he can come and assist. He's always been a bit of a whiz in the kitchen. Good, that's helpful. [friend's name] is a fantastic cook. I remember the time he made that amazing cheese and biscuit platter for our family dinner last year. Yeah, that was epic. I was amazed at how he picked out all the different types of cheeses and arranged them so beautifully. Exactly, his attention to detail is fantastic. Now, speaking of details, have you thought about the costumes yet? Of course! I've already chosen mine. I'm going to be a vampire, but not the scary kind. More like a vampire rock star. I like that. It's important to have fun with the costumes. We need to ensure everyone feels comfortable. After all, Halloween is about having fun and being creative. And it's good that you're directing this because you're always so good at organizing and making sure everything goes smoothly.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I was trying to learn how to fly? Not about flying lessons, but I remember you talked about that one time in New York when you– Oh, no! That was a while back. It was just one of those... bizarre mornings where my plane was delayed for hours and I ended up sipping coffee at Penn Station, surrounded by strange tall buildings and fractious pigeons. And how was that? Well, let me put it this way: if I had any doubts about the efficiency of anything – trains, airports, airlines – they were resolved that day. Sounds chaotic. It was. We met in Japan, and didn’t we talk about how the refusal collection here in Swansea is similar to what we had over there? It’s like every other day there’s something new to adjust or learn. Exactly! From arranging for the waste collection to writing letters – it’s funny how often we still need to interact with physical paper and boxes in the age of everything going digital. Speaking of which, I saw your post on social media the other day. You’ve been very active lately, sharing all those beautiful photos from Japan. Ah, social media isn’t just about sharing, really. It’s about connection, even if it’s a bit superficial sometimes. I found that through my posts, I’ve reconnected with a few friends and acquaintances from Japan, which has been really nice. That’s wonderful! It’s amazing how these platforms can bridge distance and time. Indeed. Plus, I’ve always loved writing letters. There’s something warm and human about receiving a handwritten note versus a generic email. I agree. While I love the convenience of digital communication, there’s something about reading someone’s words on paper that feels more… genuine? Exactly. I think in these busy times, taking the time to physically write something, take a photo, and share those snippets of life – it reminds us of the importance of slowing down. Speaking of slowing down, shall we plan the day realistically? We do have those plans for later, don’t we? Oh, right! Before we both get stuck into our academic work, I was thinking we could grab a bit to eat – maybe that new café up the hill?

I'm so late to this game, I've been running around today like a headless chicken. You would think I'd know better after being late to so many events. That's a nice turn of phrase, running around like a headless chicken. Do you know the origin of that phrase? Ah, that comes from the idea of a chicken running around wildly without a sense of direction, just chaos. Kind of how life sometimes feels when we're running late for things. Interestingly, there's a similar phrase in Welsh, “rhedodd fel ceiliog tyllog,” literally translates to "ran like a dizzy rooster," but the idea is the same. Chaos from lack of direction. Ah, you guys want to hear about my uni course? Only if it involves you not being late for class. Alright, alright, I'm not late for uni lectures... this time. My course is all about the different dialects in the English language. It’s fascinating learning how words can change so much depending on where you are. Like? For example? Well, take the word "life". In some regions, it’s pronounced with a different "i" sound, almost like "lyff". In others, it’s a flat "a" and "f" sound together. That kind of influence might be good for scrabble. I might need to use different strategies. Oh, I love that. The strategy of playing with different regional word pronunciations could really help in Scrabble. It’s about knowing your audience, really. While you’re on changing the pronunciation, what about "knight"? It’s a good one in Scrabble – but do you say it with a "k" or a "n"? That’s so funny, because in some regions, "knight" is pronounced with an "n" sound: "naight." Wait, but in scrabble, you need to play what’s on the board or the cards. How can we “play” a different pronunciation? Sure, but often, it’s not just about the letters; it’s about the combinations and what other players accept or not. If you can convince them of a different pronunciation, that could be your edge. Wait, let's plan a Scrabble tournament that takes regional dialects into account! We could have different boards or sets based on the regions we cover. That would be so much fun. We could even have mini rulebooks with pronunciation guides. And for the judges, a course on phonetics might be required!

So, how was your week? It's been alright, nothing too exciting. I was thinking about our grandkids. They're growing up so quickly. Oh, I remember that. And the way she used to insist we play dolls with her. Those were the days. Yes, and now she's making sure those same little ones get properly looked after. When we were raising our daughter, the world just seemed to be kinder, in some ways. More predictable. Nowadays, it feels like everything is moving so fast and it's hard to keep up. And technology! It's amazing how much of an impact it's had on our lives, especially on children. I remember when we just had the TV for entertainment. Now it's all about tablets and smartphones. Exactly. I don't even know how to use half the things the kids are playing with these days. But it does keep them occupied, I suppose. It does. But the problem is finding that balance. More technology can be useful, but I also worry they're missing out on good old-fashioned fun - playing outside, making up games, that sort of thing. I completely agree. But you can't turn back the clock, can you? It's about finding ways to blend the old with the new, I suppose. I guess so. It's about trying to make the best of what we have and ensuring they grow up happy, healthy, and well-adjusted. That's it exactly. It's about the values you instill in them, not just the things they play with. I hope so. Sometimes, I feel like I'm just winging it, but I know deep down we both came from good values and I hope we've passed those on.

So, how was everyone's weekend? We had a wonderful time. The kids really enjoyed swimming and exploring the nearby woods. Yeah, the natural surroundings down here are just beautiful. That sounds interesting! Do you have a version of your mum’s original recipe? I'd love to try it sometime. Oh, absolutely. I could email it to you. That sounds great! And for me, health and fitness have been about finding something sustainable. I’ve tried all sorts over the years but I’ve found that I need something I can easily fit into my day. Even just doing a few minutes of core exercises or a short walk a few times a day makes a difference.

It’s been a bit chaotic turning those into interviews but still, a success nonetheless. Congrats! Sure that takes the pressure off this year. Definitely, and it means we can also focus on the core company goals better now.  changes topic  By the way, how’s your sister?

I've decided I need more plants in my flat. I've got like three and a half plants at the moment and clearly that's not enough. I need to see this. This one – do you remember? It was tiny and now it's a bit leggy and definitely grown out of its pot. I do remember! I'm right behind you on the plant front. Just picked up a new set for my desk. That's great. Ah, Phil, did you manage any gardening this weekend or was it just football gods today? Oh, yes! Well, I did pop out for a bit but mostly I've been marked students' work. Well, after our big plans for the holidays, we should have some downtime.

Yo, mate, did you finish reading through that latest module's paperwork? It was so convoluted; I lost myself halfway through. Literally just talked about that with the others at the studios. Are you still on about the comparative study between the A5 and the M6, or is there something new on questions two and three? Yeah, yeah, totally. Like, the A5 and the M6 part makes sense, but this comparative of why the A5... I mean, what? They want us to explain why one is better than the other due to certain factors, not just historic significance or something blasé, but actually to argue for its efficiency or future use? Exactly, that's been the bane of my existence since last night. I’ve been thinking about the traffic management part in the sample from Grand Designs—how they always talk about urban planning and stuff. Maybe we could include that angle? Ooh, smart! That was my thought too, but how do we structure the argument when it’s comparative? Like, we need points for both roads’ pros and cons and then say which one wins out or something, right? I don’t know, maybe start with bullet points for each road based on what we've covered, like infrastructure maturity, potential for future development, environmental impact. Then we compare in a more structured way rather than just saying one is “better.” Yeah, or we can set certain criteria like economic, environmental, and social impacts, and see how each road fares in each area. It could be more convincing if we have clear key performance indicators they love that in academia, don't they? Totally, it proves we’ve done the homework. I was thinking maybe even finding some academic papers on comparative studies in transport design or something similar to cite. That’s a brilliant idea! Citing actual researchers, not just the TV show. Okay, so our homework for tonight: draft some KPIs or factors for comparison, find one or two articles to support our arguments, and then structure a draft for the comparative part. Sounds like a plan. I’ll start with hunting down those papers. Also, don’t forget for the A5 and M6, we should include something on the local population’s perspective or public opinion if we can find some surveys or anything like that. Good one. That’ll add depth and relevance. Alright then, let’s meet back here around 8 tomorrow and share what we’ve found.

I keep having this dream where I win the Lottery. and you save the world? Well, that would be nice but I need to decide what to do first. A trip around the world? A fancy car? A fancy house for me and my friends! Or maybe a big dog? We've always talked about getting a dog but never had space. YES! A dog! You'd have to have a big garden first, wouldn't you? I used to have a dog in London. It was just like having a puppy all over again. Yeah, but even a small dog would be nice. Maybe not a lot of fuss. Did I ever tell you about when our dog Max won a creative dog award in London? He was barely over a year old and dressed as a pirate. A dog as a pirate! I'm pretty sure that's a dream come true for any dog. Speaking of which, has anyone noticed the news today? A couple in Derbyshire won the lottery and they're buying a big farm to let all the local children play on. That's nice. I'd take that lottery win right now, however. It'd ease a lot of stress, really. What if we win the lottery and get two dogs? One doesn't feel enough for dreams! Two dogs! Dreams are free, right? You can dream as big as you want. Speaking of dreams, your mum was talking about taking the kids on a trip next year. Maybe we can turn that dream into reality instead of lottery wins. Like a holiday to Wales or something? Wales would be so cool! Yeah! Can we see mountains? Mountains, the beach, or maybe something in between. We could all vote on it and start planning little by little. Can we plan our trip to Wales right now? Not right now, but we can start thinking... Dreaming about the dream planning, I see. What can we see in Wales? There's Snowdonia, castles, even a ski resort if the weather's right. Castles! That sounds so much fun. Castles, mountains, plans, and dreams. Maybe our big family adventure next year. No lottery needed! YEAH! I’m going to tell all my friends about our trip to Wales! And when we get back, maybe we can figure out how to get those dogs you've been dreaming of.

So, I was at A&E yesterday with Rachel. You know, she was playing football with the kids and she got injured. She was carrying a ball towards the goal and then this little boy just charged at her. You should've seen the look on her face. Oh no, did she end up hurt? I'm glad it wasn't serious. Yeah, it wasn't too bad, but it's just that the whole experience was pretty... ruinous, I suppose. I mean, we arrived at A&E and it was chaos. So many people, loads of waiting. You'd think with all the advancements we've made, they'd manage to deal with patients more efficiently. Yeah, I've heard similar stories. I was just looking at online reviews and even though most people rate the care as good, the waiting times and overcrowding are huge issues. What happened to Rachel? Well, the poor girl twisted her ankle. Luckily it's not broken, just a nasty sprain. But the waiting time was over two hours! And when we finally got seen, the doctor was so brusque and seemed uninterested. That sounds terrible, especially given this is a preventable situation. I've come across these issues myself when visiting relatives in the system. It's kind of assumed we can just 'manage' these sorts of ineficiencies, but over time, they really degrade the experience for everyone. Well, it did for us yesterday. Can you imagine having to sit patiently as an adult, let alone kids? Rachel was in tears at one point. She kept asking when we'd be seen and all I could do was reassure her that it would be okay. But it's not just about the wait times. The administrative side seems to be a mammoth task. I remember when I was in there for the first time. Seems like the reception staff try their best, but there's so much of a workload. I noticed a lot of stress. Exactly! And then there's the shortage of nurses and doctors, which we all know about. But also, where's the investment in making the patient’s journey smoother? Absolutely. It's like they're focused on providing a service, but not necessarily a truly caring service. I thought we were past the point of just processing patients like an assembly line. I could go on about this all day, but at the end of the day, Rachel just needed some proper attention and some care, not to feel like a statistic in a queue.

So, I hear you've seen some of the latest financial news. What have you discovered today? Oh, yes! Well, the latest talked about global economic changes, and of course, the uncertainty caused by Brexit and the new trade agreements. People are quite worried, but as a small business owner, I've kind of seen it coming. Really? As a teacher, I'm more concerned with how it's affecting our young people, especially those looking at moving out for higher education or work opportunities. Absolutely. As a small business owner in Hove, I'm concerned about the local economy. But I've started diversifying our services earlier this year, so hopefully, we can weather this a bit better. Wise move, as always. You've always had a good head for business. Thanks. And what about you? Anything exciting happening? Well, I've decided to step down from handling classes next year. Thought I'd start freelancing, maybe teaching abroad. There's been this German program looking for English teachers in Berlin, and I love the idea of exploring Europe more while still using my skills. Interesting! That sounds like an exciting adventure. Berlin's changed a lot since my last visit. And while the Brexit uncertainty makes some things tough, it’s opened up new opportunities to explore the EU in different ways. Though, it can be quite concerning for our travel arrangements and budgets, to be honest. Exactly! But the thought of living in another country, really immersing in the culture, and probably, learning a bit of German... it's a big pull for me. It's a fantastic idea! I'm sure you'll do great. Perhaps we could meet up in Berlin sometime, if you make it over? Now that would be wonderful! We could explore a bit together, maybe over a local beer. If you think about it, we could even meet up in Hove first if traveling and planning everything seems daunting. We could make a road trip out of it. Good thought. I think a meet-up somewhere in the middle would be great. Right. We should take advantage of this chance to finally plan a proper trip. Maybe include some of our other friends? Or perhaps just us, if you're feeling tired of the socializing? [laughs] Always ready for that! But now seriously, who do you propose we invite if we plan this trip?

I've decided I need a new coat. This one is just getting so worn out. That sounds familiar. I'm the same way. Always saying that I need a new coat and then never getting around to buying one. You know what, I've kind of fallen in love with a one I saw last week. A waterproof one with a built-in scarf. I think it's perfect for London weather. Waterproof with a built-in scarf? That's smart. Are you planning on heading out when it rains? Well, actually. I've been thinking of enrolling in some courses at the local university. Oh, really? What kind of courses? Well, maybe some language courses or maybe something creative. I've always wanted to try painting or writing. That's exciting. You've always loved art. Yeah, and it might be a little something just for me. Off from work and all that. Definitely worth doing. And Woolwich has some great courses. I've heard. Yeah, it seems that way. Either way, I need something that'll keep me dry while I'm walking. Well, at least you're making good use of your evenings out. Exactly! Speaking of which, can we get the menu really quick? I could go for something warm, and maybe some mushy peas and. Or we could just stick with beer and the pub's snacks. The décor here is quite nice, by the way. Oh, I hadn't noticed the décor, but now that you mention it, the exposed brick is really cool. And they've got this great chilled classic music playing in the background. Reminds me of my uni days. Uni days. That's another subject we might want to plan for. Maybe not. But I have been watching that TV show, Happy Valley. Mind if I spoil it for you? Spoil away. I could use a recap anyway. Okay, so we don't actually need to plan anything. Just hang out, drink some beer, discuss fine art, and maybe get a new coat. I like your plan. And maybe catch up on some of that TV show...and work on that language course literature if we have a moment. Perfect. Now, what'll it be? What can I get you? The shepherd's pie sounds good, and maybe a pint of your finest. Two shepherd's pies coming right up, and perhaps two pints to follow.

So, I hear you took that trip of a lifetime last year. Round the world or nearly so. Yeah, it was incredible! I talked about it for ages but you had other things on your mind at the time. Sorry, mate! You know me, always chasing something else. So, what was the plan? Which places did you visit and hit? Well, it started off in Asia, spent some time in Japan before heading to South Korea, then down to Indonesia. From there, we moved to New Zealand for a bit, then Australia for a few weeks. Sounds epic! I've heard about the vibrant cultures and diverse landscapes in those countries. Exactly! And just like you'd expect, the diversity is incredible. The food in Japan, for instance, was a whole new level. Every region had its own specialities and it was all so delicious. And how was the weather for you? I know conditions can change a lot when you travel around the world. Well, it wasn't always sunshine and rainbows, I'm afraid! We were there in the tail end of this particularly long monsoon in Indonesia. It rained almost every day for three weeks straight. That's rough! Was it hard to deal with? It wasn't ideal, but we packed a lot of waterproof gear and made the most of it. Some days we just explored local museums or took day trips, learned to appreciate the rain in a new way. I can imagine the photos, though. Capturing moments in the rain must add a unique atmosphere. Oh, it did! I took the opportunity to shoot some really stunning shots. There's something about rain on the streets of Indonesia or in the mountains of New Zealand that just screams for a camera. You've got a knack for that. I've seen some of your stuff on social media, it's quite something. Thank you! Photography really helps me see the world differently. Even on tough days like those in the monsoon, there's beauty in it all if you look closely enough. That's a great perspective. It’s something I need to try more often, I think. Definitely! It's not just about documenting your travels either. Photography forces you to slow down and notice things you might otherwise miss in the hustle of daily life. Yeah, I get that. Sometimes I feel like everything just flies by.

Oh, so many things rushing around your head as always Grace. I wish it was just one or two things at a time, but no. You know how it is. Still juggling? Yeah – nursery, questions at work, finding time for myself... and now I've got a book club this week too, so I'll have that to add to the list. Book club? That's great! It is nice, it's just another thing. I love reading but... I just don't know when, okay? True. Juggling life with a little one's needs can be... chaotic. So, about the nursery planning - we need to finalize the schedule for the baby’s first day, and I wanted to confirm which diapers and wipes we want them to use. Of course, I can help you with that. Let's check out the nursery's recommendations and your preference list. How about we make a list and confirm with their staff? That sounds perfect, thanks. Sure thing. Now, how is little Jasper behaving? Still keeping you up at night? Only once in a while, but when he does, it's like there's an early morning wakeup call. Well, actually, it's worse because his internal clock is set to 4:30 AM. Sounds familiar. It's like the universe has a special alarm just for babies and working parents. But it's good, I'm loving every moment. It's just finding the energy to do everything else that's hard. You'll get into a routine, trust me. And don’t underestimate the power of a good afternoon nap—if you can snatch one. I wish! But really, it's finding moments of peace when I can. Like, today's my day off and we might watch a movie together after nursery drop-off. That sounds lovely! Choose something fun. You both need it. I thought so! There's this new family film on that got great reviews. Oh, perhaps you can review it and tell me if it's as good as promised. I’m always on the lookout for a good family film. Will do! Also, can we discuss our weekly plans? Since you’re staying over, maybe we can map out exactly what we're doing. Absolutely. We can even make a little schedule for the week together. It might help with organizing everything. That would be brilliant.

So, how was your week? It's been alright. Got a bit of a stressful job at times, especially when things don't go to plan, but that's life, innit? Right! And what’s new on the work front then? We're looking at some new hires starting next month and I'm kind of in charge of the initial training part. That sounds interesting! How's that going? Erm, still working it out really. But it's keeps me busy, and it’s something different. Yeah, change is good. I've been in a bit of a routine loop with work, but I've been wanting to get into some of that automation stuff, you know, to make my work more efficient. But training can be a real grind. What's wrong with being on your own? I like the independence, want to be my own boss at times. True, but autonomy in a team can work well too, if you've got trusted people around you. Plus, it keeps you on your toes, which I think is important. Definitely. It keeps life interesting, I guess. Now, have you heard the latest about Emily and Sam? No, what's the story? Apparently, there's been a bit of a misunderstanding. Well, they keep misunderstanding each other, but this time it's about where to go for holiday. Ah, classic romance, really. Communication is key. Shows you, love is not always easy, huh? Or planning holidays, it seems! On a different note, have you two see the new collection that just dropped? I saw some really snazzy pieces online the other day. Yeah, I just tried on some of the new ones. The quality is good but it's a bit pricey, if you ask me. I know what you mean but sometimes it's worth investing in something that'll last. I'm considering picking up one of those knitwear jumpers – I heard they're going to be in style for a while. I've been looking at some of the sustainable brands. They're a bit more affordable and ethically sound, which is important to me. Totally. Plus, the quality is often worth it. Yeah, I've been trying to shop more ethically too. It does take more time to find the right pieces but I feel better about it in the long run. It’s a good shift in...

Right, now I'm going to make us a proper pot of tea. To compensate for today's early chill. Fine by me, young one. It's always tea time when you've got tea, right? Aye and I'll take mine strong with one – no, two sugars. Can't have it any other way. Ah, strong tea and socialism go together, don't they? Erm, now that's a conversation I wasn't expecting to have right now. I just meant we've all, in our time, had our cups of rough tea in rough times. It just says something to sit here with you lot, doesn’t it? We've all seen our fair share of life’s storms. And we're all here now, together, with cups full and fires warm. You know, in the old days when we were running around teaching these bright young things, I'd never have expected to be discussing socialism over tea at home. For me, it's the youth. The sense of rebellion, optimism... it never dies, does it? Even if most of us did settle into more conventional lives. Still, this is a kind of settlement we never planned, really. Early retirement, the economy... we’re all here now for very different reasons than we expected when we first entered the workforce. But isn't that just the way of life? One never fully knows where the journey will end up. And here we are, with a perfectly good cup of tea and good company. Very true. And tea has always been a bit of a solace in troubled times. It’s strange, in a way. We’ve lived through so much – wars, recessions, changes in societal values... yet here we are, all retired, but still very much together, thanks to our kids and grandkids keeping us connected. Yes, and we might not be in the jobs we studied for – I spent most of my time teaching in primary – but we’ve all had our impact. We just take pride in different things now. And maybe that's the real victory, isn't it? Being proud of what you've done and who you've helped along the way, whether in the classroom or in life. I suppose so. We've brought up fine young people. And I’ve always believed that's the biggest legacy you can have. Indeed.

So, I was browsing on weekend deals yesterday and came across an idea for a family outing. Imagine a boutique micro-brewery tour and tasting out in Suffolk. It sounds fun, don't you think? You could be in beer heaven with your indispensable guide. That’s kind of you to suggest something like that. It would be fun and educational for everyone, and I suppose it’s a good change of pace from our usual dinner outings. Yeah, I'd be in. Sounds like it could be a fun outing. Though, I still get a bit nervous about tasting new beers, seeing as how I'm a beer newcomer. [laughs] Well, don't forget, your taste buds are just like your personality: shaped by what you've experienced so far. You’ll be surprised at what you might like when you try new things. Exactly, and it’ll be a relaxed atmosphere—perfect for trying out different flavors without any pressure. And it doesn’t have to be this weekend if it doesn’t fit in with everyone’s schedules. So, let’s not firmly plan it yet. Sure, I just wanted to throw it out there as an idea. Regarding schedules, funnily enough, while I was job hunting for my current role, I had to go through a CRB check, right? It was odd at first, but it made sense later for the type of job. Yeah, it’s good to have a standard in place, but I do wonder how much it helps protect the vulnerable and how much it discourages good people from jobs where it’s essential. Well, from what the HR explained, it’s supposed to be about vetting unsuitable individuals. But, if one’s background has things the check might flag—even if they're minor or unrelated to a position—it can become a barrier. I once knew someone who had issues getting a role as a teacher because of a protest they were part of years ago. True, but changing the system takes time. We could sit here and theorize or we can actually do something – make that brewery trip happen or speak up for change where we see issues in our industries. Wise words indeed. Though, I must confess, brewery sounds nice after this conversation. [laughs] [chuckles] Speaking of which, I went to a pub in London with some colleagues recently, and they had a great selection of artisanal beers.

Hey have you started today's task list yet? Mm, just finished making my breakfast and I had a look but now I’m waiting for a response from Matt before I can proceed with the project’s timeline. Did you get a weekend to yourself? Any chance of catching up with your other friends? Erm, yeah Jess is free for dinner this week if you want to get together with us three. We could do something normal this time, no Thanksgiving themes. Oh dear, I wasn’t sure if that's what was expected of me again. You can but you don’t have to - though we could do with hearing about your travel plans and how your relatives seem. They are as hilarious as ever! My little cousin managed to run around the house with no pants on while it was freezing outside because he "lost" his. Kids! We really don’t need that kind of energy right now but it sounds funny. I’ve got some pretty quirky stories too though, while on holiday. Like what? Did anything work-related come up on your mind while you were away or was it all relaxation therapy? It was all about relaxation but one of the inpatients mentioned something really interesting. He described life as being like rainbows - you only see the pretty colours through a certain angle but if you look closely enough, you find the different hues and the spectrum that makes up the whole thing. It was kind of deep and all, but it’s stuck with me since. Wow, that’s lovely, isn’t it? Sometimes I feel like that way whenever I watch a sports game or couple skate or even before they dive in the ice. It’s like there’s so much more to a sport or a person than just the surface. Exactly, that’s what I thought too. It’s like people often judge a sport by its flashy moments or so-called 'excellence' but for the skaters, the thousands of hours are the ones leading up to those final few seconds. Same for life and almost anything we do, right? Yeah. I was reading about that topic a bit on my holiday too - there was this great article on different thinking styles, especially about how different learning patterns and progress seem more like slow rainbows often too. That’s a nice reference.

So, I hear that Cassie's health has taken a turn for the worse. I'm really worried; her cancer is quite aggressive. Yes, I talked to her husband the other day. He said they're still hopeful but the treatment isn't working as well now, and the relapse is a setback. It’s so tough for them and for her friends and family. I've been thinking about offering to help with the children or anything else they might need. That's very kind of you. The kids will probably need more support now. She’s been managing most of it while she could, but seeing her like this… it’s heartbreaking. Exactly. She's such a strong person and has been so positive through all this. It’s hard to see her struggle. Speaking of struggles, we've been thinking about buying a second home in the village, but with all these new developments, the planning council seems to be very restrictive. Really? Did they reject your plans or was it more of a consultation phase? They rejected it. Now we’re considering whether this is a lost cause or if we should revisit it. I think most villages are becoming very particular about the type of development they allow. If they already think the village is overcrowded or there’s not enough infrastructure, they’re likely to be quite cautious about allowing more properties. Exactly. I’m a bit torn because we love the area and we could use the space for our family, but we’re not prepared to push plans that could harm the village over the long term. It’s important to consider the bigger picture. Maybe we should look at the village’s development plans to see where they see themselves in five or ten years. That might give us some insight into what kinds of projects they’re likely to support. Good point. We probably should. And by the way, have you seen the houses that just came up for sale? You mean in the village? No, not yet. I was waiting to check out the new listings when we had time together. There’s one that looks quite nice. A bit further from the village center, but with a huge garden and an upstairs office which could be great for me if I work from home more often. Maybe we should take a look next weekend when we’ve got some time.

I've had enough of this place already. The noise these students make is like a constant drumbeat. It's like they think they've got thirty years of youth before them, and they've got to live it every day, at maximum volume. That's because some of them have had thirty years and still act like they're eighteen. But you've got a point, it can get pretty tiresome. Tiresome? It's maddening. Like last night when that kid keeps coming in at two a.m. playing his music so loud it shakes the floor, and then I've got to go and knock on the door, just to have him act all annoyed. Who gives a two-year-old a full drum kit to play into the night? Well, from what I've observed, they don't even know how to properly use the batteries in a quiet toothbrush, so a drum kit's out of their league, for sure. But, seriously, it's got to be the broken elevators. One's always out of order. It's like they're never fixed. Yeah! Now that? That's just poor management on our end. I've written reports, I've tried calling in the engineers, and still, nothing gets done. It's like nobody cares about the little things that make the day-to-day so much more bearable. And then there's the overcomplication of the most basic tasks. I swear, we've got rules about silly things like not leaving mugs in the sink or forgetting to flush the toilet, and all it takes is a polite "hey, could you please...?" doesn't come across as scolding. It just is the elephant in the room nobody wants to talk about. Talking of which, have you dealt with the new policy about not having hot food in the kitchen? I just tried to explain that a student bought a steak tray for their microwave, and suddenly I'm the bad guy for questioning their culinary choices. Oh, the microwaved steak debacle. Yeah, I sort of got pulled into that one on the phone support for student queries. The new health and safety compliance is just overkill. A little bit of common sense could go a long way. It's like we're not trusted to handle the basics anymore. Exactly. Overregulated and yet under managed. It's like... Like what, the sense of security is more about paperwork and less about actually securing the place?

So, I was browsing on Instagram yesterday and I came across an account that uses these beautiful pictures to teach phrases in French and German. I was really struck by how much I miss learning new languages. Is that right? I remember when I was younger and I used to visit my aunts in London, we'd always try to speak a bit of French together. But never really picked it up beyond a few basics. But why didn't you two never pick up languages? All that secondary education for nothing! True. Back then, languages were an option, but I guess, like most of us, I didn't see the real point in it. Now I'm regretting it. I know what you mean. I used to be really good at French in school but never used it outside the classroom. And now all you hear is people whining about how they wish they could speak more languages. Back then, when we were travelling on package tours, we didn't really need to. Someone usually spoke the local language, and we just followed along. Oh, that brings back memories. Remember when we all went to those Christmas markets in Antwerp? We just funneled through, marveling at everything. Indeed. And the city traffic! It was chaos, but in the best way. Honestly though, I think it's easier now with all the language learning apps and YouTube. If I had those growing up, I might have tried harder. That's true. I've found myself using Duolingo and the like now. It's much more engaging than textbooks. Speaking of Antwerp, have you two heard about the festivities they’re doing there again this year? The seafront is always fun. No, but I’ve heard Herne Bay has some great Christmas shopping too. I hope I’ll make it down there this year. Don’t make that face. I'm sure you'll have time between looking after those troublesome boys of yours. And dogs too! Speaking of which, did either of you see the photos circulating about puppies in costume at Christmas markets? I did! Oh those poor things looked so bewildered but adorable. Well, I can't speak for the puppies, but I've seen some horrifying children’s birthday party outfits this season. Speaking of children, did anyone explore the Brighton Seafront lately? I've heard the new pier is still a hit.

Mum, I was at school today. They talked about the equality vote. Do you know what that is? Yes sweetie, it's talked about a lot. It's about making sure everyone has equal rights. It's about making sure no one is treated unfairly, like because of their sex, race or sexual orientation. But what does it mean for us? Well, it means you can feel safe as a boy or girl, and everyone else can too. It also means that if you want to get married when you're older, and you're with someone of the same sex, you can. It means you can choose your own way without being judged by others. So what's the problem with it then? Some people just don't understand it or feel it's not right for them. They might not know much about it or they might think it's going to change things in ways they aren't comfortable with. It also gets mixed up with complicated political stuff, which can make things even harder to understand. Mm. Well, I don't really understand or care much about it at the moment. We don't really talk about it at home, or at school. That's fair. It's a big topic but for kids it's about seeing everyone in your school as equal and being friends with people regardless of who they are or like. It's about making sure everyone is included and not left out or made to feel different. Yeah, that makes sense. Like, at school, if someone is different they are still cool, right? That's right. Just like doesn't matter if someone's birthday is different from your own, we still make sure they have a good time at their party. Yeah, mom, you always remind me of that. Like, your birthday just passed, and we celebrated it even though it was just our little family at home. Yes, that's right. And just like how you love your dad so much even though he embarrasses you sometimes with his jokes, we all can appreciate each other's quirks – and that includes what people like or who people like. Oh, yes. I couldn't tell anyone about last week when Dad sent that funny joke about marriage being like a long hallway... you know, something about ups and downs and all being fun?

I've got all these old lathe's tools. Look at this one; it's been with me since my apprenticeship days. Do you remember using this old tool, Dot? Yes, I do now that you mention it. How times have changed, huh? It's fascinating listening to your stories, Dad. I've never heard much about that period in your life. Ah, I had a laugh though. Messing about with this old lathe keeps me busy. You wouldn’t believe how many things you can make with it. Even today there's still a market for such skills, isn't there? I mean, there's trends with all the handmade things. Indeed. It's good to see that some values stick through the years. What about that wonderful meal? Looks amazing! You're a regular chef at heart with all these home-baked goods and proper sauces. Well, it's not every day we can enjoy such a proper roast, is it? Now that I'm retired, I've got the time to indulge. I’ve heard about this roast dinner recipe you made, the one with the glazed carrots. It’s legendary at family gatherings. Ah, well, it’s all about the little extra touches, isn’t it? Like that glaze. Now, where's the silly story I promised you? An anecdote? Something about the hamster? Oh, it wasn't exactly about the hamster, more about the microwave and our then excessive curiosity about its capabilities. More, more! On one of those lazy Sunday afternoons, we decided to see if we could dry out Mrs. Higgins, our poor hamster, with the science of changing the humidity inside that microwave. So, let's talk about what we've been seeing in the news lately regarding government policy.
