Right now, it's mainly about finding time for a walk when traveling like this. Are you still with the gym when you're at home? Yeah, absolutely. It's become part of my routine, just like sticking to a certain diet. You've been thinking about your diet more, right? Yeah, after retirement, my schedule changed a lot - which required me to be more aware of my diet and exercise. It's interesting how much it affects your mood and overall wellbeing. Definitely! While we're on the topic of wellbeing, did you read that travel article about how it impacts mental health? Actually, I did. It was fascinating. I think travel really helps, but maybe it's also about how you balance it with different parts of your life. Exactly! And speaking of balance, in your part-time TEFL work, do you think the career path can be sustainable? It can be, especially if you have the right mindset about it. But for me, it's more about supplementing in between other things I want to do, like volunteering. Volunteering – that's great! I've been thinking about taking that step as well. There's something so rewarding about giving back, isn't there? Yes, absolutely. Whether it's the sense of community or just the knowledge that you're making a positive difference, it's incredibly rewarding. We should look for a park to stop at when we get to Rzeszow. It's supposed to be beautiful and it would be a great place to take a walk. That’s a plan! I was looking out the window earlier and saw these huge fields. Maybe we could try to find a spot nearby. Alright, let's check the map real quick before we get too far off course. This campervan could use a break, and so could we. You know what else I realised? I started reading more since my previous travel. Have you found any good books?

Ah, now I'm going to say something that might sound a bit weird. I've been meaning to reach out to Ian Jepson, he's the gerontologist I talked to at the conference last year. He's doing some fascinating work on the role of telomeres in ageing, and if you're interested, I can set up a call. Wow, I knew telomeres were important, but I didn't realize they were so central to our understanding of ageing. Exactly! Telomeres are like the plastic tips at the end of shoelaces - they keep our DNA from unraveling, you see. As we get older, they shorten, which can lead to cellular ageing and eventually, more serious health issues. Does he have any insights about how we can slow down the shortening of telomeres? Yes, he does. He talks about lifestyle changes - diet, exercise, meditation, and even social connections. But the most surprising thing, for me, was the impact of childhood experiences and early life stress. That's a new area of study. I never thought about it like that. For me, it's hard to stick to a routine with a toddler, but if it can help in the long run... Exactly! Even small steps can make a difference. For instance, he mentioned that omega-3s, like those in oily fish, can help protect telomeres. Maybe you can sneak some into your diet? Good idea. I could try... Can I pick that up when we’re out later? Of course! Plus, it's always been a mystery to me - why weren’t the ancient civilizations like the Egyptians more concerned about gerontology? You'd think with all their interest in immortality through the pyramids and such... Yeah, immortality! I was thinking of that when we were looking at that National Geographic about the comet chasing. It made me wonder, if we were to achieve something like living forever and travel everywhere, what would happen to our changing energy resources and dependency on Earth’s resources? Ah, such a great question. If we had immortal beings, you'd think they'd have a different view on sustainability, but also, we’d run into the same issues we have now on some scale, no matter how efficient we got. The real question could be, what kind of society would we be? Would we still form families or socially structure ourselves in similar ways. I imagine immortals might be a bit like the concept of the ancient Celts and Vikings — living and dying under the sky, moving from place to place rather than settling in the same spot for centuries.

Mum, Dad, did you hear about that new restaurant that's opening up in Cleve today? I think it's gonna be really cool and they're offering a discount voucher scheme for locals. Ah, yes! I saw something about it online and thought the same, but I wasn’t sure if it was open yet. It’s about time a new place came to our area, the variety out here can be a bit disappointing. Yeah, the prices at some of those places can be a bit steep for what you get too. I've heard it's a bit of a local hotspot in town before but pricey, but with a voucher, it’s worth a try! Exactly! And from what I saw, they have like a whole line up of local specialities. It just sounds really nice for a Sunday dinner spot or something like that. That does sound wonderful. It's been so long since we've had a decent meal out as a family, just enjoying ourselves without complicated orders or rigid expectations. I’m sure it will be popular. Someone should probably book ahead though, just in case it gets crowded. But that discount would be really nice, especially if they start giving out vouchers. I think most places are doing that now, but the pressure must be on. With the new baby’s chair and all the other things we need right now, every bit counts. Absolutely, let’s keep an eye on it and maybe even go for lunch sometime this week if we can. It could be a really nice break for us all. Booking ahead is a good idea, especially if it’s popular. How about I check out their website and see if I can reserve a table? That would be great, thanks! We can just grab some things the next time we're out and then head there together. The chickens are fine aren’t they? I hope feeding them wasn’t too much trouble. Oh, no problem there! They’re actually quite a handful but also so much fun. We could probably use some more chicken feed if we’re gonna keep them, though. Yeah, I know. Either that or maybe we take turns so it’s not all on one person. It does seem like a good project for us to have, something for all of us to work on together.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time I had to explain what a hyphen was to one of my less fluent patients? It was hilarious. No, really? Was she puzzled because of the accent or just wasn't familiar with the punctuation mark? More the punctuation mark, and the fact that she was part of a family with a bunch of pre-teens and young adults, all of whom I had to teach basic English and secondary-level stuff. It was interesting keeps me grounded, alongside all the medical jargon. You'd think it's just about dispensing tablets and injections, but there's so much more human side to the job. Oh yes, I can imagine. I often have to translate digital marketing speak into plain English for some of my clients. “Pivot the content strategy to better reflect the organization's mission” becomes “Let's make sure our website says what we really do and why it matters." Exactly! So, have you done anything fun this week? Past the writing deadlines, I mean. Actually, last night I met this really interesting person online who's into studying German history and culture. We're planning a little meet-up to discuss it over coffee. It's nice to find someone passionate about the same things outside work and family. That’s cool. I used to have a patient who was super into that stuff, nice old chap who had lived through some of those periods. He always had fascinating stories and could speak German really well. He never spoke of the darker parts much, which I respect. That sounds incredible. I wish I could've met him. How the people we meet through work influence us so much, you know? Definitely. Now, about Christmas – the tree's looking a bit scraggly again, isn't it? Should we get a new one? Probably. The cat keeps knocking over the ornaments anyway. Last year it was all about finding the cat's “candy canes” under the sofa cushions after. Oh, I hadn't thought about that. Alright, we’ll get a new one. And maybe some cat-safe ornaments if such a thing exists. Yeah, definitely. Plus, the neighbours kids love climbing our almost-decorated tree just for fun. Well, we’ll make sure they're safe. Speaking of decorating, have you heard from Dave about our birthday plans? Not yet.

Right okay so I've moved in. I need to hook up the internet. I called today and apparently it arrives tomorrow. You're gonna have to wait for me to get talked through that. You called right? You got the voice prompt to talk to someone and then the waiting, the hold music? Oh God, yes. Waiting and listening to them asking me if I have broadband access at my current premises. I wish I could yell at them right now, "No, I'm trying to get broadband here!" Yeah, nothing beats listening to elevator music while waiting for essential services, is there? True. But at least I had a lamp I plugged in. So that's one thing. And we need to sort out rubbish collection. I read online we can get the bin from the council or from a shop. Do we have to decide that right away or can we figure it out later? Maybe looking for a council website first would clarify. But honestly, if the shops have them readily available, I'd just grab one. Easier for us in the moment, at least. For sure. We should also do shopping. We need some food essentials, right? Yeah, definitely basics. And while we're out, seeing if they have good local produce at the shops. It feels good to support local farmers. Well, actually, my mum was saying the nursery next door always has a sign out saying 'Local produce for sale in our shop' because they run that alongside childcare. Maybe that’s a good start. That could be a nice community connection too. Yeah, kind of like 'shop local, support the nursery' all in one. Also, seeing what cooking supplies we might need. Our kitchen is a bit bare at the moment. Exactly! And maybe while we're figuring out what we need, we can grab some first dinner supplies. You up for cooking tonight? You know how I can do a mean pasta. I'm in! And actually, I have a bottle of that nice red wine we talked about. Oh perfect! Can't go wrong with pasta and a good red. However, this leads to the important question: do we need to do banking promptly to set up direct debits and stuff? We should probably. Especially for bills. But I can probably do that during the week. Don't want to rush into that today.

Ah, I can't believe we're finally meeting up without an assignment or lecture to attend. It feels like forever since we last did this and just talked about life. Definitely unreal! I've missed our long conversations over breakfast at uni. I miss that now, the casual, chill catch-ups – before life got so busy. It's insane how fast time flies, isn't it? It feels like yesterday we were both prepping for finals, and now here we are graduated, trying to find our paths. So how is life treating you? Still working as a project co-ordinator? Yeah, it's been a whirlwind but I'm enjoying it. I've been really engaged in a project about sustainable practices in urban planning, which is really rewarding. Though, sometimes it feels like a 24/7 job! And what about your plans? Any travel ideas this year? Honestly, after the pandemic, I'm very hesitant. But my partner and I have been talking about maybe going to Greece this summer if things clear up. Just something relaxed, you know? For me, it's been a mixed bag with work. My graduate placement is interesting, but I find the transition from uni to work-life quite tough. It feels like everything's on a timer in the office, and sometimes I miss the more laid-back university vibe. Well, at least you're gaining experience, right? It's all part of the process, finding what works best for you. I've been trying really hard to keep work life from invading my entire week. It's tough, but some hobbies help. I've started baking again, which is oddly therapeutic. Baking? That's so different from what I do, but I can see how it'd be therapeutic. My stress reliever has been comedy videos. There's just something about laughing that makes the tough bits manageable. Same here. Though, my mum is getting on my case for not making more traditional Indian sweets. She's a great cook, so I feel a bit pressure to learn some of her recipes… maybe it's a project for the next holiday? That’s a great idea! I can totally imagine my mom joining in, teaching you how to make all her favorites. Speaking of family, how’s your dad been? Last I heard, he was getting into this new hobby...? Oh, yeah.

So tell me about the North East. I've never been, I've always been curious. You know, aside from what's in the media which can be a bit misleading, of course. You know, it's got quite a mixed bag. A lot of people think it’s all about industry – which is true, there’s still some of that around and it’s certainly got a strong history of that – but there's also a lot of natural beauty and culture, right? Yeah, I've always found it fascinating how diverse the North is compared to the South. You get landscapes and dialects that just don't exist elsewhere, don't you? Absolutely. The dialect is quite distinct, very similar to what you’d hear in parts of Scotland down to even Northern Ireland sometimes. Everyone’s friendly, even if places can seem a bit rough around the edges to an outsider. Rough around the edges? That’s a polite way of putting it. But I mean, that’s part of the charm, right? Exactly. It’s genuine, for sure. And the music scene! So many talented bands have come out of Newcastle and Sunderland. I mean, you see the likes of Arctic Monkeys and Maxïmo Park, but there’s a whole underground scene, too. Arctic Monkeys? They’re overrated if you ask me, but I can't deny the cultural impact. Well, at least for a while they were. Overrated, maybe. But they did a lot for putting the North East on the map when it comes to music and popular culture. And there’s so much more to it. But it's not just about the music now, is it? Tourism and investments have helped bring new life to certain areas. I’ve seen studies on how regeneration efforts have impacted the region, quite positive in many respects. Yes, that’s true. You’ve seen the old industrial sites turned into trendy loft conversions or museums. It’s really breathing new life into parts of the city. Yes, and the food’s not bad either. Oh for sure! There’s some of the best fish and chips you can find, plus all the local specialities. I mean, if you're ever in Newcastle, you have to try a stottie. Stottie?! What’s that? It’s like a large, flat bread typically filled with whatever you want – usually meat or fish, or sometimes just plain.

Nana, I was at school today. They talked about the climate change thing. I don't really understand it. Oh, well let me see if I can explain it the right way. Climate change, you see, is when the Earth’s weather becomes drastically different from the usual, like a kind of massive weather shift. You mean like it gets really hot and then really cold? Yeah, but climate change also causes things like more frequent extreme weather events. Like really heavy rains, very strong storms, or long periods of drought. And it's not just weather, it affects the whole planet. Why does this happen? Well, it's mostly because of human activities. Like when we use fossil fuels - coal, oil, and natural gas - we release a lot of carbon dioxide into the air. That’s a greenhouse gas that traps heat on the Earth. It’s like you’re wearing a blanket too thick and you get too hot. So it’s our fault then? Partly, it is. Years ago, people didn’t know that their actions could cause global warming. But now we know, so we’re trying to prevent and reverse it. I’ve heard about electric cars. Is that part of it? Exactly! Electric cars use less or no fossil fuels, so they’re better for the environment. There are also many other initiatives to reduce carbon dioxide emissions, like using solar or wind power instead of coal, and recycling. But if it really is our fault, why hasn’t the government done something about it earlier? Well, that’s a good question. It's a complex issue because it requires changes that affect how we live, work, and produce things. Plus, there are people who might lose jobs if we switch away from fossil fuels, or worry that these changes could be too expensive. Do you think we can fix it? There's hope. Lots of people, governments, and businesses around the world are working together to find solutions. It's not easy and it won't happen overnight, but if we all do our part, there’s a chance we can reduce the impact of climate change. That’s so much to think about, Nana. This seems really serious. It is serious, and it’s important for kids like you to understand it. Even though you might not feel like you can make a big difference right now, little actions can add up.

Alright so James, remember last time's "blood moon" when you grabbed the drumsticks and tried to conduct the table as though you were directing a chicken orchestra? Oh sorry, I was just channeling the lunar energy! Oh dear, the things that make me proud and cringe at the same time! Now, why don't you two show me how to properly hold a set of drumsticks during a "blood moon", if nothing else for my entertainment? Okay! You need to keep both hands at the same height, almost like holding a pair of cutlery. Yeah, or like a fork and knife! I see! A fork and knife - I like that analogy. But let's talk about proper conduct during a family dinner, shall we? We're going to travel back in time to when I was teaching and what I'd want my class or even my grandchildren to understand. Sure, and maybe this time no chicken-orchestra performances… First of all, waiting until everyone is served before you start eating. It’s a small sign of respect for those who prepared the meal and for the company. Got it – like a gentle pause for gratitude, perhaps? Also, not shoveling in food or speaking with your mouth full, manners we’re trying to get all of you boys to master. Okay, I'll try to keep the chicken shoveling to a minimum and the conversation to one statement at a time. Good! Also, saying "please" and "thank you" – it’s not just for grandmothers but for everyone who’s helping or sharing time with us. Yeah, and listening to each other when people are talking. It’s easy to get carried away in our own thoughts or jokes, but sometimes it’s important to just listen. Especially when Granny’s sharing stories about her teaching days or what we’ve missed when we’ve not been able to show up for dinner. True, I could tell stories all day! You know, one of the things I used to teach was about how meals are more than just feeding our bodies. They’re connections. So, talking, sharing, laughing together – that’s essential. I like that. Connecting with each other over food and stories feels like a pretty good life skill. Plus, when Granny’s here babysitting for us, she’s trying to share that connection too, right? So we should be mindful of that.

So, I hear you had a job interview. Yeah, actually today. Went well I think, but I've not heard back yet. Oh, that can be quite nerve-wracking, waiting to hear back isn't it? You have no idea. Every hour feels like an eternity. Indeed, I know the feeling well. It's like sitting in limbo, waiting for the right answer to be revealed. I had a similar situation a while back for my niece's teaching job. Did she get it? Yes, she was ecstatic. But the waiting part...it just takes a lot out of you. Absolutely, and it's even harder when you're looking to change paths in your life. I feel like I've been making the transition from full-on teaching to more of a background role in the school, so this would be a new chapter. That's very understandable. Changing paths can be both daunting and rewarding. I've seen so many colleagues who have done it and never looked back. But what or who is it that made you want to look this way? My daughter, partly. The school system is quite demanding, and I want to spend more time with her. Also, teaching has its moments, but the bureaucracy and paperwork can be overwhelming at times. Ah, family first, then. That's always a good reason for change, isn't it? Speaking of, how's she doing? She's fine, thanks for asking. Just getting into her own groove now. That's good to hear. She's a bright young thing. I've always wondered how it would have been if I had had kids. Sometimes the things we don't do in life can lead to as much a fulfilling path, can't they? Exactly. Different paths, different journeys. But enough about me. So, if you don't get this job, what's the plan B? We've been considering launching a little project on the side. Something related to the business side but also something we're passionate about. I've had some experience with business, but I've never owned one outright, so it's a bit of an unknown for me. That sounds exciting. Taking the leap and trying something new. Even if it fails, the experience will be invaluable. Indeed, and if it doesn't work out, we can always fall back to something more stable.

"Baby one more time" while glancing at his phone. Aaron! Stop it! I talked to your tutor the other day. He said if you need help with the voice work for your A-level project, the drama department might have some exercises for you. That’s cool, Mom. Do they have a karaoke setup? He'll never stop. Seriously though, that could be helpful for your projection and pitch. Ann, have you considered voice acting? I could ask one of my students who started a YouTube channel if they’d like to collaborate. Might just encourage him to actually sing instead. Shut up, both of you. No, seriously, its useful. We used to have a home karaoke set and it was a laugh but it also helped me with presentations at work. Your tutor might be onto something here. So, Aaron, what are you thinking about for this project? A script or poems? Oh, I’ve got some silly poem ideas. The tutor said we can do spoken word. I was thinking about doing something on traveling and its importance to people. Sounds interesting. Have you thought about technology in travel? Ah, and have you planned your trip home? We need to check the road conditions before we head in, the weather isn’t looking too great. We might have to reroute. Traffic ahead. Can we stop for lunch on the way? I’m starving. We will. But let’s choose somewhere where it’s decent. We won’t stop at the local supermarket café. What about this place we’ve had before? It's next to the park and the kids love it. Yeah, and they have good food. It might be a good break. Yay! I want mac and cheese. As long as it doesn’t end up all over the back seat. Trust you. Hey, maybe this could be part of my voice-over project, a cooking show where I just show how to make mac and cheese. You’ll be raking in commissions from Kraft by your next birthday. I'll take any commissioned work. Watch that car behind us though, looks like someone’s trying to race us. You know we’re not in a rush because of the weather, right? Yeah, let’s take our time. I need to check the traffic if there’s a better route through town. So, this might take a bit longer than expected but at least we’re not in rush hour.

I've never seen anything like it. We've hit a farm today and nearly every animal ran towards the car windows and looked at us as if they talked to us. Ah yes, that's our neighbors place up ahead, the Thompson’s. They're friendly folk, love putting on a show for the visitors. That was quite the greeting committee. I've never seen sheep right up to the car before. Oh my, there was one keeps coming backwards and forwards, putting nose to the window, I swear it was trying to ask me for a snack. I used to have a cat in London that would do just that. "Get me out, get me out" she used to say when I’d try to ignore her. It's amazing how quickly they can get your attention. I hope they don't break the car windows. Some of those noses looked sharp, or maybe I’m just paranoid after driving through a cluster of geese? Oh, never mind the geese, they just acted like they owned the motorway while the farm animals here actually interacted with the vehicle. What's the plan for when we reach the village? Should we be prepared for more animal encounters or perhaps some more traditional folk visiting us? You’ll get to see another side of the countryside. We might see some cattle and definitely will pass a few horse farms. Oh, that sounds ideal. I might even end up wanting a horse farm now. Well, you’ve got the land for it, I suppose. Though keep in mind it's a lot more work than you might think. Yes, my friend used to have sheep and it was always a challenge, especially dealing with the health and well-being of the animals. I suppose so, but there’s something so calming about animals. There is. It’s one of the reasons I enjoy driving through such areas. However, as a consultant engineer, I could perhaps design some more animal-friendly fencing or something to minimize the disruption. Ah, that’s a great idea. We could use some of those smart fences. I’d love to see such a thing. You know, like a farm where animals and cars... coexist better. Coexistence through better design is exactly what I work on. Sometimes it’s the little details that make a big difference. Well, Mrs. Thompson could probably use some advice on that if she wanted.

So, I hear that your weekend was quite busy with the school's art fair. How did it go? It was actually a great success, thanks for asking. The kids had a lot of fun and sold some beautiful pieces. Indeed, and the fair itself was very well-organized. I knew it would be. You've been part of the parent-teacher association for years and you always manage to pull off these events. Well, it's a team effort, of course. But yes, it was fun to get everyone involved, including the choir. They had a little performance which was a hit. I heard that. The choir did fantastically. It just shows how talented those kids are. And the food from the fair? I presume you tried the [traditional dish] that your sister made? The [traditional dish], yes. She made it just like Ma used to. It was spot on and everyone loved it. I had a few servings myself. I love how whenever there's an event, there's always this delicious spread. It's one of the perks of being part of this family. Indeed, the food is always one of the best parts. But the real highlight was the number of people who showed up. It was surprising, given the rain we had earlier in the day. That's always the worry, especially in this part of the country, isn't it? But it seems to have shown the community that these events are worth supporting. That it doesn't matter what the weather forecast says if there's something happening that benefits everyone. You're absolutely right, and it's not just about the art fair or the food – it's about building those community bonds. Which reminds me, we need to discuss the family holiday plans. Your idea of visiting [family member's name] in [destination] was really well-received when I mentioned it last week. Yes, I thought it was a great idea, especially since it's been a while since we saw [family member's name]. And it's always fun for the kids too. They've been asking when we're going on a trip. So, shall we finalize the dates and maybe book the train tickets soon? That’s a good idea. And don’t forget to check out [traditional recipe] when we’re there. [Family member's name] has promised to teach us how to make it.

Right okay so I had your parent’s evening today. Speaker_2 : What did mummy say about me? I don't know. You tell me. Alright so it was all positive wasn’t it, wasn’t it? Both of you are doing great. You’re making progress in everything and there’s areas where you can improve but that’s just part of the normal growth process, right? Yeah? Did she say anything about me being good at English? She did mention that you’re really enjoying reading and that you have a good grip on comprehension – that means understanding what you read, dear. I also have to say that in Maths, the teacher says you have to try to be more precise. You can be a bit faster in getting the answer but sometimes making sure each step is correct is more important than just rushing through. What about me? Did she say I was good at creative writing? Absolutely, she did! You’re quite good at coming up with stories and ideas and she said you really enjoyed the World Book Day. Which was last week, remember this? You were both quite involved. I was the Three Little Pigs. And you were the Big Bad Wolf in good disguise, I believe. Perfectly terrifying to the other children, apparently. Can we go to a real circus now? Well, we could try to find a good one that comes to town or maybe when the weather is better. I want to be a real clown. That could be quite fun. Clowns make people laugh, but you know, they also have to be very skilled and considerate. Can we cook something nasty tonight for dinner? What on earth do you mean by 'nasty'? Like something that really smells and tastes really bad. As fun as that would be, I don’t think it would be a good idea. Plus, I don’t know any recipes for prepared and served human flesh. Because it would taste like dinner at the school canteen. Alright, enough about edible human flesh. You two do have to complete your homework though, and remember, Maths requires patience and care. Can you help me with my Maths homework? Sure, but I like to hear you explain it first... Do you know what? I just want to have a simpler life like the animals in the books. Well, let’s not make things more complicated than they need to be.

I was reading Oisín's school's newsletter today. They're still looking for volunteers to supervise the Easter and Summer Fairs. You should be doing that. It's great for him to see and help the community, and a fair amount of face questions if his teacher happens to pass by. Speaker_3 : Daid, can I have some more juice? Not yet Oisín. Table manners, please. Kids and table manners - it never ends, does it? I heard about the tractor display for his birthday. He's really excited. Who is helping with that? Seamus from the Curtain Shop is saying his son can do it. They can't do it without the invitation cards. Good, he's a reliable lad. Ronan, your friends from school, might also join? And their parents too? Sure, we can't have too many onlookers, but some support is good. I'm sure the other parents will help, but the bigger problem will be the cake. Oisín still hasn't decided which one to pick. Oisín, are you listening to us? No silly, I'm just playing along. Well, there you are. You're invited too. Just don't make a mess. There you have it, a perfect blend of chaos and order. Speaking of chaos, have you heard the news about Kieran being treasurer of the local garages? No way! That's a big job for him. Is he doing well? He's doing great but he's worried about dealing with the tax side of rented houses on the estate. Tax? For garages? I thought they were just for car parking? No, it's more than that. He's dealing with insurance, land rental, and such. You know Kieran, he's quite the man. Maybe give him a few lessons on taxes and accounting. Yeah, I'll set up a meeting with someone who knows more. Daid, can we decorate the garden for the party too? Oisin, that’s a great idea! But let’s get Dad to help us with it this weekend. I hope we're not overbooking things. Remember, the rugby match is this Saturday afternoon too. So? Oisín, how's your team doing? They're winning, Daid! You're going, aren't you? Of course, what kind of father would I be if I missed his team's matches? Just make sure you’re there for both the match and the party.

So, I was pondering over some of the more…interesting word games I discovered today. Oh, which ones? I haven't talked to you in ages, and I've missed our late-night conversations about ridiculous puzzles and words. Yeah, share! We always love questions or games that make us think outside the box or use words in totally bizarre ways. Okay, so I found out about this one right? It's called "Word Chain." You know, like how you're playing telephone but with words rather than a sentence? Interesting. How does it work? Well, you start with a word, and then the next person has to come up with a word that starts with the last letter of the previous word. That sounds like a fun way to practice vocabulary and perhaps even learn a few new words! Exactly! It requires thinking quickly and looking for words you wouldn't ordinarily use in a sentence. It's fascinating how similar or vastly different words can be strung together. I love that! It's not just about word knowledge but about context, too. For sure. I can see how it could be fun with a group, but also challenging if you need to think in a more lateral way. Absolutely. It’s a bit like solving a mini-word puzzle every time someone contributes to the chain. Hey, is this different from Scrabble? I mean, they both deal with forming words, but the contexts are different. Right, because in Scrabble, the focus is on maximizing points and the structure of the board. Word Chain is more about the flow of words, not necessarily scoring or planning strategic moves. It’s more free-form, which I like. Much less pressure to be perfect. If you think about it, both can be fun but in different ways. Scrabble requires knowledge but also strategy, whereas Word Chain is more about flexibility and quick thinking. Hmm, it sounds like a great mental exercise for brainstorming or just for fun. I might try this with my mates, see if they want to give it a go. Definitely would recommend it! It's simple and adaptable. You can adjust rules if you want to make it more competitive or complex. Yeah, and I was reading about variations where you add rules like "only adjectives" or "words related to a certain theme," which I think would be fun to explore.

Remember that time we both stayed up all night trying to finish our papers and nearly fell asleep at the library? Oh, yes! We were so close to just collapsing into the bookshelves! I swear, after three hours of staring at the questions, my eyes just started closing on their own accord. But then, hearing the theme of Super Mario Bros. on loop in the background kept me going... right up until I started humming it out loud. And I was so close to napping on the table itself when suddenly, the projector started blinding us, and I woke up with a start. It's insane how much coffee we could drink that night and still fall asleep. It was like our bodies just said, "Fine, you're going to push us this far tonight, but then sleep is winning." Yeah, and afterwards, we both wrote some of the most barely coherent papers that turned out surprisingly well. Well, between the sleep deprivation and the caffeine, or maybe just the desperation, we somehow managed to meet the word count. I think the professor just assumed we both had ghost writers, but the real scriptwriter was insomnia and the entire Starlight Express soundtrack. And let's not forget the photo of us at 4 AM, surrounded by takeaway boxes, textbooks, and empty coffee cups. Oh, that picture is gold! We’re both sitting there, grinning but looking like we've seen a vision of the apocalypse and survived it. "The Night We Almost Conquered Sleep and Academic Stress!" We should frame that one and hang it somewhere together as a reminder of our, ah, "dedication." Yeah, and maybe as a warning to future students of what not to do! You know, despite all the sleep we missed, it sort of brought us closer because we realized we were both going through the same madness for the sake of academia. Absolutely. And it's funny how those moments, though crazy at the time, become fond memories. True. Like, I used to almost resent those late-night study sessions, but now... I almost miss them. Do you think if we got a group together for one of those late-night “productive” sessions now, it would just end up being a party by mistake? Oh, it definitely would. We're older now, not sure we could handle the lack of sleep anymore. Maybe now we'd just end up playing music, telling jokes, and laughing at old pictures of ourselves instead.

So, I've been going over the strategy for the first move's council planning committee meeting today. Considering how competitive it is getting to apply and secure the community centre grant, we have to ensure the application is well-structured and persuasive. Absolutely. Did the community feedback help shape the proposal at all? It was invaluable. It provided clear goals and objectives, but we've also incorporated a strong focus on sustainability and community growth – things that I know resonate with local council priorities. Good call. How are we structuring the whole content? We don't want it too heavy on detail, but enough to show we've thought about the logistics and potential impact. The accepted format in our area is a cover letter summarizing the project's aims, followed by a detailed project description, proposed budget, and a project timeline. We're also attaching supporting materials like letters of support and a risk assessment. That sounds comprehensive. What are your thoughts on handling potential questions from the council? What are we prepared to assure them in terms of potential delays or setbacks? We've anticipated many common questions, like the development timeline, potential funding shortage, impact on local traffic, etc. We have solutions prepared for most potential issues, with evidence where possible. The community centre would also provide services beyond the immediate project timeline in employment opportunities, community events, and so forth to emphasize long-term benefits. Well thought out. Should we also consider including studies or data specific to COH areas that could further reinforce our case for the community centre? Exactly. For instance, data showing a gap in local social and recreational facilities can strengthen our analysis of the community's needs and how our proposed project addresses those. Have you consulted the local business groups? Their backing could add weight to our application. Indeed. The commerce association has pledged support, and we've also received letters from local entrepreneurs and small business owners stressing the importance of having a community facility for networking and community activities that they also want to participate in. That’s been great feedback to include. We should prepare for questions on how we plan to engage residents over the project lifecycle. The council will want evidence of inclusive decision-making processes and a clear plan for gathering ongoing feedback. Absolutely, we have a comprehensive plan for community engagement that includes project updates, open forum meetings, and even a temporary website to keep everyone informed.

So, how was your week? It's been alright. Got a bit of a stressful situation at work today. We had a patient admission with deep-seated issues, and it really tested everyone's composure. Aww, that sounds tough. That’s kind of part of the job, isn’t it? You’re always dealing with something difficult and intense. Yeah, absolutely. It's mentally and emotionally draining, but at the end of the day, seeing someone improve and heal makes it all worth it. Absolutely, I couldn't do what you do. I had a lazy week – lots of planning meetings for my upcoming project and I just can't get over how early people want to have those things. Haha, that’s the life of a project co-ordinator. And project planning, isn’t it? Always trying to herd cats. The best way to describe it, really. Cat herder. Anyway, have you seen the new film “No Time to Die”? I heard mixed reviews, but I’m still planning on seeing it. Oh, I saw it over the weekend! Loved it. Daniel Craig is the perfect Bond. And who doesn't love a good spy movie? Exactly! Especially after that last Bond, I was worried. But this one... it really hits all the right buttons. Aye, definitely, it’s a great conclusion to Craig’s Bond character as well. Did you go shopping around the time you saw the movie? Just a bit. Nothing major. But I reckon I need to do the grocery shopping. Ran out of food and our cupboards are bare. Sounds like a plan. Want to grab some food together after this? I just tried this new recipe last night – a pasta with a sun-dried tomato sauce. It was amazing! That sounds perfect! I really could do with some comfort food after today. Comfort food on me! Let’s plan for later today or tomorrow night – whichever suits you better. Alright, just send me a message when you’re free. So, did you hear what’s going on with those new neighbours? Not really, care to fill me in? They came over to introduce themselves a few days ago. Bit of an odd couple, if you ask me. He’s all into those new “zero waste” living ideas, like making his own soap and using... Oh, that’s great! At least they’re trying to be more sustainable.

Oh, did you see that advert on TV? It was so cheesy; these two people arguing over whose windows and doors are more energy-efficiently sealed. Right! And the worst part is it just comes off as, like, artificial – do people really argue about that outside of commercials? Exactly! But you've got to give them credit, they're preying on basic consumer anxieties quite effectively. I mean, who doesn't want to save money and help the environment? Right, and probably many people do need better windows and doors, but to present it like there's this huge social competition going on... it's beyond me. Totally, just like the car boot sale adverts. Everyone's always trying to sell you something as if it's the "deal of the century" and you're missing out if you don't buy. Yeah, and it's always the same music too. "Car boot sale, Saturday morning, come grab a bargain!" It never changes, but somehow still works. Absolutely! Now that I'm teaching this NLP course, it's interesting how much advertising is about using different psychological techniques to make us feel we need certain products. It's pretty manipulative when you think about it. For sure. I also learned a bit about that at university. But it's crazy how effective it is, especially online shopping. People end up buying stuff they don't even need just because it was in their "recommended for you" section. Shows you what humanity is capable of – and also why I need to cut down on online window shopping! Don't worry, I do the same thing. Late-night scrolling... the next thing you know, you've got a new outfit and a kitchen appliance, neither of which are really necessary. Right! Speaking of unneeded things, have you heard about the rise in crime from people stealing from online shopping deliveries? Yeah, it's shocking. I read an article about that. People are getting really desperate, evidently. Mm, truly sad. And it's not just zero-obligation crime; it's got serious consequences. Did you hear about the new diet everyone's on at work? It's like... zero-carb or something. Do they not remember the Atkins diet from the 90s? I swear, every few years it's a different way of not eating carbs. And it’s always the same – the first week you lose a bit of water weight, then it plateaus, and then if you're like most people, you start craving pasta again.

So, I've been meaning to write something for ages, but I've been lacking inspiration. You know how it is, right? The blank page syndrome. Oh, absolutely. I've been working on a long piece about the resurgence of vinyl records. People are really getting into the tactile experience of listening to music again. Yeah, I'd totally agree. I've been into my brother's old record collection and it's fascinating to hear things the way they were originally meant to be listened to. Speaking of keepsakes, I've been meaning to start decoupage again. It's such a therapeutic activity. Anyone tried it recently? I just had a go recently with this really nice set of Easter eggs. It was fun but a bit fiddly. Do you have any tips for getting started again or troubleshooting common issues? Well, you need good scissors and a steady hand, but I'd say finding the right decoupage glue makes all the difference. Don't get the cheap stuff—it just doesn't last. Ah, thanks for the tip. I'll keep that in mind. Speaking of glue, I'm looking this up actually on my phone right now, and oh, I just got a message from some silly website. Where did I get on the mailing list for kitchen sink suppliers? These spam call things are just ridiculous. [laughs] It's like they must think everyone's sitting at home, urgently in need of a new sink. I swear, it's an epidemic. Yeah, and it's not just that. We all know mobile phone apps that are just a painful way to shop doesn't come close to beating a good brick and mortar place for that kind of thing. And then you have apps that make shopping online so much easier. I just ordered a new pair of boots from that one that just looks at your foot and says 'aha, we have exactly the right pair for you' or something. It was bizarre but effective. There's a technical term for that, actually - 'frictionless shopping'. It's both brilliant and slightly unsettling. [laughs] It certainly feels like I've been having my shopping basket filled without me so much as looking at the page. The worrying part is when the software gets it right. You could have bought something you never meant to buy just because the algorithm knows you so well.

Ah, I remember when I first arrived in this area in the 60s. It was like a whole different world. Whole council houses waiting to be occupied, and they were cheap! I recall that too! And the interview for the dentist job, the waiting room was awfully formal compared to questions back in the days. I went to a college down the road, part of my postgrad studies. I had a classmate, actually, who ended up moving here too. Recognizable name for us old timers, keeps coming up in our get-togethers. Yes, moving was quite the challenge – finding a decent place to live, especially after having to pick up jobs from interviews. Sentences of just trying to fit in. And speaking of interviews, do you remember the day the dictatorship began in Athens, and you were on your way to your postgrad course? Oh, that was a hilarious story... we were in the middle of a registration and all of a sudden people are panicking. It wasn't clear for a bit what was happening. I even took a photo of the tanks rolling down the street. I've got a whole album somewhere of old accommodation pictures. We all dealt with our fair share of DIY – it's amazing what they used to call 'loft conversions' back then! And the time differences weren't carefully calculated in travel – I remember nearly missing the start of my course because I didn’t account for time zones properly. Ah, time zones, yes. It’s all about timing. I recall my first flat… it was like it belonged back in the 50s. The owner was quite the character, kept asking if all the visitors were just 'friends'. More like tryouts for roommates! And, of course, meeting one’s future wife… that's a story for another time or couple glasses of wine. We really had our fair share of quirky accommodation and changing the place to feel more like home was an adventure in itself. Indeed, that’s what I’ve always valued about this area – everyone's had their own unique experience, but we all share such fond memories. And the students, or future students like me, mingling. You could feel the excitement and the almost shared feeling of being 'new to the area'. Did you know, my wife and I first bumped into each other at one of those local gatherings after our first faculty meetings.

So tell me Marion, what was it like working as a speech therapist? I've always admired the profession, quite complex and rewarding I imagine. Oh, yes indeed! It was incredibly rewarding. You see every client was different, each with their own set of challenges, and helping them communicate better was truly satisfying. Especially when you witness tiny victories over time. Like hearing a child speak their first word or seeing a stroke patient recover their ability to speak right? Exactly! Those moments were so heart-warming. But it could get very challenging at times too, especially with more severe cases like autism, dysphasia, and the like. I had a nephew who struggled with stuttering in early childhood. It must have been so tough for him. And yet, when he overcame it - oh, the sense of achievement was incredible for him and his parents. It's amazing how much difference targeted language therapy can make. Indeed. I've often thought about my childhood in Somerset. We didn't have all these fancy speech therapy programs back then. I had a stammer myself as a child, but it was more about just learning to live with it and hiding it than addressing it directly. That's unfortunate. It would have made such a difference for you and so many others to have access to the kind of support and therapies available now. Absolutely. But it made us very resourceful too, I suppose. Like, my grandmother always said "Just speak up, child, and talk in time." Less about speech specifically and more about asserting yourself through words and all. A simple but impactful approach. How did your family deal with it in the long run? Just accepted it as part of who I was, I think. Late in primary school, a teacher noticed and encouraged me to speak more in class, a bit like giving me a safe space. I noticed a real shift then. Later, when I became an artist, I found that visual expression became a great outlet too. Interesting, I've also seen art therapy help with communication and self-expression. Where do you find inspiration for your art now that you're retired from the gallery? Nature, family history, and my travels. I've always been drawn to the pastoral beauty of Somerset and the stories it tells. That sounds deeply personal and beautiful. I've always loved the narrative and symbolism in folk art and crafts.

So, I was browsing on Instagram yesterday and I came across an idea for a tattoo. Yeah? What was it? It was a cake with unrealistic proportions, but somehow still making you want to squeeze it. It was just so cute! Oh, isn’t that lovely! But speaking of cakes, have you guys planned anything for dinner? Ah, right actually, I was thinking we could split the cost of ingredients. I was thinking of making a keepsake cake for Christmas, something simple but memorable. You game? Absolutely! Even thought I have to check my budget, Christmas preparations can get expensive. I can buy some candies or decorations. How about we make it a potluck dinner but with a specific theme—food from around the world, perhaps? That sounds incredible! We could have various mini meals from each person's favourite cuisine. It also reduces the cost and effort, plus it's more fun that way. Perfect! I'll do Japanese food, something rice-based. I hope you don't mind. No, on the contrary! I've been meaning to try making different dishes from the cafés I've visited. I'll bring the ingredients for that. I was thinking either Italian or American, not sure yet. Either way, let's make sure we keep it minimal so we can spend more time chatting rather than prepping. Good idea. And we should definitely plan for some games or activities too, maybe some Christmas music or a film to watch afterwards. How about we finalize the theme, dishes, and budget for next week? I can also look for some deals or couple gift ideas by then. Sounds perfect and yeah, let's set a date and stick to it. Also, I heard there’s a great spot nearby for buying Christmas candy that does charity. Maybe we can pop by there after our meal? Genius, let’s suggest that to everyone. We can make it a fun activity and do good at the same time. Fantastic. So, to recap: potluck dinner, minimal cost, no set date but looking to agree on something soon, and maybe a Christmas candy shopping trip after. Seems like we’ve got everything covered. Now, who’s joining for the prep?

Mum, I was thinking about what we could do with the flat's dining room. Ah, what are you considering then? Well, the whole book collection could go into there. There's quite a bit to organize and it just feels like it’s all over the place at the moment. That could work. You could install some good shelving units and it would make a brilliant study space as well, right? Exactly, and it’s also closer to the kitchen keeps everything in one place, so would make our routine a bit smoother. That makes sense. Also, did your thesis planning go well in Cambridge? Yes, actually, I spent a bit of time with the supervisor and we ironed out a good structure now. Happy days. So you’re feeling more confident? Yes, definitely more grounded. Before, it felt too overwhelming thinking about the whole PhD. Break it down and it gets so much more manageable. Now, what about living arrangements? Are you thinking about staying in this flat long term, or should we start looking at something else if you're busy with the PhD? I think this flat will do for now. It’s convenient for university and I can manage to stay on top of rent and all that. Ah, but have you thought about perhaps moving into a shared house with some other students? Sometimes it could be a good way to get support and it would be easier to focus on work if you’re not alone and can share responsibilities. Actually, I have weighed up the pros and cons. The flat works for me at the moment because I don’t want to be in a shared situation when I have lots of study to get through. But maybe a few years down the line, a shared house would be fun for living. Fair enough, but just remember to also look after yourself and take some time off now and then. Definitely, I intend to do that. What are your plans for after you finish? I know it’s early days but, do you think about Oxford later on perhaps? Yeah, definitely an option. But for now, I intend to be a bit more open-ended and focus on getting this degree done. Maybe do some post-grad work or teach. I’ll see how it feels then. Well, that makes sense thinking ahead, but also taking each step seriously.

I did an incredible degree in linguistic's while I was doing my Master; it really opened my eyes to the diversity of languages out there, especially the evolution and historical contexts of them. Have you ever been particularly involved in the study of regional dialects or particular languages? Oh yes! I've always had an interest in regional dialects. For my part, I focused a bit more on the administrative aspect but I've also done some of my own research on how language changes over time, especially in how it reflects changes in society and keeps changing as society progresses, something you might find fascinating from an archeological perspective. That's fascinating! I've given lectures on that very subject - how archeology can give us clues not just about material culture, but also about linguistic and cultural evolution. That sounds amazing, hearing from someone actively involved in teaching and research. I remember reading a paper by a Cambridge alum where she excavated an ancient village and found evidence of an unexpected linguistic influence - it was fascinating! Ah yes, the village near Oxford where we found a rather unexpected Arab word that was so out of context it took us quite some time to decipher but it turned out to have been from early trade relations. It was quite an achievement. That's remarkable! It’s often the unexpected details that lead to the most significant discoveries. I’ve come across similar sentiments in my own work – like how certain phrases in regional dialects might trace back to historical events or cultural exchanges that aren’t widely known anymore. Absolutely, and it also happens all around us. Even in modern-day Britain, we don't often realize how much our language is a melting pot influenced by the world around us. For instance, there's a rise in Chinese loanwords due to cultural and economic influences. More and more in recent years, I’ve noticed. It’s fascinating to see Chinese language elements filtering into English, especially in city dialects. It reflects quite accurately the changing world we live in. True, and changing the way we communicate. I find it intriguing how languages can simultaneously be preserved and yet evolve so rapidly. It’s almost like they have a life of their own. Absolutely. As a coordinator for language research projects, I see this firsthand. It's not just the preservation of the past; it's also about understanding how we communicate today and perhaps, tomorrow.

So, I was browsing on TikTok yesterday and came across this video about how hard it is to be a young person today. It was about how the expectations from education and the workplace are so high, and how social media contributes to this stress. Yeah, and then the pressure to look a certain way, to have a certain kind of life. It’s insane. Like this clip where teenagers talk about how they feel they need to have their lives together at 18. I mean, I barely knew what I wanted to do when I was 18! This kind of stuff really frustrates me, you know. Like how we’re constantly compared to others, and how there’s this pressure to have perfect grades from a young age. It just creates this unhealthy competition. Exactly. And it’s not just the education system. Workplaces are becoming more demanding too. I’ve seen a lot of talk about how young people are expected to be ‘grown-up’ and professional from day one. But, at the same time, we’re told we’re lazy and entitled by the older generation. And then there’s the issue of class. For me, as someone from a working-class background, I've seen how these expectations can differ depending on where you’re from. Where I come from, the pressure isn’t so much about perfection in education; it’s more about survival. Yeah, and the cost of higher education is crazy. It feels like a barrier to so many people who could benefit from it, especially if they struggle with things like dyslexia, like I do. It’s all so exhausting. I feel like we need to raise awareness about how socio-economic factors play into it. It’s not the same burden for everyone. Totally agree. And what if you just don’t fit the traditional career mold? I’ve got friends who are struggling to find jobs because they’re not matched with their ‘expected’ career path after university. Or even just trying to find stable work in your chosen field. I’ve heard so many stories from people changing careers because the first one just wasn’t viable. It feels like sometimes we talk about these issues, but nothing really changes. I mean, look at the curriculum. How much truly prepares us for life beyond exams? Exactly. And it’s the little things, like education about finances, mental health, stuff like that.

Oh, the usual stuff then, business's as usual I suppose. How'd your day go, love? Quite busy actually. Had the usual book club on TV, and then a meeting with one of our neighbors who wants to get into investing, but is kind of stuck on questions about taxes. Oh, I see. Investing, eh? I've been thinking about that too. I've been looking at those online stock trading platforms. I know, I know, very traditional for my line of work, keeps me grounded I suppose, or something like that. You know how it is, always thinking about the bigger picture. Well grounded or just staying in your comfort zone, we'll never know. But talking about bigger picture, did you see the news about universal healthcare? I thought about making a case for that in my next lecture. Yeah, I did catch that. Seems like an interesting case study, especially how it affects the public debate over funding and such. But you won’t get anyone in the higher echelons buying into that here, at least not anytime soon. They firmly believe that the private sector is the way to go, regardless of how many people it leaves behind. Exactly. And that’s the problem – it benefits certain groups so they push that ideology at all costs, even if it’s not necessarily the best outcome for society. Ah, the politics of healthcare, perhaps one of the most complex debates we have. But isn’t that inherent in all really? Politics is never straightforward, is it? I mean, if only we could deal with these things like we approach academic debates, fairly and with all the facts... Except, unfortunately, policy isn’t based on who presents the best argument, or who’s side of the argument is most supported by research and evidence, as often as it should be. True. It’s more about who’s got the loudest voice, or in our case, who has the biggest wallet to back the lobbying. It really irks me, seriously. Definitely. But what gets me is the people who get caught up in it just because of what they’ve been told, without looking at the evidence for themselves. Right! That lack of critical thinking, it’s deeply concerning. As educators, we try to teach our students the importance of evidence-based reasoning but I sometimes wonder if we’re fighting a losing battle.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that film we saw last week? The one about the teenager who discovers she has super powers? It was hilarious. You mean 'The Adventures of Super Wendy'? Yes, it was quite amusing, wasn't it? I heard rumors there might be a sequel. A sequel, eh? I'll bet it'll have all the same jokes and nothing actually new. But you never know, maybe they'll surprise us for once. Yeah, well, let's hope for surprises! I swear, the first one had a scene where she mistakes her powers for an allergic reaction, it was beyond funny. Oh, yeah, and what about the part where she ends up accidentally turning her friend invisible? That was my favourite bit too. But have you thought about its underlying themes? Underlying themes in a film about a teenager with superpowers? What are you thinking of? Well, you know, coming to terms with one's abilities, accepting who you are, it's all quite universal. I see what you mean. It was kind of like, while the film was light-hearted, it handled awkward teenage years quite well. Interesting perspective. I didn't notice that part, but now you mention it, yeah. The way she had to hide her abilities, it kind of reflects how some teens in real life hide their talents or problems from others. Exactly. It’s those kinds of underlying messages that make films like that more than just entertainment. Speaking of hidden talents, how's Emily doing? Haven’t seen her using her art supplies lately. Ah, she's been quite busy with her new job, but I'm sure she’s still experimenting with art whenever she can. You should see her animal drawings, they're just incredible for her age. Indeed! Reminds me of the wildlife photography exhibitions we used to go to. You know, that’s something I’ve been thinking about revisiting. I miss those days, when we’d take long walks just to observe nature. We can plan a family day trip. Why not go to Rutland Water or Sherwood Forest? It’d be lovely to get everyone out and about. That sounds like a great idea. We could combine it with a picnic or a short walk. Get outside, get moving. Sure, but I suppose we’d have to check the weather. We don’t want to end up huddled together in a tent if it’s raining, although that could be fun in its own way.

Right, now I know it's exciting to visit Grandma and Grandpa, Grace but today we're driving quite a while. It's about a three-hour car journey. You both need to make sure you've used the loo before we leave, and perhaps bring a small snack and a drink if you like. Absolutely, it’s always good to be prepared for a long drive. Sure, whatever keeps you all happy and occupied. And make sure to get settled before we hit the motorway, we don’t want anyone getting restless or feeling sick from boredom. On the topic of the journey, do you think we should bring the horses out beforehand? The horses? Oh no, I don’t think that’s possible. They’re probably still in their pens at the stables, and it's not our day to ride this time. Aww, that’ll have to wait until next time. Yeah, maybe we can even plan a special horse day over the holidays. Do you think Grandpa can show us some more advanced riding techniques? Well, I’m sure Grandpa would be happy to give you some tips or even lessons if you all really want to learn more. For now, let’s focus on enjoying our visit and some family time. Speaking of family time, Grace and Lucy, how are your art projects coming along? Mine is about half done. I’m really enjoying painting this winter scene with the house in the snow. Mine’s a little different. I’m doing a self-portrait but with me riding a horse through the woods. That sounds beautiful, Lucy. And Grace, that winter scene could be perfect for a Christmas card if you want to give Grandpa that as a gift. That’s a thoughtful idea! And Grace, don’t forget to finally show me your progress on that car drawing you’ve been working on. Oh yeah! I’d almost forgotten. I’ve been designing my dream car. I put in all these cool features like a solar panel roof and a built-in mini art studio. That’s very inventive, Grace. And seriously, who knew a car could have a mini studio?

So, how was everyone's weekend? We had a nice one. My team and I had a team-building activity at work. We went to paintball. It was fun, but I did get a few welts. Paintball now, really? You're supposed to be the head of department! Hey, it was a bonding activity. A bit of fun doesn't hurt, right? And the report I've been working on? Any updates? I've heard of strictures first hand. Yeah, well speaking of which I've been meaning to tell you both the tea and the dinner party we're having here at the weekend. Speaker_2 and That’s kind of you, thank you. We’ve got a lovely spread and I thought it might be nice if the family comes along. That would be lovely. Oh, I’d love that. So, I was browsing Rotten Tomatoes yesterday and came across that new drama film. I'd really like to watch it. Ah, which one? I saw a trailer for something that looked quite interesting. Speaking of which, have you finalized the plans for the upcoming conference? You know, the one in Manchester? Yes, nearly there. Don't worry, you’ve got this. You’ve always been super organized and prepared, even under pressure. Plus, I’m sure there will be some familiar faces among the attendees, right? Yeah, we’ve got a good mix of regulars and some new faces. I’m hoping it doesn’t come across too formal. I want it to feel like a community coming together, not just some corporate event. Definitely. And have you thought about the catering? More food options than last time? Absolutely. I’m experimenting with locally sourced and more diverse options. It’s more expensive, but hopefully worth it for the quality and also the environmental aspect. That'll set you apart. I heard that’s really becoming a trend—sustainability in event management. So, I hear that there's a Scottish independence referendum coming up. What have you two fellows learned about it at school? Yeah, we've been talked about it a bit. I think some of my mates are a bit excited about it, hoping Scotland becomes its own country. But I don't fully get what questions are on the ballot and what independence really means. Well, the question on the ballot paper is pretty straightforward. “Should Scotland be an independent country?” Yeah, but what does it really mean to be independent? Think of it like Malton. If it were to be independent from the rest of Yorkshire, it would mean deciding all its own rules, laws, and how much tax is collected. Scotland already has a bit of this with its own parliament, but independence would take it much further. So, they'd leave the UK? Exactly. The UK is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. If Scotland votes for independence, they'd leave the UK. That would be a big change. Are there people who want that? Absolutely. Many people in Scotland feel this way for various reasons, from cultural identity to economic policy. I thought most Scots wanted to stay in the UK. Polls show mixed views. Scotland voted to stay in the EU during the Brexit referendum, and some think independence could better keep them aligned with Europe, or give them more control over their own policies, especially things like fisheries and oil. And if they vote yes, what happens next? If they vote yes, it's not immediate independence. There would be a transition period, possibly around the 2016 date mentioned for becoming independent, but that would be subject to negotiations with the UK government. Negotiations? Like what? Things like dividing assets, debts, military equipment, and getting Scotland its own international recognition and possibly even its own entry in the FIFA world cup. That's a lot changing. What about shared history and things? Yeah, it's a bit more complex. Think of it like moving out of a shared house where you paid for everything together, but now you want your own house. You'd need to agree on how to split things up fairly. Makes sense. So, what do you think about it? Personally, as someone from Yorkshire, I'm not really invested one way or the other, but I do think it's crucial for Scotland to get a fair decision.

Oh, did you hear that?? "Should've have gone to school more!" What is that, even?! Yeah, unreal! I mean, I love a good Yorkshire accent as much as the next person, but this elision is kind of legendary. Exactly! "Should've" instead of "should have" is one thing but "should've have"? That’s a whole new level of elision, innit? It’s like... they keeps chuckin' verbs away, innit? Oh, sorry, I'm totally getting lazy there too! It's kind of fitting in this context, though, cos it sounds like Jeremy Kyle. Exactly! Like the whole program's an invitation to chuck all your manners and grammar out the window. You know, it's funny how sometimes on Jeremy Kyle we hear elision like "gon" instead of "going to," but it's often used to highlight the lack of education or social disadvantages. It's a bit different when it's a regional accent doing it, innit? Totally. I mean, the Yorkshire accent has some fun features like glottal stops – where they drop "t"s in the middle of words – which is totally distinct and not incorrect. It’s more about how it’s perceived, right? Like, my Aunty says, "I’m goin’ doon t'market," but that's just her way of talking, not a lack of education. That’s a good point! It's easy to criticize accents we don't use ourselves or don't understand. But, also, on the show, when people are eliding the way they are, it's usually more about the perceived lack of education or, as you said, social disadvantages. True. It’s this thing Jeremy Kyle does where he's making confrontations but also kind of reinforcing certain stereotypes about who speaks “properly” and who doesn’t. It’s all a bit of mess, innit? And it’s such a missed opportunity. Instead of mocking the way people speak, they could be focusing on the real issues – lack of access to education, poverty, and health issues. Yeah, and the audience... they’re all just sitting there, nodding along, “Yeah, these people need to speak properly.” But, like, thinking about it, that idea of “proper English” is so subjective and classist, innit? Absolutely. Every region has its own way of speaking and that’s what makes language beautiful. It’s just that some accents are more “acceptable” than others in certain contexts.

Oh, did you see that last move by Sterling? Yeah, that was ridiculous wasn't it? Literally, talked about that skill the whole way down. You can just see how he outsmarts the defense so smoothly. Absolutely, and the questions his footballing days have had! Starting from that unlikely academy and ending up leading the Premier League? Exactly, and this year, especially, he's been on fire! And talking about fire keeps me thinking... Remember when we would sit in front of the telly, watching the World Cup with your mum? I have perfect memories of that. She would let us sneak down to the lounge, as long as we were back in our rooms before 10pm. And the summer of '98 was epic! Those summer days, endless football and finding innovative ways to be in front of the TV! And now, the knitting? That's turned into a bit of a tradition in our family. Someone should make a roster for next season's or even the Olympics! The Olympics! Anyone have any guesses for who’ll win gold in knitting? I'm thinking along the lines of the entire Stampede Knit Team from Canada. They're always bringing knitting to a whole new level, aren't they? I'd take that bet! Speaking of, have you heard about the new baby names book? Apparently, there's a trend of people naming their kids after sports players. Really? That doesn't bode well for a couple of decades from now when we have a team of 'Aurelians' and 'Pliskovas' playing in primary school. Imagine explaining a few decades down the line: "No, it wasn’t our favorite player at the time. It was just...classic?" Classicly odd. I wonder what names you and Emily are leaning towards. You sure you're going to reveal after all this knitting? We're thinking along nature-inspired and slightly unconventional. Nothing too overdone so as to give them the chance for their own unique identity. Wise decision! And speaking of identity, have you noticed how much the Midlands accent is being recognized in the wider British media now? Clearly, regional dialects and voices are getting more spotlights. True, it's great! Though funny thinking back, when I was just starting my PhD and there was that book that was all about preserving this very accent that used... archaic forms that even the older speakers around here wouldn't use.

Remember in The Bee Movie when Barry gets all excited about being discovered by the humans and he ends up getting all these humans paying him for his honey, but then he realizes the whole unrealistic expectation that they're all just coming out of his own hive because he thought the whole world was just one big massive hive? Yeah and then the whole thing spirals into a bee revolution against the humans where they sue humans for stealing their honey without permission. Which is actually quite... interesting, coming from a kid’s movie. Makes you think about knowledge and stuff like that, doesn't it? Even if you’re just a bee. Exactly! It’s a great moral about understanding the consequences and the impact of our actions. Unidentified : Did they even make money from that lawsuit? Well, in the movie terms, yes. In real life, there would have been many complications and legalities. But it explores this idea of owning and controlling nature versus respecting it and living alongside it. Speaking of this, it reminds me of this article I saw about these "royal fruits." Did you know most of the apples and pears from the royal estates are actually given away or sold? What? Like at Buckingham Palace or Windsor Castle? Yes, exactly. A few years back, it was news that you could actually pay to book a day to pick apples at certain royal estates. It’s a bit like a "fruit picking experience." But would that make it no longer royal if the public can pick it? Just food for thought, you know? That’s kind of like, if you make it a national park, does that mean it’s no longer royal property since everyone can visit? It’s about the distribution of wealth and power and how you view what should belong to the people versus the monarchy. I guess if we were all a republic, that would be different. If we were, that’s another topic altogether. But have you guys ever thought about what you kids would want to be when you grow up? Politics? Maybe royalty? I want to be a politician so I can make sure everyone has enough vitamins. That’s actually a great aspiration. Vitamins are important. I’ve always thought... maybe you could be the Queen, if we still had a monarchy, just so you could make sure the country always has access to enough vitamins from the start.

Oh, did I ever tell you about that time we auctioned off the furniture? Not about the furniture but I think you mentioned the various TVs. Did the old TV from Grandma's house get sold off as well? Oh, yes! It did! But that was just pre-auction, right? We never intended to sell it, but it got included by accident. Right, let me guess... it was the one with the picture tube? Yes! Exactly! The person who got it was very happy, though. I bet they thought they were getting a good deal until they realized they needed another old TV to fix it. Do you think its being used for a fun project? Probably broken down for parts or refurbished as a retro piece. You know, for interior design or those "re-use or repurpose" projects. Exactly! Good use of technology even if it is old. Speaking of technology, did you notice the town hall is setting up a digital archive? Ah, yes, technology is certainly changing the way we preserve our history, isn't it? Instead of physical archives, now we're digitizing everything. An entire archive of Thirsk's social history? That's a big project. Yes! And they're accepting community volunteers. Perhaps we could get involved? We could look into that for our class project together! You mean it as a way to learn about Thirsk's history while also contributing to preserving it. While you're at it, make sure they add a section on Thirsk’s food history… maybe with a recipe on how to make the most delicious pasty this side of the Pennines! I thought we were going to have a serious conversation about archives. Alright, alright. But seriously, if we're looking into the history of Thirsk, food has to be part of it! Especially if we're thinking about recipes from past generations. I suppose we could document the evolution of Thirsk's local cuisine through the years. That would be fascinating. Imagine if we could have an event, maybe a food festival, showcasing how things have changed or remained the same. And we could include all these older recipes! That's a great idea! We could even involve the community to try to replicate old recipes. This could be a great way to engage young people in local history, especially if we tie it to things they enjoy, like food.

So, I was browsing on the museums of northwest England last night. Did you know that today is the 175th anniversary celebration at Manchester Museum? So, I was browsing Instagram over the weekend and came across an account that uses AI-generated pictures. The results are pretty incredible. It's like they created an AI that can generate content 24/7, creative yet not thinking. Exactly! I mean, it's not just about the images, what about their next step? Music, movies, maybe even fake videos that can spread misinformation on a massive scale. Exactly the worry. And it’s kind of assumed we’re on this track. Last weekend, I went to see a live concert of my favorite indie band in Birmingham. The energy was electrifying. That sounds amazing! I wish I could go out more for events like that, but between my coursework, it’s so hard to find the time. You’ll have time after exams, definitely. Plus, the university canteen’s got this pop-up pizza café started over the weekend. We could go there next weekend and study or just hang out.

So, I was browsing on eBay yesterday and came across an almost mint condition Pokémon Red. It’s practically new. Well, that sounds exciting. But don’t forget you’ve also been saying you need a new guitar. Papa, questions. What is it, Oisin? Why does Pikachu say pikachu? He’s just very excited.
