I've heard of Harpenden, isn't that where your parents still live? Yeah, they've been there forever. It's not too far down the road from London though, so I can squeeze in occasional visits. Really? I've never actually been there. I prefer the North and its quieter, more down-to-earth pace, but I guess it has its charm where you're from right? Definitely has its own charm. And it's nice to have that mix of city accessibility with its own community feel. That does sound good. In Sunderland, we're all about the communities and having a close-knit feel. Though, let me tell you, even here, sometimes the roads can drive me mad. There's always a jam somewhere or another making me late, and usually to cricket training which is kind of ironic, right? Cricket? That's very British. How's training going? It's alright. We had a tournament last weekend that went really well though. I'm proud to say our team actually won this time. That's excellent! Well done to the team. I missed out on cricket when I was younger, maybe I need to try it again sometime. It's never too late. It's an acquired taste, though. The community behind it, though, is really what keeps people coming back, especially in places like Sunderland where it's pretty much the glue for so many Sundays. Shows there's more to it than just the game itself. Exactly. It plays a huge role in community bonding. Though, finding good pitches to play on can be a challenge here. Some of the areas around the city have side alleys or parks that are decent, but we've also had to navigate rougher playing conditions at times. That does sound challenging. How do you handle it? We just adapt, I suppose. You can't really control the pitch, but you can control how you play. We try to focus on what we're in control of – our skills, the team's strategy. Plus, it’s all part of the fun, right? And we're talking about a community that's passionate about it, so it makes the effort even more worthwhile. It's definitely all about the experience. Speaking of things beyond complete control, though, how are you finding the new bike you got for your birthday? Oh, it’s fantastic!

Does anyone know if Ming Garden or Dragon Dynasty will deliver to our area? I'm trying to surprise the others with some Chinese food for tonight and want to make sure they'll arrive before our movie starts. I'm not sure, but I can check on that now. Yeah, both Ming Garden and Dragon Dynasty have delivery options and they cover our postcode. But they might get busy so I'll just place the order straight away. That’s great, thank you. Do you know if they have any vegetarian options because Callum can't eat meat? Oh, right! Yes, they do. In fact, they always seem to have a good selection. I'll just pick something he'll like. Do you want me to pick a selection or should we just go for a standard order of everything? I think we can just go with the standard menu for now. Let's pick a variety of dishes so we have enough for everyone. And don’t forget to ask for extra sauce packets, or whatever those little spicy sauces or soy sauce are. Callum loves them. Sure, I’ll make a note of that. And how about drinks? Should we also order drinks? Yeah, let's get a case of beer and maybe some fizzy drinks. We can get a mix for everyone. Okay, I’ll take a couple of beers, but can we also get a few soft drinks as well? Not everyone is into beer. That sounds like a good balance. Alright, I've got the order in. Total it's about £45 which should cover everything we need. That sounds right. We can just split it later or consider it less stress about the money this time together. Definitely, it’s a treat. Speaking of stress, did anyone remember to pick up the new movie before we dive into food? Oops, no! I assumed you were going to. I can pick it up on the way home if I leave now. I would've but I spent the morning at the park with my little sister, trying to soak up some sun before the winter kicks in properly. Alright, no worries. It’s about 20 minutes to the shop from here, you’ll be back before the food arrives. Perfect, I'll be back. Oh, funny thinking back, remember that one time we all tried to make our own Chinese food and it was like a disaster?

So, how was your week with the NHS? As an academic's partner, I'd be really curious how the policies and legislations are affecting your practise. Oh, it was quite busy as usual. We’ve got quite a few new neighbors around now and I’ve been dealing with a fair few new patients questions about the kind of support they can get and how it's changing. That must be quite challenging, considering the constant changes in policies right? Exactly! It feels like every day there’s another new document to get through, another set of guidelines. You'd think it would be simpler, but the details change so often – it’s frustrating at times. I can imagine. As someone who’s involved with literature, I’m keen to see how the portrayal of the NHS in fiction is following these changes. Also, we discussed how well Finland does with their healthcare system. It’s a topic that keeps coming up among academics and clinicians alike. Yes, we've had a few consultants over from Finland visit our hospital last year. Their model seems to focus more on prevention and less on the burden of paperwork or strict protocols. They seem to have a more holistic approach, focusing on the wellbeing of the patient as much as their condition. That’s interesting. It’s the kind of approach I’d love to delve more into – the cultural and systemic differences that make one model more appealing or effective than another. It would be great if we could learn more from those experiences, but it’s tricky isn’t it? The NHS is huge, and making sweeping changes is always complicated. We have fantastic local examples and some innovative projects here in Liverpool that do focus on community and wellbeing, it’s promising to see the progress that can be made on a smaller scale. Yes, and yet it can feel like a constant battle between doing the best for your patients in your little corner and the wider political agenda. Exactly. And sometimes it feels like we’re tasked with making up for issues that really should be addressed in policy or resource allocation, rather than at the front line. We’re making do with what we have, but it feels like sometimes more is demanded of us with less in return. It’s that kind of overwork and underfunding that can indeed make the job even more stressful than it already is.

Ah, Phil, been a while. How're you keeping? Oh, you know, same old. Just getting by. Yeah, life's funny like that. Are you still involved with the community center? Once in a while, when they do something I'm interested in. But mostly stuck around here now. You'd be surprised how much of a part life it's become. Community can be very important, especially out here. I've been noticing how it's changed up here in L8 over the years, how would you say? Oh, it's all changed. Used to be more... rooted in the community, I suppose. Now it's mostly new faces. Don't know half their names. Interesting. You've seen the shift from big industry to... well, we're still figuring that out. Hence your community center involvement? That's part of it. But also, sometimes it feels like we're disappearing in the changes. You see these new developments, these people moving in from all over, it's hard to keep up. Absolutely. Now that I'm teaching this side of the river, it's interesting to see these changes reflected in my students' lives. There's a kind of assumed shared experience that may no longer exist. You know, it's the stories we can't pass on that hurts. My father used to tell me about the docks, jobs, all that's gone now, all gone. And with it, in some ways, our identity. I'm researching that aspect actually—stories and community identity. It's fascinating how much of our sense of self is tied up in how we work, where we come from. Except, nowadays, work is more fluid or just absent for many. Yeah, and where do these new people fit in, if they're not part of the old world? It's like they're building a new city over the old one without touching ground. That’s a great observation, Phil. This is where linguistics comes in—how language can be a binding force, or a divider, especially when old ways clash with new ones. The national corpus is a huge project that tries to take account of all these shifts, but it's a challenge. National corpus? That's something I've not even thought of. I suppose it makes sense, though—if the language reflects how we live and who we are.

So, I hear that Cassie over at educations has started running workshops online. Really? Yeah, I saw that. Thought it was a bold move but smart given the circumstances. Is it working for her? She just started this, after all. I heard it's been going well so far. People seem to appreciate the interactive element of it, and of course, it makes the content more accessible to those who can't travel. That's great for us as well, I think it could be a model for our own projects. We've been brainstorming ways to engage with a broader audience virtually. Exactly, and I think we can definitely learn from each other. It’s like the whole industry is adapting. And the content of these workshops—is it similar to the summer school programs usually offered? It's similar in spirit, but with more flexibility. She's using a mix of creative activities and traditional lectures, all tied into practical applications that can be done from home. That's really innovative. I think the key is making sure the interaction remains high quality. Otherwise it might feel quite isolated for the participants. Absolutely. We're working on some similar digital tool development for publishing, so seeing how others in the educational space are tackling this is enlightening. I’ve heard some criticism though about how it's not equitable. Not everyone has access to reliable internet or the necessary tech at home. That's a fair point, considering we’re talking about a fairly affluent demographic mostly. That’s a very real concern. But it's also pushing institutions to think more about how to bridge those gaps. There are also some free resources and grants available for those who need the support. I’ve been exploring some of these grants, actually. The idea is to reach more people locally but also to set up some international partnerships. It can be quite complex, logistically, but potentially highly rewarding. That reminds me, I’ve been meaning to sit down and go through some of those resources. We need to talk more about this, maybe schedule a meeting. Great idea. We should probably also discuss how we might collaborate on this—sharing resources, knowledge, that kind of thing. Agreed. And maybe we could also think about how we can make our own digital content more interactive. I believe that's where the future of our field is heading.

So, I was browsing TV shows yesterday and came across an Indian drama series. I started watching it; it's really captivating! That sounds interesting. Indian dramas can be really well-made, aren't they? Absolutely. And what really caught me was the opening titles. They had some English subtitles and I was thinking, "Eh, those are pretty rough." Haha, I see where you're going with this. I've noticed that sometimes, subtitles can be a bit... off when it comes to less common languages. Exactly. It was like seeing an auto-translated webpage. It started with "The tractor's moment collided with the lamp's motion." Oh, that sounds like Google Translate trying to process a Shakespearean play. Exactly! Hence my theory that Google Translate sometimes makes up words because it's more worried about grammatically correct sentences than actual meaning. Like the time it translated "Puerta" to "Door for the fox" in a Spanish textbook or whenever it makes up words that aren't in this universe. I've seen some pretty wild examples myself. Makes you appreciate the effort of human translators. Especially in literature or complex documents. Some auto-translated academic papers can be quite the read. Like, my friend once tried to translate a German novel into English using a machine and the protagonist was somehow a 'broccoli of the sea' instead of a 'sea-god'. Oh no! That's the risk when you try to automate everything. It really makes you appreciate people who are fluent or have done their due diligence in translation. Absolutely. I've been learning Hindi over the past year, actually. It's been quite a challenge but rewarding. Really? That's great! I've always thought Hindi has such a rich set of literature. Yes, it does. Plus, I teach in a class of multi-cultural children, and it's amazing how they pick up new languages. It's all about exposure and practice. Speaking of languages, have you ever tried the language learning app, Duolingo? Oh yeah, Duolingo's pretty good, but I found it a bit lacking in depth for more complex sentences. For me, it's more of a fun tool for getting the basics. I like it for maintaining recall with languages I already know but any deeper study... I prefer more comprehensive resources. I find that if I really want to learn a language properly, I need actual lessons or classes.

Right okay now I know it's exciting that Grandma and Granddad are visiting but we need to make a few arrangements before they arrive. Of course, Mum. What all do we need to do? Aye now, let's not get too carried away do we? A nice cup of tea and some homemade cake would make us right as rain. And I fancy a pint of my favorite ale, as long as I can manage to get up and about for it. Yeah, Granddad, but we need to make sure we've got enough space for you to get in and out comfortably too. Yes, that's a good point. And we'll need to make sure the pathway is clear so we can assist you without any issues. I'll manage. Me legs may be a bit creaky, but I’ll get there. Now, let's talk about the cake. What's the plan? Ah, right. I was thinking that you, could help me with that. We don’t need anything too elaborate. Just a simple sponge cake would be delightful. Sure, I can help with that. Do we need to buy anything at all or do we have all the ingredients we need? Let's check in the cupboard. Ah, we've got all we need: flour, sugar, eggs, baking powder... Oh, that's grand. I don't like buying things if we don't need to. Tell us, sweetheart, what kind of cake do you fancy? Anything with fruit? Actually, Granddad, I think a lemon drizzle would be lovely. Simple and flavorful. Aye now, that's a good idea. Now, on changing the subject to something more practical: is the guest room all set up? Yeah, I tidied up yesterday. Brought out a fresh set of sheets, made the bed, and put out fresh towels. Good lad! And have you remembered to set the thermostat for more warmth in there? Yup. I set it to 22, so it should be nice and cosy for them. That’s right, we don’t want our visitors to feel the chill. And while we’re at it, I’ve brought my walking sticks just in case the old bones need a bit of support. That’s thoughtful of you, Granddad. So Grandma and Granddad, how long do you plan on staying? We can organize our schedule accordingly. Oh, just for a few days, dear.

I keep coming across these old photos from when we lived in China. You know, the moments before we started teaching and everything was so new and exciting. Oh right. Those were the days. I almost miss it now, the energy, the culture, the students. Exactly! We had one class where everyone wanted to learn how to say "hello" and "thank you" and then they just kept repeating those phrases until I had to laugh. And how could I forget that time when we tried to cook a traditional English dinner? It was like a disaster, but the students loved it! Yes, I have that photo somewhere of your attempt at a full English. You even wore an apron! Oh god. And the look of horror on your face when you said it was "threatening" the taste buds of all our international students. But it brought us so much closer to them. They thought it was hilarious and it's still something they tease me about whenever I see them. We had some amazing students there, right? I often wonder how they're doing now. Yeah, it's hard to keep in touch with everyone but we do get updates sometimes. It's amazing to see how much they've grown and accomplished. Definitely. Like that one student who came from, I think it was Hezhou? He was shy but really dedicated. He ended up going to the UK for a master's and is now working in his field back in China. That's fantastic! I remember the progress he made during our time together. It's heartening to know all our hard work paid off in some way. More than "some way". Being part of someone's journey towards achieving their goals is a real privilege. It is. Speaking of journeys, have you thought about our next travel destination? We've both been talking about changing the scenery for a while. I've been looking into some places in Greece. The history, the landscape, the food. I think it would be wonderful. Plus, it's so much easier for us to travel internationally now that we're based in the UK again. Greece sounds perfect. The islands, the ruins, and just being somewhere new and sunny... We could relax and explore. And maybe we could take the time to visit some of our old haunts from our travels earlier, when we were just backpacking and seeing Europe for the first time.

So tell me about your weekend? It's been alright I guess. You know, just the usual. Went out with the lads after our match, got a bit drunk, and well, you can guess what happened. A wild night, then? You know, kind of regretful questions in the morning? Yeah, something like that. But this time, at least my hair wasn’t as big of a mess, right?  laughs  So how about you? You managed to sneak in some studying between your nights out, I hope? Well, I did try. But with the boys and football, it gets a bit tricky. Though, let’s be honest, even if I was stuck in the library, my mind probably would've wandered to the match. Definitely. But did I tell you about Alex's cat? She's such a wild thing. Tonight, she jumped into my lap while I was relaxing. And it was this huge bundle of fur and kindness all at once. I love pets, don't you? Oh, totally. We had dogs when I was growing up. Now I prefer the idea of a pet because they're less demanding while I'm trying to figure out my future. But the bonding is real, right? Absolutely. But back to studies – I really need to sort my priorities, you know? Next week is exam week and I haven’t even started preparing properly. We all know that feeling, right? Like you have the whole world in your head and then you realize you have exams too. Exactly! It's like my brain doesn’t want to switch from football and boys to calculus and literature. Have you tried making a study schedule? Sometimes writing it down can make it feel less overwhelming. Yeah, I think I might do that. Also, I'm considering joining that study group in the library. You going? Definitely. It's better to be struggling together than alone. Plus, I need to get used to not always relying on just my notes. Wise words indeed. So, anything else happened over the weekend? I mean, besides the usual drunken antics and studying procrastination? Actually yeah, I realised I’ve been pretty bad about my social media image lately. You know, trying to maintain this “perfect student, always doing well” facade when in reality it’s a bit chaotic. Oh yeah... I do that too sometimes. Except when you see my latest “um, why is it so hard to study?” post that somehow got more likes than my decent grades' announcement from last term.

So, I hear that your grandmother is coming to visit soon. We should have some fun plans lined up for her, what do you think about a picnic out in the park? That sounds lovely! Are we still on for the weekend? I think the weather should be fine if it stays like this – no sign of rain this week. Yeah, let's definitely do that. Make sure to bring a portable Wii so we can play some Fifa outside. Erm, maybe not. Seems a bit much even if it is outside. She might not be keen on too much game-playing. Oh, true. Let’s keep it simple then. Maybe we can plan a walk along the River Eden. She’s always enjoyed those. I was thinking we could actually combine a little village tour with the walk. There's an old mill not too far from here that's been around since the 1700s. We could show her that and also visit the village shop. Lovely idea. And it will give her a chance to see the quaint side of Hunsonby as well. Definitely. Also, what’s the plan for her accommodation? Are we keeping the cabin room for her specifically or will we have to shuffle? I was thinking we can give her the spare room over the garage. It’s bright and spacious, and she’ll have her own bathroom, so it should be perfect. Sounds good. I’ll talk to Jim at the cottage office to confirm everything is ready by the time she arrives. And what about food? Shall we start prepping some of the things she likes? She's mentioned she loves traditional Irish fare if it’s homemade. Maybe we can have some champ and steak for Sunday dinner? That would be lovely. We can prep everything in advance. Yes, that's a great idea. There’s also talk of a new Fifa coming out soon. You sure you won’t join us after all for a friendly game? She does enjoy watching us play but I don’t know if she’s prepared for a match. Nah, I think we'll leave that to the young ones. However, have you guys given any thought about those cups that got broken during the last FIFA tournament? It’s like... wasn’t that Tim who knocked over one? Yeah. Look, he didn’t mean to.

Right okay so I think that's all of the vegetables beans and's egg fried rice mixed veg. Oh and don't forget the sauce. Oh yeah sauce, right. Still it's all the same, isn't it? Just water questions. It's not just water, it's the type of water. You can't just use any type of water, right? Erm, yeah and it's also about how water is keeps changing right due to changes in the environment and public health knowledge and stuff like that, isn't it? Even tap water can be acidic or have fluoride or stuff. Yeah absolutely. So what, we should all carry around testing kits to check before drinking? Probably not necessary but you get my point. It's not just water, there's more to it. True. But in the end, it's just about staying hydrated, right? Exactly. Now speaking of hydration, have you guys decided what we're gonna drink with it? Yeah but is it even different? Isn't bottled water just filtered tap water sometimes, while the tap water here in Brighton is quite good? That's right, the council does do a good job with the water. I agree, I always drink right from the tap here. But maybe we could try that new artisanal water brand they started selling here, I read it's local and from springs and stuff. Or we could just stick with beer and the lounge. Everyone laughs. Alright, if one of you can set the blackberry phone up to the TV, we can watch Netflix a bit too, maybe. On it. Speaking of Netflix, does anyone remember that classic movie we watched last week? Oh yeah! The one with changing the SAT NAV instructions. Yeah, it was pretty funny, especially when it kept saying "Turn left for forty-seven kilometres and then just keep going straight". Classic! Reminds me of last summer when we got completely lost walking around Brighton, and took about three hours to get back to the coast. Haha! You all looked like you were out on a real adventure! We did make up some amazing excuses. And all that sunburn. Anyway, this reminds me that... Do you need your contact lenses, I think I saw glasses lying around here? Ah, thanks! I really wish I could see things like we used to, without needing youth-dependent tech like that, huh?

Oh, did you see the first line's "never worked and long-term unemployed"? That's what I am. No way! I didn't. It's got quite a few strong words there. Sorry, but questions are always kind of ginger conversations isn't it? What kind of narrative would you spin about that part of your history? Oh well, you never know when your narrative might be set for a reboot! For now, it's mostly a tale about a time in search for my purpose before we dive into those soccer scores you spoke of. Manchester United did quite well, didn't they? I used to be big into football. Sentiments of football and belonging to a community were among the few things that genuinely kept me going when I feel lost. Yeah, they gave a decent show. But I find you more interesting than the latest Premier League matches. You didn't work for a while, then became a freelance TEFL teacher? That's a great pivot. You must have amazing stories from that time, preparing students or running into cultural misunderstandings? Oh, stories! The stories I have from teaching. There's this one student who would only understand 'football', and so in every lesson he tried to steer the conversation back to the beautiful game. It was charming, but challenging . I love those moments, where teaching is as much about shared interests as it is about the subject matter. For me, it’s all about empathy and finding common ground. Like when I’m leading my exam prep classes in Poland, it’s tough seeing the pressure on them. Some of them remind me of myself, preparing for high-stakes tests when I was younger. More pressure than ever, it seems! And the blurred boundaries between being a teacher and a pseudo-mother. You end up worrying about them more than you should, don't you? Absolutely! I’ve even found myself googling more about SAD and ways to cope when I see some of my students struggling more than usual. Like, feeling nostalgic for home is one thing but it can be debilitating. Did you ever run into that while you were teaching abroad? Oh, the homesickness. Living abroad almost makes you realize how much of your identity is tied to where you’re from and what's familiar. I found coping with it by taking on freelance projects that allowed me to move around and get involved with the local communities.

So, I hear you've seen some of the latest first dates. How have they been? You know, aside from Ian who seemed like a nice chap but was silent as the grave? [laughs] Yes! I really understood why he was quiet now, the poor guy was just nervous – but silence questions his status as a good conversationalist and potential partner. He wasn’t bad, really. It was just unfortunate timing – and of course, as soon as I said “it was me”, he suddenly became loud and even boastful about his job, which was not exactly impressive to me. Oh, you spoke with him again after the date? How did the conversation go beyond the silent evening? It just felt like a bit of an overcompensation. It was good in a way though because it gave us something to talk about, but I wasn’t sure if it was genuine or just trying too hard. Trust me, sometimes it’s just better to acknowledge that a date didn’t go well and move on rather than spend time overanalyzing it. But for the next few dates, I’m making a note to not judge the quiet ones so harshly. One moment they might be shy or awkward, but who knows what they're like outside of the pressure of a first date? That's fair. It’s a lot like job interviews sometimes - the really nice people often don't come across as assertive or confident right away, but they have so much more to offer once you scratch beneath the surface. Speaking of which, in my job as a conference events co-ordinator, we always have to be prepared for anything. I deal with these really pushy exhibitors, and I've learned that it's not about being the loudest, but about holding your ground while still being polite and clear in what you want or expect. Seems like the quiet ones may just be sharpening their knives, as they say. Exactly. Anyway, another funny one was this guy who insisted on buying me a drink, which isn't a bad gesture, but when I asked for a glass of white wine he looked at me like I'd insulted him. What’s wrong with white wine? I don't know, maybe because I'm a 'lady’. This meme of the 'chill aesthetic' and all, but it was bizarre. Yeah, or maybe he just assumed all women like cider or beer and didn't consider wine an option?

So, I hear you've seen some of the latest teaching trends. What have you discovered? Oh, there's been a lot of buzz about using comprehensive resources for language teaching. Most of these resources need to be quite holistic to capture all the nuances and complexities of the language. Yeah, I've had similar experiences. It's hard to find materials that cover everything, especially cultural and historical contexts that students often miss. Absolutely. I've been meaning to set up my own teaching methodology module based on that. It’s something I’ve been exploring for my PhD, seeing how those resources can be effectively integrated into the classroom. I can imagine. You've also had Chinese guests, have you not? Yes, actually. It was interesting because we discussed the layout of the park, and they were quite curious about how we planned certain areas, like the space around the lime trees. Lime trees, eh? What did they make of those? Did they have any in China? They didn’t really mention lime or any other specific tree by name, but they mentioned something about ecological and biodiverse gardens, which might be their equivalent. They were quite fascinated by the concept of our park though, the way everything is designed. Speaking of nature, have you also discussed with them about pandas or bears in China? Ah, yes. The pandas were a big topic as expected, especially conservation efforts. But actually, in China, brown bears are more common, and we’re talking about the Tibetan plateau and surrounding regions for those. Fascinating stuff. Wildlife enthusiasts would love China for sure, including the landscapes and all. We also talked about countryside touring and how challenging driving in rural China can be for those used to a different infrastructure, especially getting to places like the Isle of White locally requires some planning ahead. Yes, I recall reading about the ins and outs of rural areas there. The challenges but also the experiences that are unique to that setting. Exactly, that’s what I’ve been trying to experience. For example, there’s this wonderful story about a boy catching a pigeon in rural China for his family’s dinner. The community aspect came up a lot in their stories. Really? That’s quite the anecdote. Yes. I also inquired about Tibet and their perspectives as Chinese citizens. It was quite nuanced — both thinking about current political aspects and just their experiences visiting.

[Beginning to set GPS] Alright, so we’re going to visit the city for the weekend. I’ve already got all the bookings sorted. That was fast. So what’s this place we’re staying at like? It’s a bit outside the city centre but very close to the main attractions. And the reviews are pretty good; the apartment has its own kitchen and there’s also a place nearby that does a fabulous Sunday brunch. That sounds like my kinda place. What's our plan for the first day? I’ve arranged for us to meet up with some friends who are also visiting over the weekend. There’s likely going to be a pub crawl on the first night and the next day we can explore the city and maybe hit up the new art museum. A pub crawl sounds fun. Do you reckon we’ll need to plan for public transport to get around? If we’re staying outside the centre, yes, we might want to look into getting a travel card for the weekend. I’ve already got the directions saved on the GPS and we can use that for the first few days. Good thinking. Let me just check my phone and make sure I’ve got everything downloaded. [Checking her own phone] And I sent over the itinerary for the trip. Did you have a chance to look at it yet? Just getting there. But based on what you’ve told me so far, it sounds like we’re good to go. Just a few more details to confirm. But yeah, we’re all set. Should we leave early to avoid any traffic? I’ve checked the forecast and it’s supposed to be clear. But leaving at 7:30 should give us plenty of time to get to the airport and check-in. Sounds like a plan. So at 7:30 we’re leaving. Exactly. And don’t forget to pack layers; it might get a bit chilly in the evenings. Got it. Layers packed. Great! Now, who’s gonna be in charge of music on the road? You are. [Laughs] Only if you’re driving. Deal. Perfect. Now, let’s enjoy the drive and when we get to the destination... [Interrupting] Let’s enjoy the moment and take it all in! Could you provide me with such details? That will allow me to craft a conversation based on what can be relevant and interesting between these two speakers, given their relationship, location, and the activity at hand.

Oh, did I ever tell you about's Dad's story when he caught the flu? He was bedridden and couldn't move for two days, insisting he was the original Typhoid Mary. Aye, yeah, you did. That's why I always have a handy thermometer and loads of flu meds in the house, eh? I’ve learned a thing or two about dealing with illness after I had to look after my sister through a nasty bout of pneumonia last year. It’s amazing how something affects not just the person who’s ill but everyone around, isn’t it? Definitely. Makes you appreciate your own health more, you know? Speaking of health, what about the whole waiting list in the NHS? I feel like I've been on the NHS's waiting list for a GP appointment indefinitely since I moved back to Doncaster. It’s a nightmare, especially in the smaller towns. My mum had similar issues last year. She had this ear infection that wouldn’t clear up, and it took what felt like forever to get an appointment with a specialist. Yeah, and then when you finally get seen, it’s often assumed you can just 'manage' your condition instead of actually treating it. Exactly. It feels like they keep pushing private healthcare on you. But I mean, look at the cost, it’s ridiculous. I’m not in a position where I can shell out for private health without skipping some bill or another. That’s why I’m glad I’ve got a good work scheme that helps with things like private insurance. Not ideal, but it’s better than nothing. And let’s not start on the side of commerce, where healthcare seems more a luxury than a right. The idea that good healthcare should be based on your bank balance is just absurd, isn’t it? Absolutely bonkers. But talking of changing the world, what are your views on the newest education policies? I mean, I was lucky I got into some reasonable student debt for university, but now I see all these new plans and it feels like they want to make university only accessible for the privileged few. Again, it’s about those who can afford to afford it. The new student loan interest rates and job requirements post-graduation... Yeah. It feels like everything’s set up for you to fail.

So, I hear that Cassie from work is getting a divorce. Oh really? That's such a shame. She and Alex were always together since uni, weren’t they? Yeah. It's been quite a shock to everyone. She just mentioned it lightly, but you could tell she's really struggling with it. Yeah, I'd totally understand. Divorce can be so complicated, especially when you’ve been together for a long time. And the two of them were always so supportive of each other. Exactly. She’s actually been having a bit of a tough time at work, too. The pressure of managing her new project has been quite overwhelming. That makes sense. Work stress can easily add to personal stress, especially during difficult times. Do you think she’s open to talking about it or would she rather we just let her be for now? She's been quite open about it with us at work, actually. But sometimes she just needs a bit of space. I think it’s just good that she feels trusted among us. It’s also funny because the other day at work, we were discussing break-ups and how different people react. Really? Interesting topic. Yeah, we were talking about how everyone kind of assumed that the more 'stable' people would deal with a break-up more 'rationally', but it’s not always the case. Cassie, for instance, everyone thought she’d take it really well because she’s been so patient and understanding in her relationships. And yet, as you said, she’s finding it really tough. Exactly. It just goes to show that you can’t judge a person's strength based on their personality or how they appear to others. And then on the other hand, people who can come across as quite less stable or more emotional, they can actually deal with these things amazingly. Right! It’s also funny because another colleague, Tom, who can be quite hot-headed, he’s really been supportive of Cassie and has been rallying everyone to make sure she knows she’s not alone. Ah, I like that about Tom. He can be quite rough around the edges but he's got a good heart. And it's surprising how much kindness and emotional intelligence some of these people have when it comes to situations like this. Speaking of which, I had a patient the other day who had a really tough break-up.

So kids, I was thinking we might do a bit of an activity this week. We can learn about these old legends and folk tales that have been passed down from our ancestors. Mummy, can we do something with dragons? Yeah! And knights! Why dragons and knights? Oh, isn't that lovely! But do you know, those weren't just about fighting and fire, they often centred around the ideas of good and evil, and I think we can find some very interesting tales from England. But why are there always dragons in these stories? 'Cause they're awesome! They are, aren't they? But in early British stories, they often symbolized threats or challenges, not just fire-breathing creatures but metaphors for troubles that people faced. What kind of troubles? Well, in one tale, a dragon was said to be causing trouble in a village, destroying crops and scaring people. But in the story, it turns out the dragon wasn't evil - it was just a guardian or a symbol. Oh, like maybe it was protecting something. Exactly! And often, the hero of the story would learn the dragon's true reason and they would figure out how to live together peacefully or to address the real problem. It's a bit like solving puzzles, right? Like puzzles? I love puzzles! Exactly, and as we read more of these stories, we'll also talk about what they tell us about "good" and "evil" doesn't always mean what you think. It's about the choices we make and treating others fairly and with kindness. So it’s not always clear who's good or bad? No, a lot of the times, the "bad" characters in these stories were also just facing their own challenges or had been treated unfairly. It's about understanding why people and creatures in these stories behave the way they do. Can we draw these stories then? Absolutely, but also, we can act them out. If you're up for it, over the next few days, we can choose a few stories and work them into little plays. You can have characters, and even the puppets you made could be in them. Puppets! Can we use those we made with Auntie? Yes, we can use any puppets or props. It'll be so much fun. And while we're at it, I think we can also make some treats that were popular in those times we're reading about - maybe some simple pastries or something.

So, how was the school filming trip yesterday. It was fun. The kids really enjoyed it and they did a great job. I was impressed with their acting skills. Yeah, I had a blast! We got to act out a scene and then shoot it. It was so cool to see how everything turns out on camera. Me too! I was the one who accidentally spilled the fake blood but they said it made the scene even better.  laughs  So how is ANON's leg. You were limping a bit yesterday. It was sore for a while after the gym earlier today. But I think I just overdid it a bit. Should be fine by tonight. Did the gym hurt it more or less from before? Well, I tried to be careful but sometimes it still bothers me, especially with the running machines. It's mostly okay as long as I don't push it too hard. Next time you should grab a lighter weight and fewer reps for the weights. Yeah, maybe try a different machine this time. You don't want to hurt it further. Yeah, good idea. Where did you get that doughnut? Stunned at the café after we came back from school. It was a post-gym celebration! Ah, the lure of carbs... A well-deserved treat, however. Next time maybe opt for something a bit healthier for your post-workout.  laughs  Yeah, you need your protein and carbs post-workout but maybe not the entire doughnut. Actually, that jogging machine at the gym has been doing miracles for my flexibility. You should try it. Yeah, I tried the jogging machine a bit. It felt weird since my leg's been hurting. But maybe it could help in some way? There's also the elliptical if running feels too much. It's really good on the joints. Yeah, that jogging machine seems like a good idea. Maybe for tomorrow’s workout session. Either way, don’t push too much, okay? Will do! Hopefully by tomorrow it won’t bother me as much. Let's just make sure to keep the care for ANON's leg in mind. If it's really bothering you, maybe we should take a few days off and just do some low-impact exercises or just rest altogether. Yeah, like stretching or something. That’s a good idea. Maybe we can just do some light yoga or pilates for a bit?

Ah, George, welcome back to the city. Thanks John. Nice surprise. Hope you didn’t mind I dropped by without warning. Not at all, just down on my two days off here. How's business been treating you since last? Ah, you know, up and down days like always. We had a pretty good sale recently though, those gadget boot sales did surprisingly well. Always right at the forefront, aren’t you? Well, when times change, keeps changing with them. Keeps me on my toes, I suppose. That it does. I’ve been dealing with quite the stir since the latest curriculum update came through. Seems like our education system keeps morphing faster than any of us can keep up. Is that so? Well, change’s always been a bit unpredictable. Keeping up with everything is a full time job, I reckon. Indeed. Between adjusting to new teaching methods and adapting to changing student needs, I barely have time to sleep. Must keep you or your students engaged. Now that progressive thinking is more trendy than ever, it’s no surprise there’re constant updates. I’ve voted with the Green Party since they took over, but even they seem to need some refining in their policies nowadays. Ah, politics. Always changing, yet so often feels like we’re just rehashing previous discussions. But I agree, it's an interesting time. The political landscape... really is more fluid now. Shows there’s still some hope for progress, I suppose. But it proves tough to keep the progress steady. As much as we advance socially, politically, environmentally, all these areas seem just as quick to slip back or get ignored. Perhaps just the nature of growth, right? Ups and downs. Could be. But personally, as an educator, it's disheartening to see areas like physical and mental health being pushed to the side. Our new health module’s got a focus on it, but sometimes I feel like it's just not enough. Health. Well, my sister-in-law’s run a small health food shop here in Hove for years. She’s been urging for more focus on locally sourced, organic produce. Got me thinking about my own diet more. Maybe I should take her advice more seriously and reduce the pastries I have during breaks. Well, I can't speak for pastries, but knowing your late starts to mornings, a bit of health food might be good for you.

I've decided I need more plants in my flat. I just can't resist these little green things. That sounds familiar. I recently got a little succulent for my desk. They're quite low maintenance. That's exactly why I got started! But have you seen the tiny one I got the other day? It's totally cute. Yeah, I saw your post about it. And have you tried propagating any? Oh, I wish! I've heard it's a bit tricky for beginners, but I'm determined to try. It's quite rewarding, though, when you see a new leaf sprout. Definitely, but sometimes I wish they didn't need so much light. Well, you could always consider a terrarium if want low maintenance and a more enclosed environment. That's a great idea, actually. I might look into it. You should. And between us, I've been meaning to get into recycling my fashion. I'm thinking this is a perfect moment to start. That is a fantastic idea. You’re always on top of the game with that. It’s about being more conscious, isn’t it? This endless cycle of fast fashion is unsustainable. Absolutely, and I’ve noticed a shift in brands starting to provide more sustainable options, which is really positive. Yeah, some are starting to catch on that consumers want more than just the cheapest option. Exactly. Though, I do struggle sometimes; finding good deals while also considering the environment isn’t easy. It’s true, but there are ways around it. Thrift shopping, swapping with friends... Shopping at charity shops is a big one for me. I love finding hidden gems and it really makes me think about what I’m buying. It’s a mindset change, but it's so worth it. Plus, I've been following some of these sustainable fashion influencers, and it’s inspiring. Can you recommend any? Yeah, definitely. There’s one person in particular who has almost entirely based her content around sustainable fashion and living zero-waste. She has complete freedom with her brand because she works directly with the consumers who care about these issues. That’s really interesting. I’d love to hear more about her. Her name is Emily and she’s based in Scotland. Her brand is all about slow fashion, repair, and repurpose. She even offers workshops on sewing and mending.

So, I was grading papers over the weekend. How was your weekend? I was busy preparing for my conference presentation and couldn't stop thinking about my talked about Killer Whales. You know how TV violence affects children, right? Oh, yes, very interesting topic – do you have any insights? Well, I was watching a documentary, Killer Whales are so intelligent and social that they even share food – and of course, that fracturing of packs is similar to how social dynamics can be affected by violent stimuli in kids. Fascinating, I didn't know about that, but it does makes sense in a way. And today I was at the library and I stumbled upon that old Blue Peter badge book. Did you ever get any badges when you were a kid? Yeah! I wanted that Art Badge so badly. I made a mosaic, which was the project, and I thought it was so much fun. I barely remember, but I recall going on about it for weeks. Maybe it was for the Wildlife Conservation badge, I think or maybe something else. Nowadays, I’m more interested in ecological and ethical aspects of studying animals but still, that badge system was good for kids. Yeah, it encouraged creativity and responsibility in a way that a lot of modern programs don’t, really. What about you, have you gotten into any arty projects lately? Actually, I did an adult class in glasswork last year. It was a bit of a chaos but also incredibly therapeutic. That’s great! I’ve been meaning to try something like that. But it's tough with the inconsistent hours we have as lecturers. Absolutely, teaching’s a varied profession but it keeps us on our toes, right? How’s your research going? I saw that you’re looking into the effects of squatting on mental health. Yes, it's quite confronting but also enlightening. The resilience of people dealing with homelessness and how art can be a form of empowerment is really interesting. Art for therapy, in a way. I often think about bringing those types of activities into my lectures as well. It’s all about making learning accessible and engaging. That's definitely something. Did you watch that new TV series... I forget the name... about the social care system? You mean, 'Save Me'? Yes, that show was quite raw. It really highlighted the humanity and despair behind the system.

I seen some of them photos you took. You have a good camera. Oh, thank you! It's just a hobby. Had more time for it since I retired. Indeed. Speaking of photos, did you hear about the hostel on questions? It's just so overpriced and yet the state of them is miserable. Yes! I've heard about it, actually went there once with some friends. And how was it? Not great. The room was small and stuffy, the mattresses were worn out. And they charge through the roof. It's a scandal. I read that in the paper. The same issue with the abattoirs. They should be better run. Yes! It's unfair that people go hungry while the conditions are such. It's all about profit, isn't it? Little thought for the people or for the environment. That's true. I remember when this town was full of hardworking people, plenty of small shops. Now everything is high street chains. And the job opportunities. It's tough for kids nowadays. Indeed, the workforce seems different now. More automated, technology-focused. I worry for my grandchildren. Getting a decent education seems harder than ever. It’s all about money and politics, they don’t care about the human side doesn’t seem it. I think there’s still good education out there. It's just not always equitably distributed or accessible to all. More focus should be on practical skills and real-world application. The world needs good engineers, carpenters, and even skills like photography! I've always loved taking my car apart and fixing it myself. Even now, though my son says he’ll do most of it for me, I like to do it when I can. That's just it. We need more hands-on skills in schools. I've taught students who can work wonders on computers but struggle with the basics of physical repairs. And it's not just the skills. The care for what we do, respect for labour and work, that seems lost somehow. I saw something on TV the other day about the decline of small farms and shops. It's sad to think they often worked themselves to the bone with little reward. That's a great point, though it's a bit off-topic. What can we do, though? We can't all just keep complaining. One thing we can do is support local endeavors.

So tell me about your previous role in recruitment. It was interesting. It was a quite demanding job. I was at a reputable recruitment firm, placing candidates across various sectors, mostly in various high tech industries. There was quite a bit of pressure because it was all about finding the right candidate for the client as quickly as possible. That sounds intense. Was there a lot of variation between clients and job openings? There was, actually. We worked with big tech companies, biotech firms, and sometimes even government bodies. Each job required a very different set of skills and experience, so it was essential to be able to understand the client's needs quickly and accurately. And I can imagine that you've seen trends change over the years, right? Oh, absolutely. One of the biggest changes I've noticed is the importance of digital literacy. These days, even if a person doesn't want a job directly related to tech, they still need to be proficient with digital tools and platforms. That was not always the case, but even roles like sales or marketing now require a high level of digital competence. That's really interesting, actually. I've been working on evaluating academic literacy for our university's course modules. I find the transition from high school to university quite challenging, especially for students who may not have had the same level of exposure to academic writing. What specific areas do you find students struggle with most? Well, I'd say one of the biggest struggles is summarization and critical analysis. For many students, it's hard to go beyond understanding the content to actually critically assess it and condense it into a coherent summary. Another area is properly citing sources - adhering to different citation styles can be quite confusing, especially if students haven't had to do it before. That's the same issue we faced in the recruitment world - sourcing and citations! Companies, especially the tech ones, are really strict about plagiarism and ensuring everything is properly referenced. It's interesting to see that similar issues confront students in an academic setting. Exactly. It's really about learning to communicate complex information in a structured and professional manner, which I think is something we're not always teaching explicitly. I think that's so important. I often found that candidates who could demonstrate these skills in an interview - the ability to critically analyse and present information - those were often the ones who stood out.

Oh, so I'm Hannah, from Bradford. I'm doing a Master's in History. How about you all? I'm Chris, I'm from just down the road, Wigan. I work part-time as a sales assistant but now I’m back to studying a bit – I’m looking at some kind of vocational qualification. Hey, I’m Megan, born and bred in Bolton. I’ve just started my grad program in Education. Nice to meet everyone! And I'm Neeta, from Manchester. Well, technically I’m from India, but I've been living in Manchester since I was 10, so I guess you could say northern England's home too! Interesting mix here. You all sound from around our part of the world. Definitely. It’s nice to finally meet some people I didn’t already know from our university. You know, we’re always in a rush for lectures or assignments, never really take the chance to chat. That’s true. Sometimes I find myself running into the same people in the library but never really say hello. Yeah, especially as an international student, it can be tough to break in with the 'established' groups. But honestly, the university has been really helpful in organizing events and stuff for us internationals. That's good to know, Neeta. Speaking of, anyone else here from the North? I've been trying really hard to keep my northern accent intact here, but all the southerners keep 'informing' me I don't sound northern enough… Classic! Don't worry, Chris. Your accent is fine. Maybe it’s the fact we all have different kinds of northern accents together that’s throwing people off, blurred the lines a bit. Absolutely. There's like a spectrum from Miner's slang and all the way to...whatever a stereotypical 'northern' accent is supposed to be. True. I grew up in Bolton, so sometimes people say I sound like I’m from nearby. But when I visit family back in Bradford, they're like "Megan, ye don't sound like a proper Yorkshire lass no more!" Exactly! Maybe our job here is to reclaim regional identity. I mean, I've had a friend who's half from the North and half from elsewhere, and he’s like, "I just end up talking in general Northern for convenience." That's a... relatable situation. So, Neeta, coming from the Indian diaspora, have you found any... cultural adjustments moving to Manchester?

So, I was browsing this weekend. I came across an article about recruitment in the military. You'd think that nowadays people would be all about the computers and high-tech, but actually, they seem to really be focusing on physical fitness still. Yeah, that doesn't surprise me, though. The basics of military service are still kind of rooted in physical prowess and discipline. True, but when I think about the future of warfare, it's all cybersecurity and drones. Yet, they still want you to be able to run a certain distance in a certain time. Crazy when you think about it. Well, you can't just have everyone behind a laptop screen. The military still requires a very physical type of soldier. Plus, the mental and physical resilience is paramount. I can see why they focus on that. Also, another thing caught my eye. They're still predominantly male and white? I thought we'd be beyond that by now. It's a very slow process, unfortunately. Even though the army is trying to diversify, it's not happening fast enough. And the structure itself, it's still very much based on traditional ranks and hierarchies. Mm, it's like they're running the military like a corporation from the 50s. You need to bring in younger, fresher ideas. Maybe, but also, the military isn't just about technology or diversity – it's about tradition and ensuring that soldiers are always ready for anything, physically and mentally. It can't just be about having the latest gadgets. Which is fair. But it's like, when I saw the ad, they were showing people climbing over obstacles and shooting things. It's so different from the reality of modern conflicts, which are more about strategy and technology. Maybe I'm just really biased towards tech side of things, but it seems like a focus on fitness over other skills is misplaced. Well, skills are important, but so is discipline and physical capability. Maybe it's just that the military’s recruitment strategy hasn't caught up yet. It’s a good point. I was also looking at magazines for work. You know, for event planning. Some of them are really pushing for sustainable events. I mean, all the corporate zero-waste initiatives are sorta sweet, but when it comes to conferences and events, the logistical nightmare of trying to make them eco-friendly just makes me laugh.

So, I hear that James from MEDS will be joining our's film shootings soon. He’s been quite talkative about his upcoming works. Yeah, the whole unrealistic studios he visits. He always brings up that indispensable time-lapse tech now, the one he bought with his savings. And isn’t that one of the most expensive bits of kit he could’ve picked up? I mean, it looks amazing with the footage he’s been presenting. But for us, we got to keeps it practical. As architects, our hands are tied with budgets and stuff. Tell me about it – always dealing with clients who just want to save on costs despite our efforts to design something visually striking. Exactly, whereas James gets to just play around with new gear because it’s part of making his art, us...we have to build within constraints. It's not so much about creativity, more about compromise. And yet, both film and architecture require a vision, right? But in different ways. That’s true. Sometimes I think filmmakers have it easy in that way. We’re constantly fighting for our view to be represented. Not to mention the political agendas involved in both our fields. I’ve been noticing lately, the environmental politics in the projects we're being asked to work on - it can't just be about aesthetics anymore, it's about sustainability, too. Totally. We were visiting this site last week for a new office building design, and the owners keep stressing we’re ‘future-proofing’ but that’s code for ‘make it green because it doesn’t cost much extra, it’s the trendy thing to do.’ Greenwashing! Haven’t we all had one of those ‘sustainable design’ briefs from clients who just don’t care a single bit, they want the label without the practice. If only we could couple aesthetics with environmentally friendly practices without it being an extra cost. There must be a market demand here, no? We could try to pitch that as a unique selling point. But sometimes I feel like we are also navigating uneasiness of people not really wanting to spend on real environmental changes because it might mean less profit. Which sorta brings us to the dating world too, no? It’s about those internalized values and almost unintentional greenwashing. Ah, dating is a whole different level of greenwashing. I’ve been on dates thinking I’ve found someone with similar views when it turns out they’re just using that to sound like a good person while they’re...

Right okay so I think it's time we figured out how we's going to manage our spare cash. Now I know some folk would say forget about it let it sit, but I think it's better if we've got a plan in place. Aye now, the old saying is a penny saved is a penny earned. But times have changed isn't that so? But even so, it's wise to make provision. But why not just put it into a good old savings account and set it aside. That way, keeps it safe and still earns a bit in interest. Yeah, but with interest rates so low, it hardly feels worthwhile. Maybe there's better ways to make our money work for us? That's what I was thinking too. Crypto, stocks, bonds, even a bit of a side hustle perhaps. Careful with that crypto, I've seen people go bust before. I never got around to that crypto fad. I couldn't figure out if it was for buying stamps or exotic fruits. Maybe a more traditional investment would be safer. Like a high-interest savings account or a managed fund. Yeah, that sounds reasonable. We need something stable. Speaking of money, I saw there's a sale on at Halfords today for bikes. Should we look at getting a bike each? Hmm, that's an interesting idea. Could save on travel expenses if we cycle to work, and it's good exercise too. Oh, I don't think I could learn to cycle again! I fell off once as a child and never looked back! Never looked back at cycling that is. I just thought, if we matched it up right it'd be quite a fun way to get around. Plus, we can take some nice rides out in the countryside round here. Yeah, Sussex has some great cycling routes. It might be a good idea. And if we need to, we could also just use a bike from the Boris Bike service. Wait, Boris Bike? Yes, the Santander Cycles. Oh, the pay-as-you-go bikes. They're a convenient option if you're not looking to own one or haul one back and forth. That could be a great way to try it out too. We could even plan a little trip somewhere. Maybe Brighton? Brighton's a great idea. We could plan a day there, check out the SeaLife center, and then make it across to the South Downs Way for a bike ride.

So, I was browsing on the internet yesterday and came across an interesting article about AI and today's job market. Have you seen anything like that? Ah yes, I think everyone is talking about that these days. There was a video from MIT that I watched last week which was quite eye-opening – suggesting that while AI is kind of replacing traditional jobs, it's also creating new and entirely different ones. It's kind of paradoxical but makes sense when you think about it. That does sound quite compelling. I've also been reading about how it could potentially make certain jobs obsolete in the near future, like administrative work. Like your job? Ha! Well, kind of, but our work is a bit unique. It’s like, half is admin but the other half is understanding and adapting to language from all over the world - which even the best AI still has trouble with. Got it, I see your point. So, as a corpus administrator, your role seems to have a creative and interpretive side to it which is quite hard to automate. Exactly. I hope so, anyway! Now, talking about jobs... have you seen the new vacancies for civil engineers in Cambridge? Yeah, they're all over the place. With all the new development in the area, there’s plenty of demand. I also saw a couple of articles discussing the politics around it though - Ah, yes, I saw something about how it’s affecting house prices isn’t it? Exactly! The more buildings, the higher the demand, which in turn hikes up the prices. Some community groups are protesting, saying it’s pricing out the locals. It’s a tough one because on one hand, it’s great for the economy, creating more jobs and the like, but it’s also a concern for the community. Exactly. Speaking of tough topics, did you hear about the health concerns regarding phone usage and internet addiction? Oh, absolutely. It's really scary especially considering we are both in a field that requires extensive use of digital technology. Right? I've started trying to limit my phone use after work, trying to leave it on zero notifications or something so I don't get that constant pull. That's smart. I've also been trying to read more and maybe pick up a new hobby. Did you try that new recipe you came across?

So, how was your week? It's been alright. Got a bit of a stressful job at times, especially when dealing with challenging clients, but it's not all the time. Right! Same here. I work with elderly people and sometimes, you need to have a bit of patience. But it’s rewarding isn’t it? You make a difference in their lives. Absolutely. I've had my share of stressful shifts as a nurse too, but there's nothing like the feeling of helping someone during a difficult time. Definitely. You get to see the little things, like a patient smiling when you’ve helped them with something they struggle with. It's a very rewarding job. And I bet you’ve seen some interesting things as carers too. You probably have some great stories. Oh, loads. This one time, I had a patient who hated a certain TV show and would always complain about it. One day, she unexpectedly enjoyed an episode and even laughed out loud! It was funny because we couldn’t believe it! And at work, I’ve got a colleague who is always talking about her this new diet she is trying. Anyone else dealing with colleagues like that? Or is it just me? Yeah, I know someone at work who is always trying new diets. But the problem is, she also really fancies a good curry. She can't decide which one to prioritise, so ends up not sticking to either! Haha, can relate. My colleague really fancies trying everything new, even the fussy eating plans. And then she always ends up at the hospital because she doesn’t properly follow the advice and ends up with issues. Oh dear, excessive fussiness isn’t good for one’s health. Seems like the elderly prefer traditional meals though, a nice roast or a warm pie. I noticed that at our retirement home, when we prepare traditional English food, everyone is happier. That’s interesting. While I was dealing with a patient who was really picky and would only eat certain foods, I tried to introduce new foods that were similar but with a twist. Surprisingly, she liked it! It’s about presentation, isn’t it? Yeah, presentation does work! And also getting them involved in the cooking process sometimes. Makes the meal more appealing. That’s a good technique. I do that with the folks I care for too.
